B. At age 18, or on entering college at any age ✔ KEY
The student becomes an "eligible student" at 18 or on attending a postsecondary institution.
C. On graduating from high school, whatever the age
Graduation alone does not transfer FERPA rights; age 18 or postsecondary attendance does.
D. At age 21, the age set for all federal privacy laws
FERPA sets 18, and there is no single age for all federal privacy laws.
Rationale: FERPA gives parents rights over their child's education records until the student turns 18 or attends a postsecondary institution, at which point the student becomes an "eligible student" and the rights transfer. Schools may still disclose to parents in limited situations, such as when the student is a tax dependent or in a health or safety emergency.
References: FERPA — 34 CFR 99.3 and 99.5: eligible student and transfer of parental rights
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

53. nce-s-eth-053 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · HIPAA and FERPA basics for counselors · medium · In review

A middle school counselor jots brief notes after student meetings to jog her memory. A parent asks to see "everything the school has" on his son. Under FERPA, which condition would keep the counselor's notes outside the definition of education records?
A. They are typed on a school computer and saved in the student's file
Placing notes in the student file makes them part of the education record.
B. They are shared with the student support team to plan interventions
Once notes are revealed to others, the sole-possession exclusion is lost.
C. They are labeled "confidential" and locked in the main office cabinet
A label and a lock do not change status if others in the office can access them.
D. They are used only as her memory aid and are not shown to anyone else ✔ KEY
Sole-possession records kept as a personal memory aid and not shared are excluded from education records.
Rationale: FERPA excludes from "education records" notes that are kept in the sole possession of the maker, used only as a personal memory aid, and not accessible or revealed to any other person except a temporary substitute. Once such notes are shared, placed in the student file, or used to make decisions, they become education records that parents may inspect.
References: FERPA — 34 CFR 99.3 definition of education records: sole-possession exclusion
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

54. nce-s-eth-054 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · HIPAA and FERPA basics for counselors · hard · In review

A client at a HIPAA-covered clinic reads her records and asks the counselor to change an intake note that lists past alcohol misuse, which she says is wrong. The counselor reviewed the intake carefully and believes the note is accurate and complete. What does the HIPAA Privacy Rule require?
A. Delete the note, because clients control the content of their own records
Clients may request amendment, but the provider is not required to accept a change it finds inaccurate.
B. Refuse to discuss it, because clients may view but not seek changes to records
HIPAA gives individuals an explicit right to request amendment of their records.
C. Answer in writing; if denied, explain why and let her file a disagreement ✔ KEY
A denial must be written, give the basis, and tell the client she may submit a statement of disagreement.
D. Amend it only if a supervisor agrees, then send the change to all insurers
Supervisor approval is not the HIPAA standard, and blanket disclosure to insurers violates minimum necessary.
Rationale: Under 45 CFR 164.526, individuals may ask a covered entity to amend their protected health information. The entity may deny the request if the information is accurate and complete, but it must respond in writing within set time limits, state the basis for denial, and explain the right to file a statement of disagreement that is then linked to the record. Disclosures of the amendment follow the minimum necessary standard.
References: HIPAA — 45 CFR 164.526 Amendment of protected health information
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

55. nce-s-eth-055 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · NBCC Code of Ethics · medium · In review

A counselor is licensed in her state, holds the National Certified Counselor (NCC) credential, and is a member of the American Counseling Association. Which ethical standards apply to her professional conduct?
A. The ACA Code, the NBCC Code and her licensing board's rules all apply ✔ KEY
Each body binds her through a separate tie: membership, certification and licensure.
B. Only the state board rules, since licensure overrides voluntary codes
Licensure does not cancel obligations she accepted by joining ACA and holding the NCC.
C. Only the NBCC Code, since national certification outranks state law
National certification does not outrank state law; licensure regulates legal practice.
D. Only whichever code is strictest, as the others then fall away entirely
All applicable codes remain in force; she is accountable to each body separately.
Rationale: Counselors are often bound by several codes at once. ACA members agree to follow the ACA Code of Ethics, NCCs and applicants are bound by the NBCC Code of Ethics, and licensees must follow the rules and code adopted by their state board. Each body can act on a violation within its own authority, so the counselor attends to all of them.
References: NBCC Code of Ethics — Application to NCCs and applicants · ACA Code of Ethics — Preamble and Purpose: application to ACA members
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

56. nce-s-eth-056 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · NBCC Code of Ethics · medium · In review

A National Certified Counselor receives a public reprimand from her state licensing board for a documentation lapse. She wonders whether she must tell NBCC, since the matter was handled by the state. What does the NBCC Code of Ethics expect?
A. No notice is needed, as NBCC reviews only complaints that clients file
NBCC can act on licensure discipline as well as on client complaints.
B. She reports the board action to NBCC within the time the Code sets ✔ KEY
The NBCC Code requires NCCs to report disciplinary actions by licensing boards to NBCC.
C. She tells NBCC only if the board fully revokes or suspends her license
The reporting duty is not limited to revocation or suspension.
D. She waits for the renewal form and mentions it at her next recertification
The Code sets a reporting window rather than deferring disclosure to renewal.
Rationale: The NBCC Code of Ethics requires NCCs to report to NBCC disciplinary actions taken by licensing or credentialing bodies, along with certain legal matters, within a set period (60 days in recent versions). This lets NBCC decide independently whether action on the certification is warranted.
References: NBCC Code of Ethics — NCC duty to report licensure discipline and legal actions to NBCC
⚑ Check: Confirm the current NBCC Code wording on self-reporting duties and the 60-day window cited in the rationale.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

57. nce-s-eth-057 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · counselor impairment and self-care · medium · In review

Two months after her father's death, a counselor finds herself tearful and distracted in sessions with several bereaved clients, and she lost track of one client's risk disclosure last week. What is her MOST appropriate course of action?
A. Keep her full caseload, since staying busy is the best way to work through grief
Continuing unchanged after a missed risk disclosure puts clients at risk of harm.
B. Quietly close her practice to new and current clients without notice to them
Abrupt closure without notice or transfer amounts to client abandonment.
C. Seek help and consultation, and limit or transfer cases until she can serve safely ✔ KEY
C.2.g directs impaired counselors to seek assistance and limit, suspend or end services as needed.
D. Disclose her loss to grieving clients so that they can support her in sessions
Using clients for support reverses roles and serves the counselor's needs, not the clients'.
Rationale: ACA C.2.g directs counselors to monitor themselves for signs of impairment, seek assistance for problems that reach the level of impairment, and limit, suspend or terminate professional responsibilities until it is safe to resume. Consultation, personal counseling and a temporary transfer of affected cases protect clients without abandoning them.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — C.2.g Impairment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

58. nce-s-eth-058 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · counselor impairment and self-care · easy · In review

After three years of working mainly with survivors of violent crime, a counselor notices that she now sees the world as unsafe, distrusts strangers, and has intrusive images from clients' stories. Which term BEST describes this?
A. Vicarious trauma ✔ KEY
Vicarious trauma is a lasting change in the helper's beliefs about safety and trust from empathic exposure to trauma.
B. Countertransference
Countertransference is the counselor's reaction to a particular client, often tied to the counselor's own history.
C. Simple job burnout
Burnout is exhaustion and cynicism from workload and conditions, not a shift in trauma-related schemas.
D. Moral distress
Moral distress arises when one cannot act on what one believes is ethically right.
Rationale: Vicarious traumatization, described by McCann and Pearlman, is a cumulative change in the counselor's inner experience and core beliefs, such as safety, trust and control, that results from empathic engagement with clients' trauma. It differs from burnout, which stems from work conditions, and calls for supervision, caseload balance and self-care as part of ethical practice (ACA C.2.g).
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counselor burnout, vicarious trauma and self-care · ACA Code of Ethics — C.2.g Impairment
⚑ Check: Confirm the Gladding chapter locator for vicarious trauma vs burnout; the McCann & Pearlman attribution is standard.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

59. nce-s-eth-059 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · professional organizations and their roles · easy · In review

A counselor wants to join the American Counseling Association division that focuses on multicultural counseling and that endorsed the Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies. Which division should she join?
A. ASGW
The Association for Specialists in Group Work focuses on group work and its best practices.
B. ACES
The Association for Counselor Education and Supervision focuses on training and supervision.
C. IAMFC
The International Association of Marriage and Family Counselors focuses on couple and family work.
D. AMCD ✔ KEY
The Association for Multicultural Counseling and Development focuses on multicultural counseling.
Rationale: The Association for Multicultural Counseling and Development (AMCD) is the ACA division devoted to multicultural and diversity issues, and it developed the Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies with ACA endorsement. ACA divisions each serve a specialty area, such as group work (ASGW), counselor education (ACES) and family counseling (IAMFC).
References: MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — AMCD development and ACA endorsement of the competencies · Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Professional organizations and ACA divisions
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

60. nce-s-eth-060 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · professional organizations and their roles · medium · In review

A counselor educator is preparing a slide that matches counseling bodies with their roles. Which pairing is accurate?
A. CACREP: issues licenses that let counselors practice in each state
CACREP accredits graduate programs; it does not license anyone.
B. Chi Sigma Iota: the international honor society of the counseling field ✔ KEY
Chi Sigma Iota is the counseling academic and professional honor society.
C. NBCC: accredits master's and doctoral counseling graduate programs
NBCC certifies individual counselors and administers the NCE; CACREP accredits programs.
D. State licensing board: awards the National Certified Counselor title
The NCC is awarded by NBCC; state boards grant licenses to practice.
Rationale: Chi Sigma Iota is the international honor society for counseling students, professional counselors and counselor educators, promoting scholarship, leadership and excellence. CACREP accredits programs, NBCC grants national certification such as the NCC, and state boards license counselors and enforce state practice law.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Professional organizations: Chi Sigma Iota, NBCC, CACREP and state boards
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

61. nce-s-eth-061 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · duty to warn and protect · hard · In review

The California Supreme Court decided Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California twice, in 1974 and again on rehearing in 1976. How did the 1976 decision change the clinician's obligation?
A. It framed it as a duty to protect, met by warning or other reasonable steps ✔ KEY
Tarasoff II held a duty to use reasonable care to protect the victim, which warning may or may not satisfy.
B. It removed any duty, ruling that therapy privilege outweighs third parties
The court reaffirmed liability, stating that the protective privilege ends where public peril begins.
C. It limited the duty to cases in which the client has already hurt someone
The duty concerns foreseeable future violence against an identifiable victim, not past harm.
D. It required clinicians to call the police after any client voices anger
The duty arises from a serious threat of violence, not ordinary expressions of anger.
Rationale: Tarasoff I (1974) held that a therapist had a duty to warn a foreseeable victim. On rehearing, Tarasoff II (1976) restated this as a broader duty to protect: when a therapist determines, or should determine, that a client poses a serious danger of violence to another, the therapist must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim, which may include warning, notifying police or other steps.
References: State law — Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1974, 1976) and state duty-to-protect law · ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm and Legal Requirements
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

62. nce-s-eth-062 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · duty to warn and protect · easy · In review

A counselor relocates her practice to a new state. A colleague tells her that "duty to warn works the same everywhere because of Tarasoff." What is the MOST accurate response?
A. Tarasoff is a federal ruling, so every state follows the same rule
Tarasoff was a California Supreme Court case, not a federal ruling binding all states.
B. Duty to warn applies only to psychiatrists, not licensed counselors
State duty-to-protect laws commonly cover licensed mental health professionals, including counselors.
C. States differ, so she must learn her new state's duty-to-protect law ✔ KEY
Some states mandate action, some permit disclosure, and some have no statute, so she checks local law.
D. The ACA Code sets one duty-to-warn rule that replaces state statutes
The ACA Code defers to legal requirements and does not replace state statutes.
Rationale: Tarasoff was a California decision. States have since adopted different approaches: some impose a mandatory duty to warn or protect, some permit but do not require disclosure, and some have no statute or case law. Counselors must know the law in each state where they practice, including what triggers the duty and what actions discharge it.
References: State law — Duty-to-warn/protect statutes: mandatory, permissive or none · ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm and Legal Requirements
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

63. nce-s-eth-063 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · ACA Code of Ethics structure · medium · In review

The Preamble of the 2014 ACA Code of Ethics lists core professional values of the counseling profession. Which of the following is one of those core values?
A. Protecting the field's public image
Reputation of the profession is not listed among the Preamble's core values.
B. Maximizing cost-effectiveness
Cost-effectiveness is not a core professional value in the Preamble.
C. Deferring to client families
The Code emphasizes client autonomy, not deference to family on treatment.
D. Promoting social justice ✔ KEY
Promoting social justice is one of the core professional values listed in the Preamble.
Rationale: The Preamble names the profession's core values: enhancing human development throughout the life span; honoring diversity and embracing a multicultural approach; promoting social justice; safeguarding the integrity of the counselor-client relationship; and practicing in a competent and ethical manner. It also lists the ethical principles of autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence, justice, fidelity and veracity.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — Preamble: core professional values and fundamental principles
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

64. nce-s-eth-064 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · termination and referral · hard · In review

A client's partner has twice confronted the counselor in the parking lot after sessions and left threatening voicemails. The counselor no longer feels safe continuing the relationship. Under the ACA Code of Ethics, what may the counselor do?
A. End services by letter right away, giving no referrals, since the threat is not her fault
Even when termination is justified, the counselor offers pretermination counseling and referrals as appropriate.
B. Terminate, since threats from someone close to the client are an accepted reason ✔ KEY
A.11.c permits termination when the counselor is in jeopardy of harm by someone in a relationship with the client.
C. Continue indefinitely, because ending services would punish the client for the partner
The Code does not require counselors to keep working while in jeopardy of harm.
D. Invite the partner into joint sessions to resolve the conflict before any decision
Bringing a threatening person into sessions raises risk and is not required before termination.
Rationale: A.11.c states that counselors may terminate when they are in jeopardy of harm by the client or by another person with whom the client has a relationship. Counselors still provide pretermination counseling and recommend other service providers when necessary, and they document the reasons and safety steps taken.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.c Appropriate Termination
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

65. nce-s-eth-065 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · termination and referral · medium · In review

A counselor realizes that a client's severe eating disorder requires specialized care beyond her competence. She offers three referrals to qualified providers, but the client declines all of them and asks to keep seeing her. What does the ACA Code of Ethics direct?
A. Continue, since the client's wish to stay outweighs the competence concern
Client preference does not permit practice outside competence when serious risk is present.
B. Keep working with her but drop eating-related goals from the treatment plan
Ignoring the main clinical problem does not address the risk and is not what the Code directs.
C. Discontinue the counseling relationship once the referrals have been offered ✔ KEY
A.11.a states that if clients decline the suggested referrals, counselors discontinue the relationship.
D. Ask a friend with eating-disorder training to coach her by phone each week
Informal coaching is not supervision or consultation and does not establish competence.
Rationale: A.11.a provides that when counselors lack the competence to help a client, they avoid entering or continuing the relationship, know culturally and clinically appropriate referral resources, and suggest them. If the client declines the suggested referrals, the counselor discontinues the relationship, handling the transition with care to avoid abandonment.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.a Competence Within Termination and Referral
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

66. nce-s-eth-066 · Social and Cultural Diversity · multiple relationships and boundary crossings · medium · In review

At the final session, a client who immigrated from the Philippines brings her counselor a small box of homemade pastries to thank her, explaining that in her family such gifts express respect. How should the counselor approach this gift?
A. Weigh its value, the client's motive, the relationship and cultural meaning ✔ KEY
A.10.f directs counselors to consider the relationship, monetary value, and the client's and counselor's motives.
B. Decline it politely, since the Code bars all gifts from current clients
The Code recognizes that small tokens of appreciation may be acceptable and does not bar all gifts.
C. Accept it, then offer a gift of equal value back so that the two are even
Reciprocal gift-giving is not required and can blur the professional relationship.
D. Accept it only if the client agrees to put the gift in writing beforehand
The Code sets factors to weigh, not a written agreement, for small gifts.
Rationale: A.10.f recognizes that in some cultures small gifts are a token of respect and gratitude. When deciding whether to accept, counselors consider the therapeutic relationship, the monetary value of the gift, the client's motivation for giving it, and the counselor's motivation for accepting or declining. Refusing a modest, culturally meaningful gift can itself harm the relationship.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.10.f Receiving Gifts
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

67. nce-s-eth-067 · Assessment and Testing · informed consent and its required elements · easy · In review

A counselor has a guardian's consent to give a career interest inventory to a 17-year-old student. Under the ACA Code of Ethics, what must the counselor explain to the student before the assessment?
A. The raw scoring keys, so she can check the scoring on her own later on
Sharing scoring keys would compromise test security and is not part of informed consent.
B. Nothing until results are in, so that her answers stay honest and unbiased
E.3.a requires the explanation before the assessment, not after.
C. Only the time the inventory will take, since interest tests are low risk
Low risk does not remove the duty to explain the nature, purpose and use of results.
D. Its nature and purpose and who will use the results, in words she grasps ✔ KEY
E.3.a requires explaining nature, purposes and specific use of results in understandable language.
Rationale: E.3.a requires counselors, before an assessment, to explain its nature and purposes and the specific use of results by potential recipients, in terms and language the client can understand. This applies to low-stakes instruments too, and with minors the counselor also involves parents or guardians as appropriate.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — E.3.a Explanation to Clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

68. nce-s-eth-068 · Assessment and Testing · scope of practice and competence · medium · In review

A counselor running a workshop on test anxiety wants to photocopy several items from a published, copyrighted achievement test to use as practice handouts. What is the ethical issue?
A. None, as long as the counselor removes the publisher's name from each page
Removing attribution makes the problem worse; it does not grant permission.
B. Copying items without permission breaks test security and publisher rights ✔ KEY
E.10 requires maintaining test security and not reproducing published tests without permission.
C. It is acceptable only if the handouts are collected and shredded at the end
Collecting handouts does not cure unauthorized reproduction or exposure of items.
D. It is allowed for any educational purpose under the fair use of all tests
Exposing secure items can invalidate the test for future takers; fair use does not cover this.
Rationale: E.10 directs counselors to maintain the integrity and security of tests and assessment techniques consistent with legal and contractual obligations, and not to appropriate, reproduce or modify published assessments without acknowledgment and permission from the publisher. Exposing items also threatens the validity of the test for future examinees.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — E.10 Assessment Security
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

69. nce-s-eth-069 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · supervision and consultation responsibilities · medium · In review

A licensed counselor agrees to provide clinical supervision for a new graduate working toward licensure. Under the ACA Code of Ethics, what should the supervisor do at the start of the relationship?
A. Start case review at once and discuss evaluation only when problems arise
Delaying the discussion of evaluation denies the supervisee informed consent.
B. Ask the supervisee to waive any right to appeal a negative evaluation
Supervisees must be told of due process and appeal mechanisms, not asked to waive them.
C. Review policies, evaluation methods and due process for appeals with her ✔ KEY
F.4.a builds informed consent into supervision, including policies and due process appeal.
D. Rely on the graduate program's handbook, since it covers all expectations
Post-degree supervision needs its own informed consent; a school handbook does not cover it.
Rationale: F.4.a requires supervisors to incorporate the principles of informed consent and participation into supervision, informing supervisees of the policies and procedures to which supervisors are to adhere and the mechanisms for due process appeal of individual supervisor actions. Many supervisors put this in a written supervision agreement that also covers evaluation, emergencies and fees.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — F.4.a Informed Consent for Supervision
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

70. nce-s-eth-070 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · supervision and consultation responsibilities · medium · In review

A counselor's close friend asks her to serve as the licensure supervisor for the friend's adult son, who just finished a counseling degree. The counselor is confident she could be fair. What does the ACA Code of Ethics direct?
A. Accept, provided she documents the friendship in the supervision file
Documentation does not cure the loss of objectivity the Code warns about.
B. Accept, but have a second supervisor sign his final evaluation as well
A co-signer does not remove the conflict in the ongoing supervisory relationship.
C. Accept if the son agrees in writing that their personal ties will not matter
Supervisee consent does not resolve the supervisor's inability to stay objective.
D. Decline, since she may be unable to judge him with full objectivity ✔ KEY
F.3.d bars supervisory relationships with friends or family members where objectivity is at risk.
Rationale: F.3.d states that supervisors are prohibited from engaging in supervisory relationships with individuals with whom they have an inability to remain objective, such as friends or family members. The counselor's own confidence does not settle the matter; the safer course is to decline and help the son find another qualified supervisor.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — F.3.d Friends or Family Members
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

71. nce-s-eth-071 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · telehealth and technology ethics · easy · In review

A group practice is moving from paper charts to a cloud-based electronic health record. Under the ACA Code of Ethics, what should counselors tell clients about this change?
A. Nothing, because record storage is an internal business decision only
H.5.a requires informing clients how records are kept electronically.
B. How records are stored, including encryption and archive retention ✔ KEY
H.5.a lists the type of encryption and security and archival storage as things clients are told.
C. That electronic records are fully secure and cannot ever be breached
Counselors acknowledge the limits of technology security rather than promising it is perfect.
D. That clients must sign a waiver of all liability for any data breach
Liability waivers are not part of the Code and do not replace security duties.
Rationale: H.5.a directs counselors to maintain electronic records in accordance with relevant laws and to inform clients how records are maintained electronically, including the type of encryption and security assigned to the records and whether, and for how long, archival storage is kept. HIPAA's Security Rule adds administrative, physical and technical safeguards for electronic records.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — H.5.a Records · HIPAA — Security Rule safeguards for electronic PHI (45 CFR Part 164, Subpart C)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

72. nce-s-eth-072 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · confidentiality and its limits · medium · In review

The mother of a 14-year-old client calls after the third session and asks the counselor to tell her "everything he says," noting that she has legal custody and pays for services. The teen has asked that his talks stay private. What is the counselor's BEST approach?
A. Respect her rights, clarify what will be shared, and keep safety limits clear ✔ KEY
B.5.b asks counselors to respect parental rights while explaining the confidential nature of counseling.
B. Give her full session details, since a parent who pays controls the record
Payment does not entitle a parent to all session content, and full disclosure can damage trust.
C. Refuse to speak with her at all, since the teen asked for complete privacy
Ignoring a custodial parent disregards the parent's legal rights and responsibilities.
D. End counseling, since the parent and teen want different things from it
Differing wishes are common and are worked through, not a reason to terminate.
Rationale: B.5.b directs counselors to inform parents and guardians about the role of counselors and the confidential nature of the counseling relationship, consistent with legal and custodial arrangements, and to respect the inherent rights and responsibilities of parents. Ideally the counselor sets these terms with parent and minor at the outset: general progress may be shared, specific content stays private, and safety concerns are disclosed.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.5.b Responsibility to Parents and Legal Guardians
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

73. nce-s-eth-073 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · record keeping and documentation · easy · In review

A counselor at a community clinic is reviewing her progress notes before an internal audit. Which entry BEST reflects what belongs in a progress note?
A. A near-verbatim transcript of everything the client said during the hour
Transcripts are excessive and expose more private material than the record needs.
B. Client presentation, interventions used, response, risk status and plan ✔ KEY
A progress note documents observable presentation, the service provided, the client's response, risk and the next steps.
C. The counselor's guesses about the private lives of the client's coworkers
Speculation about third parties is not clinically necessary and should not be recorded.
D. A list of the counselor's own feelings and frustrations about the client
Personal reactions belong in supervision or consultation, not in the clinical record.
Rationale: Progress notes should be timely, accurate and objective, recording what services were provided and why, how the client responded, any risk findings, and the plan. ACA B.6.a asks counselors to create and maintain records needed to provide professional services. Excess detail, speculation about others and counselor feelings add risk without clinical value.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Progress note content: presentation, interventions, response, risk and plan · ACA Code of Ethics — B.6.a Creating and Maintaining Records and Documentation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

74. nce-s-eth-074 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · record keeping and documentation · medium · In review

A week after writing a progress note in the clinic's electronic record, a counselor realizes she entered the wrong medication dose that the client reported. How should she correct the error?
A. Delete the original note and write a new one dated to the session day
Deleting and back-dating destroys the original entry and can look like falsification.
B. Edit the dose in the original note quietly so the record reads correctly
An unmarked change hides that the record was altered and when.
C. Leave the note as written, since signed entries may not be changed later
Known errors should be corrected; leaving false information harms care.
D. Add a dated, signed addendum noting the error and the correct dose ✔ KEY
An addendum corrects the record while keeping the original visible and showing who changed it and when.
Rationale: Records are corrected in a way that keeps the original entry visible and marks the correction with the date and the counselor's signature: a single line through the error on paper, or a dated addendum or amendment in an electronic record. Erasing, overwriting or back-dating can be viewed as falsifying records. Accurate correction protects both care and the record's integrity.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Correcting errors: late entries and addenda that preserve the original entry · ACA Code of Ethics — B.6.a Creating and Maintaining Records and Documentation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

75. nce-s-eth-075 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · record keeping and documentation · hard · In review

A counselor saw a couple in joint sessions and also met once with each partner alone. After the couple separates, one partner, a 42-year-old man, asks for a copy of "the whole file." The other partner has not given consent. What does the ACA Code of Ethics direct?
A. Release only the parts of the record that relate directly to him ✔ KEY
B.6.e limits access in multiple-client records to the parts that relate to the requesting client, without other clients' confidential material.
B. Release the entire file, since he took part in most of the sessions
The file includes his partner's confidential material, including her individual session.
C. Refuse all access, since couple records belong to the counselor alone
Clients have a right to reasonable access to their records; a blanket refusal is not supported.
D. Release the file only after his former partner reviews and edits it
Letting one client edit the record is improper and does not protect either client.
Rationale: ACA B.6.e states that in situations involving multiple clients, counselors provide individual clients with only those parts of records that relate directly to them and do not include confidential information related to any other client. Setting rules for couple records at the start, including how individual sessions are documented, prevents disputes later.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.6.e Client Access
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

76. nce-s-eth-076 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · ethical decision-making models · easy · In review

A counselor promised a client she would call him back with a referral by Friday. On Friday, her schedule is overloaded, but she makes the call before leaving work. Which of Kitchener's moral principles does this action MOST directly reflect?
A. Justice
Justice concerns fairness and equal treatment, not keeping a specific promise.
B. Veracity
Veracity is truthfulness; the act here is honoring a commitment.
C. Fidelity ✔ KEY
Fidelity means being faithful to commitments and promises made to clients.
D. Autonomy
Autonomy is respect for the client's right to make his own choices.
Rationale: Kitchener's principles include autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice and fidelity, with veracity often added in later work. Fidelity refers to honoring commitments and being trustworthy, which builds the trust the counseling relationship depends on.
References: Forester-Miller & Davis (Practitioner's Guide to Ethical Decision Making) — Moral principles: autonomy, justice, beneficence, nonmaleficence, fidelity (and veracity)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

77. nce-s-eth-077 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · ethical decision-making models · medium · In review

A nonprofit agency fills open counseling slots by giving priority to clients with private insurance. A counselor argues that slots should go first to clients with the most severe needs, regardless of payer. Which moral principle is the counselor MOST directly invoking?
A. Justice, the fair allocation of services and resources ✔ KEY
Justice concerns fairness and equitable distribution of services, which is the issue raised.
B. Fidelity, keeping promises made to current clients
No promise to a particular client is at stake in the policy dispute.
C. Veracity, being truthful with clients about services
The concern is how services are allocated, not honesty in disclosure.
D. Autonomy, respecting each client's freedom of choice
Clients' self-determination is not the issue in how slots are assigned.
Rationale: Justice means treating people fairly and distributing services equitably; treating clients differently requires a rationale that is relevant to the difference. Prioritizing by ability to pay rather than clinical need raises a justice concern, and counselors may advocate within the agency for fairer policies.
References: Forester-Miller & Davis (Practitioner's Guide to Ethical Decision Making) — Moral principles: justice as fairness and equitable treatment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

78. nce-s-eth-078 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · ethical decision-making models · hard · In review

A competent 55-year-old client decides to leave a stable job to open a risky small business. She is not in danger, but her counselor believes the move will cause her great stress and financial harm and is tempted to keep steering sessions toward talking her out of it. Which two principles are MOST in tension?
A. Justice and fidelity, since the client may lose her income
Neither fair distribution nor a broken promise is at issue.
B. Veracity and justice, since the plan affects her family too
Truthfulness and fairness are not the competing values in this choice.
C. Fidelity and veracity, since she has set her goals for therapy
No commitment or truthfulness conflict drives the counselor's dilemma.
D. Autonomy and beneficence, since her choice and welfare differ ✔ KEY
Her right to self-determination conflicts with the counselor's wish to do good for her.
Rationale: Autonomy is respect for a competent client's right to make her own decisions; beneficence is the duty to promote her welfare. When a client's free choice differs from what the counselor believes is good for her, and no serious harm is foreseeable, autonomy generally prevails. The counselor can explore consequences openly without imposing her own values (ACA A.4.b).
References: Forester-Miller & Davis (Practitioner's Guide to Ethical Decision Making) — Moral principles: autonomy versus beneficence · ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

79. nce-s-eth-079 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · licensure, credentialing and professional identity · medium · In review

A counselor holds a full, unencumbered license in her home state, which belongs to the Counseling Compact. She obtains a privilege to practice in another member state to see a client there by video. Whose practice laws govern her work with that client?
A. Only her home state's laws, since the privilege rests on that license
The privilege is based on the home license, but practice follows the remote state's laws.
B. The laws of the member state where the client is located during care ✔ KEY
Under the Compact, a privilege holder must follow the laws and rules of the remote state where the client is located.
C. Only federal rules, since telehealth across states is federally run
Counseling practice is regulated by states; no federal license governs it.
D. The Compact Commission's own national practice act for counselors
The Commission administers the Compact; it does not replace state practice acts.
Rationale: The Counseling Compact lets a counselor with an unencumbered license in a home member state practice in other member states through a privilege to practice. While using that privilege, the counselor is subject to the laws and regulations of the remote state where the client is located, and that state may act against the privilege. ACA H.1.b likewise notes that distance counselors may be subject to the laws of the client's location.
References: Counseling Compact — Privilege to practice: adherence to the laws and rules of the remote state · ACA Code of Ethics — H.1.b Laws and Statutes
⚑ Check: Compact privileges were not yet being issued in every member state when written; confirm current operational status and the "law of the client's state" framing against the Compact text.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

80. nce-s-eth-080 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · licensure, credentialing and professional identity · hard · In review

A counselor holds an associate-level counseling license that, under her state's law, requires practice under an approved supervisor. She also holds the NCC credential. A friend urges her to open a solo private practice, saying "the NCC shows you're qualified." What determines whether she may practice independently?
A. Her NCC, since national certification overrides tiered state licenses
National certification is voluntary and does not authorize practice or override state law.
B. Her degree, since a CACREP master's permits independent counseling
A degree is a requirement for licensure, not a legal authorization to practice.
C. Her state's law for her license tier, which limits independent work ✔ KEY
The scope and conditions of each license tier are set by state law; an associate license requires supervision.
D. Her own judgment of her skills, since competence is self-assessed
Competence matters ethically, but self-assessment cannot expand a legal scope of practice.
Rationale: State licensure law defines who may practice counseling and under what conditions, including tiered licenses for counselors still completing supervised experience. National certification such as the NCC is a voluntary professional credential and does not grant the legal right to practice. ACA C.2.a also directs counselors to practice only within the boundaries of their credentials.
References: State law — Counselor licensure tiers: associate licenses and supervision requirements · ACA Code of Ethics — C.2.a Boundaries of Competence
⚑ Check: Associate-level license titles and supervision rules vary by state; confirm the general framing.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

81. nce-s-eth-081 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · licensure, credentialing and professional identity · easy · In review

A state's counselor law is described as a "title act" rather than a "practice act." What does a title act do?
A. It limits who may use a protected title such as "licensed counselor" ✔ KEY
A title act restricts use of the protected professional title to people who hold the credential.
B. It limits who may perform counseling services for a fee in the state
Restricting the activity itself is what a practice act does.
C. It sets the standards that graduate programs must meet to accredit
Program standards are set by accreditors such as CACREP, not by state title laws.
D. It requires every counselor in the state to hold national certification
National certification is voluntary and is not created by a state title act.
Rationale: A title act protects the use of a professional title, so only credentialed people may call themselves, for example, a licensed professional counselor. A practice act goes further and defines the scope of practice, restricting who may perform the regulated activities. Most states now regulate both the title and the practice of counseling.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Credentialing: licensure, certification, title and practice acts
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

82. nce-s-eth-082 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor advocacy and social justice · medium · In review

A counselor who works with many clients facing eviction testifies before a state legislative committee in support of a bill to expand tenant protections. In the ACA Advocacy Competencies, which domain does this work fall under?
A. Client/student domain, through direct client empowerment
Client-level work helps an individual build self-advocacy skills or acts for one client.
B. School/community domain, through community collaboration
Community collaboration joins local groups; legislative testimony targets public policy.
C. Clinical domain, through individual treatment planning
There is no clinical domain in the competencies; treatment planning is not advocacy.
D. Public arena domain, through social/political advocacy ✔ KEY
Influencing legislation and public policy is social/political advocacy in the public arena.
Rationale: The ACA Advocacy Competencies describe three domains: client/student, school/community and public arena, each with an "acting with" and an "acting on behalf" level. Testifying to lawmakers to change policy that affects many clients is social/political advocacy in the public arena. ACA A.7.a supports advocacy at individual, group, institutional and societal levels.
References: ACA Advocacy Competencies — ACA Advocacy Competencies: client/student, school/community and public arena domains · ACA Code of Ethics — A.7.a Advocacy
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

83. nce-s-eth-083 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor advocacy and social justice · medium · In review

A counselor notices that several clients from the same apartment complex report asthma flare-ups from mold, and the landlord ignores repair requests. Which action BEST represents systemic rather than client-level advocacy?
A. Help one client draft a letter to the landlord about her own unit
Supporting one client's self-advocacy is valuable but stays at the client level.
B. Teach each affected client coping skills for the stress of the mold
Coping skills address individual distress, not the conditions causing it.
C. Work with a tenants' group and housing officials on building repairs ✔ KEY
Collaborating with community groups to change the conditions affecting many tenants is systems advocacy.
D. Refer each client separately to a legal aid office for their claims
Individual referrals address each case one at a time rather than the system.
Rationale: Client-level advocacy helps a particular client access resources or self-advocate. Systemic advocacy targets the policies, institutions or conditions that create barriers for many people, often by collaborating with community groups. When counselors see a pattern across clients, the MSJCC and ACA A.7.a support intervening at the institutional and community levels, with client consent for any case-specific action.
References: MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling and advocacy interventions: institutional and community levels · ACA Code of Ethics — A.7.a Advocacy
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

84. nce-s-eth-084 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor advocacy and social justice · medium · In review

A 29-year-old client who is Deaf tells her counselor that her employer keeps refusing to provide an interpreter for staff meetings. She is articulate, knows her rights, and wants to handle it herself, but feels discouraged. Which advocacy approach BEST fits this situation?
A. Call the employer's human resources office on the client's behalf
Acting for a client who wants to self-advocate undercuts her autonomy and needs consent.
B. Help her identify strengths and plan her own self-advocacy steps ✔ KEY
Empowerment, acting with the client, fits a capable client who wants to advocate for herself.
C. Focus sessions on accepting the workplace as it currently operates
Encouraging adjustment to discrimination ignores the systemic barrier she faces.
D. File a formal discrimination complaint to a federal agency for her
Filing for her overrides her stated wish to act on her own behalf.
Rationale: At the client level, the ACA Advocacy Competencies distinguish empowerment (acting with clients to build self-advocacy) from advocacy on their behalf. When a client is able and wants to act for herself, the counselor helps her recognize strengths, identify resources and plan steps. ACA A.7.b requires client consent before counselors advocate on a client's behalf.
References: ACA Advocacy Competencies — Client/student empowerment: acting with clients before acting on their behalf · ACA Code of Ethics — A.7.b Confidentiality and Advocacy · Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — ACA Advocacy Competencies: client/student empowerment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

85. nce-s-eth-085 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · counselor impairment and self-care · easy · In review

A counseling intern says self-care is "a personal lifestyle choice that has nothing to do with ethics." How does the 2014 ACA Code of Ethics treat counselor self-care?
A. As a private matter outside the scope of professional standards
The Code directly links self-care to meeting professional responsibilities.
B. As required only for counselors who are already showing impairment
Self-care is framed as ongoing and preventive, not only a response to impairment.
C. As a duty that applies only to supervisors overseeing trainees
The expectation applies to all counselors, not only supervisors.
D. As part of the professional responsibility to serve clients well ✔ KEY
The Code expects counselors to engage in self-care to best meet their professional responsibilities.
Rationale: The introduction to Section C of the ACA Code states that counselors engage in self-care activities to maintain and promote their emotional, physical, mental and spiritual well-being to best meet their professional responsibilities. Standard C.2.g adds that counselors monitor themselves for impairment and refrain from offering services when impaired.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — Section C Introduction (self-care); C.2.g Impairment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

86. nce-s-eth-086 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · counselor impairment and self-care · medium · In review

A counselor in solo practice is diagnosed with a progressive neurological illness. She is fully able to work now but knows sudden decline is possible. Under the ACA Code of Ethics, what should she do to protect her clients?
A. Prepare a plan naming a colleague to handle clients and records ✔ KEY
C.2.h calls for a plan for transfer of clients and files if the counselor becomes incapacitated.
B. Close her practice right away, since any illness is an impairment
A diagnosis alone is not impairment; she may practice while able, with planning and monitoring.
C. Tell each client her full diagnosis so they can decide whether to stay
Full medical disclosure is not required and may shift focus from clients' needs.
D. Rely on her family to contact clients if she becomes unable to work
Family members are not qualified to manage confidential records or clinical transitions.
Rationale: ACA C.2.h directs counselors to prepare a plan for the transfer of clients and the distribution of records to an identified colleague or records custodian in case of incapacitation, death or termination of practice, often called a professional will. Under C.2.g, she continues to monitor for signs of impairment and limits practice if it appears.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — C.2.h Counselor Incapacitation, Death, Retirement, or Termination of Practice · ACA Code of Ethics — C.2.g Impairment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

87. nce-s-eth-087 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · ACA Code of Ethics structure · easy · In review

A new clinical supervisor wants the section of the 2014 ACA Code of Ethics that covers supervisor gatekeeping, evaluation of supervisees and counselor educator duties. Which section should she read?
A. Section D
Section D, Relationships With Other Professionals, covers colleagues, employers and consultation, not supervision duties.
B. Section E
Section E, Evaluation, Assessment, and Interpretation, covers testing and assessment of clients.
C. Section F ✔ KEY
Section F, Supervision, Training, and Teaching, addresses supervision, evaluation and gatekeeping, and counselor educator duties.
D. Section I
Section I, Resolving Ethical Issues, covers ethics complaints, conflicts with law and cooperation with committees.
Rationale: The 2014 ACA Code has nine sections: A The Counseling Relationship; B Confidentiality and Privacy; C Professional Responsibility; D Relationships With Other Professionals; E Evaluation, Assessment, and Interpretation; F Supervision, Training, and Teaching; G Research and Publication; H Distance Counseling, Technology, and Social Media; and I Resolving Ethical Issues. Gatekeeping and supervisee evaluation appear in Section F.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — Section F Supervision, Training, and Teaching (F.6.b Gatekeeping and Remediation)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

88. nce-s-eth-088 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · ACA Code of Ethics structure · medium · In review

A counselor asks whether the 2014 ACA Code of Ethics tells counselors exactly which decision-making model to use when facing a dilemma. Which statement is accurate?
A. It requires the Forester-Miller and Davis model for all ethics cases
The Code names no single required model.
B. It expects a credible model able to bear public scrutiny, not a set one ✔ KEY
The Code asks counselors to use a credible model whose application can withstand scrutiny.
C. It ranks its standards so higher sections settle conflicts automatically
The Code does not rank its standards to resolve dilemmas mechanically.
D. It leaves decision making entirely to each employer's written policy
Employer policy does not replace the counselor's ethical decision-making duty.
Rationale: The Purpose section and standard I.1.b note that no single decision-making model is best for every situation, so counselors are expected to use a credible model that can bear public scrutiny of its application. Counselors also consult, document their reasoning, and draw on ethical principles and the Code's standards.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — Purpose; I.1.b Ethical Decision Making
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

89. nce-s-eth-089 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · NBCC Code of Ethics · medium · In review

A counselor's National Certified Counselor (NCC) credential lapsed eight months ago after she did not recertify. Her website, business cards and email signature still list "NCC." What is the ethical concern?
A. She is misrepresenting a credential she no longer holds ✔ KEY
Listing a lapsed credential misleads the public about her qualifications.
B. There is none, since she met the standard when she earned it
A credential may be claimed only while it is current and in good standing.
C. It is a concern only if a client is harmed by her services
Misrepresentation is a violation whether or not harm results.
D. It is a concern only for her state license, not certification
The issue is her claim of national certification, which NBCC governs.
Rationale: Both the NBCC Code of Ethics and ACA C.4.a require counselors to represent their credentials accurately. Continuing to list a lapsed certification misleads clients and the public. She should remove the designation at once or complete the steps to reinstate it.
References: NBCC Code of Ethics — Accurate representation of credentials and qualifications · ACA Code of Ethics — C.4.a Accurate Representation
⚑ Check: Confirm that the current NBCC Code of Ethics addresses misrepresenting a lapsed credential; the exact directive number is not cited.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

90. nce-s-eth-090 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · NBCC Code of Ethics · medium · In review

A counselor who just passed the NCE posts a list of questions she remembers from the exam in an online study group to help friends who test next month. How is this viewed under NBCC standards?
A. As acceptable, since the items came from her own memory
Recalled items are still secure exam content; the source does not change that.
B. As acceptable, as long as she posts the items anonymously
Anonymity does not make sharing secure content ethical.
C. As a concern only if her friends end up passing the exam
The breach occurs when content is shared, whatever the result.
D. As a breach of exam security that can put her NCC at risk ✔ KEY
Sharing secure exam content violates NBCC standards and may lead to sanctions.
Rationale: NBCC requires applicants and certificants to protect the security of its examinations, and disclosing recalled exam content is a violation that can lead to sanctions such as denial or revocation of certification. Exam security protects the validity of the credential for every counselor who holds it.
References: NBCC Code of Ethics — Examination security and integrity of the certification process
⚑ Check: Confirm that the NBCC Code of Ethics (rather than only the candidate agreement) addresses examination security.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

91. nce-s-eth-091 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · professional organizations and their roles · easy · In review

A newly hired high school counselor wants to join the national professional association for school counselors that publishes a national model for school counseling programs. Which organization is it?
A. AMHCA
The American Mental Health Counselors Association serves clinical mental health counselors.
B. ASCA ✔ KEY
The American School Counselor Association publishes the ASCA National Model.
C. NBCC
NBCC is a certification board, not a membership association for school counselors.
D. CACREP
CACREP accredits graduate programs; it is not a membership association.
Rationale: The American School Counselor Association (ASCA) is the national association for school counselors and publishes the ASCA National Model, a framework for comprehensive school counseling programs, along with its own ethical standards for school counselors.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Professional organizations: ASCA and the ASCA National Model
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

92. nce-s-eth-092 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · professional organizations and their roles · medium · In review

A state counseling board wants to join a national organization made up of state counselor licensing boards that works on issues such as license portability and consistent regulatory standards. Which organization fits this description?
A. CSI
Chi Sigma Iota (CSI) is the counseling honor society for students and professionals.
B. ACA
The American Counseling Association (ACA) is a membership association of individual counselors, not of boards.
C. AASCB ✔ KEY
The American Association of State Counseling Boards (AASCB) brings together state counselor licensing boards on regulatory issues such as portability.
D. NBCC
The National Board for Certified Counselors (NBCC) certifies individuals and develops exams; its members are not state boards.
Rationale: The American Association of State Counseling Boards (AASCB) is the organization of state counselor licensing boards. It works on regulatory consistency, licensure portability and public protection. ACA serves individual members, NBCC grants national certification and develops exams, and CSI is the profession's honor society.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Credentialing bodies: AASCB, NBCC and state licensure boards
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

93. nce-s-eth-093 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · confidentiality and its limits · hard · In review

A 15-year-old client reveals that she has been cutting her thighs and has had thoughts of "not waking up." Her father emailed the counselor that morning demanding to know what his daughter talks about. She begs the counselor not to tell her parents anything. What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Complete a risk assessment, then plan with her what parents must learn ✔ KEY
Risk must be assessed first; safety information is then shared with parents with the teen involved.
B. Reply to the father's email with a full summary of what she disclosed
Disclosure before assessing risk and without the teen's involvement shares more than needed.
C. Keep the disclosure private, since she asked that nothing be shared
A minor's request cannot override the duty to protect when safety is at stake.
D. Tell her sessions will stop unless she tells her parents herself today
Threatening to end services is coercive and risks abandonment of an at-risk teen.
Rationale: Self-injury and passive suicidal ideation call first for a structured risk assessment. If the assessment shows risk, ACA B.2.a permits disclosure to protect the client, and with a minor the counselor involves the teen in deciding how parents are told, sharing only what is needed for safety (B.2.e). The father's general demand for content is handled separately, balancing parental rights with the teen's privacy (B.5.b).
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm; B.2.e Minimal Disclosure · ACA Code of Ethics — B.5.b Responsibility to Parents and Legal Guardians
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

94. nce-s-eth-094 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · multiple relationships and boundary crossings · hard · In review

A father in individual counseling for depression asks his counselor to testify as an expert in his upcoming custody trial and to recommend that he receive primary custody. He says, "You know me better than anyone." What should the counselor do?
A. Agree, since a long alliance gives her the best basis for an opinion
Familiarity from treatment is not a basis for a forensic opinion and creates a dual role.
B. Agree if the other parent and both attorneys consent to her testimony
Consent of others does not cure the conflict between therapeutic and forensic roles.
C. Write a letter supporting custody instead of appearing at the hearing
A custody recommendation in writing is the same forensic opinion in a different form.
D. Explain she cannot give a custody opinion and refer him to an evaluator ✔ KEY
E.13.c bars evaluating current clients for forensic purposes; a neutral evaluator is the proper source.
Rationale: ACA E.13.c states that counselors do not evaluate current or former clients, clients' romantic partners or clients' family members for forensic purposes. A treating counselor lacks the neutrality and full information a custody evaluation requires. If legally compelled, she may testify as a fact witness with appropriate consent, describing treatment rather than recommending custody.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — E.13.c Client Evaluation Prohibited · ACA Code of Ethics — A.6.e Nonprofessional Interactions or Relationships (Other Than Sexual or Romantic)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

95. nce-s-eth-095 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · record keeping and documentation · hard · In review

A client with adjustment disorder learns his insurer will pay for more sessions only for "a serious diagnosis." He asks his counselor to record major depressive disorder, and the practice manager says, "Everyone does it." What should the counselor do?
A. Record major depression, since the client has consented to the code
Client consent does not make a false diagnosis to an insurer honest or legal.
B. Keep the accurate diagnosis and discuss other payment or care options ✔ KEY
Diagnoses must be accurate; the counselor can explore sliding fees, self-pay or referral.
C. Record major depression only until the client's finances stabilize
A time-limited false diagnosis is still fraudulent billing.
D. Follow the manager's direction, since the practice bears the billing risk
Employer pressure does not excuse misrepresentation; the counselor is personally accountable.
Rationale: Counselors provide proper diagnoses (ACA E.5.a) and are accurate, honest and objective in reports to third parties, including insurers (C.6.b). Upcoding a diagnosis to obtain payment is insurance fraud and can also harm the client through an inaccurate permanent record. The counselor addresses the financial barrier through legitimate options instead.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — E.5.a Proper Diagnosis; C.6.b Reports to Third Parties
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

96. nce-s-eth-096 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · confidentiality and its limits · hard · In review

A client signed a release last month letting her counselor share records in her divorce case. On the same day, the counselor receives a subpoena for the records from the spouse's attorney and a signed letter from the client revoking the release. What should the counselor do?
A. Send the records, since the release was valid when the subpoena was issued
Revocation applies to future disclosures; nothing has yet been released in reliance on it.
B. Ignore the subpoena, since the client has now withdrawn her permission
A subpoena is a legal document that must receive a timely response.
C. Honor the revocation, respond to the subpoena, and seek a court order ✔ KEY
The revocation stops voluntary release; the counselor responds without disclosing and asserts privilege.
D. Send a summary only, since that limits what the spouse's side will see
Any disclosure now lacks valid consent or a court order.
Rationale: A client may revoke an authorization in writing, and the revocation applies to any disclosure not yet made. A subpoena alone is not a court order, so the counselor responds in a timely way, notifies the client, asserts privilege on her behalf, consults an attorney, and discloses only what a court orders, limiting it to what is necessary (ACA B.2.c and B.2.e).
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.c Court-Ordered Disclosure · HIPAA — 45 CFR 164.508(b)(5) Revocation of authorizations
⚑ Check: Subpoena response and revocation handling vary by state and court rules; confirm the general guidance.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

97. nce-s-eth-097 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · duty to warn and protect · medium · In review

After a careful risk assessment, a counselor concludes that she must notify a man whom her client, a 31-year-old warehouse worker, has credibly threatened to stab. What information should she share when she makes the call?
A. The client's full diagnosis, treatment history and recent session notes for context
Diagnosis, history and notes go well beyond what is needed to protect the man.
B. Nothing that names the client, so the client's privacy is kept fully intact
A warning that does not identify the source of danger may not let the man protect himself.
C. Only the essential facts: who poses the threat and the nature of the danger ✔ KEY
B.2.e directs that only essential information is revealed when disclosure is required.
D. Whatever the man asks about the client, since the duty overrides all privacy
The duty to protect permits a limited disclosure, not open access to the client's information.
Rationale: When serious and foreseeable harm requires a disclosure, ACA B.2.e limits it to essential information. In a warning, that means enough for the person to protect themselves, such as the source and nature of the threat, without diagnosis or treatment details. Where possible, the client is told about the disclosure beforehand and involved in the decision.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.e Minimal Disclosure · ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm and Legal Requirements
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

98. nce-s-eth-098 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · duty to warn and protect · hard · In review

The father of an adult client calls a counselor and says his son has been talking about "getting even" with his ex-partner's new boyfriend and has been driving past the boyfriend's home. The client has said nothing like this in session. How should the counselor BEST view the father's report?
A. As risk information to assess promptly, since some state laws treat it as able to trigger a duty ✔ KEY
Courts in some states (e.g., Ewing v. Goldstein) have held that a family member's report to the therapist can trigger the duty to protect.
B. As hearsay that cannot create any duty, because only the client's own words count in law
This is not true in every jurisdiction; some courts have held otherwise, and clinically the report must be assessed.
C. As grounds to warn the boyfriend at once, before speaking with the client about any of it
A warning without assessment skips the step that tells the counselor whether the risk is serious and foreseeable.
D. As a confidentiality breach by the father, which the counselor should report to the client
The father did not breach any duty, and treating the call this way ignores a possible risk to an identifiable person.
Rationale: Information about a client's dangerousness does not have to come from the client to be clinically and legally significant. In Ewing v. Goldstein (2004), a California appellate court held that a family member's report to the therapist could trigger the statutory duty to protect. Counselors assess such reports promptly, consult, and follow the law of their own state.
References: State law — Ewing v. Goldstein (Cal. Ct. App. 2004): family member communications and the duty to protect · ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm and Legal Requirements
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

99. nce-s-eth-099 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · duty to warn and protect · easy · In review

A counseling student asks why many textbooks now use the phrase "duty to protect" rather than "duty to warn." Which answer is MOST accurate?
A. Duty to protect applies only to suicide risk, while duty to warn covers harm to others
Both terms concern danger to others; suicide risk is handled under separate standards.
B. Duty to protect requires that police be called first, before any other step is taken
No single required first step applies; options depend on the case and on state law.
C. Duty to protect means the counselor shares liability for any harm the client commits
The term describes the clinician's obligation to act reasonably, not automatic liability.
D. Protecting may involve steps besides a warning, such as hospitalization or police contact ✔ KEY
The 1976 Tarasoff ruling framed the duty as reasonable care to protect, which a warning alone may or may not meet.
Rationale: The 1976 Tarasoff decision held that when a therapist determines a patient presents a serious danger of violence to another, the therapist must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim. Warning the victim is one option; others include notifying police, arranging hospitalization, or intensifying treatment. State laws define which actions discharge the duty.
References: State law — Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1976): duty to use reasonable care to protect
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

100. nce-s-eth-100 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · mandated reporting of abuse and neglect · medium · In review

An agency counselor tells her supervisor that a 9-year-old client described being burned with a cigarette by a parent's partner. The supervisor says, "I'll take care of the report." Two days later, the counselor cannot confirm that any report was made. What should she do?
A. Wait for the supervisor to follow up, since the agency chain of command now owns it
In most states the mandated reporter's duty is personal and is not met by telling a supervisor.
B. Make the report herself now, since telling a supervisor does not discharge her duty ✔ KEY
Mandated reporting duties generally rest on the individual; she must make sure a report is made promptly.
C. Ask the child about the burn in more detail first, so the report will be complete
Investigating is the role of child protective services; more questioning can harm the child and the case.
D. Call the parent's partner to hear his account before deciding whether to report
Contacting the alleged abuser can put the child at further risk and is not the counselor's role.
Rationale: In most jurisdictions a mandated reporter's obligation is individual: informing a supervisor or administrator does not relieve the counselor of the duty to make sure a report reaches child protective services or law enforcement within the required time. Agency procedures can support reporting but do not replace it. The counselor should report and document the date, time and agency contacted.
References: State law — Child abuse reporting statutes: individual duty of mandated reporters and reporting timelines
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

101. nce-s-eth-101 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · mandated reporting of abuse and neglect · hard · In review

A 40-year-old father in counseling for anger tells his counselor that last week he struck his 6-year-old with a belt, leaving welts. He says it will not happen again and that counseling is how he is "fixing it." He asks the counselor to keep it private. What should the counselor do?
A. Keep it confidential, since the client is already in treatment for the very problem
Being in treatment does not remove the legal duty to report suspected child abuse.
B. File the required report and discuss it with the client, as reviewed in informed consent ✔ KEY
Mandated reporting applies when the client is the alleged abuser; the counselor can stay engaged and transparent.
C. Report only if the client strikes the child again, since this was a single incident
Reporting laws do not wait for repeated abuse; one incident with injury can trigger the duty.
D. End counseling and refer him elsewhere, so a new provider can decide about reporting
Referring out evades the duty and abandons a client who is seeking help.
Rationale: Child abuse reporting laws apply regardless of whether the person disclosing is the victim, a witness, or the alleged perpetrator, and they do not exempt clients who are already in treatment. Because reporting is a limit of confidentiality, it should be covered in informed consent at the start. Counselors can report while staying engaged and supporting the client's change efforts.
References: State law — Child abuse reporting statutes: duty applies to disclosures by alleged perpetrators · ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm and Legal Requirements
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

102. nce-s-eth-102 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · mandated reporting of abuse and neglect · easy · In review

A new school counselor hesitates to report a suspicion of neglect because she fears the family will sue her if child protective services finds nothing. What should her supervisor tell her?
A. She should wait for proof, since a report that turns out unfounded can lead to liability
The standard is reasonable suspicion, not proof, and good-faith reports are protected.
B. She may report anonymously, which is the only way to avoid being named in a lawsuit
Mandated reporters usually must identify themselves; protection comes from good-faith immunity.
C. State laws give immunity for reports made in good faith, even if abuse is not found ✔ KEY
All states grant immunity from liability for good-faith reports, and failing to report can carry penalties.
D. She should get the parents' consent before reporting, which protects her from a suit
Parental consent is not required to report and seeking it could put the child at risk.
Rationale: Mandated reporters must report when they have reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect. State laws, consistent with federal CAPTA requirements, protect people who report in good faith from civil and criminal liability even when the report is not substantiated. By contrast, knowingly failing to report can bring fines or other penalties.
References: State law — Good-faith immunity for child abuse and neglect reporters; penalties for failure to report
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

103. nce-s-eth-103 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · HIPAA and FERPA basics for counselors · medium · In review

A billing specialist at a HIPAA-covered group practice asks a counselor to forward complete session notes for every client so claims can be submitted faster. Which HIPAA principle MOST directly applies?
A. Minimum necessary: share only the information that is needed to process the claims ✔ KEY
For payment and operations uses, the minimum necessary standard limits what staff may access.
B. Right of access: staff have the same rights to full records that clients themselves do
The right of access belongs to the individual client, not to workforce members.
C. Treatment exception: anyone in the practice may see full notes without any limits
Billing is a payment function, not treatment, and is subject to minimum necessary limits.
D. Breach notification: clients must be told each time a billing staff member views notes
Breach notification applies to impermissible disclosures, not routine permitted access.
Rationale: The HIPAA Privacy Rule requires covered entities to limit uses and disclosures of protected health information to the minimum necessary to accomplish the purpose. Claims usually need dates, codes and diagnoses, not full session content. The minimum necessary standard does not apply to disclosures to other providers for treatment, but billing is a payment function.
References: HIPAA — Privacy Rule minimum necessary standard (45 CFR 164.502(b), 164.514(d))
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

104. nce-s-eth-104 · Professional Counseling Orientation and Ethical Practice · HIPAA and FERPA basics for counselors · easy · In review

A counselor opening a private practice that bills health insurance electronically is setting up her intake paperwork. Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, what must she give new clients?
A. A full copy of her case notes from every past client so they can judge her methods
Sharing other clients' records would itself be a serious privacy violation.
B. A signed waiver giving up their right to see their own records for the treatment term
HIPAA gives clients a right of access; providers may not require waiving it.
C. A written guarantee that no information will be shared without their permission ever
HIPAA and law permit some disclosures without authorization, so this promise is inaccurate.
D. A Notice of Privacy Practices, with a good-faith effort to get written acknowledgment ✔ KEY
Direct treatment providers give the notice at first service and try to obtain acknowledgment of receipt.
