Morning tremor and sweating relieved by drinking suggest physical dependence, so the counselor should arrange medical evaluation to determine the appropriate withdrawal management setting before the client stops. ASAM Dimension 1 (acute intoxication and withdrawal potential) guides this decision.
References: ASAM Criteria — Dimension 1: acute intoxication and/or withdrawal potential · DSM-5-TR — Alcohol Withdrawal: features and complications
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

372. nce-s-clf-132 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · substance use and addictive disorders · medium · In review

A 16-year-old is referred after cannabis is found in his backpack. He uses most days and his grades are slipping. He says, "Weed is natural. It doesn't hurt anybody." Which counselor response BEST reflects a motivational rather than a confrontational approach?
A. "Research shows cannabis harms the teen brain, so you need to stop now."
Leading with warnings and demands is the righting reflex and tends to increase resistance.
B. "Until you admit you have a problem, counseling will not help you much."
Requiring the client to accept a label is a confrontational stance MI avoids.
C. "It feels pretty harmless to you. What, if anything, concerns you about it?" ✔ KEY
A reflection followed by an open question rolls with discord and invites the teen's own reasons for change.
D. "Your parents and school are worried, so let's agree that you quit today."
Pressing for a commitment the teen has not voiced bypasses his ambivalence and autonomy.
Rationale: Motivational interviewing avoids arguing, labeling, and the righting reflex, which tend to provoke sustain talk, especially in adolescents sensitive to autonomy. Instead, the counselor reflects the client's view and asks open questions that evoke the client's own concerns and reasons for change. Research does not support confrontational approaches for substance use.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — The righting reflex; responding to sustain talk and discord · SAMHSA TIP 35 — Motivational approaches with adolescents
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

373. nce-s-clf-133 · Assessment and Testing · neurodevelopmental disorders · medium · In review

A 32-year-old seeks an ADHD evaluation for lifelong disorganization, forgetfulness, and trouble finishing tasks at work and home. Which statement about diagnosing ADHD in adults under DSM-5-TR is accurate?
A. Five symptoms in a domain are needed for those aged 17 and older ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR lowers the threshold to five symptoms in a domain for older adolescents and adults.
B. Six symptoms in a domain are needed at every age, adults included
Six symptoms are required for children up to age 16; five for those 17 and older.
C. Impairment from symptoms must be documented from before age 7
DSM-5 replaced age 7 with several symptoms present before age 12; impairment need not be documented then.
D. Symptoms need to appear in only one setting, such as the workplace
Several symptoms must be present in two or more settings.
Rationale: For ADHD, children up to age 16 need six or more symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, while adolescents aged 17 and older and adults need five or more. Several symptoms must have been present before age 12 and in two or more settings. Adult presentations often show more inattention and inner restlessness than overt hyperactivity.
References: DSM-5-TR — Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Criterion A (symptom thresholds by age)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

374. nce-s-clf-134 · Assessment and Testing · neurodevelopmental disorders · medium · In review

An autistic 8-year-old speaks in full sentences but struggles with back-and-forth conversation and making friends. His insistence on sameness and great distress at small changes markedly interfere with functioning across settings. How should severity be recorded under DSM-5-TR?
A. Assign one overall level, based mainly on his measured IQ
Severity is not based on IQ; intellectual impairment is recorded with a separate specifier.
B. Rate social communication and restricted behaviors separately ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR rates the level of support needed separately for each of the two domains.
C. Assign a support level only if he has intellectual disability
Severity levels are recorded for all autistic individuals, with or without intellectual disability.
D. Use only the more impaired domain to set one combined level
The domains are rated separately, so a child may need different levels of support in each.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR asks clinicians to specify current severity of autism spectrum disorder separately for social communication and for restricted, repetitive behaviors, using levels 1 (requiring support), 2 (requiring substantial support), and 3 (requiring very substantial support). Severity can change across contexts and over time, and it is recorded alongside specifiers for intellectual and language impairment.
References: DSM-5-TR — Autism Spectrum Disorder: severity levels for each domain
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

375. nce-s-clf-135 · Assessment and Testing · schizophrenia spectrum disorders · medium · In review

Two weeks after giving birth, a 28-year-old suddenly develops delusions and disorganized speech. She has no manic or depressive symptoms. With treatment, she returns fully to her prior level of functioning after 10 days. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Schizophreniform disorder, with good prognostic features
Schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms lasting at least 1 month.
B. Major depressive disorder, with peripartum onset
No depressive episode is described.
C. Schizophrenia, first episode, currently in acute episode
Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for at least 6 months.
D. Brief psychotic disorder, with peripartum onset ✔ KEY
Psychotic symptoms lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, beginning within 4 weeks postpartum, fit this diagnosis and specifier.
Rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires at least one of delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech (plus possibly grossly disorganized behavior), lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning. The "with peripartum onset" specifier applies when onset is during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum. Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency, and clinicians should also consider an underlying bipolar disorder.
References: DSM-5-TR — Brief Psychotic Disorder: criteria and specifiers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

376. nce-s-clf-136 · Assessment and Testing · schizophrenia spectrum disorders · easy · In review

Parents of a 17-year-old report that over 8 months he has pulled away from friends, his grades have dropped, he neglects hygiene, and he has become suspicious and voices odd ideas. He has no clear hallucinations or fixed delusions and does not use substances. What is the MOST appropriate action?
A. Refer for a full evaluation, as these may be early signs of psychosis ✔ KEY
A decline in functioning with emerging odd beliefs can signal a prodrome; early evaluation and intervention improve outcomes.
B. Reassure the parents that these are typical changes during adolescence
A marked, sustained decline with suspiciousness goes beyond typical adolescent change.
C. Diagnose schizophrenia, since negative signs have lasted over 6 months
Schizophrenia requires an active phase of at least 1 month of Criterion A symptoms, which is not present.
D. Wait to act until hallucinations or delusions have clearly appeared
Waiting for frank psychosis delays care; a long duration of untreated psychosis worsens outcomes.
Rationale: Prodromal signs of schizophrenia often include social withdrawal, declining school or work performance, poor self-care, and attenuated positive symptoms such as unusual beliefs or suspiciousness. These signs do not establish a diagnosis, but they warrant prompt referral for comprehensive evaluation, because shorter duration of untreated psychosis is associated with better outcomes. DSM-5-TR lists attenuated psychosis syndrome as a condition for further study.
References: DSM-5-TR — Schizophrenia: development and course (prodromal phase) · DSM-5-TR — Conditions for Further Study: Attenuated Psychosis Syndrome
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

377. nce-s-clf-137 · Assessment and Testing · personality disorders · easy · In review

A 30-year-old cannot decide what to wear or what to order at a restaurant without reassurance from her mother. She agrees with others even when she disagrees, for fear of losing their support, feels helpless when alone, and quickly began a new relationship after a breakup. Which personality disorder BEST fits?
A. Avoidant personality disorder
Avoidant PD centers on fear of criticism and rejection leading to social avoidance, not a need to be taken care of.
B. Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic PD involves attention seeking and shallow, shifting emotion.
C. Dependent personality disorder ✔ KEY
Difficulty making everyday decisions, fear of disagreeing, and urgently seeking a new relationship fit dependent PD.
D. Borderline personality disorder
Borderline PD involves unstable identity, affect, and relationships, not submissive reliance for everyday decisions.
Rationale: Dependent personality disorder, in Cluster C, is a pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive, clinging behavior and fears of separation. Criteria include difficulty making everyday decisions without excessive advice, difficulty expressing disagreement, feeling helpless when alone, and urgently seeking another relationship when one ends.
References: DSM-5-TR — Dependent Personality Disorder: criteria and differential diagnosis
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

378. nce-s-clf-138 · Assessment and Testing · personality disorders · hard · In review

A 45-year-old manager follows rules rigidly, misses deadlines because work is never perfect enough, will not delegate, is reluctant to spend money, and has let friendships lapse because of work. He sees his ways as simply "the right way." He reports no intrusive thoughts or rituals. Which statement is MOST accurate?
A. OCD fits best, since his perfectionism counts as an obsession
Perfectionism that is experienced as correct is a trait, not an intrusive, unwanted obsession.
B. OCPD fits; his traits form a pattern without true obsessions ✔ KEY
His pervasive, ego-syntonic perfectionism, rigidity, and miserliness, without obsessions or compulsions, fit OCPD.
C. OCPD can be diagnosed only when OCD is also present with it
OCPD does not require OCD; the two may co-occur but are distinct.
D. Narcissistic PD fits, since he sees his own way as superior
His focus is on order and control, not grandiosity or a need for admiration.
Rationale: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and control at the expense of flexibility and efficiency, including excessive devotion to work, reluctance to delegate, and miserly spending. Unlike OCD, it involves no true obsessions or compulsions, and the traits are usually ego-syntonic. The two can co-occur, but neither requires the other.
References: DSM-5-TR — Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder: differential diagnosis (OCD)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

379. nce-s-clf-139 · Human Growth and Development · eating disorders · medium · In review

Parents of a 7-year-old say he eats only a handful of familiar foods and refuses new textures. A pediatrician has ruled out a medical cause. Which finding would MOST support avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) rather than ordinary picky eating?
A. He refuses most vegetables and prefers plain pasta at dinner
Food preferences like this are common in young children and do not show clinical significance.
B. He eats more readily when meals are served in a favorite bowl
This is a typical childhood preference with no sign of nutritional or functional impact.
C. He complains that many new foods look strange or smell bad to him
Sensory dislikes occur in both picky eating and ARFID, so they do not distinguish them.
D. He now relies on nutritional supplements and growth has faltered ✔ KEY
Faltering growth and dependence on supplements are among the consequences that define ARFID.
Rationale: ARFID requires an eating disturbance that leads to at least one of: significant weight loss or faltering growth in children, significant nutritional deficiency, dependence on enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplements, or marked interference with psychosocial functioning. Picky eating without these consequences is developmentally common. ARFID also differs from anorexia nervosa in lacking body image disturbance.
References: DSM-5-TR — Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder, Criterion A
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

380. nce-s-clf-140 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · eating disorders · medium · In review

A 20-year-old in outpatient counseling for anorexia nervosa says her recent blood work was "totally normal," so she no longer needs to see her physician. Which counselor response is MOST accurate?
A. Normal labs do not rule out serious risk, so medical monitoring should continue ✔ KEY
Laboratory results can be normal despite serious medical risk, so ongoing medical monitoring remains part of care.
B. Normal labs show she is medically stable and can pause physician visits for now
Normal labs do not establish medical stability in anorexia nervosa.
C. Medical monitoring is needed only if she begins to report purging behaviors
Restriction alone carries significant medical risk; monitoring is not limited to purging.
D. The counselor can track her physical health during sessions in place of a doctor
Medical monitoring is outside counseling scope and requires a qualified medical provider.
Rationale: Anorexia nervosa has one of the highest mortality rates among mental disorders, and laboratory values can remain normal even when risk is serious. Treatment is multidisciplinary: the counselor coordinates with a medical provider who monitors physical health throughout care, and helps the client see monitoring as part of recovery rather than a sign of failure.
References: NICE guidelines — NG69 Eating disorders: recognition and treatment, physical health monitoring · DSM-5-TR — Anorexia Nervosa: functional consequences and laboratory findings
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

381. nce-s-clf-141 · Assessment and Testing · neurocognitive disorders · medium · In review

A nursing home resident with moderate Alzheimer's disease has, over the past 2 days, become much more confused, drowsy at times and agitated at others, and unable to keep her attention on a conversation. Staff say, "Her dementia is just getting worse." What should the counselor do?
A. Agree that this is expected decline and update her care plan
Alzheimer's disease progresses gradually; an abrupt change over days is not expected progression.
B. Begin reminiscence sessions to help reorient her to the past
Reminiscence does not address a possible acute medical cause of the change.
C. Alert medical staff promptly, as this may signal a delirium ✔ KEY
Acute onset, fluctuating alertness, and inattention suggest delirium, which needs urgent medical evaluation.
D. Repeat a cognitive screen in a month to compare the scores
Waiting a month delays care for a potentially serious, treatable medical cause.
Rationale: Delirium is a disturbance in attention and awareness that develops over hours to days, fluctuates, and is caused by a medical condition, substance, or medication. People with major neurocognitive disorder are at higher risk, and delirium superimposed on dementia is often missed because staff attribute the change to the dementia. Any abrupt change in cognition calls for prompt medical evaluation.
References: DSM-5-TR — Delirium: criteria, risk factors, and differential diagnosis (major neurocognitive disorder)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

382. nce-s-clf-142 · Human Growth and Development · grief and loss · easy · In review

A month after her grandfather died, a 4-year-old keeps asking when he will be finished being dead and come home. Her parents worry that something is wrong. What BEST explains her questions?
A. Her questions show a denial that calls for treatment
This reflects normal cognitive development, not pathological denial.
B. Young children often do not yet see death as permanent ✔ KEY
Preschoolers commonly view death as temporary or reversible; irreversibility is understood later.
C. She is showing early signs of prolonged grief disorder
Her questions are developmentally expected, and too little time has passed for that diagnosis.
D. She is too young to grieve, so the topic should wait
Young children do grieve and benefit from simple, honest explanations.
Rationale: Children gradually develop an understanding of death's components: irreversibility (permanence), nonfunctionality (the body stops working), universality (all living things die), and causality. Preschoolers often think of death as temporary, like sleep or a trip. Adults can help by using clear, concrete words such as "died" rather than euphemisms, answering repeated questions patiently, and including children in mourning rituals as appropriate.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Death, dying, and bereavement: children's understanding of death · Worden (Grief Counseling) — Grieving children: developmental understanding of death
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

383. nce-s-clf-143 · Social and Cultural Diversity · grief and loss · easy · In review

A 52-year-old's former husband, with whom she stayed close after their divorce, died suddenly. His family did not invite her to the funeral, coworkers seem puzzled that she is upset, and she says she has "no right" to grieve. Which concept BEST describes her experience?
A. Anticipatory grief
Anticipatory grief occurs before an expected death; this death was sudden.
B. Prolonged grief disorder
Nothing indicates the duration or impairment required for prolonged grief disorder.
C. Chronic grief
Chronic grief refers to excessively long mourning, not grief that lacks social recognition.
D. Disenfranchised grief ✔ KEY
Grief that is not openly acknowledged, socially supported, or publicly mourned is disenfranchised grief.
Rationale: Disenfranchised grief, a term introduced by Doka, describes grief that is not openly acknowledged or socially supported, such as the death of a former spouse, an unrecognized partner, a pet, or a pregnancy loss. Lack of social recognition removes supports and rituals and can complicate mourning. Counselors can validate the loss and help clients create their own ways to mourn.
References: Worden (Grief Counseling) — Mediators of mourning: social mediators and socially unrecognized losses
⚑ Check: The term is Doka's; Worden discusses socially unspeakable/negated losses among social mediators. SME to confirm the Worden locator wording.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

384. nce-s-clf-144 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · grief and loss · medium · In review

The husband of a woman with advancing ALS says he already grieves the losses of her voice and their plans for retirement. He feels guilty "mourning someone who is still here." Which counselor response is MOST helpful?
A. Normalize his anticipatory grief and help him face both loss and time left ✔ KEY
Anticipatory grief is a normal response to expected loss; counseling can attend to it while supporting time together.
B. Advise him to set the grief aside until after she has died, to stay strong
Suppressing grief is not recommended and adds to his guilt and isolation.
C. Explain that grieving now shows a detachment that could harm her care
Anticipatory grief does not indicate harmful detachment and should not be pathologized.
D. Assure him that grieving now means he will grieve far less after she dies
Anticipatory grief does not reliably reduce grief after the death, so this promise is misleading.
Rationale: Anticipatory grief is mourning that begins before an expected death, often in response to a series of losses during a progressive illness. It is normal and may include guilt, sadness, and fatigue. Worden notes that it does not necessarily shorten or lessen grief after the death; counselors can normalize it, address the losses already occurring, and help the family make meaningful use of the time remaining.
References: Worden (Grief Counseling) — Anticipatory grief
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

385. nce-s-clf-145 · Assessment and Testing · crisis and disaster response · easy · In review

A counselor returns from a meeting to four voicemails from clients. Which client should the counselor contact FIRST?
A. A client who reports her panic attacks are back and she cannot sleep
This is distressing and needs follow-up, but it shows no imminent danger.
B. A client who is furious about a custody ruling and wants to vent today
Anger about a court ruling warrants a call but shows no stated risk of harm.
C. A client who has written goodbye letters and given away her pet cats ✔ KEY
Goodbye letters and giving away belongings are preparatory behaviors that signal acute suicide risk.
D. A client who missed his appointment and would like to reschedule it
A routine scheduling request has the lowest priority.
Rationale: Crisis triage puts imminent risk to life first. Preparatory behaviors, such as writing goodbye notes or giving away valued possessions, are among the strongest warning signs of suicide and call for immediate contact and risk assessment, for example with the C-SSRS. Other clients' needs are real but can be addressed afterward.
References: C-SSRS — Suicidal behavior: preparatory acts or behavior
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

386. nce-s-clf-146 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · crisis and disaster response · hard · In review

After a high school student dies by suicide, the principal asks the school counselor to lead the response. Which action BEST reduces the risk of suicide contagion among students?
A. Set up a lasting memorial on campus where students can gather and grieve
Permanent or prominent memorials can glamorize the death; postvention guidance favors time-limited, low-key options.
B. Share facts without method details and screen students most at risk ✔ KEY
Safe messaging plus identifying and reaching out to vulnerable students are core postvention steps.
C. Avoid any mention of the death so that students do not become upset
Silence fuels rumors and leaves grieving students without support.
D. Explain that stress caused the death, so students have a simple answer
Attributing suicide to a single cause oversimplifies it and can lead others to identify with it.
Rationale: Postvention aims to support grief and prevent contagion. Recommended steps include sharing accurate information in small groups or classrooms without describing the method, avoiding glamorizing or simplifying the death, offering time-limited and low-key memorial options, and actively identifying and reaching out to students at elevated risk, such as close friends, those with prior suicidal behavior, and those exposed to the death.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Crisis counseling in schools: responding after a suicide
⚑ Check: Content follows AFSP/SPRC "After a Suicide: A Toolkit for Schools," which is not on the approved source list; the Gladding locator is a general crisis-counseling citation.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

387. nce-s-clf-147 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · intimate partner violence · hard · In review

A client who recently left an abusive partner says he keeps appearing wherever she goes and texts her details about her day. She plans to change all her passwords and delete her accounts tonight. Which counselor response is MOST appropriate?
A. Plan with her first, since sudden changes may alert him and raise risk ✔ KEY
Abrupt loss of access can signal to an abuser that the victim is acting and may escalate danger, so changes are planned as part of safety planning.
B. Urge her to block him and delete every account tonight to cut off his access
This may feel protective but can provoke escalation and destroy evidence of stalking.
C. Reassure her that tracking her is unlikely unless he holds her phone
Shared accounts, spyware, location sharing, and tracking devices allow monitoring without physical access.
D. Suggest she meet with him in person to demand that he stop following her
Confronting a stalking ex-partner can increase risk; contact decisions belong in safety planning.
Rationale: Technology-facilitated abuse and stalking are common after separation, which is itself a high-risk period. Safety planning considers how the abuser may be monitoring the client (shared accounts, location sharing, spyware, trackers), uses a safer device for sensitive contacts, documents incidents for possible legal action, and times changes so they do not alert the abuser. Connecting the client with a domestic violence advocate adds specialized expertise.
References: SAMHSA TIP 57 — Trauma-informed principles: safety and client choice · Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling survivors of intimate partner violence
⚑ Check: Technology-safety guidance comes from NNEDV Safety Net materials, which are not on the approved source list; citations are general.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

388. nce-s-clf-148 · Human Growth and Development · intimate partner violence · medium · In review

A mother says her 6-year-old was "asleep upstairs" during her partner's assaults on her and was never hit, so the girl has not been affected. Since the mother left, the child has had nightmares, startles easily, and clings to her at bedtime. Which statement is MOST accurate?
A. Children who are not hit themselves seldom show lasting effects
Children exposed to IPV show emotional and behavioral effects comparable to those of directly abused children.
B. Her symptoms most likely reflect a normal phase at her age
Nightmares, startle, and clinging after exposure to violence are trauma-related signs, not a typical phase.
C. Young children forget such events, so focus on the mother
Young children are affected by violence they overhear, and they need their own assessment and support.
D. Hearing or seeing IPV can cause trauma reactions in children ✔ KEY
Witnessing or overhearing violence against a caregiver is a traumatic exposure that can produce trauma symptoms.
Rationale: Children often see or hear IPV even when parents believe they are asleep or unaware. DSM-5-TR PTSD criteria for children 6 years and younger specifically include witnessing traumatic events occurring to others, especially primary caregivers. Exposed children may show sleep problems, hyperarousal, regression, and clinginess, and benefit from trauma-informed assessment and a strengthened caregiver relationship.
References: DSM-5-TR — Posttraumatic Stress Disorder for Children 6 Years and Younger, Criterion A2 · SAMHSA TIP 57 — Trauma across the life span: children exposed to violence
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

389. nce-s-clf-149 · Human Growth and Development · developmental life transitions · medium · In review

A 53-year-old client says that since her youngest child left for college, she wanders the house feeling useless. Her husband, by contrast, is enjoying the extra time together. Based on life-span research on the empty nest, which factor MOST increases the risk that launching children will be a painful transition?
A. Having a spouse who adjusts to the change faster
A spouse adapting faster may highlight the contrast, but research does not identify it as the main risk factor.
B. An identity built mainly around the parenting role ✔ KEY
Empty-nest distress is most likely when a parent has invested identity chiefly in parenting and has few other roles to turn to.
C. Launching the last child after the age of fifty
Timing that fits social expectations (on-time launching) is usually easier; age over fifty is not itself the risk factor.
D. Children who move to a college far from the home
Distance may add sadness, but most parents adjust well regardless; the key risk lies in how central parenting is to the self.
Rationale: Most parents adjust well to the empty nest, and many report relief and improved marital satisfaction. Distress is more likely when parenting has been the core of a person's identity, when other roles are thin, or when children leave off-time. Counseling can help the client build roles and meaning beyond active parenting.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Middle adulthood: launching children and the empty nest
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

390. nce-s-clf-150 · Human Growth and Development · developmental life transitions · easy · In review

Parents worry that their 22-year-old son has "failed to launch." In two years he has moved apartments three times, switched jobs twice, and ended two relationships. He is curious and hopeful about his future. Within Arnett's theory of emerging adulthood, how is this pattern BEST understood?
A. Instability, a typical feature of emerging adulthood ✔ KEY
Arnett names instability in love, work and residence as one of the defining features of emerging adulthood.
B. Identity diffusion that shows his development stalled
Diffusion (Marcia) means neither exploring nor committing; he is actively exploring, so the label does not fit.
C. Role confusion left over from an unresolved adolescence
Arnett frames these moves as normative for the age period, not as a failure of Erikson's adolescent stage.
D. Delayed launching caused by overinvolved, enmeshed parents
Nothing in the stem points to enmeshment; frequent change is expected in this period.
Rationale: Arnett describes emerging adulthood (roughly ages 18–25) by five features: identity explorations, instability, self-focus, feeling in-between, and possibilities. Frequent changes of residence, work and partners are expected. Counselors can reframe parents' worry while still supporting the young adult's goal setting.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Emerging adulthood (Arnett): features of the period
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

391. nce-s-clf-151 · Human Growth and Development · developmental life transitions · medium · In review

A 47-year-old client works full time, is raising two teenagers, and now helps her mother, who has early dementia, with meals, bills and appointments. She is exhausted, snaps at her children, and feels guilty that she is "failing everyone." What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Urge her to move her mother into a memory care facility
Placement may become an option, but directing it first ignores her values and skips assessment.
B. Explore early conflicts with her mother that fuel the guilt
Family history may matter later, but her current overload and well-being take priority.
C. Assess her caregiving load and link her to respite support ✔ KEY
For a "sandwich generation" caregiver, assessing strain and connecting her with respite, services and shared care is the practical first step.
D. Advise her to cut back her hours at work to free up time
Reducing work may add financial stress and is a decision for her after options are explored.
Rationale: Midlife adults who care for both children and aging parents (the "sandwich generation") face role overload that raises the risk of depression and burnout. Counselors first assess the demands and resources, then help the client mobilize respite, family sharing of tasks and community services, and address guilt and self-care.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Middle adulthood: caring for aging parents
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

392. nce-s-clf-152 · Human Growth and Development · developmental life transitions · medium · In review

Four months after the birth of their first child, a couple seeks counseling. They argue about night feedings and chores, and both say they feel less close than before. Which statement BEST reflects research on the transition to parenthood?
A. Their conflict signals a poor match that a baby has exposed
A dip in satisfaction after a first birth is common and does not by itself show the couple is mismatched.
B. Satisfaction usually rises soon after a first child arrives
On average, relationship satisfaction declines modestly rather than rises after the first birth.
C. Strain mostly reflects postpartum mood in the birth parent
Postpartum mood should be screened, but strain on the couple is common even without a mood disorder.
D. Satisfaction often dips, less so when care is shared fairly ✔ KEY
Research shows a common decline in satisfaction that is smaller when partners share caregiving and chores in a way both see as fair.
Rationale: Studies of the transition to parenthood find that relationship satisfaction often declines after a first child, driven by sleep loss, role change and disputes over the division of labor. Couples who share child care and household tasks fairly, and who hold realistic expectations, show less decline. Counseling can target these modifiable factors.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Early adulthood: transition to parenthood and marital satisfaction
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

393. nce-s-clf-153 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · chronic illness and disability · hard · In review

A 39-year-old client with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis had seemed at peace with her diagnosis. After a new relapse, she is again angry, tearful and asking "why me?" Her counselor wonders if earlier progress was lost. Which understanding of adjustment to chronic illness BEST fits?
A. Adjustment is often cyclical, and reactions return as the illness changes ✔ KEY
Contemporary adjustment models describe nonlinear, recurring reactions, especially when the illness course shifts.
B. Her anger shows she skipped a stage and must now go back and finish it
Rigid stage sequences are not supported; people do not need to complete stages in a fixed order.
C. Once a client reaches acceptance, a return of grief signals a new disorder
Renewed grief after a relapse is expected, not evidence of a new mental disorder.
D. Her distress points to a failed treatment that calls for a higher level of care
An expected emotional response to a relapse does not by itself warrant a higher level of care.
Rationale: Models of psychosocial adaptation to chronic illness and disability describe reactions such as shock, anxiety, depression, anger and acknowledgment as overlapping and recurring rather than a fixed sequence. Changes in the illness, such as a relapse, can bring earlier reactions back. Counselors normalize this cycling and help the client re-engage coping resources.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Rehabilitation counseling: psychosocial adaptation to chronic illness and disability
⚑ Check: Confirm Gladding (8th ed.) covers nonlinear psychosocial adaptation (e.g., Livneh & Antonak); a rehabilitation counseling text may be a better citation.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

394. nce-s-clf-154 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · chronic illness and disability · medium · In review

A 50-year-old with chronic low back pain for three years also meets criteria for major depressive disorder. He tells the counselor, "Once the doctors fix my back, my mood will fix itself, so counseling can wait." Which response BEST reflects current understanding of chronic pain and depression?
A. Agree to pause counseling until medical treatment of the pain ends
Waiting leaves the depression untreated, and the two conditions reinforce each other.
B. Explain that his pain is likely psychological and needs no medical care
Chronic pain is real and needs medical care; implying it is "all in his head" damages trust.
C. Explain that pain and low mood feed each other and both can be treated ✔ KEY
Pain and depression are linked in both directions; psychological care can lift mood and lessen pain's grip on daily life.
D. Refer him to a pain clinic and close his counseling case for now
Coordinating with a pain clinic can help, but closing the case abandons treatment of his depression.
Rationale: Chronic pain and depression are closely linked, each worsening sleep, activity, and outlook in a cycle. Guidelines for chronic pain recommend psychological approaches such as CBT or ACT alongside medical care to reduce distress and disability. Counselors treat the depression now and coordinate with the medical team rather than waiting for the pain to resolve.
References: NICE guidelines — NG193 Chronic pain (primary and secondary) in over 16s: psychological therapy (CBT, ACT)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

395. nce-s-clf-155 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · chronic illness and disability · easy · In review

A counselor works with a 68-year-old man who has cared for his wife with Parkinson's disease for six years. He reports feeling trapped, worn out and resentful, and the counselor wants a standard measure of how much strain caregiving places on him. Which instrument is designed for this purpose?
A. Mini-Mental State Examination
The MMSE screens cognitive impairment, not the strain caregiving places on a caregiver.
B. Zarit Burden Interview ✔ KEY
The Zarit Burden Interview measures perceived caregiver burden across health, finances, social life and the relationship.
C. Geriatric Depression Scale
The GDS screens for depression in older adults; it does not measure caregiving strain.
D. Beck Hopelessness Scale
The BHS measures negative expectations about the future, not caregiver burden.
Rationale: Caregiver burden is the physical, emotional, social and financial strain of caring for an ill or disabled person. The Zarit Burden Interview is a widely used self-report measure of it. High burden predicts caregiver depression and poorer health, so counselors screen for it and link caregivers to respite, support groups and services.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Assessment with older adults and caregivers: caregiver burden measures
⚑ Check: Confirm Hays (Assessment) names the Zarit Burden Interview; the fact is standard but the citation locator is uncertain.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

396. nce-s-clf-156 · Social and Cultural Diversity · spiritual and religious concerns · easy · In review

A counselor uses the FICA tool to take a brief spiritual history at intake. The letters stand for Faith or belief, Importance or influence, a third element, and Address in care. What does the "C" ask about?
A. Conflict between faith and treatment
Conflicts may surface, but "C" in FICA does not stand for conflict.
B. Coping skills learned from faith
Faith-based coping may arise in the interview, but it is not what "C" names.
C. Commitment to religious practice
Level of practice may come up under importance, but "C" is not commitment.
D. Community the person belongs to ✔ KEY
The "C" in FICA asks whether the client is part of a spiritual or religious community and whether it is a support.
Rationale: Puchalski's FICA is a brief spiritual history: Faith or belief (what gives meaning), Importance or influence (how beliefs shape life and health choices), Community (membership in and support from a spiritual community), and Address in care (how the client wants these addressed in treatment). It lets counselors assess spirituality respectfully without imposing values.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Spirituality in counseling: spiritual assessment
⚑ Check: FICA (Puchalski) components are standard; confirm Gladding mentions FICA or substitute a spirituality-in-counseling source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

397. nce-s-clf-157 · Social and Cultural Diversity · spiritual and religious concerns · hard · In review

After a cancer diagnosis, a 61-year-old devout client says, "God is punishing me for my sins. Maybe this is what I deserve." She has stopped attending services and feels abandoned. In Pargament's research on religious coping, how is her response BEST classified, and what is it linked to?
A. Negative religious coping, tied to poorer adjustment ✔ KEY
Punishing-God reappraisals and feeling abandoned by God are negative religious coping, which predicts more distress.
B. Positive religious coping, tied to better adjustment
Positive coping includes benevolent reappraisals and seeking spiritual support, not a punishing-God view.
C. A deferring coping style, tied to passive acceptance
Deferring means leaving problems to God; her statement is about punishment and abandonment.
D. Spiritual bypassing, tied to avoidance of emotion
Spiritual bypassing uses spiritual ideas to avoid feelings; she is expressing distress, not avoiding it.
Rationale: Pargament distinguished positive religious coping (benevolent reappraisal, seeking spiritual support, collaborative problem solving) from negative religious coping (punishing-God reappraisal, feeling abandoned by God, questioning God's power). Negative religious coping is associated with greater depression and poorer health outcomes. Counselors assess for it and may collaborate with clergy when the client wishes.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Spirituality in counseling: religious coping
⚑ Check: Pargament's positive/negative religious coping (RCOPE) is well established; confirm the Gladding locator or cite a spirituality-specific source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

398. nce-s-clf-158 · Social and Cultural Diversity · spiritual and religious concerns · medium · In review

Eight months after her infant died, a client who has always been devout says she is furious at God and ashamed of feeling that way. She fears her anger means she has lost her faith. The counselor does not share her religion. Which response is MOST appropriate?
A. Suggest she set aside spiritual topics until her grief eases
Avoiding her spiritual struggle leaves a central part of her grief unaddressed.
B. Reassure her that a loving God would not want her to be angry
This imposes a theological view and may deepen her shame.
C. Normalize anger at God as a common struggle and explore it ✔ KEY
Spiritual struggles such as anger at God are common after loss; exploring them openly reduces shame and supports meaning making.
D. Refer her to clergy since faith is outside the counselor's role
Clergy consultation may help with consent, but spiritual concerns are within a counselor's scope when they affect well-being.
Rationale: Spiritual struggles, such as anger at God, doubt, or conflict with a faith community, are common after trauma and loss and are linked to distress when unaddressed. Counselors respond within the client's own framework, normalize the struggle, and explore it without imposing beliefs. Collaboration with clergy is an option the client can choose.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Spirituality in counseling: addressing spiritual concerns · ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

399. nce-s-clf-159 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · sleep-wake concerns · easy · In review

A veteran with PTSD has the same trauma-related nightmare several nights a week. His counselor has him write down the dream, change the storyline in any way he chooses, and rehearse the new version in imagery for a few minutes each day. Which intervention is this?
A. Cognitive processing therapy
CPT targets stuck points in beliefs about the trauma; it does not rescript dreams.
B. Imagery rehearsal therapy ✔ KEY
Imagery rehearsal therapy has clients change a recurring nightmare and rehearse the new version while awake.
C. Stimulus control therapy
Stimulus control re-links the bed with sleep; it does not change dream content.
D. Systematic desensitization
Systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with a fear hierarchy, not dream rescripting.
Rationale: Imagery rehearsal therapy (IRT) treats recurring nightmares, including PTSD-related ones. The client rewrites the nightmare in any way desired and rehearses the new script while awake, which often reduces nightmare frequency and distress. It can be used alongside trauma-focused therapy.
References: VA/DoD CPG — Management of PTSD: treatment of trauma-related nightmares (imagery rehearsal therapy)
⚑ Check: Confirm the strength of the current VA/DoD PTSD CPG recommendation on IRT for nightmares; the item only asks for the definition.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

400. nce-s-clf-160 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · sleep-wake concerns · easy · In review

A 56-year-old client being treated for depression says he sleeps eight hours yet nods off while driving. His wife says he snores loudly and sometimes stops breathing and gasps at night. He also wakes with headaches and has high blood pressure. What should the counselor do?
A. Begin CBT-I with sleep restriction to consolidate sleep
Sleep restriction can worsen sleepiness and is not suited to a likely breathing disorder.
B. Teach sleep hygiene and review it again in two weeks
Sleep hygiene does not treat a possible breathing disorder, and the delay is unsafe given drowsy driving.
C. Treat the sleepiness as a symptom of his depression
Snoring, apneas and morning headaches point to a medical sleep problem, not only depression.
D. Refer him to his physician for a sleep apnea evaluation ✔ KEY
Loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, sleepiness and hypertension suggest obstructive sleep apnea, which needs medical evaluation.
Rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea is a breathing-related sleep disorder marked by snoring, gasping or breathing pauses during sleep, and daytime sleepiness despite adequate sleep time. It is confirmed by polysomnography and treated medically. Untreated apnea can worsen mood and raises accident risk, so counselors refer promptly and continue mental health care.
References: DSM-5-TR — Breathing-related sleep disorders: obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

401. nce-s-clf-161 · Career Development · career and vocational concerns · medium · In review

A 66-year-old retired engineer spent his first months of retirement traveling and finishing house projects. Now, about a year in, he feels let down, bored and unsure what his days are for. In Atchley's phases of retirement, which phase is he MOST likely in?
A. Honeymoon
The honeymoon phase is the early period of freedom and activity he has already moved past.
B. Reorientation
Reorientation follows disenchantment, as the retiree builds a realistic new routine.
C. Disenchantment ✔ KEY
Disenchantment is the letdown that can follow the honeymoon, when retirement does not meet expectations.
D. Termination
Termination is the end of the retirement role, often through illness or a return to work.
Rationale: Atchley described retirement phases: preretirement, honeymoon, disenchantment, reorientation, stability (routine), and termination. Not every retiree passes through each phase. Counselors can normalize disenchantment and help the client find meaningful roles such as volunteering, part-time work or learning.
References: Sharf (Career Development Theory) — Late career and retirement: adjustment to retirement
⚑ Check: Atchley's phases are standard NCE content; confirm Sharf (6th ed.) presents them or cite Berk (late adulthood: retirement).
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

402. nce-s-clf-162 · Career Development · career and vocational concerns · easy · In review

A 63-year-old accountant plans to leave her full-time firm job next year. She does not want to stop working completely, so she is lining up part-time tax preparation work to ease the move into full retirement. What is this type of work called?
A. Bridge employment ✔ KEY
Bridge employment is paid work after leaving a career job and before full retirement.
B. Career plateauing
A plateau is a point where advancement stalls within a career, not a step toward retirement.
C. Role disengagement
Disengagement theory describes withdrawal from roles; she is staying engaged in work.
D. Maintenance stage
Super's maintenance stage involves holding one's place in a career, not shifting to new part-time work.
Rationale: Bridge employment is part-time, temporary or self-employed work that links a career job and full retirement. It can provide income, structure and social contact, and it is linked to better adjustment for many older workers. Career counselors help older clients weigh bridge options alongside finances, health and values.
References: Sharf (Career Development Theory) — Late career: older workers and bridge employment
⚑ Check: Confirm Sharf uses the term bridge employment; Berk (late adulthood, retirement) is an alternative locator.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

403. nce-s-clf-163 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · child abuse and neglect · medium · In review

A 9-year-old tells her school counselor, "My uncle does things to me at night that I don't like, but you can't tell anyone." She looks scared and stops talking. Which response BEST fits recommended practice for handling a sexual abuse disclosure?
A. Promise to keep her secret so she will feel safe telling more
The counselor is a mandated reporter and cannot promise secrecy; a broken promise harms trust.
B. Stay calm, thank her for telling, avoid leading questions, report ✔ KEY
A calm, supportive response with minimal open questions protects the child and later investigation; reporting is required.
C. Ask if her uncle touched her private parts so the facts are clear
This is a leading question that can contaminate her account for any later forensic interview.
D. Gather a full, detailed account now so she will not need to retell
Detailed questioning is the role of trained forensic interviewers, not the school counselor.
Rationale: When a child discloses sexual abuse, counselors stay calm, believe and thank the child, use the child's own words, ask only minimal open-ended questions needed to establish reasonable suspicion, explain honestly that they must tell people who can help, and report promptly. Detailed or leading questioning can distress the child and compromise the investigation.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm and Legal Requirements · State law — Mandated reporting of suspected child abuse
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

404. nce-s-clf-164 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · child abuse and neglect · hard · In review

A counselor has seen a 7-year-old for six months for anxiety. After a report of possible abuse, the CPS caseworker asks the counselor to conduct the investigative interview, since "she already trusts you." The counselor has no forensic interview training. What should the counselor do?
A. Agree, since an existing alliance will help her disclose more
Trust does not make a treating counselor a proper forensic interviewer; mixing roles harms both.
B. Agree if the caseworker watches and records the session live
Observation does not solve the dual role or the lack of forensic training.
C. Interview her alone first, then pass the notes on to the caseworker
Investigative questioning by the therapist risks contaminating evidence and the therapy relationship.
D. Decline the forensic role and support a trained interviewer's work ✔ KEY
Treating counselors avoid forensic roles with their own clients; a trained interviewer, often at a child advocacy center, conducts it.
Rationale: Forensic interviews are fact-finding interviews conducted by trained interviewers using structured, nonleading protocols, often at a child advocacy center. A treating counselor's role is therapeutic, and the ACA Code bars counselors from evaluating their own current or former clients for forensic purposes. The counselor can support the child and cooperate within the law while keeping roles separate.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — E.13.c Client Evaluation Prohibited
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

405. nce-s-clf-165 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · military and veteran populations · medium · In review

A counselor in a small rural town sees a 34-year-old Army National Guard member just home from deployment. Compared with many active-duty service members, which stressor is MORE characteristic of Guard and Reserve members and their families?
A. Frequent moves between distant bases that uproot the children
Frequent permanent change of station moves are more typical of active-duty families.
B. Living in base housing within a closely knit military unit
Base housing and on-post community are features of active-duty life, not Guard life.
C. Distance from military supports and strain on civilian jobs ✔ KEY
Guard and Reserve families often live far from installations and must leave and return to civilian jobs.
D. Fewer total deployments over the course of an enlistment
Fewer deployments would lessen stress; the distinct burden lies in the civilian-military shift and limited support.
Rationale: National Guard and Reserve members move rapidly between civilian and military life. Their families often live far from installations and military support services, may be surrounded by civilians who do not understand deployment, and face disruption to civilian employment and income. Counselors in community settings help connect them to resources and address these transition stressors.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling military populations: Guard and Reserve families
⚑ Check: Content is standard; confirm Gladding addresses Guard/Reserve distinctions or cite a military counseling source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

406. nce-s-clf-166 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · couples and family concerns · medium · In review

An 11-year-old lives with her father and stepmother on weekends. She enjoys baking with her stepmother but then feels guilty and turns cold toward her, saying, "Mom would be hurt if she knew I liked her." Which intervention BEST addresses this loyalty conflict?
A. Help her mother give clear permission to like her stepmother ✔ KEY
Explicit permission from the biological parent eases the child's loyalty bind most directly.
B. Have her stepmother step in as her primary mother on weekends
Asking the stepmother to replace her mother intensifies the loyalty conflict.
C. Advise the father to limit contact between the two households
Cutting contact does not resolve her guilt and may harm her relationship with her mother.
D. Tell her the guilt is a sign the stepfamily is not yet working
Loyalty conflicts are common in stepfamilies and do not mean the family is failing.
Rationale: Children in stepfamilies often feel that caring for a stepparent betrays the absent biological parent. These loyalty conflicts ease when both biological parents explicitly permit the child to have a good relationship with the stepparent, and when the stepparent is presented as an additional adult rather than a replacement.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Remarried families: loyalty conflicts and stepfamily development
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

407. nce-s-clf-167 · Human Growth and Development · aging and older adults · medium · In review

A 64-year-old woman has taken custody of her two grandchildren because her daughter has a severe opioid use disorder. She loves them but says, "This was supposed to be my time." She is tired, short on money, and lies awake worrying about her daughter. Which concern is MOST characteristic of custodial grandparents?
A. A loss of interest in the grandchildren caused by aging
Nothing suggests lost interest; she loves the children and is stressed by the load.
B. An early sign of cognitive decline from added demands
Fatigue and worry do not indicate cognitive decline.
C. Rivalry with the grandchildren's other set of grandparents
Rivalry is not a characteristic theme for custodial grandparents.
D. Off-time role strain together with grief over her daughter ✔ KEY
Raising grandchildren is an off-time role, often with financial strain and grief or anger about the adult child.
Rationale: Grandparents raising grandchildren in skipped-generation households take on an unexpected, off-time parenting role. They often face financial strain, health demands, legal and school hurdles, social isolation from peers, and grief, anger or worry about the adult child whose problems led to the arrangement. Counselors address both the practical load and the losses.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Late adulthood: grandparents rearing grandchildren (skipped-generation families)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

408. nce-s-clf-168 · Social and Cultural Diversity · LGBTQ+ clients and minority stress · hard · In review

A 20-year-old client says, "I'm probably gay. I've started going to an LGBTQ+ student group so I'm not so alone, but I'm not ready to say I like it about myself, and I haven't told my family." In Cass's model of homosexual identity formation, which stage BEST fits?
A. Identity comparison
In comparison the person first considers "I might be gay" and weighs the alienation; she has moved past this to seeking out community.
B. Identity tolerance ✔ KEY
In tolerance the person accepts "I probably am gay" and seeks contact with gay communities, tolerating rather than fully accepting the identity.
C. Identity acceptance
Acceptance brings a more positive view of the identity and more contact; she still only tolerates it.
D. Identity pride
Pride involves strong immersion and often anger at heterosexist society, which she does not show.
Rationale: Cass described six stages: identity confusion, comparison, tolerance, acceptance, pride, and synthesis. In tolerance, the person acknowledges a probable gay identity and seeks out others to reduce isolation, while still merely tolerating the identity. Stage models are useful lenses but not every client follows them in order.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling LGBTQ+ individuals: sexual identity development (Cass model)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

409. nce-s-clf-169 · Social and Cultural Diversity · LGBTQ+ clients and minority stress · medium · In review

Religious parents of a 15-year-old who has come out as lesbian tell the counselor they cannot approve of her identity, but they love her and want to keep her safe. Which statement BEST reflects family acceptance research on LGBTQ+ youth?
A. Only her parents' full agreement with her identity lowers risk
Research shows benefit from reducing rejecting behaviors even before full acceptance.
B. Parental views matter little once teens find support from peers
Family acceptance and rejection have strong effects on youth health even with peer support.
C. Reducing rejecting behaviors lowers risk, even without agreement ✔ KEY
Family rejecting behaviors predict higher suicide, depression and substance risk; reducing them helps even without full agreement.
D. Teens facing rejection mainly benefit from moving out of the home early
Leaving home early raises risks such as homelessness; strengthening family support is preferred.
Rationale: Research from the Family Acceptance Project found that LGBTQ+ youth from highly rejecting families had far higher rates of suicide attempts, depression and substance use, while family acceptance was protective. Because even modest reductions in rejecting behaviors help, counselors can work with ambivalent families on specific behaviors, such as stopping slurs and supporting the teen at school, while respecting their values.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling LGBTQ+ individuals: family acceptance and rejection
⚑ Check: Finding is from Ryan et al. (Family Acceptance Project); confirm Sue & Sue (9th ed.) discusses it or add a source with the original study.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

410. nce-s-clf-170 · Social and Cultural Diversity · acculturation and immigration stress · medium · In review

A 30-year-old woman resettled as a refugee three months ago after fleeing armed conflict. Through an interpreter she reports nightmares and poor sleep, and says she is worried about losing her apartment and about relatives still in a refugee camp. What should the counselor focus on FIRST?
A. Address safety and resettlement needs while building trust ✔ KEY
Trauma-informed, phase-oriented care starts with safety, stability and trust, including practical resettlement needs.
B. Begin detailed trauma narration to process her war memories
Detailed trauma processing comes after stabilization, not at the start amid housing insecurity.
C. Encourage her to adopt local customs to speed her adjustment
Pushing assimilation ignores her culture and can raise acculturative stress.
D. Teach her to set aside thoughts of her relatives in the camp
Her worry is realistic; suppressing it is neither feasible nor helpful.
Rationale: Refugees carry pre-migration trauma, migration losses and ongoing post-migration stressors such as housing, finances and separated family. Trauma-informed care begins with safety, stabilization and trust, uses qualified interpreters, and attends to practical needs before any trauma-focused work. Current stressors often drive distress as much as past events.
References: SAMHSA TIP 57 — Trauma-informed principles: safety and trustworthiness; refugee and immigrant populations
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

411. nce-s-clf-171 · Social and Cultural Diversity · acculturation and immigration stress · easy · In review

A Korean immigrant family has lived in the United States for six years. The 15-year-old son speaks mostly English, wants to date, and argues that his parents' rules are "old-fashioned." His parents, who still speak mainly Korean, feel they are losing him. Which concept BEST describes this family conflict?
A. Typical adolescent rebellion unrelated to culture
Developmental strivings play a role, but the cultural gap is central to this conflict.
B. Marginalization of the son from both of his cultures
He is engaging with the host culture, not rejected by both cultures.
C. Cultural encapsulation of the parents' worldview
Cultural encapsulation (Wrenn) describes counselors who view others only through their own culture.
D. An intergenerational acculturation gap in the family ✔ KEY
Children often acculturate faster than parents, creating gaps in values and language that fuel conflict.
Rationale: An intergenerational acculturation gap arises when children adopt the host culture's language and values faster than their parents. The gap can strain communication, shift family roles, and heighten parent-child conflict. Counselors help family members understand each other's positions and find bicultural ground.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Immigrant and refugee families: acculturation conflicts between generations
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

412. nce-s-clf-172 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · self-injury · hard · In review

Within two weeks, four ninth graders at a high school are found to be cutting after one student posted photos of her wounds online. The principal asks the school counselor how the school should respond. Which plan is MOST consistent with best practice for self-injury in schools?
A. Hold an assembly showing the warning signs and methods of cutting
Describing methods to large groups can spread self-injury through social contagion.
B. Meet each student alone, assess risk, inform parents, limit spread ✔ KEY
Individual assessment, parent notification and steps to curb contagion are core to a school protocol.
C. Start a support group where the four students share their cutting
Groups focused on sharing self-injury can reinforce it and spread it among members.
D. Keep the cutting from parents so students keep trusting staff
Parents of minors at risk should be informed; secrecy leaves students without home support.
Rationale: School responses to self-injury emphasize individual risk assessment (including suicide risk), parent notification, referral for treatment, and limiting social contagion. Counselors avoid large-group presentations about methods and process groups centered on self-injury, and they may address related online sharing. Students are offered support in a calm, nonjudgmental way.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — School counseling: responding to self-injury and contagion · ACA Code of Ethics — B.5.b Responsibility to Parents and Legal Guardians
⚑ Check: Best-practice content is standard (e.g., Walsh; ASCA); confirm the Gladding locator or cite a school self-injury protocol source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

413. nce-s-clf-173 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · psychopharmacology basics for counselors · hard · In review

A counselor coordinating care for a client with bipolar I disorder learns that the psychiatrist is switching her from lithium to valproate. To support her in keeping medical appointments, the counselor wants to understand the lab monitoring involved. Which monitoring is MOST closely tied to valproate rather than lithium?
A. Kidney function and thyroid hormone levels
Kidney and thyroid monitoring is a hallmark of long-term lithium treatment.
B. Hydration status and daily salt intake
Dehydration and salt changes affect lithium levels, not valproate.
C. Liver function tests and platelet counts ✔ KEY
Valproate carries risks to the liver and blood platelets, so these are monitored.
D. Regular white blood cell counts for safety
Routine white cell monitoring is linked to clozapine, not valproate.
Rationale: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range; monitoring includes blood levels, kidney and thyroid function, and attention to hydration and salt. Valproate monitoring focuses on liver function and blood counts, including platelets, and it carries serious risks in pregnancy. Counselors do not interpret labs but can encourage adherence to monitoring and communicate concerns to the prescriber.
References: NICE guidelines — CG185 Bipolar disorder: monitoring physical health with lithium and valproate
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

414. nce-s-clf-174 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · psychopharmacology basics for counselors · medium · In review

A client who takes sertraline started St. John's wort on her own last week. In session she is restless and sweating, with shivering, muscle twitching, a racing heart and diarrhea. She says the symptoms began yesterday and are getting worse. What should the counselor recognize and do?
A. Possible serotonin syndrome needing urgent medical care ✔ KEY
Combining serotonergic agents can cause serotonin syndrome, which can become life-threatening and needs urgent care.
B. A panic attack to treat with breathing and grounding
Muscle twitching, diarrhea and sweating after adding a serotonergic herb point to a medical reaction, not panic.
C. SSRI discontinuation symptoms that will pass on their own
She has not stopped the SSRI; she added another serotonergic agent.
D. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from her antidepressant
NMS is linked mainly to antipsychotics and features severe rigidity, not twitching after adding an herb.
Rationale: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity, often when an SSRI is combined with another serotonergic agent such as St. John's wort, tramadol, triptans or an MAOI. Signs include agitation, sweating, tremor or twitching, rapid heart rate, diarrhea and fever. Counselors do not manage medications but should recognize warning signs and direct the client to urgent medical care.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Psychopharmacology for counselors: antidepressant adverse effects
⚑ Check: Clinical facts are standard; confirm Gladding covers serotonin syndrome or cite a psychopharmacology reference.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

415. nce-s-clf-175 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · psychopharmacology basics for counselors · easy · In review

A client who has taken a prescribed benzodiazepine daily for six years tells her counselor she is "done with pills" and plans to stop it all at once this weekend. Why should the counselor urge her to talk with her prescriber before stopping?
A. Stopping will cause relapse of her anxiety in all cases
Anxiety may return, but that is not certain and is not the main safety concern.
B. Stopping suddenly will lower her tolerance to alcohol use
This is not the key risk of abrupt benzodiazepine discontinuation.
C. Stopping is unsafe only if she took more than prescribed
Dependence develops with long-term use at prescribed doses too.
D. Abrupt withdrawal can bring severe effects like seizures ✔ KEY
Sedative withdrawal after long-term use can include seizures, so a supervised taper is needed.
Rationale: Long-term benzodiazepine use produces physiological dependence even at prescribed doses. DSM-5-TR sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic withdrawal can include autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, insomnia, anxiety, hallucinations and grand mal seizures. Counselors support the client's goal and urge a medically supervised taper.
References: DSM-5-TR — Sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic withdrawal: criteria
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

416. nce-s-clf-176 · Human Growth and Development · military and veteran populations · easy · In review

Two months into her husband's deployment, a mother says their 4-year-old has started wetting the bed again, clings to her at daycare drop-off, and asks every night when Daddy is coming home. What guidance should the counselor give?
A. These signs point to a likely trauma disorder needing intensive care
Regression and clinging are common reactions to a parent's absence and do not by themselves suggest a trauma disorder.
B. Brief regression is common; keep routines and give honest reassurance ✔ KEY
Young children often regress during deployment; stable routines, simple honest answers and connection help.
C. Avoid mentioning her father so she is not reminded of his absence
Avoiding talk of the parent increases confusion; keeping him present through photos and messages helps.
D. Tell her Daddy will be home soon to calm her fears about his return
False reassurance can backfire; age-appropriate, honest information is better.
Rationale: Children's reactions to deployment vary by age. Preschoolers often show regression, clinginess and sleep problems; school-age children may show irritability or school problems; adolescents may take on adult roles or act out. Counselors help the at-home parent keep routines, give honest age-appropriate explanations, maintain connection with the deployed parent, and watch for persistent difficulties.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Early childhood: stress, separation and regression in young children
⚑ Check: Content is standard deployment-cycle guidance; Berk does not address deployment directly, so a military family source may be preferable.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

417. nce-s-clf-177 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · school and academic concerns · medium · In review

A 14-year-old has missed 15 school days this term. Each morning he leaves home on time, then spends the day at a friend's house playing video games. He forged notes so his parents would not find out, and he shows no worry about school itself. Which pattern does this BEST fit?
A. School refusal due to anxiety about being away from home
School refusal involves emotional distress, often staying home with parents' knowledge.
B. School refusal driven by fear of a specific school setting
He shows no fear of school; he is avoiding it to do something more appealing.
C. Truancy, hidden from parents and without school anxiety ✔ KEY
Truancy is typically concealed from parents, lacks marked anxiety, and may involve conduct problems.
D. Avoidance linked to depression and loss of interest at school
Nothing points to depressed mood; he is actively seeking a rewarding activity elsewhere.
Rationale: School refusal involves emotional distress about attending, and the child usually stays home with the parents' knowledge. Truancy involves absence concealed from parents, little anxiety about school, and often conduct or peer-related problems. The distinction guides intervention: anxiety-focused exposure for refusal, versus behavioral contracts, parental monitoring and school engagement for truancy.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — School counseling: attendance problems, school refusal and truancy
⚑ Check: Distinction follows Berg/Kearney; confirm the Gladding locator or cite a school-attendance source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

418. nce-s-clf-178 · Assessment and Testing · neurocognitive disorders · hard · In review

Over 2 years, a 57-year-old engineer has made crude remarks to strangers, lost interest in his grandchildren, shown little concern when his wife cries, and begun eating sweets compulsively. He still recalls recent events and finds his way around town without trouble. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease
Alzheimer's disease typically begins with prominent decline in learning and memory, which is relatively spared here.
B. Major neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies, early stage
Lewy body NCD features fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism, none of which are described.
C. Frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder, behavioral variant ✔ KEY
Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, and hyperorality with relatively spared memory and spatial skills fit the behavioral variant.
D. Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, late onset
There is no elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, or episodic course; the change is gradual and progressive.
Rationale: The behavioral variant of frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder requires three or more of: behavioral disinhibition; apathy or inertia; loss of sympathy or empathy; perseverative, stereotyped, or compulsive behavior; and hyperorality or dietary change, along with prominent decline in social cognition or executive abilities. Learning, memory, and perceptual-motor function are relatively spared. Onset is often in midlife, so the presentation is easily mistaken for a psychiatric or "midlife" problem.
References: DSM-5-TR — Major or Mild Frontotemporal Neurocognitive Disorder, Criterion C1 (behavioral variant)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

419. nce-s-clf-179 · Assessment and Testing · neurocognitive disorders · easy · In review

A 79-year-old with a known neurocognitive disorder now relies on her son to pay her bills and set out her daily medications because she makes repeated errors on her own. Under DSM-5-TR, what does this change MOST directly indicate?
A. Deficits now interfere with independence, so major NCD fits ✔ KEY
Needing help with complex instrumental activities such as bills and medications marks the functional threshold for major NCD.
B. A delirium is now present on top of her existing disorder
Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and awareness, which is not described.
C. Her cognitive test scores must now fall in the severe range
The mild/major distinction rests mainly on functional independence, not on a single test cutoff.
D. The cause of her disorder must have shifted to vascular
A change in functional level says nothing about a change in etiological subtype.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR separates mild from major neurocognitive disorder chiefly by function. In mild NCD the deficits do not interfere with independence in everyday activities, although greater effort or compensatory strategies may be needed. In major NCD they do, at minimum requiring assistance with complex instrumental activities such as paying bills or managing medications.
References: DSM-5-TR — Major Neurocognitive Disorder, Criterion B; Mild Neurocognitive Disorder, Criterion B
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

420. nce-s-clf-180 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · neurocognitive disorders · medium · In review

A daughter caring for her father with moderate Alzheimer's disease says he asks several times each evening where his late wife is. Each time she reminds him that her mother died, he sobs as if hearing it for the first time. Which guidance should the counselor offer?
A. Keep reminding him of the death so that the fact is gradually relearned
Repeated reorientation to a painful fact he cannot retain causes fresh grief each time without lasting learning.
B. Ask his physician to raise his sedative dose for the evening hours
Medication is not the first response to distress that can be eased by changing how caregivers respond.
C. Avoid the subject entirely and leave the room whenever he raises it
Withdrawing leaves him alone with distress and does not meet the emotional need behind the question.
D. Respond to the feeling behind the question, then gently redirect him ✔ KEY
Acknowledging the emotion (for example, that he misses her) and redirecting reduces distress without repeated re-traumatizing news.
Rationale: In moderate dementia, a person often cannot retain new information, so repeated correction brings repeated fresh grief. Caregivers are usually taught to respond to the emotion behind a question, offer comfort, and redirect to a soothing activity. Counselors also support caregivers with psychoeducation, skills training, and attention to their own strain, as dementia guidelines recommend.
References: NICE guidelines — NG97 Dementia: supporting carers (psychoeducation and skills training) · Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Late adulthood: Alzheimer's disease and caregiving
⚑ Check: Validation-and-redirect is standard caregiver teaching rather than a quoted NICE recommendation; SME to confirm locators.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

421. nce-s-clf-181 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · obsessive-compulsive and related disorders · medium · In review

A 63-year-old with hoarding disorder faces eviction because her apartment is blocked by stacked items. Her landlord has offered to send a crew to clear it out over one weekend. Which approach is MOST consistent with effective treatment of hoarding?
A. Support the weekend cleanout, since clearing the space ends the disorder
Forced cleanouts may solve an immediate crisis but are distressing and often followed by rapid reaccumulation.
B. CBT building sorting and decision skills with practice in discarding ✔ KEY
CBT for hoarding targets motivation, organizing and decision-making skills, graded discarding, and reduced acquiring.
C. Insight-oriented talk about her childhood losses before any sorting
Exploring history alone does not change saving and acquiring behavior and delays needed work.
D. Have the counselor decide which items to discard to speed progress
Decisions made for the client undercut her own decision-making practice, which is central to treatment.
Rationale: Hoarding disorder involves persistent difficulty discarding possessions because of a perceived need to save them and distress at discarding, leading to clutter that compromises living areas. Cognitive-behavioral treatment for hoarding uses motivational work, skills training in organizing and decision-making, graded exposure to sorting and discarding, and practice resisting acquiring. Externally imposed cleanouts tend to be traumatic and rarely produce lasting change.
References: DSM-5-TR — Hoarding Disorder: diagnostic features and functional consequences · Corey (Theory & Practice) — Cognitive behavior therapy: skills training and exposure
⚑ Check: Hoarding-specific CBT (Steketee & Frost) is not in the approved source library; treatment content cited to general sources. SME to confirm.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

422. nce-s-clf-182 · Assessment and Testing · obsessive-compulsive and related disorders · hard · In review
