A 27-year-old is completely certain that her nose is grotesquely misshapen, although others see nothing unusual. She checks mirrors for hours and has had two rhinoplasties, which left her more distressed. She is now seeking a third surgeon. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?
A. BDD with absent insight; more surgery is unlikely to ease her distress ✔ KEY
Total conviction is coded as BDD with absent insight/delusional beliefs, and cosmetic procedures rarely relieve BDD.
B. Delusional disorder, somatic type, as her conviction is fixed and total
DSM-5-TR codes delusional appearance beliefs as BDD with absent insight rather than as delusional disorder.
C. BDD with good insight; a skilled surgeon will likely resolve her concern
Complete conviction is not good insight, and surgery typically fails to resolve or worsens BDD symptoms.
D. No disorder applies, because she has sought medical rather than mental care
Many people with BDD seek cosmetic rather than mental health treatment; the pattern fully meets BDD criteria.
Rationale: Body dysmorphic disorder involves preoccupation with perceived flaws not observable or slight to others, with repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking. Insight is specified as good or fair, poor, or absent insight/delusional beliefs; a person completely convinced of the flaw still receives BDD, not a psychotic diagnosis. Many people with BDD seek cosmetic procedures, which seldom improve and can worsen symptoms, so referral for CBT and medication evaluation is indicated.
References: DSM-5-TR — Body Dysmorphic Disorder: insight specifiers; associated features (cosmetic treatment)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

423. nce-s-clf-183 · Assessment and Testing · obsessive-compulsive and related disorders · medium · In review

A 14-year-old with OCD spends hours arranging objects and touching doorframes until things feel "just right." His parents mention that between ages 7 and 10 he had repeated eye blinking and grunting that have since stopped. Which DSM-5-TR specifier should be added to his OCD diagnosis?
A. With poor insight
Insight specifiers depend on his beliefs about the obsessions, which are not described.
B. With panic attacks
No abrupt surges of intense fear are described.
C. With absent insight
Nothing suggests he is fully convinced his obsessional beliefs are true.
D. Tic-related ✔ KEY
The tic-related specifier applies to a current or past history of a tic disorder.
Rationale: OCD is specified as tic-related when the person has a current or past history of a tic disorder. Tic-related OCD is more common in males with childhood onset and often involves symmetry, ordering, and "just right" concerns rather than harm or contamination themes. Past tics count, so a careful developmental history matters.
References: DSM-5-TR — Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: specify if tic-related
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

424. nce-s-clf-184 · Assessment and Testing · neurodevelopmental disorders · hard · In review

A 9-year-old with average intellectual ability reads slowly and makes many decoding errors. A school team is considering specific learning disorder with impairment in reading. Under DSM-5-TR, which requirement must be met?
A. A large gap between full-scale IQ and reading achievement scores
DSM-5 dropped the IQ-achievement discrepancy requirement; skills must instead be well below age expectations.
B. Difficulty persisting 6 months despite help aimed at that skill ✔ KEY
Criterion A requires difficulties persisting at least 6 months despite interventions that target them.
C. A formal diagnosis made only after the child reaches age 12
Specific learning disorder is typically identified in the early school years; there is no age 12 threshold.
D. Proof that the difficulty also appears in mathematics and writing
Impairment may involve one domain only; reading, written expression, and mathematics are specified separately.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR requires difficulties learning and using academic skills that have persisted for at least 6 months despite targeted intervention, with skills substantially and quantifiably below those expected for age (confirmed by standardized achievement measures and comprehensive clinical assessment). Onset is in the school-age years, and the difficulties are not better explained by intellectual disability, sensory problems, or inadequate instruction. The older IQ-achievement discrepancy model is no longer required.
References: DSM-5-TR — Specific Learning Disorder, Criteria A and B
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

425. nce-s-clf-185 · Human Growth and Development · neurodevelopmental disorders · easy · In review

In DSM-5-TR, deficits in adaptive functioning for intellectual developmental disorder are assessed in which three domains?
A. Verbal, perceptual, and processing speed
These resemble index scores from intelligence tests, not adaptive functioning domains.
B. Sensory, motor, and expressive language
These are developmental skill areas, not the three DSM-5-TR adaptive domains.
C. Conceptual, social, and practical ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR assesses adaptive functioning in the conceptual, social, and practical domains.
D. Cognitive, emotional, and behavioral
This is a general psychological triad, not the DSM-5-TR adaptive framework.
Rationale: Intellectual developmental disorder requires deficits in intellectual functions and in adaptive functioning, with onset during the developmental period. Adaptive functioning covers the conceptual (academic), social, and practical (self-management) domains. Severity is set by adaptive functioning in these domains rather than by IQ alone, because adaptive functioning determines the level of support needed.
References: DSM-5-TR — Intellectual Developmental Disorder, Criterion B and severity table
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

426. nce-s-clf-186 · Assessment and Testing · neurodevelopmental disorders · easy · In review

For the past year, a 10-year-old girl has shown seven inattentive symptoms of ADHD, such as losing materials and drifting off during lessons, but only two hyperactive-impulsive symptoms. Symptoms began before age 12 and appear at home and school. Which presentation should be specified?
A. Predominantly inattentive presentation ✔ KEY
Inattention criteria are met while hyperactivity-impulsivity criteria are not, which defines this presentation.
B. Combined presentation
Combined presentation requires both symptom criteria to be met for the past 6 months.
C. Predominantly hyperactive presentation
She has only two hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, below the threshold.
D. Other specified ADHD
Full criteria are met, so a specified presentation of ADHD applies.
Rationale: ADHD presentations reflect the past 6 months: combined (both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity criteria met), predominantly inattentive (inattention met, hyperactivity-impulsivity not), or predominantly hyperactive/impulsive (the reverse). Children need six or more symptoms in a domain; those 17 and older need five. Girls are more often seen with the inattentive presentation, which can delay recognition.
References: DSM-5-TR — Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: specify current presentation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

427. nce-s-clf-187 · Assessment and Testing · schizophrenia spectrum disorders · easy · In review

Which of the following is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
A. Persecutory delusions
Delusions are positive symptoms, an addition to normal experience.
B. Disorganized speech
Disorganized speech is a separate symptom domain, not a negative symptom.
C. Auditory hallucinations
Hallucinations are positive symptoms.
D. Avolition ✔ KEY
Avolition, a decrease in self-initiated purposeful activity, is a core negative symptom.
Rationale: Negative symptoms reflect a loss or reduction of normal functions. DSM-5-TR highlights diminished emotional expression and avolition as especially prominent in schizophrenia; others include alogia, anhedonia, and asociality. Negative symptoms account for much of the long-term disability in schizophrenia and respond less well to antipsychotic medication than positive symptoms.
References: DSM-5-TR — Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders: key features (negative symptoms)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

428. nce-s-clf-188 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · schizophrenia spectrum disorders · hard · In review

A 45-year-old in treatment for severe depression arrives with his wife, who says he has barely spoken or eaten for 3 days. In session he stays mute, holds a stiff, odd posture for long periods, and resists when the counselor gently offers him a cup of water. What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Begin behavioral activation to restart his routine and appetite
Behavioral activation cannot address a possible medical emergency that needs urgent evaluation first.
B. Use silence and patience until he is ready to talk in session
Waiting delays care for catatonia, which can lead to dehydration and other serious complications.
C. Arrange urgent medical evaluation for possible catatonia today ✔ KEY
Mutism, posturing, and negativism suggest catatonia, which needs urgent medical care and is often highly treatable.
D. Ask his wife to keep a food log and report back next week
A week of monitoring is far too slow when he is not eating or drinking and may be catatonic.
Rationale: Catatonia is diagnosed when three or more of twelve psychomotor features are present, such as stupor, mutism, posturing, catalepsy, and negativism. It can occur with depressive, bipolar, psychotic, or medical conditions and may become life-threatening through dehydration, malnutrition, or autonomic instability. It typically responds to medical treatment, so the counselor's first job is to get the client to urgent medical and psychiatric evaluation.
References: DSM-5-TR — Catatonia Associated With Another Mental Disorder (Catatonia Specifier)
⚑ Check: Placed under schizophrenia spectrum because catatonia sits in that DSM-5-TR chapter; the client here has depression.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

429. nce-s-clf-189 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · schizophrenia spectrum disorders · medium · In review

A 24-year-old has just been discharged after a first episode of schizophrenia and is moving back home. His parents are frightened and often criticize him for "lying around," and his mother has given up her job to watch him constantly. Which intervention is MOST likely to reduce his risk of relapse?
A. Family psychoeducation that lowers criticism and overinvolvement ✔ KEY
High expressed emotion predicts relapse, and family interventions that reduce it lower relapse rates.
B. Advising the family to limit contact with him until he stabilizes
Reducing contact removes support and does not teach the family more helpful ways to respond.
C. Individual insight therapy exploring his early family relationships
Insight-oriented therapy is not an evidence-based relapse-prevention approach for schizophrenia.
D. Encouraging his parents to confront his low motivation more firmly
Firmer confrontation increases criticism, a component of high expressed emotion linked to relapse.
Rationale: Expressed emotion describes family attitudes of criticism, hostility, and emotional overinvolvement toward a member with a mental illness. High expressed emotion reliably predicts relapse in schizophrenia. Family psychoeducation and family intervention teach relatives about the illness, problem-solving, and calmer communication, and they reduce relapse and rehospitalization.
References: NICE guidelines — CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: family intervention · Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Psychoeducational family therapy and expressed emotion
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

430. nce-s-clf-190 · Assessment and Testing · personality disorders · easy · In review

A 34-year-old arrives in a flamboyant outfit and calls the counselor "my new best friend" at their first meeting. She is upset when attention shifts away from her, speaks dramatically but vaguely, and her emotions change quickly. This pattern has lasted since her late teens. Which personality disorder BEST fits?
A. Narcissistic personality disorder
Narcissistic personality centers on grandiosity, entitlement, and need for admiration rather than shallow, shifting emotion.
B. Histrionic personality disorder ✔ KEY
Attention-seeking, rapidly shifting shallow emotion, impressionistic speech, and overestimating intimacy fit histrionic personality.
C. Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality centers on abandonment fears, unstable identity, and self-harm, which are not described.
D. Dependent personality disorder
Dependent personality centers on needing others to make decisions and fear of being alone.
Rationale: Histrionic personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of excessive emotionality and attention-seeking beginning by early adulthood. Features include discomfort when not the center of attention, rapidly shifting and shallow emotions, use of appearance to draw attention, impressionistic speech lacking detail, theatrical expression, suggestibility, and viewing relationships as more intimate than they are. At least five of eight criteria are required.
References: DSM-5-TR — Histrionic Personality Disorder, diagnostic criteria
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

431. nce-s-clf-191 · Assessment and Testing · personality disorders · hard · In review

Since adolescence, a 29-year-old has avoided almost all new relationships and job promotions, believing she is inferior and certain to be rejected. She also has marked fear of being judged when eating or speaking in front of others. How does DSM-5-TR describe avoidant personality disorder in relation to social anxiety disorder?
A. Social anxiety disorder must be ruled out before avoidant PD is given
DSM-5-TR does not make social anxiety disorder an exclusion for avoidant personality disorder.
B. Avoidant PD is diagnosed only when fear is limited to one situation
Avoidant personality disorder is pervasive across contexts, not limited to a single situation.
C. The two are unrelated, as one is a mood state and the other a trait
DSM-5-TR describes heavy overlap between them; neither is a mood disorder.
D. They overlap heavily and both may be diagnosed if each is fully met ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR notes great overlap, possibly alternative conceptualizations, and both can be diagnosed when criteria are met.
Rationale: Avoidant personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation beginning by early adulthood. DSM-5-TR notes so much overlap with social anxiety disorder that they may be alternative conceptualizations of the same or similar conditions. When criteria for both are met, both may be diagnosed; avoidant PD tends to reflect a broader, identity-level sense of inadequacy across most interpersonal settings.
References: DSM-5-TR — Avoidant Personality Disorder: differential diagnosis (social anxiety disorder)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

432. nce-s-clf-192 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · personality disorders · medium · In review

Early in counseling, a client with borderline personality disorder calls the counselor several times a week between sessions, often late at night, and feels rejected when calls are not returned at once. The counselor is growing frustrated. Which response BEST reflects an effective treatment frame?
A. Return every call at once so she does not feel abandoned in a crisis
Unlimited availability is unsustainable, can reinforce crisis behavior, and risks counselor burnout.
B. Tell her calls between sessions are not allowed under any condition
A blanket ban leaves her without coaching support and may feel like the rejection she fears.
C. Set clear, agreed limits on contact, with brief skills-coaching calls ✔ KEY
A collaborative, consistent frame with planned coaching contact supports skill use while protecting the work.
D. Refer her elsewhere, since frequent calls show she is not yet ready
Frequent contact is a treatment target, not a reason to abandon the client.
Rationale: Evidence-based treatments for borderline personality disorder share a clear, consistent treatment frame agreed with the client. In dialectical behavior therapy, between-session phone coaching is brief and focused on applying skills, with limits the therapist observes and explains openly. A predictable frame reduces fears of abandonment, discourages reinforcement of crisis behavior, and is supported by consultation for the counselor.
References: Linehan (DBT Skills Training Manual) — DBT treatment modes: between-session phone coaching and observing limits
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

433. nce-s-clf-193 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · eating disorders · easy · In review

An adult client meets criteria for binge-eating disorder and asks which psychological treatment has the strongest evidence. Which approach should the counselor describe as first-line?
A. Eating-disorder-focused cognitive behavioral therapy ✔ KEY
CBT focused on eating, including guided self-help, is the first-line psychological treatment for binge-eating disorder.
B. A strict diet plan aimed mainly at quick weight loss
Dieting is not a treatment for binge eating and rigid restriction can intensify the binge cycle.
C. Long-term psychodynamic therapy as the sole treatment
Psychodynamic therapy lacks the evidence base that CBT has for binge-eating disorder.
D. Hypnosis to suppress cravings for specific trigger foods
Hypnosis is not an evidence-based first-line treatment for binge-eating disorder.
Rationale: Clinical guidelines recommend eating-disorder-focused CBT for binge-eating disorder, often beginning with a guided self-help program and moving to group or individual CBT if needed. Treatment targets regular eating, the binge cycle, triggers, and the over-evaluation of shape and weight. Weight loss is not the primary aim, and restrictive dieting can maintain binge eating.
References: NICE guidelines — NG69 Eating disorders: treating binge eating disorder (guided self-help; group CBT-ED)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

434. nce-s-clf-194 · Assessment and Testing · eating disorders · medium · In review

A 17-year-old has lost a significant amount of weight over a year through restrictive eating. She intensely fears weight gain and judges herself almost entirely by her shape. Her physician notes that, despite the loss, her weight remains within the normal range for her age and height. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Anorexia nervosa, restricting type, with mild severity
Anorexia nervosa requires significantly low body weight, which is not present here.
B. Other specified feeding or eating disorder (atypical AN) ✔ KEY
Atypical anorexia nervosa is listed under OSFED when all AN criteria are met except low weight.
C. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, adolescent onset
ARFID excludes restriction driven by concerns about body shape or weight.
D. Bulimia nervosa, low frequency and limited duration
No binge eating or compensatory behaviors are described.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR lists atypical anorexia nervosa as an example of other specified feeding or eating disorder: all criteria for anorexia nervosa are met except that, despite significant weight loss, weight is within or above the normal range. Medical risks can be serious despite a normal-appearing weight, so these clients need the same medical monitoring and specialized care as those with anorexia nervosa.
References: DSM-5-TR — Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder: atypical anorexia nervosa
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

435. nce-s-clf-195 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · eating disorders · medium · In review

Parents of a 14-year-old recently diagnosed with anorexia nervosa ask what treatment the eating disorder team will recommend. She is medically stable for outpatient care. Which description BEST fits family-based treatment (FBT) for adolescent anorexia?
A. The teen meets alone with a therapist to explore the roots of her illness
FBT is family based and does not focus on uncovering causes; individual insight work is a different model.
B. Parents step back from meals so that the teen regains a sense of control
FBT does the opposite in its first phase, placing parents in charge of restoring healthy eating.
C. The family first explores how parenting errors caused the eating disorder
FBT takes an agnostic stance on cause and explicitly avoids blaming parents.
D. Parents take charge of renourishment at first, then gradually hand it back ✔ KEY
FBT empowers parents to lead renourishment first, then returns control to the teen as she recovers.
Rationale: Family-based treatment (the Maudsley approach) is a leading evidence-based treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa and is reflected in guideline recommendations for eating-disorder-focused family therapy. It proceeds in phases: parents take charge of restoring healthy eating, control over eating is gradually returned to the adolescent, and then broader adolescent development is addressed. The model does not blame parents and separates the illness from the young person.
References: NICE guidelines — NG69 Eating disorders: anorexia nervosa in children and young people (eating-disorder-focused family therapy)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

436. nce-s-clf-196 · Assessment and Testing · depressive disorders · hard · In review

A 26-year-old in a major depressive episode brightens noticeably when friends invite her out, then sinks again. She sleeps far more than usual, eats much more, describes her arms and legs as feeling "like lead," and has long been crushed by small hints of criticism. Which specifier BEST fits?
A. With melancholic features
Melancholic features involve loss of reactivity to pleasant events, early waking, and decreased appetite, the reverse of this picture.
B. With anxious distress
Anxious distress involves tension, restlessness, worry, and fear, which are not described.
C. With atypical features ✔ KEY
Mood reactivity plus hypersomnia, increased appetite, leaden paralysis, and rejection sensitivity define atypical features.
D. With mixed features
Mixed features require manic or hypomanic symptoms during the episode, which are absent.
Rationale: The "with atypical features" specifier requires mood reactivity (mood brightens in response to positive events) plus at least two of: significant weight gain or increased appetite, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, and a long-standing pattern of sensitivity to interpersonal rejection. Criteria for melancholic features or catatonia must not be met in the same episode. Despite its name, this pattern is common.
References: DSM-5-TR — Specifiers for Depressive Disorders: with atypical features
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

437. nce-s-clf-197 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · bipolar disorders · medium · In review

A 32-year-old nurse with bipolar I disorder, stable on medication, is about to switch to rotating night shifts. Her past manic episodes followed weeks of disrupted sleep. Which counseling focus is MOST consistent with interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (IPSRT)?
A. Keep daily routines and sleep-wake times as steady as she can ✔ KEY
IPSRT stabilizes daily rhythms, especially sleep, because disruptions can trigger mood episodes.
B. Explore early memories to find the roots of her mood swings
Uncovering childhood roots is not the IPSRT focus on present rhythms and relationships.
C. Dispute the irrational beliefs that drive her elevated moods
Disputing irrational beliefs comes from REBT, not IPSRT.
D. Build a fear hierarchy for in-vivo exposure to her workplace
Exposure hierarchies treat anxiety disorders; they do not address rhythm disruption.
Rationale: Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy, developed by Ellen Frank, holds that disruptions to daily routines and sleep-wake cycles can trigger mood episodes in people with bipolar disorder. Clients track daily rhythms (for example, with a social rhythm metric), work to keep them regular, and address interpersonal problems and role transitions. A shift to night work is a classic rhythm disruption to plan for.
References: IPSRT — Social rhythm stabilization and the social rhythm metric
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

438. nce-s-clf-198 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · anxiety disorders · hard · In review

A 22-year-old nursing student has fainted twice while watching blood draws and now avoids clinical rotations. She has specific phobia, blood-injection-injury type. When planning exposure, which added technique is MOST suited to this phobia type?
A. Progressive muscle relaxation before and during each exposure
Relaxation can deepen the drop in blood pressure behind fainting, so it is generally avoided for this type.
B. Applied tension, tensing large muscles to keep blood pressure up ✔ KEY
Applied tension counters the vasovagal blood pressure drop that causes fainting in this phobia type.
C. Interoceptive exposure to dizziness by spinning in a chair first
Interoceptive exposure targets fear of bodily sensations in panic disorder, not vasovagal fainting.
D. Slow diaphragmatic breathing to lower her heart rate and arousal
Lowering arousal does not address, and may worsen, the vasovagal response.
Rationale: Unlike other specific phobias, the blood-injection-injury type often involves a vasovagal response: a brief rise in heart rate and blood pressure followed by a sharp drop that can cause fainting. Applied tension teaches the client to tense large muscle groups to raise blood pressure while being exposed to feared stimuli. Relaxation-based methods are generally avoided because they can make fainting more likely.
References: DSM-5-TR — Specific Phobia: blood-injection-injury type (vasovagal fainting response)
⚑ Check: Applied tension (Öst) is not described in DSM-5-TR; no approved source names it directly. SME to confirm or add a citation.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

439. nce-s-clf-199 · Assessment and Testing · trauma- and stressor-related disorders · hard · In review

A 38-year-old meets full criteria for PTSD after a violent home invasion. She also reports that she often feels as though she is watching herself from outside her body and that the world seems dreamlike and unreal. These experiences are not caused by substances or a medical condition. How should this be diagnosed?
A. PTSD plus a separate diagnosis of depersonalization/derealization disorder
When these symptoms occur as part of PTSD, they are captured with the specifier, not a separate disorder.
B. Acute stress disorder, as dissociative symptoms are central to that diagnosis
Full PTSD criteria are already met, and acute stress disorder is limited to the first month after trauma.
C. PTSD with delayed expression, given the presence of dissociative symptoms
Delayed expression refers to full criteria not being met until at least 6 months after the event.
D. PTSD with dissociative symptoms, noting depersonalization and derealization ✔ KEY
The dissociative specifier applies to persistent or recurrent depersonalization or derealization in PTSD.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR allows PTSD to be specified "with dissociative symptoms" when the person also has persistent or recurrent depersonalization (feeling detached from oneself, as an outside observer) or derealization (the world feels unreal, dreamlike, or distant), not attributable to substances or a medical condition. Recognizing this subtype matters because dissociation can affect pacing and stabilization in trauma-focused treatment.
References: DSM-5-TR — Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: specify with dissociative symptoms
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

440. nce-s-clf-200 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · substance use and addictive disorders · medium · In review

A 36-year-old with opioid use disorder has taken prescribed buprenorphine for 8 months and has not used illicit opioids. In a recovery group, peers tell him he is "not really clean" and urge him to stop the medication. He asks the counselor what to think. Which response is MOST consistent with best practice?
A. Agree that full recovery requires tapering off all opioid medicines soon
No fixed endpoint is required; stopping medication early raises the risk of relapse and overdose.
B. Suggest he follow the group's view, since peer support predicts recovery
Peer support is valuable, but the group's advice here conflicts with the evidence on medication for OUD.
C. Affirm that MOUD is effective treatment, and support talking to his prescriber ✔ KEY
Medication for OUD is evidence-based treatment, and medication decisions belong with the client and prescriber.
D. Advise him to keep his medication secret from others in the recovery group
Encouraging secrecy does not address stigma or help him find supportive recovery settings.
Rationale: Medications for opioid use disorder, such as buprenorphine, methadone, and extended-release naltrexone, reduce illicit use, overdose deaths, and other harms. Taking prescribed medication as directed is treatment, not "substituting one addiction for another." Counselors should challenge stigma, support informed choices, coordinate with prescribers, and help clients find MOUD-friendly recovery supports; duration of medication is individualized, and discontinuing it raises relapse and overdose risk.
References: SAMHSA TIP 63 — Part 1: MOUD effectiveness; Part 4: counseling and peer support for clients on MOUD
⚑ Check: SME to confirm the TIP 63 part numbers in the locator.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

441. nce-s-clf-201 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · grief and loss · easy · In review

Two years after her husband died, a 70-year-old has returned to her volunteer work and made new friends. She still talks to him at his grave on their anniversary and keeps his watch on her nightstand. Her adult children ask the counselor to help her "finally let go." Which response BEST reflects current grief theory?
A. Agree that she must give up the attachment before she can heal
Older "letting go" models have given way to the view that healthy bonds with the deceased can continue.
B. Explain that a lasting bond with him can coexist with a full life ✔ KEY
Continuing bonds, and Worden's fourth task of finding an enduring connection, describe adaptive grief.
C. Assess her for prolonged grief disorder due to the grave visits
She is functioning well; occasional rituals of connection are not signs of prolonged grief disorder.
D. Suggest she put his watch away to signal the grief has ended
Keeping meaningful objects can be part of a healthy continuing bond; removing them is not required.
Rationale: Contemporary grief theory views ongoing connection with the deceased as compatible with healthy adaptation. Worden's fourth task of mourning is to find an enduring connection with the deceased while embarking on a new life, and the continuing bonds perspective holds that memories, rituals, and inner conversations can support coping. Concern arises when connection prevents re-engagement in life, which is not the case here.
References: Worden (Grief Counseling) — Task IV: find an enduring connection with the deceased while embarking on a new life
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

442. nce-s-clf-202 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · crisis and disaster response · easy · In review

Using James and Gilliland's six-step crisis model, a counselor has defined the problem with a client whose house burned down, ensured his safety, and offered support. The client is now calmer. Which step comes NEXT?
A. Obtaining his commitment to a plan
Commitment is the sixth and final step, after alternatives are explored and a plan is made.
B. Making a concrete plan with him
Planning is the fifth step and follows examining alternatives.
C. Redefining the core problem again
Defining the problem is the first step, which has already been completed.
D. Examining alternatives with him ✔ KEY
After the three listening steps, the fourth step is examining alternatives.
Rationale: James and Gilliland's six-step model has three listening steps (defining the problem, ensuring client safety, providing support) followed by three acting steps (examining alternatives, making plans, obtaining commitment). Assessment runs throughout all six steps, and safety is monitored continuously, but the sequence guides the counselor from understanding to action.
References: James & Gilliland (Crisis Intervention Strategies) — Six-step model of crisis intervention
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

443. nce-s-clf-203 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · intimate partner violence · medium · In review

During a risk assessment, a client experiencing partner abuse discloses several things about her partner. Which disclosure MOST strongly signals elevated risk of lethal violence and calls for urgent safety planning?
A. He has choked her until she could barely breathe in the past ✔ KEY
Prior non-fatal strangulation is one of the strongest known predictors of later intimate partner homicide.
B. He often yells and calls her names when he gets home late
Verbal abuse is harmful but is a weaker predictor of lethality than strangulation.
C. He grew up in a home where his father hit his mother often
Childhood exposure to violence is a risk factor for perpetration but a weaker lethality marker.
D. He sulks and won't speak to her for days after arguments
Withdrawal after conflict does not signal elevated lethality.
Rationale: Lethality assessment in intimate partner violence focuses on factors linked to homicide, such as prior strangulation, access to firearms, threats to kill, escalating frequency or severity, extreme jealousy, and a recent or planned separation. Non-fatal strangulation markedly raises the risk of later homicide and may leave few visible injuries, so counselors should ask about it directly and respond with urgent safety planning and advocacy referrals.
References: James & Gilliland (Crisis Intervention Strategies) — Intimate partner violence: assessing lethality
⚑ Check: The strangulation-lethality link comes from Campbell's Danger Assessment research, which is not in the approved library; SME to confirm the James & Gilliland locator.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

444. nce-s-clf-204 · Human Growth and Development · neurodevelopmental disorders · medium · In review

A 3-year-old has delays in speech, motor skills, and self-care, but cannot yet complete standardized intellectual testing in a valid way. The evaluating team plans to reassess in a year. Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis BEST fits for now?
A. Intellectual disability, mild
Severity cannot yet be reliably assessed, so a specified level of intellectual disability is premature.
B. Global developmental delay ✔ KEY
This diagnosis is reserved for children under 5 who miss milestones in several areas and cannot yet be reliably assessed.
C. Autism spectrum disorder, level 1
No social communication deficits or restricted, repetitive behaviors are described.
D. Language disorder, expressive type
Delays extend well beyond language to motor and self-care areas.
Rationale: Global developmental delay is diagnosed in children under age 5 when they fail to meet expected milestones in several areas of intellectual functioning and the clinical severity cannot be reliably assessed, often because the child is too young for standardized testing. It requires reassessment after a period of time.
References: DSM-5-TR — Global Developmental Delay
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

445. nce-s-clf-205 · Assessment and Testing · substance use and addictive disorders · hard · In review

A 44-year-old previously met full criteria for alcohol use disorder. For the past 5 months he has met no criteria except strong cravings, which come mainly when he passes his old bar. He lives at home, not in a controlled setting. Which specifier applies?
A. In sustained remission, since he has gone months without drinking
Sustained remission requires 12 months or longer without meeting criteria other than craving.
B. No remission specifier, because his ongoing craving is a criterion
Craving is the one criterion explicitly allowed during remission, so it does not block the specifier.
C. In early remission, as only craving has been present for 5 months ✔ KEY
Early remission applies after 3 months but less than 12 months with no criteria met except craving.
D. In early remission, in a controlled environment, given the time
He lives at home; the controlled-environment specifier is for settings where access is restricted.
Rationale: For substance use disorders, "in early remission" applies when, after full criteria were met, none have been met for at least 3 months but less than 12 months, with the exception of craving. "In sustained remission" requires 12 months or longer. "In a controlled environment" is added only when the person is in a setting where access to substances is restricted.
References: DSM-5-TR — Alcohol Use Disorder: remission specifiers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

446. nce-s-clf-206 · Assessment and Testing · anxiety disorders · medium · In review

A 30-year-old violinist is comfortable at parties, in meetings, and on dates, but for a year has felt intense dread before solo recitals, fearing the audience will judge her shaking hands. She has started declining solo work. If criteria for social anxiety disorder are met, which specifier applies?
A. With panic attacks
No abrupt surges of intense fear are described, and this specifier does not capture the restricted context.
B. Generalized type
DSM-5 removed the generalized specifier for social anxiety disorder.
C. With poor insight
Social anxiety disorder has no insight specifier in DSM-5-TR.
D. Performance only ✔ KEY
This specifier applies when the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public.
Rationale: Social anxiety disorder may be specified "performance only" when the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public. People with this pattern are often impaired mainly in professional or academic roles that require performing, while ordinary social interactions are comfortable. DSM-5 replaced the older "generalized" specifier with this narrower one.
References: DSM-5-TR — Social Anxiety Disorder: specify if performance only
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

447. nce-s-clf-207 · Human Growth and Development · trauma- and stressor-related disorders · medium · In review

A 4-year-old was in a serious car crash 3 months ago. Since then she repeatedly crashes toy cars together while making siren noises, cries when buckled into her car seat, and clings to her parents at bedtime. She shows no visible distress during the crash play. How should the counselor understand the repetitive play?
A. Play reenactment can express intrusion symptoms in young children ✔ KEY
For children 6 and younger, intrusive memories may appear as play reenactment and need not look distressing.
B. The play is ordinary for her age and unrelated to the crash itself
Repetitive play that mirrors the trauma, alongside avoidance and clinging, points to a trauma response.
C. Because she seems calm during the play, PTSD can be ruled out here
DSM-5-TR notes that intrusive memories in young children may not appear distressing.
D. The play shows the trauma is resolved and needs no further attention
Ongoing reenactment with avoidance and distress at reminders suggests the trauma is not resolved.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR includes separate PTSD criteria for children 6 years and younger. Intrusion symptoms may take the form of play reenactment, and spontaneous intrusive memories may not appear distressing. The avoidance and negative-cognition clusters are combined, so only one symptom from that combined group is needed. Counselors should assess such play in context and involve caregivers in trauma-focused treatment.
References: DSM-5-TR — Posttraumatic Stress Disorder for Children 6 Years and Younger, Criterion B
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

448. nce-s-clf-208 · Human Growth and Development · aging and older adults · medium · In review

A 73-year-old retired teacher with no history of anxiety reports four months of constant worry, a racing heart, restlessness and poor sleep. She recently began two new medications and says, "I just feel keyed up all the time." What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Begin weekly CBT for generalized anxiety and give a worry log
CBT may help later, but new-onset anxiety in late life needs a medical cause ruled out before a psychological plan is set.
B. Teach slow breathing and suggest she cut back on her caffeine
Coping tips are reasonable but skip the key step of checking for medical and medication causes of her symptoms.
C. Encourage a medical review of her health and new medications ✔ KEY
Late-onset anxiety often has medical or medication contributors (e.g., thyroid, cardiac, drug effects), so medical review comes first.
D. Reassure her that worry is a normal response to growing older
Persistent anxiety is not a normal part of aging; dismissing it reflects ageist assumptions and delays care.
Rationale: Anxiety that first appears in later life is more often linked to medical illness, medication side effects or interactions, or early cognitive change than anxiety that began earlier. Older adults also tend to describe anxiety in somatic terms. Counselors coordinate a medical evaluation first, then provide evidence-based psychological treatment such as CBT, which is effective for older adults.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Late adulthood: physical health, medication use and mental health
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

449. nce-s-clf-209 · Human Growth and Development · aging and older adults · hard · In review

A home-health aide refers an 83-year-old man who lives alone. His home has spoiled food, piled-up mail and no working heat, and he has missed his heart medication for weeks. No one else is involved in his care. He tells the counselor, "I'm fine. Leave me be." Which response BEST fits the counselor's obligations?
A. Assess his safety and capacity and follow state rules on reporting to APS ✔ KEY
Self-neglect that threatens health is reportable to Adult Protective Services in most states, and capacity shapes the response; both must be assessed.
B. Honor his stated wishes and close the case, since he is a competent adult
His capacity has not been assessed, and serious self-neglect may trigger reporting duties regardless of his preference.
C. Arrange for him to move to a nursing home before the cold weather comes
Counselors do not unilaterally relocate adults; least-restrictive options and his rights must be weighed through proper channels.
D. Ask the aide to keep watching and decide again at the next monthly visit
No heat and missed cardiac medication are current dangers; waiting a month risks serious harm.
Rationale: Elder self-neglect, an older adult's failure to meet his own basic needs in ways that threaten health or safety, is the most common type of case reported to Adult Protective Services, and most states treat it as reportable. Counselors balance respect for autonomy against safety by assessing decision-making capacity and immediate risk, following state reporting law, and favoring the least-restrictive supports.
References: State law — Adult protective services statutes: self-neglect and vulnerable-adult reporting · ACA Code of Ethics — B.2.a Serious and Foreseeable Harm and Legal Requirements
⚑ Check: Whether self-neglect is reportable, and who is a mandated reporter of vulnerable-adult maltreatment, varies by state; SME to confirm the "most states" framing.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

450. nce-s-clf-210 · Human Growth and Development · aging and older adults · easy · In review

During a community talk on aging, an attendee says, "Getting old means your mind goes and you end up lonely and miserable." Which statement BEST reflects life-span research on typical aging?
A. Memory and reasoning decline steeply for most people after age sixty
Some abilities slow, but steep, global decline is not typical of normal aging; it suggests a neurocognitive disorder.
B. Most older adults become more depressed as their social circles shrink
Smaller networks reflect chosen focus on close ties; depression is not a normal outcome of aging.
C. Crystallized knowledge and processing speed both fall sharply with age
Processing speed slows, but crystallized knowledge such as vocabulary is stable or grows into late life.
D. Emotional well-being is often stable or better, though processing slows ✔ KEY
Older adults often report steady or improved emotional well-being, while fluid abilities like speed show gradual slowing.
Rationale: Research finds that emotional well-being tends to hold steady or improve in late adulthood. Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory explains that older adults focus on fewer, more meaningful relationships and positive emotional experience. Cognitively, processing speed and some fluid abilities slow, but crystallized knowledge stays stable, and severe decline is not a normal part of aging.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Late adulthood: socioemotional selectivity theory; fluid vs crystallized intelligence
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

451. nce-s-clf-211 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · self-injury · medium · In review

A high school teacher tells the school counselor that a 15-year-old in her class has cuts on her arm. The teacher says, "She is just doing it for attention, so I plan to ignore it so I don't reward it." How should the counselor BEST respond to the teacher?
A. Agree that ignoring it is wise, since attention can reinforce cutting
Ignoring self-injury leaves the student without assessment or help and rests on a common myth about its purpose.
B. Explain cutting usually eases distress, and arrange to see the student ✔ KEY
Self-injury most often regulates painful emotion, and the student needs a prompt, calm assessment that includes suicide risk.
C. Ask the teacher to tell the student to stop and to check her arms daily
Demands and body checks by staff tend to increase shame and secrecy and are not a substitute for assessment.
D. Suggest the teacher discuss self-injury with the whole class that day
Class discussion of self-injury can spread it through social contagion and exposes the student.
Rationale: Nonsuicidal self-injury is most often used privately to relieve intense negative emotion, not to gain attention. Even when it is not suicidal, it is a risk factor for later suicide attempts, so any student who self-injures needs an assessment that includes suicide risk. Counselors consult with staff to replace the "attention" myth with a calm, supportive referral pathway.
References: DSM-5-TR — Conditions for Further Study: Nonsuicidal self-injury disorder (functions and course) · Linehan (DBT Skills Training Manual) — Self-harm as an emotion-regulation behavior
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

452. nce-s-clf-212 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · self-injury · medium · In review

A 16-year-old has cut herself repeatedly for a year and has made one suicide attempt. She has intense mood swings and frequent conflict with her parents. Which treatment approach has the STRONGEST research support for reducing self-harm in adolescents like her?
A. Dialectical behavior therapy adapted for teens, with family skills work ✔ KEY
DBT for adolescents, which includes caregivers in skills training, has randomized trial support for reducing self-harm.
B. Client-centered therapy offered weekly in a supportive, open format
Supportive therapy builds rapport but has weaker evidence than DBT-A for reducing repeated self-harm.
C. Psychoeducation for her parents alone, with no individual sessions
Parent education helps but cannot replace skills training and individual treatment for a high-risk teen.
D. A peer support group where members discuss their self-harm stories
Groups that focus on sharing self-harm can increase contagion and are not an evidence-based first choice.
Rationale: Dialectical behavior therapy for adolescents (DBT-A) combines individual therapy, multifamily skills groups (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness, and walking the middle path), phone coaching and team consultation. Randomized trials show it reduces self-harm and suicide attempts in adolescents with repeated self-harm.
References: Linehan (DBT Skills Training Manual) — DBT skills modules; adaptation for adolescents and families
⚑ Check: DBT-A trial evidence (Mehlum et al., 2014; McCauley et al., 2018) is not in the approved source list; SME to confirm the Linehan locator covers the adolescent adaptation.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

453. nce-s-clf-213 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · sleep-wake concerns · medium · In review

A 76-year-old widow goes to bed at 8 p.m., lies awake for hours, naps twice a day, and gets up at 7 a.m. feeling unrested. She asks the counselor whether she should ask her doctor for a sleeping pill. Which recommendation is MOST appropriate?
A. A sleeping pill, since medication works best for insomnia in later life
Sedative-hypnotics raise the risk of falls, confusion and dependence in older adults and are not first-line.
B. More time in bed and longer naps so that she can catch up on lost sleep
Extra time in bed and naps weaken sleep drive and fragment night sleep further.
C. CBT for insomnia, including less time in bed and fewer daytime naps ✔ KEY
CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia at any age; limiting time in bed and naps builds sleep drive and consolidates sleep.
D. Acceptance that broken sleep is normal aging and needs no treatment
Sleep becomes lighter with age, but distressing insomnia with daytime effects is treatable and should not be dismissed.
Rationale: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is the recommended first-line treatment for chronic insomnia, including in older adults. Sleep restriction (or the gentler sleep compression) matches time in bed to actual sleep, and limiting naps strengthens sleep drive. Hypnotic medications carry added risks of falls and cognitive effects in later life.
References: AASM Clinical Practice Guideline (Insomnia) — CBT-I and sleep restriction therapy for chronic insomnia (strong recommendation)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

454. nce-s-clf-214 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · sleep-wake concerns · easy · In review

A factory worker was moved to a permanent overnight shift six months ago. He cannot stay asleep when he goes to bed at 9 a.m. and fights to stay awake at work around 4 a.m. His sleep was normal on his old day schedule. Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Hypersomnolence disorder
Hypersomnolence involves excess sleepiness despite adequate main sleep, not a mismatch with a work schedule.
B. Insomnia disorder
His sleep loss is explained by a circadian mismatch with his shift, which a circadian diagnosis better captures.
C. Delayed sleep phase type
Delayed sleep phase is a late internal clock, not a problem caused by night-shift work.
D. Circadian disorder, shift work type ✔ KEY
Insomnia during the sleep period and sleepiness during work, tied to a night-shift schedule, defines shift work type.
Rationale: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder, shift work type, involves insomnia during the major sleep period and/or excessive sleepiness during the major awake period, associated with a shift work schedule such as night work. Counseling supports sleep scheduling, light management and protecting daytime sleep.
References: DSM-5-TR — Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: shift work type
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

455. nce-s-clf-215 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · school and academic concerns · medium · In review

A new principal asks the high school counselor to serve as the full-time state testing coordinator and to handle discipline for tardy students. The counselor is concerned that these duties will leave little time for students. Which response BEST reflects the ASCA National Model?
A. Accept both duties, since the principal sets the counselor's role
The ASCA model expects counselors to advocate for an appropriate role rather than simply absorb noncounseling duties.
B. Use data on student needs to propose shifting noncounseling duties ✔ KEY
The model calls for using data and an annual agreement with the principal to keep most time on direct and indirect student services.
C. Refuse both duties and file a complaint with the district office
Refusal and escalation damage collaboration; the model favors data-based advocacy with the principal first.
D. Take on discipline only, since it gives contact with at-risk students
ASCA lists handling discipline as inappropriate for counselors because it conflicts with the helping role.
Rationale: The ASCA National Model recommends that school counselors spend about 80% of their time in direct and indirect services to students. Coordinating schoolwide testing and administering discipline are listed as inappropriate duties. Counselors use data and an annual administrative conference to advocate for a role focused on academic, career and social/emotional development.
References: ASCA National Model — Appropriate vs inappropriate activities for school counselors · Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — School counseling: the ASCA National Model
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

456. nce-s-clf-216 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · school and academic concerns · easy · In review

An 11th grader studies hard and knows the material, but during exams her heart pounds, her mind goes blank, and she thinks, "If I fail this, my future is over." Her grades are dropping. Which intervention should the school counselor offer FIRST?
A. Relaxation training plus work on her catastrophic test thoughts ✔ KEY
Test anxiety responds well to combined arousal-reduction and cognitive restructuring, which target both parts of her reaction.
B. A referral for psychoeducational testing for a learning disability
She knows the material; the pattern points to anxiety during tests, not a learning disability.
C. More hours of studying each night so she feels better prepared
She is already prepared; more study does not address the anxiety that blocks retrieval.
D. A request to excuse her from exams for the rest of the semester
Avoidance maintains anxiety and does not build the skills she needs.
Rationale: Test anxiety has physiological (arousal), cognitive (worry and catastrophic thinking) and behavioral parts. Cognitive behavioral approaches that combine relaxation or systematic desensitization with cognitive restructuring, plus test-taking skills when needed, are well supported. Avoidance tends to strengthen the anxiety.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — School counseling: test anxiety interventions · Corey (Theory & Practice) — Cognitive behavior therapy: relaxation training and cognitive restructuring
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

457. nce-s-clf-217 · Human Growth and Development · school and academic concerns · medium · In review

A 9-year-old in a gifted program reads at a high school level and debates ethics with adults, yet melts down when he loses a board game and struggles to make friends his age. His parents ask how he can be "so mature and so immature." Which concept BEST explains this?
A. A twice-exceptional profile that signals a hidden learning disability
Twice-exceptional means giftedness with a disability; nothing here indicates a disability.
B. Emotional immaturity caused by too much praise for his intellect
This blames parenting without evidence; uneven development is common in gifted children.
C. Asynchronous development across his intellectual and social growth ✔ KEY
Gifted children often develop unevenly, with intellect far ahead of social and emotional skills that match their age.
D. Early signs of a disruptive mood dysregulation disorder pattern
DMDD requires severe, frequent outbursts and persistent irritability across settings; this is not described.
Rationale: Asynchronous development means a gifted child's intellectual abilities run well ahead of social, emotional or physical development. This uneven profile can produce frustration, perfectionism and difficulty finding peers. Counselors normalize the pattern for families, support social-emotional skills, and help the child find intellectual peers.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Middle childhood: giftedness, creativity and talent
⚑ Check: The term "asynchronous development" comes from gifted-education literature (Columbus Group; Silverman); SME to confirm Berk covers it or swap the reference.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

458. nce-s-clf-218 · Career Development · career and vocational concerns · medium · In review

A 29-year-old Army veteran led a 12-person logistics team for six years. Applying for civilian jobs, his resume lists military job codes and unit titles, and he has had no interviews. He says, "Nobody out here values what I did." What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Steer him toward entry-level roles until he gains civilian work history
This undervalues his experience and could lead to underemployment.
B. Give an interest inventory to find a field unrelated to his service
His issue is translating proven skills, not a lack of known interests.
C. Explore his anger at civilians as a possible sign of combat trauma
His frustration is an understandable response to rejection; nothing suggests a trauma reaction.
D. Help him translate his military duties into civilian skills and terms ✔ KEY
Translating military roles into transferable civilian skills, using tools like the O*NET military crosswalk, is a key first step.
Rationale: Many veterans have strong leadership, logistics and technical skills that civilian employers do not recognize when described in military language. Career counselors help veterans identify transferable skills, translate job codes and titles into civilian terms (for example, with the O*NET military crosswalk), and connect with veteran employment resources.
References: Sharf (Career Development Theory) — Career counseling with special populations: transferable skills and occupational information
⚑ Check: Veteran-specific content may not be covered directly in Sharf; SME to confirm the locator.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

459. nce-s-clf-219 · Career Development · career and vocational concerns · easy · In review

A career counselor is screening clients for a program that serves people who are underemployed. Which client BEST fits the definition of underemployment?
A. A nurse who left work by choice to care for her newborn twins
Leaving the labor force by choice is not underemployment.
B. An engineer stocking shelves part time who wants full-time work ✔ KEY
Working part time involuntarily in a job well below his training fits underemployment.
C. A teacher on summer break who will return to her job in the fall
A planned seasonal break from a full-time job is not underemployment.
D. A laid-off welder who has been looking for a job for six months
Someone without a job who is seeking work is unemployed, not underemployed.
Rationale: Underemployment describes working fewer hours than desired (involuntary part-time work) or in a job that does not use one's education, skills or experience. It is associated with lower well-being and job satisfaction, much as unemployment is, so counselors address both the practical job search and its emotional toll.
References: Sharf (Career Development Theory) — Adult career crises and transitions: unemployment and underemployment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

460. nce-s-clf-220 · Career Development · career and vocational concerns · medium · In review

A 44-year-old woman with top performance reviews has been passed over three times for vice president. Each time, a man with a similar record was chosen. She tells her counselor, "I must not be leadership material." Which counselor response is BEST?
A. Focus on assertiveness training to correct her leadership weaknesses
This assumes a personal deficit and ignores the strong evidence of her performance.
B. Suggest she lower her goals to match what the company is likely to offer
Lowering goals accepts a barrier as fixed and undermines her career self-efficacy.
C. Help her weigh structural barriers to advancement, not just self-blame ✔ KEY
The pattern fits a glass ceiling; exploring systemic barriers counters self-blame and opens options for action.
D. Advise her to file a discrimination lawsuit against the firm at once
Legal action is her decision to make after exploring options, not the counselor's directive.
Rationale: The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier that limits women's advancement to top leadership despite qualifications. Women may internalize such barriers as personal failings. Counselors help clients recognize contextual and systemic barriers, preserve career self-efficacy, and consider strategies such as mentoring, sponsorship, advocacy or a move to another organization.
References: Sharf (Career Development Theory) — Career development of women: barriers to advancement · MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling and advocacy interventions: addressing systemic barriers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

461. nce-s-clf-221 · Career Development · career and vocational concerns · hard · In review

A college sophomore has clear interests in health and science but has not declared a major. She says, "I'm bad at making big choices; I don't trust myself to pick right." A counselor using social cognitive career theory wants to build her career decision self-efficacy. Which strategy would be MOST powerful?
A. Hand her more printed details on each major so she can study them
She already knows her interests; more information does not build confidence in deciding.
B. Tell her firmly that she has what it takes to make a strong decision
Verbal persuasion is a weaker source of self-efficacy than direct success experiences.
C. Have her watch peers describe how they each chose their own majors
Vicarious learning helps, but it is less powerful than her own successes.
D. Set graded decision tasks she can complete and succeed at herself ✔ KEY
Mastery experiences, personal success at the task, are the strongest source of self-efficacy in Bandura's and SCCT's view.
Rationale: Social cognitive career theory (Lent, Brown and Hackett) draws on Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy: performance accomplishments (mastery), vicarious learning, verbal persuasion, and physiological and emotional states. Mastery experiences are the most powerful. For indecision rooted in low decision-making confidence, counselors structure small, achievable decision steps.
References: Sharf (Career Development Theory) — Social cognitive career theory: sources of self-efficacy; career decision self-efficacy
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

462. nce-s-clf-222 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · couples and family concerns · medium · In review

A counselor trained in divorce mediation is helping a couple reach a parenting and property agreement. In the third session, the wife privately asks the counselor to also see her for individual therapy for depression after the divorce is final. What should the counselor do?
A. Stay in the neutral mediator role and refer her to another therapist ✔ KEY
Taking one party as a therapy client would compromise mediator neutrality; a referral meets her need without a role conflict.
B. Agree, since therapy would begin only after the mediation has ended
Even later, the role change could appear to favor her and undermine the husband's trust in the agreement.
C. Begin individual sessions now so her depression does not slow progress
Concurrent therapy with one party creates a clear conflict of interest in mediation.
D. Ask the husband's permission and then see her alone if he agrees to it
Consent does not remove the conflict created when the mediator becomes one party's therapist.
Rationale: Divorce mediation is a neutral, task-focused process for reaching agreements; it is not therapy. When one party seeks a therapeutic relationship, the counselor clarifies roles and refers to avoid a conflict of interest that would compromise impartiality. The ACA Code addresses role changes and serving multiple clients whose interests may conflict.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.6.d Role Changes in the Professional Relationship; A.8 Multiple Clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

463. nce-s-clf-223 · Human Growth and Development · couples and family concerns · easy · In review

Parents of a 13-year-old are alarmed that she now argues about clothes, chores and bedtime and rolls her eyes at their rules. She has good grades, close friends, and still talks with them about school. What should the counselor tell the parents?
A. The bickering may signal early oppositional defiant disorder
ODD involves a persistent, pervasive pattern of hostility; mild, everyday conflict with good functioning is not ODD.
B. Mild conflict over daily issues is common in early adolescence ✔ KEY
Parent-teen conflict over everyday matters rises in early adolescence and usually reflects normal striving for autonomy.
C. Firm limits with no discussion will end the conflict quickest
An authoritarian style tends to escalate conflict; warmth with reasoned limits works better.
D. Letting her set her own rules will reduce tension at home
A permissive approach removes needed structure; teens still benefit from monitoring and clear limits.
Rationale: Parent-adolescent conflict over everyday issues typically increases in early adolescence as teens seek autonomy, and it usually declines later. Severe, constant conflict is not normal and warrants attention. Authoritative parenting, which pairs warmth with clear, explained limits and gradually expanded autonomy, is linked to the best adolescent outcomes.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Adolescence: parent-child relationships, autonomy and conflict
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

464. nce-s-clf-224 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · couples and family concerns · medium · In review

A family lost their home and business in a wildfire. In counseling, they argue about what went wrong but also describe neighbors who helped and a shared faith that "we will rebuild." A counselor using Froma Walsh's family resilience framework would MOST likely focus on which task?
A. Finding the family member whose symptoms carry the family stress
Locating an identified patient fits other systems models, not Walsh's strengths-based resilience focus.
B. Tracing the family's patterns of fusion back over three generations
Multigenerational tracing is a Bowenian task, not the core of the resilience framework.
C. Strengthening shared meaning, connection and joint problem-solving ✔ KEY
Walsh's key processes are belief systems, organizational patterns and communication/problem-solving, all built on family strengths.
D. Rearranging the family hierarchy so the parents hold firmer power
Restructuring hierarchy is a structural family therapy goal, not the main resilience focus.
Rationale: Walsh's family resilience framework views families facing adversity as challenged, not damaged. It strengthens three domains of key processes: belief systems (making meaning of adversity, a positive outlook, transcendence and spirituality), organizational patterns (flexibility, connectedness, social and economic resources) and communication/problem-solving (clarity, open emotional sharing, collaborative problem-solving).
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Family resilience (Walsh): key processes in family functioning
⚑ Check: Walsh's framework is primary in Walsh (2016), Strengthening Family Resilience; SME to confirm the Goldenberg locator.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

465. nce-s-clf-225 · Social and Cultural Diversity · spiritual and religious concerns · medium · In review

A 35-year-old client mentions that during worship at her Pentecostal church she speaks in tongues and sometimes feels the Holy Spirit move through her. She works, has close relationships, and shows no other unusual experiences. How should the counselor BEST understand these reports?
A. As possible psychotic symptoms that call for a psychiatric referral
Experiences accepted within the client's faith community, with intact functioning, are not evidence of psychosis.
B. As accepted religious practices within her own faith community ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR cautions that experiences sanctioned by a person's culture or religion should not be judged as symptoms.
C. As dissociative episodes that need a structured diagnostic interview
DSM-5-TR excludes trance states that are a normal part of broadly accepted religious practice.
D. As avoidance of her problems that should become a focus of treatment
Nothing suggests her faith practice is causing problems; treating it as avoidance imposes the counselor's values.
Rationale: Clinicians must judge unusual experiences in the context of the client's cultural and religious norms. Practices such as glossolalia are normative in some traditions and are not symptoms when they occur within accepted religious contexts and do not cause distress or impairment. DSM-5-TR notes that dissociative disorder diagnoses do not apply to states that are a normal part of broadly accepted cultural or religious practice.
References: DSM-5-TR — Cultural concepts and distinguishing culturally sanctioned experiences from psychopathology; dissociative disorders exclusion for religious practice · ACA Code of Ethics — E.5.b Cultural Sensitivity
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

466. nce-s-clf-226 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · chronic illness and disability · easy · In review

A 27-year-old is referred eight months after a moderate traumatic brain injury from a car crash. He forgets what was discussed, tires quickly, and becomes irritable when sessions run long. Which adjustment to counseling is MOST appropriate?
A. Long open-ended sessions so he can explore at his own pace
Long, unstructured sessions tax attention and fatigue after brain injury.
B. Insight-focused talk therapy without memory aids or notes
Without memory supports, he is unlikely to retain or use session content.
C. Fewer sessions spaced far apart to reduce his frustration
Wide spacing weakens retention; short, frequent, structured sessions fit better.
D. Short, structured sessions with written summaries and aids ✔ KEY
Shorter sessions, concrete structure, repetition and written notes compensate for memory and fatigue problems after TBI.
Rationale: Clients with traumatic brain injury often have deficits in memory, attention, processing speed and emotional regulation, along with fatigue. Counselors adapt by using shorter, structured sessions, repetition, written summaries and external aids, involving family when appropriate, and coordinating with rehabilitation and neuropsychology providers.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling clients with disabilities: adapting counseling to cognitive impairment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

467. nce-s-clf-227 · Social and Cultural Diversity · chronic illness and disability · hard · In review

A 30-year-old client who was born deaf comes to counseling, with a sign language interpreter, for stress at work. She mentions proudly that she is active in the Deaf community. The counselor plans to begin by helping her grieve the loss of hearing. Why is this plan MOST problematic?
A. It imposes a loss frame on an identity she holds as cultural ✔ KEY
Many culturally Deaf people view deafness as a linguistic and cultural identity, not a loss to grieve.
B. Grief work is not suitable when an interpreter is in the room
Interpreters do not rule out any type of counseling work; the problem is the counselor's assumption.
C. Stage models say grief over hearing ends by early adulthood
No such rule exists; the issue is that she does not experience her deafness as a loss.
D. Counselors should refer deaf clients to a deaf counselor only
Culturally competent hearing counselors can serve Deaf clients; automatic referral is not required.
Rationale: Disability identity varies. Many people who are culturally Deaf (capital D) see themselves as members of a linguistic and cultural minority with its own language, such as ASL, rather than as people with a deficit. Applying a medical or loss model without asking the client imposes the counselor's worldview. Counselors explore how clients define their own identity and focus on the presenting concern.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling individuals with disabilities: disability identity and Deaf culture
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

468. nce-s-clf-228 · Social and Cultural Diversity · LGBTQ+ clients and minority stress · medium · In review

A 72-year-old transgender woman who transitioned in her forties must move into assisted living after a stroke. She says, "I fought my whole life to be myself. I'm terrified the staff will misgender me or that I'll have to hide again." Which counselor response is BEST?
A. Reassure her that staff are trained, so her worries are probably unfounded
Her fears reflect real risks documented for LGBTQ+ older adults; dismissing them invalidates her.
B. Suggest she keep her history private until she knows the staff better
Advising concealment adds to minority stress and puts the burden of others' bias on her.
C. Explore her fears and help her find and advocate for affirming facilities ✔ KEY
Validating her fears and helping her identify affirming care and supports addresses both her distress and real barriers.
D. Focus on her stroke recovery, since gender identity is a settled matter
Her identity is settled, but her safety and dignity in care are urgent present concerns.
Rationale: Transgender older adults often carry histories of discrimination and may lack family support. Many fear mistreatment, misgendering or pressure to go back into the closet in long-term care. Counselors validate these fears, help clients locate LGBTQ+-affirming providers and aging resources, and advocate for respectful, competent care.
References: MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling and advocacy interventions at the institutional level · Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling LGBTQ+ individuals; counseling older adults
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

469. nce-s-clf-229 · Social and Cultural Diversity · LGBTQ+ clients and minority stress · hard · In review

A 26-year-old bisexual man in a relationship with a woman says his family calls his bisexuality "a phase," while gay friends tell him he is "really straight now." He feels he belongs nowhere. Which concept BEST describes this source of minority stress?
A. Internalized homonegativity that he holds about his own identity
Internalized stigma is a self-directed belief; here the invalidation comes from others.
B. Bisexual erasure from both straight and gay communities ✔ KEY
Bisexual people often face invalidation from both heterosexual and gay or lesbian communities, sometimes called double discrimination.
C. Identity confusion, the first stage of Cass's identity model
Cass describes stages of gay and lesbian identity; it does not capture rejection from two communities.
D. Heterosexual privilege that protects him from any minority stress
Being in a different-gender relationship does not remove the stigma and invisibility bisexual people face.
Rationale: Bisexual people experience unique minority stressors, including bisexual erasure (denial that bisexuality is real or lasting) and binegativity from both heterosexual and gay or lesbian communities. This double marginalization can limit community support and is linked to higher rates of depression and anxiety than among gay and lesbian peers.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling LGBTQ+ individuals: bisexual invisibility and double discrimination
⚑ Check: Confirm the Sue & Sue chapter discusses bisexual erasure/binegativity and double discrimination.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

470. nce-s-clf-230 · Social and Cultural Diversity · acculturation and immigration stress · hard · In review

A 38-year-old woman who entered the country without documentation seeks counseling for panic, poor sleep and constant fear that she will be separated from her children. At intake she hesitates and asks, "Will you tell anyone about my status?" What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Explain confidentiality and its limits, which do not include her status ✔ KEY
Immigration status is not a mandated reporting category; explaining confidentiality and its true limits builds the safety she needs.
B. Record her status in detail so that the clinical file is fully complete
Counselors record what is clinically needed; detailed status notes add risk without clinical benefit.
C. Refer her to an immigration attorney before beginning counseling work
Legal referral may help later, but her immediate question is about confidentiality and her panic needs care.
D. Tell her you cannot discuss her legal status because of agency policy
Deflecting her question deepens fear and mistrust; she needs a clear answer about confidentiality.
Rationale: Undocumented clients live with chronic fear of detention and family separation, which can cause anxiety, depression and trauma symptoms. Fear of disclosure is a major barrier to care. Counselors clearly explain confidentiality and its actual limits (such as risk of harm or child abuse), note that immigration status is not a reportable matter, and document only what is clinically necessary.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.1.d Explanation of Limitations; A.2.b Types of Information Needed · Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling immigrants and refugees: undocumented status and fear of disclosure
⚑ Check: No general mandate requires counselors to report immigration status, but some funded programs or states may have specific rules; SME to confirm the general framing.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

471. nce-s-clf-231 · Social and Cultural Diversity · acculturation and immigration stress · medium · In review

A 58-year-old woman who immigrated from rural China two years ago is brought in by her daughter. She reports headaches, fatigue and poor appetite, says her doctor found nothing wrong, and insists, "I am not crazy. I do not need to talk about feelings." Which approach is BEST?
A. Explain that her physical symptoms are really depression in disguise
Relabeling her experience early challenges her worldview and is likely to end engagement.
B. Ask her daughter to describe her mother's emotions on her behalf
This sidelines the client and may breach her preferences about what is shared within the family.
C. Tell her counseling can begin only once she accepts a diagnosis
Requiring acceptance of a diagnosis is a barrier and does not fit her cultural view of help-seeking.
D. Respect her view of the symptoms and offer practical, active help ✔ KEY
Starting with her own framing and offering concrete, problem-focused help builds credibility with less acculturated clients.
Rationale: Less acculturated clients from many cultures underuse counseling, may express distress through somatic complaints, and may see emotional talk as stigmatizing. Sue and Sue describe culturally responsive engagement: accept the client's explanation of the problem, coordinate with medical care, and offer active, structured, practical help. An early, felt benefit (what Sue and Sue call gift giving) builds the counselor's credibility.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Asian Americans: somatic expression of distress; credibility and gift giving
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:
