573. nce-s-trt-038 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · collaborative treatment planning · medium · In review

A 45-year-old man with obsessive-compulsive disorder is nervous about exposure and response prevention and asks whether there are other options. Which response BEST reflects shared decision making?
A. Tell him ERP is the evidence-based choice, so the plan cannot change
Insisting on one option without exploring his concerns and preferences removes him from the decision.
B. Let him choose any approach he likes without discussing the evidence
Shared decision making requires the counselor to bring evidence; deferring entirely abandons that role.
C. Review the options, evidence and his concerns, then decide jointly ✔ KEY
Shared decision making combines the counselor's knowledge of the evidence with the client's values and preferences in a joint choice.
D. Postpone treatment planning until his anxiety about ERP has resolved
Delaying planning leaves him untreated; fear of ERP is something to discuss and plan for, not wait out.
Rationale: Evidence-based practice integrates the best research evidence, clinical expertise and client characteristics, values and preferences. In shared decision making the counselor explains the options with their benefits and burdens, explores the client's concerns, and arrives at a plan together. Here that might include explaining how ERP is graded and client-paced.
References: APA CPG — Evidence-based practice: integrating patient values and preferences into treatment decisions
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

574. nce-s-trt-039 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · collaborative treatment planning · medium · In review

A 19-year-old Mexican American client with depression tells her counselor that decisions in her family are made together and that she wants her mother involved in her care. Which approach to the treatment plan is MOST culturally responsive?
A. Include her mother in planning as she wishes, keeping core methods ✔ KEY
Cultural adaptation honors her value of family involvement while keeping the active ingredients of effective treatment.
B. Keep the plan individual, since adult clients decide treatment alone
This imposes an individualistic worldview and ignores the client's own stated wish for family involvement.
C. Assume every Latina client prefers family therapy over individual work
This stereotypes the client; adaptation should follow her stated preferences, not group generalizations.
D. Ask her mother to set the goals because she is the family decision maker
The client remains the decision maker about her own care; involving family does not mean handing over her goals.
Rationale: Culturally adapted treatment adjusts how a plan is delivered (who is involved, language, metaphors, goals framed in the client's values) while preserving the core components of effective treatment. The adaptation should be driven by the individual client's stated values, here familismo and collective decision making, rather than by assumptions about a group.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Culturally appropriate intervention strategies: collectivism and family involvement · MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling and advocacy interventions: integrating client worldview into counseling
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

575. nce-s-trt-040 · Assessment and Testing · progress monitoring and outcome measures · easy · In review

A group practice announces that it is adopting measurement-based care. Which practice BEST describes this approach?
A. Giving a symptom inventory at intake and again at discharge only
Pre-post measurement evaluates results after the fact but cannot guide treatment while it is happening.
B. Routinely scoring brief measures and using them to guide treatment ✔ KEY
Measurement-based care means regular standardized measurement whose results are reviewed with the client and used to adjust treatment.
C. Basing progress notes on the counselor's sense of client improvement
Clinical judgment alone tends to miss clients who are not improving or are getting worse.
D. Sending yearly satisfaction surveys to all of the practice's clients
Satisfaction surveys are program evaluation; they do not track an individual client's symptoms over time.
Rationale: Measurement-based care is the systematic administration of brief, validated measures (for example, the PHQ-9 or GAD-7) at regular intervals, with results reviewed with the client and used to inform clinical decisions. It improves detection of clients who are not responding.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Use of assessment in counseling: monitoring client progress with standardized measures
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

576. nce-s-trt-041 · Assessment and Testing · progress monitoring and outcome measures · hard · In review

A counseling center begins giving the Outcome Questionnaire-45 (OQ-45) before every session and sends counselors color-coded alerts based on expected recovery curves. According to research on this kind of routine outcome monitoring with feedback, which clients benefit MOST?
A. Clients who are improving faster than their expected recovery curve
On-track clients do about as well with or without feedback; they are not where the largest gains appear.
B. Clients whose intake scores fell within the normal, nonclinical range
Clients starting in the functional range have little room to improve, so feedback adds little for them.
C. Clients in brief treatment who are seen for only one or two sessions
Feedback needs repeated measurement over time to identify a trajectory and prompt a change in course.
D. Clients flagged as not on track, who are at risk of deteriorating ✔ KEY
Feedback alerts help counselors notice and respond to not-on-track clients, improving their outcomes and reducing deterioration.
Rationale: The OQ-45 measures symptom distress, interpersonal relations and social role functioning. Lambert and colleagues found that giving counselors feedback on clients predicted to be not on track, especially paired with clinical support tools that review alliance, motivation and supports, improved outcomes and reduced deterioration. Counselors on their own tend to underestimate which clients are getting worse.
References: Lambert (Outcome Monitoring) — OQ-45 feedback and alerts for clients not on track · Hays (Assessment) — Outcome assessment and routine outcome monitoring
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

577. nce-s-trt-042 · Assessment and Testing · progress monitoring and outcome measures · medium · In review

A 56-year-old client's scores on a weekly anxiety measure have risen by more than the measure's reliable change index since intake, and she arrives at session five looking tense. How should the counselor respond to this deterioration?
A. Keep the current plan, since symptoms often worsen before improving
Assuming early worsening is expected ignores the warning sign; reliable deterioration predicts poor outcome if unaddressed.
B. Discharge her and refer elsewhere because treatment is not working
Abrupt discharge without exploring the cause is premature and risks abandonment.
C. Review scores with her, explore causes and revise the plan together ✔ KEY
Sharing the data, checking the alliance, stressors and fit of the plan, and adjusting collaboratively is the recommended response.
D. Stop giving the measure, because her rising scores may upset her more
Dropping measurement removes the information needed to respond; the scores should be discussed openly.
Rationale: Reliable deterioration on an outcome measure is a signal to act, not to wait. The counselor discusses the change with the client, assesses risk, explores the alliance, life events and treatment fit, and adjusts the plan, consulting or referring for added services if needed. Documenting the change and the response is part of good practice.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Monitoring progress: reliable change and responding to nonresponse · Wiger (Documentation) — Progress notes and treatment plan updates when progress stalls or reverses
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

578. nce-s-trt-043 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · safety planning · medium · In review

A 28-year-old client had a suicidal crisis over the weekend. He did not use his safety plan, saying it "didn't feel real" and that he had forgotten where he put it. He is now safe and engaged. What should the counselor do with the plan?
A. Revise it with him, find the barriers and make each step more usable ✔ KEY
Safety plans are living documents; reviewing what got in the way and rewriting steps in his words makes the plan more usable.
B. Replace it with a written no-suicide contract that he agrees to sign
No-suicide contracts lack evidence of preventing suicide and do not give the client coping steps.
C. Set the plan aside, since he has shown that safety planning fails him
One unused plan points to barriers to fix, not a reason to abandon an evidence-supported intervention.
D. Keep the original plan but tell him to read it once a day as homework
Repeating an unchanged plan ignores why it failed; it needs collaborative revision first.
Rationale: The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention is developed collaboratively, written in the client's own words, kept somewhere easy to reach (such as a phone), and reviewed and revised after crises. Asking what got in the way of using each step lets the counselor and client make the plan realistic.
References: Stanley-Brown SPI — Reviewing and revising the safety plan; identifying barriers to using each step
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

579. nce-s-trt-044 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · safety planning · easy · In review

While adding crisis resources to a safety plan, a 17-year-old client asks what happens if she contacts 988. Which description is accurate?
A. It is a line that sends police to the caller's location on every contact
Most 988 contacts are resolved by phone, text or chat; emergency dispatch is reserved for imminent danger.
B. It connects her by call, text or chat to trained crisis counselors 24/7 ✔ KEY
988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers call, text and chat access to trained crisis counselors at any hour.
C. It is reserved for people who are in the middle of a suicide attempt
988 serves anyone in suicidal, mental health or substance use crisis, or worried about someone else.
D. It is a text-only service that answers messages during business hours
988 is available by phone, text and chat around the clock.
Rationale: The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline became the national three-digit number in the United States in July 2022. It routes calls, texts and chats to trained crisis counselors 24 hours a day. In a Stanley-Brown safety plan it belongs in the step listing professionals and agencies to contact in a crisis.
References: SAMHSA 988 Lifeline — 988 by call, text or chat, 24/7 · Stanley-Brown SPI — Step 5: professionals and agencies to contact in a crisis
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

580. nce-s-trt-045 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · SMART goals and measurable objectives · easy · In review

A counselor writes this objective for a client with panic disorder: "Client will reduce panic attacks from four per week to one or fewer per week, as recorded in a daily panic log." Which SMART element is missing?
A. A specific behavior that is targeted for change
The objective names a specific behavior: the frequency of panic attacks.
B. A way to measure progress toward the objective
The daily panic log and the counts per week make the objective measurable.
C. A target that is realistic for this client
Reducing attacks to one or fewer per week is a reasonable, attainable target for treated panic disorder.
D. A time frame for reaching the stated target ✔ KEY
The objective gives no date or number of weeks, so it is not time-bound.
Rationale: SMART objectives are specific, measurable, achievable (attainable), relevant and time-bound. Adding a time frame, such as "within 10 weeks," tells the client and counselor when to judge whether the objective was met and supports documentation of medical necessity and progress.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Treatment plans: writing behaviorally measurable, time-bound objectives
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

581. nce-s-trt-046 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · matching level of care to need · hard · In review

A 34-year-old client with severe depression has worsened despite three weeks in an intensive outpatient program (three hours, three days a week). He is not suicidal, lives with a supportive spouse, and can stay safe at night, but he needs structured treatment most of each weekday. Which level of care BEST fits?
A. Weekly individual outpatient counseling plus a medication review
This is less intensive than the IOP he is already failing in, so it would be a step down when he needs a step up.
B. Continued IOP at the same schedule for another three weeks
He is worsening at this intensity; continuing unchanged does not match his increased need.
C. A partial hospitalization program attended most of each weekday ✔ KEY
PHP offers several hours of daily structured treatment while he returns home at night, matching his need without 24-hour care.
D. Admission to a locked inpatient psychiatric unit for stabilization
He has no imminent risk and can stay safe at home, so 24-hour inpatient care would be more restrictive than needed.
Rationale: Levels of care run from outpatient to intensive outpatient (about 9 or more hours a week for adults), partial hospitalization (about 20 or more hours a week, usually most of each weekday), and 24-hour residential or inpatient care. The best match is the least restrictive level that meets current need; worsening in IOP without imminent danger points to PHP.
References: LOCUS (AACP) — Level-of-care intensity: intensive outpatient versus partial hospitalization
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

582. nce-s-trt-047 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · matching level of care to need · medium · In review

Which client presentation MOST clearly meets criteria for inpatient psychiatric hospitalization rather than a less restrictive level of care?
A. A man with chronic passive death wishes, no plan, and strong supports
Passive ideation without plan or intent, with supports, can usually be managed in outpatient care with safety planning.
B. A woman with a plan, intent and access to means who cannot stay safe ✔ KEY
Imminent risk with a plan, intent, access to means and inability to maintain safety requires 24-hour protective care.
C. A teen with worsening grades and conflict who refuses to go to school
Functional decline without imminent danger calls for outpatient or intensive outpatient services, not hospitalization.
D. A man with panic attacks who missed work twice this month from fear
Panic with some missed work is treated effectively on an outpatient basis.
Rationale: Inpatient hospitalization is reserved for clients who are an imminent danger to themselves or others, or who are so impaired they cannot care for themselves, and who cannot be kept safe at a less restrictive level. Suicidal ideation with a plan, intent, access to means and an inability to engage in safety planning is the classic indication.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Crisis counseling: suicide risk and the decision to hospitalize
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

583. nce-s-trt-048 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · coordination of care and referral · medium · In review

A 20-year-old client in counseling for perfectionism mentions that she has been vomiting after most meals, has lost 15 pounds in two months, and feels dizzy when she stands up. The counselor has no eating disorder training. What is the BEST course of action?
A. Continue the current work and add eating concerns to future goals
Purging with rapid weight loss and dizziness signals possible medical danger that cannot wait for future sessions.
B. End counseling now and give her a list of eating disorder programs
Abruptly ending services without a coordinated transition risks abandonment.
C. Read about eating disorders and begin treating them in next session
Reading alone does not provide the training and supervision needed to practice within competence.
D. Arrange a prompt medical exam and specialist referral with a release ✔ KEY
Her symptoms need urgent medical evaluation, and care should be coordinated with a qualified specialist with her consent.
Rationale: Purging, rapid weight loss and dizziness can indicate electrolyte imbalance or other medical instability, so a prompt medical evaluation comes first. Because eating disorder treatment falls outside this counselor's competence, the counselor coordinates a referral to a qualified provider with a signed release, supporting the transition rather than abandoning the client.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — C.2.a Boundaries of Competence; A.11.a Competence Within Termination and Referral
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

584. nce-s-trt-049 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · discharge and aftercare planning · easy · In review

A 42-year-old client is completing an intensive outpatient program for depression and will step down to weekly counseling. Which aftercare step does the MOST to reduce the risk that he drops out after discharge?
A. Book his first outpatient visit with a named counselor before he leaves ✔ KEY
A confirmed appointment with a named provider, made before discharge, is a warm handoff that improves follow-through.
B. Give him a list of local counselors to call once he feels he needs one
Leaving the client to make contact on his own increases the chance that no follow-up happens.
C. Tell him to return to the program if symptoms come back after discharge
This plans only for relapse and leaves a gap in continuing care.
D. Mail a copy of his discharge summary to his home address after he leaves
A summary sent to the client does not connect him to the next provider.
Rationale: The period right after leaving a more intensive level of care carries elevated risk of disengagement and relapse. Effective aftercare planning schedules the next appointment before discharge, shares records with the receiving provider with consent, and updates the safety and relapse prevention plans.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Discharge summaries and aftercare recommendations
⚑ Check: Warm-handoff and pre-discharge scheduling are standard continuity-of-care practice; confirm Wiger is the best fit or cite a SAMHSA continuity-of-care source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

585. nce-s-trt-050 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · stages of change and treatment readiness · easy · In review

A 50-year-old client was referred by his physician for heavy cannabis use. He says, "It helps me relax. I don't see what the problem is." Which intervention BEST matches his stage of change?
A. Help him set a quit date and list strategies for handling cravings
Quit dates and coping plans are action-stage tasks; pushing them now tends to raise resistance.
B. Teach relapse prevention skills for high-risk situations he may face
Relapse prevention fits the action and maintenance stages, after change has begun.
C. Build rapport and offer nonjudgmental feedback to raise awareness ✔ KEY
In precontemplation, consciousness raising and nonconfrontational feedback help the client begin to consider change.
D. Confront his denial firmly so that he accepts that he has a problem
Confrontation increases defensiveness and is not supported for clients in precontemplation.
Rationale: A client who sees no problem is in precontemplation. Stage-matched work at this point builds the relationship, raises awareness through information and personalized feedback, and explores the client's own view of the behavior. Action-oriented tasks fit later stages.
References: Transtheoretical Model — Precontemplation: consciousness raising and stage-matched processes of change · Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Avoiding the righting reflex and reducing discord
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

586. nce-s-trt-051 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · stages of change and treatment readiness · hard · In review

A counselor uses a decisional balance exercise with a client who is weighing whether to stop gambling. According to research on the Transtheoretical Model, how does decisional balance typically shift as people move from precontemplation toward action?
A. The cons of changing rise steadily until they overtake the pros
This reverses the pattern; perceived cons of change tend to decrease as people progress.
B. The pros of changing increase until they come to outweigh the cons ✔ KEY
Pros of change rise across stages and typically cross over the cons before the action stage.
C. Pros and cons both stay stable, and only self-efficacy shifts
Self-efficacy does rise, but decisional balance also shifts in a predictable way across stages.
D. Pros and cons drop together as the client stops thinking about it
Movement toward action involves more, not less, weighing of the pros of change.
Rationale: Decisional balance is the weighing of the pros and cons of changing. In precontemplation the cons outweigh the pros; the two are roughly balanced in contemplation, which feeds ambivalence; and the pros come to outweigh the cons before action. Prochaska described the pros as rising more steeply than the cons fall (the strong and weak principles).
References: Transtheoretical Model — Decisional balance across the stages of change; strong and weak principles of progress
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

587. nce-s-trt-052 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · SMART goals and measurable objectives · easy · In review

A counselor-in-training writes "Client will have healthier relationships" as the only entry under objectives in a treatment plan. Her supervisor explains how goals and objectives differ. Which statement BEST describes that difference?
A. A goal states a broad aim; objectives are measurable steps toward it ✔ KEY
Goals describe the desired end state in broad terms; objectives break the goal into specific, observable, time-limited steps that show progress.
B. A goal is set by the counselor; objectives are chosen by the client
Both goals and objectives are developed collaboratively; authorship is not what separates them.
C. A goal lists the interventions; objectives list the diagnoses treated
Interventions and diagnoses are separate parts of the plan; neither defines the goal or the objective.
D. A goal is reached in one session; objectives take the full treatment
This reverses the relationship: objectives are the shorter-term steps, and the goal is the longer-term outcome.
Rationale: In treatment planning, a goal is a broad, long-term statement of what the client hopes to achieve, such as healthier relationships. Objectives translate that goal into specific, measurable, time-bound steps (for example, using an "I" statement in two disagreements per week for four weeks, recorded in a log). The supervisee's entry is a goal, so it still needs measurable objectives beneath it.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Treatment plans: distinguishing long-term goals from measurable short-term objectives
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

588. nce-s-trt-053 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · SMART goals and measurable objectives · medium · In review

A 27-year-old client with severe social anxiety rarely speaks in groups larger than three people. At intake, her counselor writes the objective: "Client will give a 10-minute presentation to her 200-person department within two weeks." Which SMART criterion does this objective MOST clearly fail?
A. Specific, because it does not say which behavior will change
The behavior (a 10-minute presentation to a named audience) is clearly specified.
B. Measurable, because a presentation cannot be counted or observed
Giving a presentation is directly observable and easy to verify, so the objective is measurable.
C. Achievable, because the step is too large for her starting point ✔ KEY
Jumping from avoiding groups of three to presenting to 200 people in two weeks is not realistic; graded steps are needed.
D. Time-bound, because it does not include any deadline for change
The objective includes a clear deadline of two weeks, so it is time-bound.
Rationale: SMART objectives are Specific, Measurable, Achievable (attainable), Relevant and Time-bound. An objective can be precise and measurable yet still fail if it is not realistic given the client's current functioning. Setting an unattainable first step invites failure and discouragement; a graded series of objectives, such as speaking once in a small meeting, then a larger one, fits the client's starting point and the logic of gradual exposure.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Treatment plans: objectives that are realistic and attainable for the client's current level of functioning
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

589. nce-s-trt-054 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · collaborative treatment planning · medium · In review

A 44-year-old man seeks counseling for stress after losing his job. During the intake, he mentions drinking six to eight beers most nights but says, "That is not why I am here." The counselor believes the drinking is a major concern. How should the counselor approach the treatment plan?
A. List alcohol abstinence as the primary goal since it is most urgent
Imposing a goal the client has rejected undermines the alliance and is likely to increase resistance and dropout.
B. Decline to treat the job stress until he agrees to address drinking
Making care conditional on accepting the counselor's agenda is coercive and ignores the client's stated needs.
C. Leave drinking out of the plan and the sessions to keep the alliance
Ignoring a clinically significant concern avoids conflict but fails the client; it should be explored respectfully.
D. Start with his job stress goal and openly explore links to drinking ✔ KEY
Beginning with the client's priority builds engagement while the counselor transparently shares the concern and explores how drinking affects his stress.
Rationale: Collaborative treatment planning starts from the goals the client brings while allowing the counselor to share clinical concerns honestly. Here the counselor can begin with job-loss stress, voice the concern about drinking without imposing it, and use a motivational approach to explore how alcohol affects sleep, mood and coping. Plans built jointly and consistent with the client's circumstances are more likely to succeed.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.1.c Counseling Plans: counselors and clients work jointly to devise counseling plans · Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Focusing process: negotiating a shared agenda when client and counselor priorities differ
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

590. nce-s-trt-055 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · collaborative treatment planning · hard · In review

A 63-year-old Vietnamese immigrant client nods and agrees to every goal the counselor proposes during treatment planning, then misses the next two sessions. She has said she was raised to defer to doctors and teachers. Which response is MOST likely to produce a truly collaborative plan?
A. Ask her to sign the plan as written since she already agreed to it
Her agreement may reflect deference rather than true endorsement; a signature does not make the plan collaborative.
B. Invite her priorities indirectly, such as what she hopes will change ✔ KEY
Open, respectful questions about her own hopes let her shape the plan without having to openly contradict an authority figure.
C. Refer her to a counselor who is also from a Vietnamese background
Shared ethnicity does not guarantee a good match, and referral skips the counselor's own task of adapting the process.
D. Let her family set the treatment goals because she defers to others
Family input may be welcome if she wants it, but handing goal-setting to others removes her voice entirely.
Rationale: Agreement is not the same as collaboration. When a client's cultural norms discourage disagreeing with authority, quick assent to every proposal and later missed sessions suggest the plan does not reflect her priorities. Culturally responsive planning reduces the power gap by asking about her hopes, concerns and preferred pace in indirect, respectful ways, checking understanding, and revising the plan with her.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Culturally appropriate intervention: deference to authority and indirect communication styles · ACA Code of Ethics — A.1.c Counseling Plans: plans consistent with the abilities, temperament and circumstances of clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

591. nce-s-trt-056 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · coordination of care and referral · medium · In review

A counselor works as a behavioral health care manager in a primary care clinic that uses the collaborative care model. She tracks every patient's PHQ-9 scores in a registry and reviews the caseload weekly with a consulting psychiatrist. What is the main purpose of the registry review?
A. To spot patients who are not improving so treatment can be adjusted ✔ KEY
Systematic caseload review flags patients not responding so the team can change treatment, the treat-to-target core of collaborative care.
B. To transfer every depressed patient to the psychiatrist's own care
In collaborative care the psychiatrist consults on the caseload; patients stay with their primary care provider and care manager.
C. To produce billing records that replace the clinical progress notes
A registry supports clinical decision-making; it does not replace progress notes or exist mainly for billing.
D. To find patients who no longer need any primary care involvement
The model keeps behavioral health care inside primary care; it is not designed to remove patients from it.
Rationale: Integrated behavioral health in primary care often follows the collaborative care model: a primary care provider, a behavioral health care manager and a consulting psychiatrist share a defined caseload. Measurement-based tracking in a registry and regular systematic caseload review identify patients who are not reaching targets, prompting changes in medication or psychotherapy. This treat-to-target approach is a key reason the model improves depression outcomes.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Clinical mental health counseling settings: integrated behavioral health in primary care · Lambert (Outcome Monitoring) — Measuring and monitoring progress to identify clients not on track
⚑ Check: Collaborative care (registry, care manager, psychiatric consultant, treat-to-target) is well established in the AIMS/Unutzer literature; confirm Gladding edition discusses integrated care in this detail or swap to a more specific source if added to the library.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

592. nce-s-trt-057 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · coordination of care and referral · easy · In review

During a routine visit, a family physician learns that a 35-year-old patient has been having panic attacks. She walks the patient down the hall, introduces him by name to the clinic's counselor, and explains why she thinks they should meet that same day. What is this practice called?
A. A cold referral
A cold referral gives the patient a name or number to call later, with no direct introduction.
B. A case conference
A case conference is a meeting among professionals about a client, not a live introduction of the client.
C. A warm handoff ✔ KEY
A warm handoff is a direct, in-person introduction from one provider to another, ideally during the same visit.
D. A consultation
Consultation is professional-to-professional advice; the patient is not transferred to the consultant's care.
Rationale: A warm handoff occurs when one provider personally introduces a patient to another, explaining the reason for the connection, often in the same visit. Compared with handing the patient a phone number, it transfers the trust built with the first provider, reduces stigma and logistical barriers, and increases the chance that the patient actually begins behavioral health care.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Clinical mental health counseling settings: referral and integrated care with medical providers
⚑ Check: Confirm the Gladding edition names the warm handoff explicitly; the concept is standard in integrated-care literature (e.g., AHRQ).
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

593. nce-s-trt-058 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · discharge and aftercare planning · medium · In review

A 39-year-old client has met her treatment goals for generalized anxiety and will be discharged from an outpatient agency. Her counselor is preparing the discharge summary. Which entry is MOST essential to include?
A. A full transcript of the client's comments during the final session
Verbatim session content is not required and adds detail that is not needed for continuity of care.
B. Progress on each treatment goal and the aftercare recommendations ✔ KEY
A discharge summary documents why treatment ended, progress on each goal, status at discharge and the aftercare plan.
C. The counselor's personal reactions to the client across treatment
Counselor reactions belong in supervision, not in the client record that may follow her to future providers.
D. A copy of every weekly anxiety score the client has ever obtained
Scores are already in the record; the summary reports overall change rather than reproducing every data point.
Rationale: A discharge (closing) summary gives future providers and reviewers a concise picture of the episode of care: reason for referral and for discharge, diagnosis, services provided, progress toward each treatment-plan goal, condition at discharge, and specific aftercare recommendations and referrals. Linking discharge to the plan's goals shows that treatment ended for a clinical reason and supports continuity of care.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Discharge summary: reason for discharge, progress toward goals, and aftercare recommendations
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

594. nce-s-trt-059 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · safety planning · hard · In review

A 46-year-old client with recurring suicidal thoughts keeps a handgun in his bedside drawer. He has no current plan or intent and is working on a safety plan with his counselor. He says the gun is for protection and he does not want to sell it. Which approach is MOST consistent with best practice?
A. Ask him to sign a contract promising not to harm himself with the gun
No-suicide contracts lack evidence of preventing suicide and do nothing to reduce access to lethal means.
B. Accept his choice and leave lethal means out of the safety plan to respect autonomy
Respecting autonomy does not mean skipping lethal means counseling; access to a firearm is a major risk factor.
C. Tell him counseling cannot continue until the firearm leaves the home
An ultimatum damages the alliance and may push him out of care, which raises rather than lowers risk.
D. Explore temporary off-site storage with someone he trusts during a crisis ✔ KEY
Collaborative lethal means counseling seeks temporary, acceptable ways to put time and distance between the client and the firearm.
Rationale: Making the environment safe is a core step of the Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention. Lethal means counseling works collaboratively, respecting the client's values while finding acceptable options, such as temporary storage with a trusted friend, a locked safe with the key held by someone else, or ammunition stored separately. Because suicidal crises are often brief, added time and distance from a firearm can be lifesaving.
References: Stanley-Brown SPI — Step 6: Making the environment safe (lethal means counseling)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

595. nce-s-trt-060 · Research and Program Evaluation · program evaluation and needs assessment · hard · In review

An agency compares two depression programs by dividing each program's total cost by the number of clients who achieved remission, finding $2,400 per remission for one and $3,100 for the other. Outcomes are not converted to dollar values. Which type of analysis is this?
A. Cost-benefit analysis
Cost-benefit analysis expresses outcomes in dollars (such as savings from fewer hospital days) and compares them with costs.
B. Summative needs assessment
A needs assessment identifies unmet needs before or during planning; it does not compare program costs per outcome.
C. Cost-effectiveness analysis ✔ KEY
Cost-effectiveness analysis compares programs on cost per unit of a nonmonetary outcome, such as cost per remission.
D. Formative process evaluation
Formative or process evaluation examines how a program is running so it can be improved, not its cost per outcome.
Rationale: Both analyses weigh costs against results, but they express results differently. Cost-benefit analysis converts outcomes into monetary terms so that benefits and costs can be compared directly, often as a benefit-cost ratio. Cost-effectiveness analysis keeps outcomes in natural units, such as remissions or symptom-free days, and reports the cost per unit of outcome, which suits counseling programs whose results are hard to price.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Program evaluation: cost-benefit versus cost-effectiveness analysis
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

596. nce-s-trt-061 · Research and Program Evaluation · program evaluation and needs assessment · medium · In review

A school district adopts an evidence-based bullying prevention curriculum, but after one year bullying reports have not declined. Teachers report that they often skipped lessons to make time for test preparation. What should the program evaluator examine FIRST?
A. Whether the curriculum's original research trials were published
The curriculum is already evidence-based; reviewing its publication history does not explain the local result.
B. Whether the curriculum was delivered with fidelity as designed ✔ KEY
Skipped lessons suggest poor implementation fidelity; a program not delivered as designed cannot be judged ineffective.
C. Whether a different curriculum would cost the district less
Cost comparisons may come later, but they do not address why this program did not produce the expected outcome.
D. Whether students liked the curriculum more than last year's
Satisfaction is a weak proxy for outcome and does not address the reported gaps in delivery.
Rationale: Fidelity (treatment integrity) monitoring checks whether a program is delivered as intended in dose, content and quality. When outcomes disappoint, evaluators first ask whether the program was actually implemented; otherwise a failure of delivery is mistaken for a failure of the program. Involving stakeholders such as teachers, students and administrators in the evaluation helps uncover implementation barriers like competing demands on class time.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Program evaluation: implementation (process) evaluation and treatment fidelity; stakeholder involvement
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

597. nce-s-trt-062 · Research and Program Evaluation · research design basics · easy · In review

A researcher randomly assigns college students to receive either four or eight sessions of mindfulness training and then compares their scores on a perceived stress scale. In this study, what is the dependent variable?
A. Scores on the perceived stress scale ✔ KEY
The dependent variable is the outcome measured to see whether it changes in response to the manipulated variable.
B. The number of mindfulness sessions
The number of sessions is manipulated by the researcher, which makes it the independent variable.
C. The random assignment of the students
Random assignment is a design feature that controls for group differences; it is not a variable being measured.
D. The college the students are enrolled in
The college is a constant or possible extraneous variable, not the outcome under study.
Rationale: The independent variable is what the researcher manipulates or uses to form groups (here, four versus eight sessions). The dependent variable is the outcome measured to see whether it depends on the independent variable (here, perceived stress scores). A quick test: the dependent variable is the effect, measured after the cause is varied.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Research design: independent and dependent variables
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

598. nce-s-trt-063 · Research and Program Evaluation · research design basics · medium · In review

A college counseling center compares students who signed up for a new resilience workshop with students who chose not to attend. At pretest, workshop students already reported more social support and higher motivation. Workshop students show greater gains at posttest. Which threat to internal validity is MOST important here?
A. Maturation of both groups over the full semester
Maturation would affect both groups similarly over the same period, so it does not explain the difference between groups.
B. Testing effects from taking the same pretest
Both groups took the pretest, so practice effects would not explain why one group gained more.
C. Instrumentation changes in the outcome measure
Nothing suggests the measure or its scoring changed between pretest and posttest.
D. Selection bias from groups that chose themselves ✔ KEY
Students chose their own group and differed at pretest, so preexisting differences may explain the gains.
Rationale: Selection is the main threat in quasi-experimental designs that compare nonequivalent groups without random assignment. When participants choose whether to receive the intervention, the groups can differ in motivation, support or other traits that also affect the outcome. Pretest differences are a warning sign; random assignment, matching or statistical controls such as ANCOVA reduce, but in quasi-experiments do not eliminate, this threat.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Quasi-experimental designs: selection as a threat to internal validity
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

599. nce-s-trt-064 · Research and Program Evaluation · research design basics · medium · In review

A researcher first analyzes outcome scores from 200 clients in a grief support program. She then interviews 15 clients whose scores did not improve to understand why the program did not help them. Which research design is she using?
A. An exploratory sequential mixed methods design
An exploratory sequential design starts with qualitative data and uses it to build or guide a later quantitative phase.
B. An explanatory sequential mixed methods design ✔ KEY
An explanatory sequential design collects quantitative data first, then qualitative data to explain the quantitative results.
C. A convergent parallel mixed methods study design
A convergent design collects both types of data at about the same time and compares them, rather than in sequence.
D. A practitioner-led action research design
Action research is cyclical inquiry by practitioners to improve their own practice; the defining feature here is the quant-then-qual sequence.
Rationale: Mixed methods research combines quantitative and qualitative data in one study. In an explanatory sequential design, the quantitative phase comes first and the qualitative phase follows to explain unexpected or important quantitative findings, such as why some clients did not improve. In an exploratory sequential design the order is reversed, and in a convergent design both strands are collected together and merged.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Mixed methods designs: explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential and convergent
⚑ Check: Design names follow Creswell & Plano Clark; confirm Erford uses the same labels (older texts say "sequential explanatory" and "concurrent triangulation").
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

600. nce-s-trt-065 · Research and Program Evaluation · research design basics · hard · In review

A research team plans a randomized trial of a new intervention for adults with severe depression, some of whom report suicidal ideation. One team member proposes a no-treatment control group to get the cleanest comparison. Which comparison condition is MOST ethically defensible?
A. Treatment as usual, so control clients still receive standard care ✔ KEY
An active treatment-as-usual comparison answers the research question without withholding needed care from high-risk clients.
B. A no-treatment group, provided participants give informed consent
Consent does not make it acceptable to withhold effective care from severely depressed, at-risk participants.
C. A placebo pill group, so neither group knows which they received
An inert placebo still withholds active treatment and is a poor match for a psychotherapy intervention.
D. A six-month waitlist group with no contact until the waiting ends
A long waitlist without monitoring delays care and leaves suicidal risk unassessed, which is not defensible here.
Rationale: Researchers must minimize harm to participants. When an effective standard treatment exists and participants are at serious risk, withholding care for the sake of a cleaner comparison is hard to justify. Comparing the new intervention with treatment as usual (an active control) keeps everyone in care. Waitlist or no-treatment controls are more defensible for low-risk problems, short delays, and with monitoring and a plan to offer treatment afterward.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — G.1.e Precautions to Avoid Injury: researchers take reasonable precautions to avoid causing physical, emotional or social injury to participants · Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Ethics in research: control groups and withholding treatment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

601. nce-s-trt-066 · Research and Program Evaluation · statistics used in outcome research · easy · In review

A study comparing a new group intervention with a waitlist reports Cohen's d = 0.50 on a measure of anxiety. Using Cohen's conventional benchmarks, how large is this effect?
A. Negligible
Effects below about 0.20 are usually described as negligible; 0.50 is well above that.
B. Small
A small effect is about d = 0.20.
C. Medium ✔ KEY
Cohen described d = 0.50 as a medium effect.
D. Large
A large effect is about d = 0.80 or above.
Rationale: Cohen's d expresses the difference between two group means in standard deviation units. Cohen's conventional benchmarks are 0.20 for a small effect, 0.50 for a medium effect and 0.80 for a large effect. Unlike a p value, an effect size describes how much difference an intervention makes and does not depend on sample size.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Effect size: Cohen's d benchmarks of .20, .50 and .80
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

602. nce-s-trt-067 · Research and Program Evaluation · statistics used in outcome research · medium · In review

A trial reports that clients receiving a sleep intervention improved 5 points more on an insomnia scale than controls, with a 95% confidence interval for the difference of 2 to 8 points. Which interpretation is MOST accurate?
A. Ninety-five percent of treated clients improved between 2 and 8 points
The interval describes uncertainty about the average group difference, not the range of individual client changes.
B. The difference is significant at .05 because the interval excludes 0 ✔ KEY
A 95% interval that does not contain zero corresponds to rejecting the null hypothesis of no difference at alpha = .05.
C. The study has a 5% chance of being repeated with the same 5-point result
Confidence level is not a probability of replicating the exact point estimate.
D. The intervention has a large effect because the whole interval is positive
An interval above zero shows a reliable difference, not a large one; effect size needs a standardized measure.
Rationale: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the population parameter, here the true mean difference. If the procedure were repeated many times, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true value. When a 95% interval for a difference excludes zero, the result is statistically significant at the .05 level. The interval's width also shows precision: narrower intervals reflect more precise estimates.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Inferential statistics: confidence intervals and their relation to hypothesis testing
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

603. nce-s-trt-068 · Research and Program Evaluation · statistics used in outcome research · hard · In review

A client's score on a depression measure drops from 38 to 26. The reliable change index for this measure is 8 points, and the cutoff separating clinical from nonclinical populations is 20. Using the Jacobson and Truax approach, how should this change be classified?
A. Recovered, since the change is larger than the reliable change index
Recovery requires both reliable change and a final score past the cutoff; 26 is still above 20.
B. Unchanged, since the final score is still in the clinical range
A 12-point drop exceeds the 8-point reliable change index, so the change is larger than measurement error.
C. Deteriorated, since the score has not yet fallen below the cutoff
Deterioration means reliable change in the worse direction; this client's score improved.
D. Improved, since the change is reliable but the cutoff is not crossed ✔ KEY
The 12-point drop exceeds the reliable change index, but 26 remains in the clinical range, so the client is improved, not recovered.
Rationale: Jacobson and Truax defined clinically significant change with two criteria: the change must be reliable (larger than expected from measurement error, judged by the reliable change index) and the client must move from the dysfunctional range into the functional range past a cutoff. Clients meeting both are recovered; reliable change without crossing the cutoff is improved; no reliable change is unchanged; reliable worsening is deteriorated. This distinguishes meaningful change for one client from mere statistical significance in a group.
References: Lambert (Outcome Monitoring) — Reliable change index and clinical cutoff (Jacobson & Truax) for classifying client change · Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Clinical versus statistical significance
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

604. nce-s-trt-069 · Assessment and Testing · matching level of care to need · medium · In review

A 52-year-old client drinks about a fifth of vodka daily and wants to stop. The last time he quit on his own, he had a withdrawal seizure and was taken to an emergency department. He has stable housing and a supportive sister. Which recommendation is MOST appropriate as the first step?
A. Begin weekly outpatient counseling with a goal of stopping alcohol use within two weeks
Weekly outpatient care offers no medical monitoring; stopping abruptly with his seizure history puts him at serious risk.
B. Enroll him in an intensive outpatient program and have him taper his drinking on his own
A self-directed taper is unreliable and unsupervised; IOP does not provide the medical management his withdrawal risk requires.
C. Refer him for medically monitored withdrawal management before planning ongoing treatment ✔ KEY
A history of withdrawal seizures signals high withdrawal risk, so medically supervised withdrawal management is the safe first step.
D. Arrange a stay in a sober living home so he can stop drinking in an alcohol-free setting
Sober living provides a substance-free environment but no medical care; it does not address dangerous withdrawal.
Rationale: Level-of-care decisions in addiction treatment consider several dimensions, and acute intoxication and withdrawal potential is assessed first because it can be life-threatening. A prior withdrawal seizure with heavy daily drinking signals high risk for complicated alcohol withdrawal. He should first receive medically monitored withdrawal management; his supportive environment can then help him step into an appropriate ongoing level of care.
References: ASAM Criteria — Withdrawal potential dimension: history of withdrawal seizures and medically monitored withdrawal management
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

605. nce-s-trt-070 · Assessment and Testing · matching level of care to need · medium · In review

A 36-year-old teacher meets criteria for mild alcohol use disorder. She has no withdrawal symptoms or medical problems, is motivated to cut back, and lives with a supportive partner. Her counselor recommends a 28-day residential program "just to be safe." What is the MAIN concern with this recommendation?
A. It places her at a more intensive level than needed and may disrupt her work and supports ✔ KEY
Care should be the least intensive level that safely meets her needs; residential care would pull her from her job and partner without clinical need.
B. Residential programs are designed only for clients who have already failed outpatient care
Placement is based on current multidimensional need, not on a required sequence of failed lower levels.
C. A 28-day stay is too short to change a drinking pattern that has lasted for several years
The problem is not the length of the stay but that residential care is not indicated for her at all.
D. Her motivation shows she does not need any formal treatment for her alcohol use at this time
Motivation is a strength, but she still meets criteria for a disorder and can benefit from outpatient treatment.
Rationale: Placement criteria aim to match clients to the least intensive level of care that is safe and effective, based on a multidimensional assessment. Over-placement wastes resources and can harm clients by disrupting protective factors such as employment, family and community ties. With no withdrawal risk, no medical or psychiatric complications and a supportive home, outpatient treatment fits this client.
References: ASAM Criteria — Multidimensional assessment and placement in the least intensive level of care that is safe and effective
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

606. nce-s-trt-071 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · evidence-based treatment selection · medium · In review

A 58-year-old retired nurse has had trouble falling and staying asleep at least four nights a week for over a year. Medical and substance-related causes have been ruled out, and she would prefer not to take sleep medication. Which psychological treatment has the strongest evidence as a first-line approach?
A. Sleep hygiene education given on its own, such as limiting caffeine and keeping a dark room
Sleep hygiene is a useful component, but guidelines advise against using it alone because it is not effective as a single therapy.
B. Psychodynamic therapy aimed at uncovering the early conflicts that are keeping her awake
Psychodynamic therapy is not an established first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.
C. Progressive muscle relaxation practiced in session, with no change to her sleep schedule
Relaxation can help, but alone it lacks the support of the multicomponent package that restructures sleep behavior.
D. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, including stimulus control and sleep restriction ✔ KEY
CBT-I is the recommended first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults, with strong research support.
Rationale: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a multicomponent treatment that combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive work on sleep-related beliefs and sleep hygiene education. Clinical practice guidelines strongly recommend it as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults. Sleep hygiene education is helpful as part of the package but is not recommended as a stand-alone therapy.
References: AASM Clinical Practice Guideline (Insomnia) — Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia: strong recommendation for multicomponent CBT-I; sleep hygiene not recommended as a single therapy
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

607. nce-s-trt-072 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · evidence-based treatment selection · hard · In review

A 33-year-old client with bipolar I disorder takes lithium as prescribed. Her mood episodes tend to follow disruptions such as overnight shifts, travel across time zones and conflicts with her partner. Her psychiatrist asks the counselor to provide an adjunctive psychotherapy suited to this pattern. Which approach BEST fits?
A. Exposure and response prevention focused on reducing her worry about future mood swings
ERP is a treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder and does not target the rhythm disruptions linked to her episodes.
B. Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy to stabilize daily routines and address conflicts ✔ KEY
IPSRT was developed for bipolar disorder; it regularizes sleep and daily routines and addresses interpersonal problems that trigger episodes.
C. Person-centered therapy alone, letting her choose the focus of each session as it unfolds
A supportive nondirective approach does not provide the structured rhythm and interpersonal work her pattern calls for.
D. Psychoanalytic therapy several times weekly to explore unconscious roots of her moods
Intensive psychoanalytic therapy is not an evidence-based adjunct for bipolar disorder and does not target rhythm stability.
Rationale: Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (IPSRT), developed by Ellen Frank, combines interpersonal psychotherapy with behavioral work on stabilizing daily routines and sleep-wake cycles. It rests on the idea that disrupted social rhythms destabilize circadian functioning and can trigger mood episodes in bipolar disorder. It is used as an adjunct to medication, which fits a client whose episodes follow schedule disruptions and relationship conflicts.
References: IPSRT — Social rhythm stabilization and interpersonal problem areas as an adjunct to medication in bipolar disorder
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

608. nce-s-trt-073 · Research and Program Evaluation · progress monitoring and outcome measures · hard · In review

An experienced counselor declines to use session-by-session outcome measures, saying, "After 20 years, I can tell when a client is getting worse." Which research finding MOST directly challenges this view?
A. Clinicians rarely predict which clients will deteriorate; measure-based alerts flag most ✔ KEY
Studies comparing clinician predictions with actuarial alerts found that therapists identified very few deteriorating clients, while measures flagged most of them.
B. Experienced clinicians tend to underestimate how much progress their clients are making
Research suggests the opposite bias: clinicians tend to overestimate client improvement.
C. Most clients who get worse in counseling say so openly to their counselor within a session
Clients often do not voice deterioration directly, which is one reason structured measures are useful.
D. Standardized measures are accurate only when they are given at intake and at the final session
Pre-post measurement cannot detect deterioration while there is still time to respond; frequent monitoring is the point.
Rationale: Research on routine outcome monitoring found that clinicians, including experienced ones, are poor at predicting which clients will deteriorate, while statistical early-warning systems based on expected recovery curves identify most of them. Clinicians also tend to overrate their own effectiveness. Feedback from frequent standardized measures helps counselors catch clients who are not on track and change course before dropout or treatment failure.
References: Lambert (Outcome Monitoring) — Clinician judgment versus actuarial prediction in detecting client deterioration
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

609. nce-s-trt-074 · Research and Program Evaluation · progress monitoring and outcome measures · easy · In review

A counselor plans to track a client's anxiety with a brief standardized self-report measure over the course of treatment. When should the counselor give the measure for the FIRST time?
A. Once the client has learned the coping skills, so the scores show what they have gained
Waiting until skills are learned removes the starting point needed to show how much the client has changed.
B. At the midpoint of treatment, when the counselor is deciding whether to change approaches
A midpoint score has nothing to be compared against unless an earlier baseline was taken.
C. At intake or before treatment starts, to set a baseline for comparing later scores ✔ KEY
A pretreatment score is the baseline against which every later score is compared.
D. At the final session, so the counselor can document the client's status at discharge
A discharge score alone cannot show change; it needs a baseline taken before treatment.
Rationale: Progress monitoring depends on a baseline: a measurement taken at intake or before treatment begins. Later scores are interpreted relative to that starting point, which allows the counselor to judge whether change is meaningful. Without a baseline, improvement or deterioration cannot be shown.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Outcome assessment: establishing a baseline before treatment for progress monitoring
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

610. nce-s-trt-075 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · discharge and aftercare planning · medium · In review

A 41-year-old client has met all the goals in her treatment plan for depression, and her scores have stayed in the nonclinical range for two months. She says she feels ready to stop. Her counselor would like to keep meeting weekly to "work on deeper issues." What should the counselor do?
A. Continue weekly sessions, since further personal growth is still possible for the client
Continuing when goals are met and the client wants to stop serves the counselor's agenda, not a clinical need.
B. Review her gains, plan for maintaining them, and discharge her with an option to return ✔ KEY
When the client no longer needs counseling, the counselor ends it with a planned discharge and aftercare guidance.
C. End services at this session without further discussion, since the treatment goals are met
Ending abruptly skips the review, relapse-prevention planning and aftercare that a planned discharge includes.
D. Write new long-term goals in the plan so that continued weekly sessions are justified
Adding goals the client did not ask for to justify services is not collaborative and is ethically questionable.
Rationale: Counselors end counseling when it is reasonably apparent that the client no longer needs assistance, is unlikely to benefit or is being harmed. A planned discharge reviews progress toward goals, consolidates gains, identifies early warning signs and coping strategies, and tells the client how to return if needed. The client's readiness and goal attainment, not the counselor's wish to continue, guide the decision.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.c Appropriate Termination · Wiger (Documentation) — Discharge summary: progress toward goals and aftercare recommendations
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

611. nce-s-trt-076 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · safety planning · easy · In review

A new counselor asks why the agency uses a written safety plan with clients at risk of suicide instead of asking them to sign a "no-suicide contract." Which explanation is MOST accurate?
A. A signed contract legally shields the counselor, but it is too formal for most clients
No-suicide contracts offer no reliable legal protection, and formality is not the main problem with them.
B. A contract is the better tool, but a safety plan takes less session time to complete
Contracts are not the better tool, and a good safety plan takes time to build collaboratively.
C. A safety plan replaces the need for any further suicide risk assessment of the client
A safety plan supplements ongoing risk assessment; it does not replace it.
D. A safety plan builds specific coping steps, while a contract lacks evidence of benefit ✔ KEY
Safety plans give clients concrete steps and resources for a crisis; no-suicide contracts lack research support and can give false reassurance.
Rationale: No-suicide contracts ask a client to promise not to harm themselves but give them nothing to do in a crisis, lack evidence of effectiveness and may give counselors false reassurance. A safety plan, such as the Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention, is developed collaboratively and lists warning signs, internal coping strategies, social contacts, people to ask for help, professional and crisis resources, and steps to make the environment safer.
References: Stanley-Brown SPI — Safety planning as an alternative to no-suicide contracts
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

612. nce-s-trt-077 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · stages of change and treatment readiness · medium · In review

A 47-year-old client who has smoked for 30 years tells his counselor that he has picked a quit date two weeks from now, bought nicotine patches and told his family. Which counselor response BEST matches his current stage of change?
A. Help him build a specific quit plan that anticipates triggers and names his coping steps ✔ KEY
He is in preparation, so the task is to firm up a concrete, workable action plan.
B. Give him information about the health risks of smoking to raise his awareness of them
Consciousness raising fits precontemplation; he is already convinced and taking steps.
C. Explore his mixed feelings by listing the pros and cons of smoking and of quitting
A decisional balance exercise suits contemplation, when the client is still ambivalent about changing.
D. Focus on preventing relapse in the months after he has stayed smoke-free for a while
Relapse prevention for sustained change belongs to the maintenance stage, which he has not reached.
Rationale: In the Transtheoretical Model, the preparation stage describes people who intend to act within about the next month and have already taken small steps, such as setting a date or buying supplies. Stage-matched interventions in preparation help the client turn intention into a concrete plan, anticipate obstacles and strengthen commitment. Interventions suited to earlier stages can feel redundant to a client who has already decided.
References: Transtheoretical Model — Preparation stage: intention to act within 30 days and stage-matched action planning
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

613. nce-s-trt-078 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · stages of change and treatment readiness · hard · In review

A 29-year-old client stopped using methamphetamine eight months ago but used again for three days after a breakup. She tells her counselor, "I'm back at square one." According to Prochaska and DiClemente's model, which statement BEST reflects how relapse is understood?
A. Relapse sends most people back to precontemplation, so change must restart from the start
Only a small share of people who relapse regress to precontemplation; most do not start over.
B. Relapse after six months shows the client had not truly reached the maintenance stage
Relapse can occur from maintenance; it does not mean the earlier progress was not real.
C. Relapse is common, and most people recycle to contemplation or preparation and try again ✔ KEY
The spiral model shows that most people who relapse recycle to contemplation or preparation and draw on what they learned.
D. Relapse shows that the stages of change model does not apply to stimulant use disorders
The model has been applied across many addictive behaviors, including stimulant use, and expects relapse.
Rationale: Prochaska, DiClemente and Norcross described change as a spiral rather than a straight line. Relapse is common, and most people who relapse do not regress all the way to precontemplation; they recycle to contemplation or preparation and try again, often with lessons from earlier attempts. Framing relapse this way helps counselors counter the client's "square one" thinking and reduce shame.
References: Transtheoretical Model — Spiral model of change: relapse and recycling through the stages
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

614. nce-s-trt-079 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · coordination of care and referral · hard · In review

A client's primary care physician calls the counselor to coordinate care and asks for "everything you have," including the private process notes the counselor keeps separate from the client's clinical record. Under HIPAA, which statement is accurate?
A. HIPAA bars the counselor from sharing any client information with a physician without consent
HIPAA allows disclosure of protected health information to another provider for treatment; it does not bar all sharing.
B. The physician may obtain the process notes because they are part of the client's medical record
Psychotherapy notes kept separate from the record are not part of the general medical record and receive extra protection.
C. All records, process notes included, may be sent because disclosure for treatment is permitted
The treatment exception does not cover psychotherapy notes, which need specific authorization.
D. The process notes need the client's specific authorization; record information may be shared ✔ KEY
Psychotherapy notes generally need a separate authorization, while information in the clinical record may be shared for treatment.
Rationale: HIPAA gives psychotherapy notes, the counselor's separate notes analyzing session content, special protection: most disclosures, including to other providers, require the client's specific authorization. Information in the clinical record, such as diagnosis, treatment plan, symptoms and progress summaries, may be disclosed to another provider for treatment purposes. Many counselors still obtain a release before coordinating care, and state law or ethics codes may require stricter consent.
References: HIPAA — Privacy Rule 45 CFR 164.508(a)(2): authorization required for psychotherapy notes; 164.506 disclosures for treatment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

615. nce-s-trt-080 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · SMART goals and measurable objectives · easy · In review

A 30-year-old client seeks counseling because panic attacks keep her from driving on the highway to work. Her counselor adds this objective: "Client will walk 30 minutes three times a week for the next eight weeks, as recorded in an exercise log." Which SMART criterion is this objective MOST likely to fail?
A. Measurable, because walking cannot be counted or recorded in any reliable way
Walking time and frequency are easy to record in a log, so the objective is measurable.
B. Relevant, because it is not clearly tied to the problem the client came in for ✔ KEY
Nothing links walking to her highway-driving panic, so the objective does not fit her presenting concern.
C. Time-bound, because the objective does not give any time period for the change
The objective states an eight-week period, so it is time-bound.
D. Specific, because the objective does not state how often or how long she will walk
The objective names the activity, duration and frequency, so it is specific.
Rationale: SMART objectives are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. This objective is precise, countable and time-limited, but it does not connect to the client's stated problem of panic while driving on highways. Relevant objectives flow from the presenting concern and the goal, such as graded driving exposure tracked in a log.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Treatment plans: objectives linked to the presenting problem and long-term goals
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

616. nce-s-trt-081 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · collaborative treatment planning · medium · In review

A 30-year-old man with a mild intellectual disability lives in a group home and is starting counseling for anger after conflicts with a housemate. The group home manager offers to write his treatment goals for him to save time. What is the BEST approach?
A. Build goals with him in plain words with visual aids, inviting staff input if he agrees ✔ KEY
Adapting the process to his abilities keeps him at the center of planning, with staff involved only with his consent.
B. Accept the manager's goals, since staff observe his daily behavior more than he can report
Staff observations are useful input, but letting staff set his goals removes him from his own treatment planning.
C. Write the goals in standard clinical language and read them aloud to him for his signature
Having him sign a plan he did not shape, in language he may not understand, is not meaningful collaboration.
D. Delay planning until a court-appointed guardian can be found to decide on his goals
Nothing indicates he lacks capacity or has a guardian; a disability alone does not remove his right to participate.
Rationale: Counselors and clients work jointly to devise counseling plans that fit the client's abilities, developmental level and circumstances. For a client with an intellectual disability, collaboration means adapting the process, using plain language, concrete examples and visual supports, rather than handing planning to others. Support staff can contribute valuable information when the client agrees.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.1.c Counseling Plans: plans consistent with the abilities, developmental level and circumstances of clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

617. nce-s-trt-082 · Research and Program Evaluation · program evaluation and needs assessment · easy · In review

At the end of its first full year, a middle school's peer mediation program is evaluated so the school board can decide whether to continue funding it. Which type of evaluation is this?
A. Formative evaluation
Formative evaluation gathers feedback during a program to improve it, not to judge it for a funding decision.
B. Needs assessment
A needs assessment identifies gaps before a program is designed; it does not judge an existing program.
C. Single-subject design
A single-subject design tracks one person's behavior across phases, not a whole program's worth.
D. Summative evaluation ✔ KEY
Summative evaluation judges a program's overall effectiveness at the end of a cycle to inform decisions such as continuing funding.
Rationale: Summative evaluation takes place at the end of a program or program cycle and judges its overall merit or effectiveness, often to inform decisions about continuing, expanding or ending it. Formative evaluation, by contrast, happens while a program is running and is used to improve it. A board deciding on future funding needs a summative judgment.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Program evaluation: formative vs summative evaluation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

618. nce-s-trt-083 · Research and Program Evaluation · program evaluation and needs assessment · medium · In review

To estimate the need for youth mental health services in a county, an agency analyzes existing census data, school dropout rates, juvenile arrest records and emergency department visits for self-harm. No residents or providers are contacted directly. Which needs assessment method is the agency using?
A. Key informant approach
This method gathers views from knowledgeable people such as clinicians or community leaders, who were not contacted here.
B. Community forum approach
A community forum invites residents to public meetings to voice needs; no residents were involved.
C. Social indicators approach ✔ KEY
This method infers need from existing public statistics such as census, school and health records.
D. Field survey of residents
A field survey collects new data directly from a sample of residents, which the agency did not do.
Rationale: Needs assessments can draw on several methods. The social indicators approach infers community need from existing public data, such as census figures, health statistics and school or court records. Key informant interviews, community forums and field surveys all collect new information directly from people. Many needs assessments combine methods because existing data alone may miss what residents and providers see.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Needs assessment methods: key informants, community forums, surveys and social indicators
⚑ Check: Confirm that the Erford text names the social indicators approach among needs assessment methods; the method itself is standard (Warheit, Bell & Schwab).
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

619. nce-s-trt-084 · Research and Program Evaluation · program evaluation and needs assessment · medium · In review

An evaluator of a new parenting program at a community center records how many sessions are offered, who attends, whether the target families of toddlers are being reached and whether facilitators cover each planned module. She does not yet measure changes in parenting. Which type of evaluation is she conducting?
A. Outcome evaluation
An outcome evaluation measures changes in participants, such as parenting skills, which she is not yet doing.
B. Process evaluation ✔ KEY
Process evaluation examines how a program is delivered: reach, attendance and whether it runs as planned.
C. Needs assessment
A needs assessment identifies gaps before a program is built; this program is already running.
D. Cost-benefit study
A cost-benefit study compares program costs with outcomes converted to dollars; no costs are examined here.
Rationale: Process (implementation) evaluation asks whether a program is being delivered as intended and to the intended population, tracking things like attendance, reach and coverage of planned content. Outcome evaluation asks whether participants changed as a result. Process data also help interpret outcomes, because a program that is not delivered as planned cannot fairly be judged ineffective.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Program evaluation: process vs outcome evaluation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

620. nce-s-trt-085 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · coordination of care and referral · medium · In review

A counselor in a rural clinic refers a 66-year-old client with worsening depression to a telepsychiatry service for a medication evaluation. The client signs a release so the two providers can share information. What should the counselor do to BEST complete the referral?
A. Follow up to confirm the appointment took place and share relevant information as agreed ✔ KEY
Closing the loop confirms the client connected with care and lets both providers coordinate treatment.
B. Give the client the service's phone number and leave the scheduling and follow-up to him
Passing on a number without follow-up is a passive referral and raises the risk that the client never connects.
C. End counseling once the referral is made, since the psychiatrist now manages his depression
A medication evaluation adds to counseling; ending services would leave the client without psychotherapy.
D. Wait to discuss the referral until his next monthly session in case he brings it up himself
Waiting passively for the client to raise it can leave a worsening depression without timely follow-up.
Rationale: A referral is complete only when the client actually connects with the new service. Good care coordination includes helping the client schedule, confirming the appointment occurred, and, with consent, sharing information so both providers work from the same plan. Active follow-up matters especially for older or rural clients, who may face transportation, technology or access barriers.
