Understanding the client's worldview, and the real barriers behind it, guides culturally responsive goals such as advocacy.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Worldview: locus of control and locus of responsibility quadrants
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

735. nce-s-cou-115 · Social and Cultural Diversity · multicultural counseling competencies · hard · In review

At intake, a counselor briefly asks a Latina client whether she minds working with a counselor of a different ethnicity. He never returns to culture, even when she later describes ethnic bias from her supervisor. In Day-Vines and colleagues' broaching continuum, which style does this MOST reflect?
A. Avoidant
An avoidant counselor does not raise race or culture at all; this counselor did raise it once.
B. Infusing
An infusing counselor builds attention to culture and social justice into all of their work, well beyond the session.
C. Isolating ✔ KEY
An isolating counselor broaches culture in a superficial, one-time way to satisfy an obligation, then drops it.
D. Integrated/congruent
An integrated/congruent counselor broaches routinely and links the client's cultural experiences to the presenting concerns.
Rationale: Broaching is the counselor's consistent, open invitation to explore how race, ethnicity and culture bear on the client's concerns. Day-Vines and colleagues described a continuum of broaching styles: avoidant, isolating, continuing/incongruent, integrated/congruent and infusing. Raising culture once and never connecting it to the client's experience is the isolating style.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Broaching race and culture in counseling: Day-Vines broaching continuum
⚑ Check: Verify the broaching style names and order against Day-Vines et al. (2007) and confirm Sue & Sue covers them.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

736. nce-s-cou-116 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · crisis intervention models · medium · In review

A counselor deployed to a family assistance center after a mass shooting will use Psychological First Aid (PFA) as developed by the National Child Traumatic Stress Network and National Center for PTSD. Which practice is NOT one of the PFA core actions?
A. Linking survivors with needed collaborative services
Linkage with collaborative services is one of the eight PFA core actions.
B. Gathering information on current needs and worries
Information gathering about current needs and concerns is a PFA core action.
C. Offering information on coping with stress reactions
Providing information on coping is a PFA core action.
D. Asking survivors to recount the event in detail ✔ KEY
PFA does not require survivors to describe the event in detail; pressing for a detailed account can be distressing and resembles debriefing, which PFA avoids.
Rationale: PFA's eight core actions are contact and engagement, safety and comfort, stabilization, information gathering on current needs and concerns, practical assistance, connection with social supports, information on coping, and linkage with collaborative services. It is evidence-informed, flexible and non-intrusive, and it does not push survivors to retell or process their trauma.
References: Psychological First Aid Field Operations Guide (NCTSN/NCPTSD) — The eight PFA core actions
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

737. nce-s-cou-117 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · trauma-informed interventions · medium · In review

A counselor using trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (TF-CBT) with a 9-year-old has completed psychoeducation and parenting skills, relaxation, affective modulation and cognitive coping. Following the PRACTICE sequence, which component comes NEXT?
A. In vivo mastery of trauma reminders
In vivo mastery follows the trauma narrative and is used only when the child avoids safe reminders.
B. Conjoint child-parent sessions
Conjoint sessions, often used to share the narrative with the caregiver, come after the narrative is developed.
C. Enhancing future safety
Enhancing safety is the final component of the PRACTICE sequence.
D. Trauma narrative and processing ✔ KEY
After the stabilization skills, the child gradually develops and processes a narrative of the trauma.
Rationale: TF-CBT, developed by Cohen, Mannarino and Deblinger, follows the PRACTICE components: Psychoeducation and Parenting skills, Relaxation, Affective modulation, Cognitive coping, Trauma narrative and processing, In vivo mastery, Conjoint child-parent sessions and Enhancing safety. Coping skills are built first so the child can tolerate the gradual exposure of the trauma narrative.
References: NICE guidelines — PTSD (NG116): trauma-focused CBT for children and young people
⚑ Check: The PRACTICE order is from Cohen, Mannarino and Deblinger; confirm NICE NG116 is an acceptable citation or swap to a source that describes the model.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

738. nce-s-cou-118 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · trauma-informed interventions · medium · In review

After a year at a child advocacy center, a counselor notices lasting changes in her own beliefs: she now sees the world as unsafe, distrusts adults around her own children, and has intrusive images drawn from clients' accounts. Which term BEST describes her experience?
A. Burnout
Burnout is exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness from workload and work conditions; it need not involve trauma-related changes in beliefs.
B. Vicarious trauma ✔ KEY
Vicarious trauma is a cumulative change in the helper's inner world, such as beliefs about safety and trust, from empathic engagement with clients' trauma.
C. Compassion satisfaction
Compassion satisfaction is the positive fulfillment helpers draw from their work, the opposite of her experience.
D. Countertransference
Countertransference is the counselor's reaction to a particular client rooted in her own history, not a cumulative shift in worldview.
Rationale: Vicarious trauma (McCann and Pearlman) is a lasting shift in a helper's beliefs about safety, trust and control that results from repeated exposure to clients' trauma. Compassion fatigue (Figley) emphasizes the emotional cost of caring, including secondary traumatic stress, while burnout stems from work conditions. Remedies include supervision, caseload balance, peer support and personal self-care.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counselor wellness: burnout, compassion fatigue and vicarious trauma · ACA Code of Ethics — C.2.g Impairment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

739. nce-s-cou-119 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · trauma-informed interventions · easy · In review

While talking about an assault, a client begins to dissociate: she stares blankly, speaks in a monotone, and says the room feels "far away." What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Guide her to name things she can see and feel her feet on the floor ✔ KEY
Grounding techniques that engage the senses and body bring her back into the present moment and her window of tolerance.
B. Encourage her to keep going so the memory can be fully processed today
Continuing while she is dissociated is unlikely to be therapeutic and can overwhelm her further.
C. Ask her to close her eyes and picture the memory in greater detail
Closing her eyes and deepening the memory increases the risk of further dissociation.
D. Interpret her dissociation as resistance to the work of the session
Dissociation is a protective response to overwhelming arousal, not resistance to be interpreted.
Rationale: When a client dissociates or becomes flooded, trauma-informed counselors first re-establish safety and present-moment awareness through grounding, such as the 5-4-3-2-1 senses exercise, feeling the feet on the floor, holding an object or naming the date and place. Trauma processing resumes only when the client is back within her window of tolerance.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Crisis and trauma counseling: grounding and stabilization
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

740. nce-s-cou-120 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · trauma-informed interventions · medium · In review

In eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), the client holds the disturbing image, negative belief and body sensations in mind while the counselor leads sets of eye movements, and distress ratings are taken until they fall toward zero. In Shapiro's eight-phase protocol, which phase is this?
A. Preparation
Preparation builds the relationship, explains EMDR and teaches calming skills before memories are processed.
B. Assessment
Assessment identifies the target image, negative and positive cognitions and baseline ratings without bilateral stimulation.
C. Desensitization ✔ KEY
Desensitization uses sets of bilateral stimulation while the client attends to the target, until the SUD rating approaches 0.
D. Reevaluation
Reevaluation happens at the start of the next session to check whether earlier gains have held.
Rationale: Francine Shapiro's EMDR protocol has eight phases: history taking, preparation, assessment, desensitization, installation, body scan, closure and reevaluation. Bilateral stimulation (eye movements, taps or tones) is used during desensitization, installation of the positive cognition and the body scan. EMDR is recommended by several PTSD practice guidelines.
References: APA CPG — PTSD guideline (2017): EMDR as a conditionally recommended psychotherapy
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

741. nce-s-cou-121 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · Adlerian therapy · medium · In review

During a lifestyle assessment, an Adlerian counselor asks a 38-year-old client to describe a single, specific incident from early childhood that she can picture clearly, including what she felt at the time. The counselor is LEAST concerned with whether the memory is factually accurate. What is the main purpose of gathering these early recollections?
A. To uncover repressed trauma so it can be worked through in transference
Recovering repressed material and working it through in the transference is a psychoanalytic goal, not the Adlerian use of early memories.
B. To reveal her private logic and core convictions about self, others and life ✔ KEY
Adlerians treat early recollections as projective: the memories a person keeps reflect present convictions, goals and basic mistakes in the lifestyle.
C. To identify the conditioned stimuli that first triggered her current anxiety
Locating conditioned stimuli is a behavioral assessment task; Adlerians are not seeking a learning history of specific triggers.
D. To confirm the accuracy of her family history before choosing a diagnosis
Adlerians value early recollections for what the client selects and how she tells it, not for historical accuracy or diagnosis.
Rationale: In Adlerian lifestyle assessment, early recollections are single, specific memories, usually from before about age 10. Because people remember events consistent with their current view of life, the memories serve as a projective window into private logic, goals and basic mistakes. Factual accuracy matters little; the themes and the client's stance within the memory matter most.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Adlerian Therapy: lifestyle assessment and early recollections
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

742. nce-s-cou-122 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · Adlerian therapy · easy · In review

An Adlerian counselor asks a client who feels stuck in a low mood to close his eyes and recall a pleasant memory, notice the feelings that come with it, then recall a painful memory and notice how his feelings shift, and then return to the pleasant one. The aim is to show him that he can influence his feelings by what he chooses to think about. This is called:
A. Rational emotive imagery
Rational emotive imagery (REBT) has the client imagine a feared event and change the emotion by changing the belief, not alternate pleasant and painful memories.
B. Acting as if
Acting as if invites the client to behave as though he were already the person he wishes to be, not to switch between memories.
C. The push-button technique ✔ KEY
The push-button technique alternates pleasant and unpleasant images so the client sees he can "push the button" for the feeling he wants.
D. Systematic desensitization
Systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with a graded fear hierarchy; it is a behavioral fear-reduction method.
Rationale: The Adlerian push-button technique teaches that feelings are not simply things that happen to us. By deliberately calling up pleasant and then unpleasant memories and noticing the emotional shift, the client learns he can create or change feelings by what he chooses to focus on, which supports responsibility and encouragement.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Adlerian Therapy: reorientation techniques (push-button technique)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

743. nce-s-cou-123 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · Adlerian therapy · easy · In review

A 15-year-old who failed her first algebra test tells her school counselor she is "just bad at math" and wants to drop the class. She studied every evening for the next test and raised her score to a C. Which counselor response BEST reflects the Adlerian use of encouragement?
A. "You're so smart. I was sure you would get an A one of these days."
This is praise that rates the person and sets an outcome standard; Adlerians distinguish such praise from encouragement.
B. "A C is still a C. Let's set a firm goal of a B on the next test."
This focuses on the shortfall and raises the bar, which can deepen discouragement rather than build courage.
C. "Maybe math just isn't your thing. Many people do fine without it."
This colludes with her discouraged belief that she lacks ability, which is the mistaken conviction to be challenged.
D. "You studied each night, and your score rose. Your effort paid off." ✔ KEY
Encouragement recognizes effort and improvement, building the courage and faith in herself that she can grow.
Rationale: Adlerians view many problems as rooted in discouragement, and they see encouragement as the most powerful method for change. Encouragement focuses on effort, improvement and the person's strengths, and it is not contingent on success. Praise, by contrast, rewards outcomes and can teach that worth depends on performing well.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Adlerian Therapy: encouragement as a core process
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

744. nce-s-cou-124 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · person-centered therapy · medium · In review

Carl Rogers (1957) proposed six conditions that are necessary and sufficient for therapeutic personality change. Besides the counselor's congruence, unconditional positive regard and empathy, which condition describes the state of the client entering the relationship?
A. The client is incongruent, being vulnerable or anxious ✔ KEY
Rogers specified that the client is in a state of incongruence, vulnerable or anxious; this is one of the six conditions.
B. The client has insight into the childhood origins of distress
Insight into childhood origins is a psychodynamic aim and was not among Rogers's conditions.
C. The client agrees to specific, measurable treatment goals
Measurable goal setting is more typical of behavioral and brief approaches; Rogers did not require it.
D. The client has received an accurate diagnosis from the counselor
Rogers considered diagnosis unnecessary for change and potentially harmful to the relationship.
Rationale: Rogers's six conditions are: two persons are in psychological contact; the client is incongruent, vulnerable or anxious; the counselor is congruent in the relationship; the counselor experiences unconditional positive regard; the counselor experiences empathic understanding of the client's internal frame of reference; and the client at least minimally perceives the counselor's regard and empathy. He held that no particular technique, insight or diagnosis was required.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-Centered Therapy: necessary and sufficient conditions for change
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

745. nce-s-cou-125 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · person-centered therapy · easy · In review

A 60-year-old client caring for his wife with dementia asks his counselor, "Just tell me straight: should I move her into a memory care facility or not?" Which counselor response is MOST consistent with a person-centered, nondirective stance?
A. "Most families in your situation find a facility is the better choice."
This gives advice from the counselor's frame of reference and shifts the decision away from the client.
B. "Let's list the pros and cons this week and score each one at home."
A structured decision task is a directive, problem-solving move rather than following the client's experience.
C. "You feel torn, and you wish someone would tell you what is right." ✔ KEY
This empathic reflection stays in his frame of reference and trusts his capacity to reach his own decision.
D. "Perhaps your guilt about her illness is what makes deciding so hard."
This is an interpretation that imposes the counselor's hypothesis about the cause of his difficulty.
Rationale: Person-centered counselors trust the client's actualizing tendency and capacity for self-direction. Rather than advising, assigning tasks or interpreting, they offer accurate empathy, genuineness and unconditional positive regard, so the client can explore his own experience and arrive at his own choice.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-Centered Therapy: nondirective stance and the client as expert
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

746. nce-s-cou-126 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · person-centered therapy · medium · In review

A counseling student is summarizing common criticisms of the person-centered approach for a theories exam. Which criticism is MOST often raised?
A. It casts the counselor as an expert who interprets the client's hidden motives
This describes classical psychoanalysis; person-centered counselors avoid the interpretive expert role.
B. Its low structure may not suit clients who want or expect active direction ✔ KEY
Critics note that a nondirective stance can leave some clients, including many from cultures that expect an active helper, without enough guidance.
C. It depends heavily on standardized testing and diagnosis to guide treatment
Rogers de-emphasized testing and diagnosis, so this is the opposite of the approach.
D. It treats the therapeutic relationship as secondary to specific techniques
The relationship is the core of person-centered therapy, which places little weight on techniques.
Rationale: Person-centered therapy is praised for its emphasis on the relationship and the client's resources, and its core conditions are well supported by alliance research. Common criticisms are that it can be too passive or unstructured for clients in crisis or those who expect direction, and that some practitioners reduce it to simple reflection without real presence.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-Centered Therapy: limitations and criticisms; multicultural perspective
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

747. nce-s-cou-127 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · existential therapy · medium · In review

A 29-year-old client has been offered a job abroad and says he feels anxious about the choice because no one can make it for him and he will have to live with the results. How would an existential counselor MOST likely view this anxiety?
A. As normal anxiety that comes with freedom and can spur growth and choice ✔ KEY
Existentialists see normal anxiety as an unavoidable part of facing freedom and responsibility, and as a potential source of growth.
B. As a symptom to be reduced quickly with relaxation and breathing skills
Symptom reduction is a behavioral aim; existential counselors do not try to eliminate normal anxiety.
C. As the result of repressed impulses breaking through his ego defenses
This is a psychoanalytic account of anxiety, not an existential one.
D. As the product of an irrational demand that he dispute in homework
Disputing irrational demands is REBT; existential therapy treats this anxiety as a meaningful response to real givens.
Rationale: Existential therapy distinguishes normal anxiety, a fitting response to freedom, responsibility, death and isolation, from neurotic anxiety, which is out of proportion and blocks living. Rollo May described normal anxiety as something to face, not remove, because it can motivate authentic choice. The counselor helps the client own his freedom rather than escape the discomfort.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Existential Therapy: normal and neurotic anxiety; freedom and responsibility
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

748. nce-s-cou-128 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · existential therapy · hard · In review

Which pairing of existential theorist and contribution is accurate?
A. Viktor Frankl: the four ultimate concerns of death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness
The four ultimate concerns were described by Irvin Yalom, not Frankl.
B. Irvin Yalom: logotherapy and the will to meaning as the primary human motivation
Logotherapy and the will to meaning are Frankl's contributions.
C. Rollo May: the I-Thou relationship as the basis of genuine human encounter
The I-Thou relationship comes from the philosopher Martin Buber, though existential counselors draw on it.
D. Rollo May: bringing existential ideas to American therapy and writing on anxiety ✔ KEY
May was a key figure in introducing existential thought to U.S. psychotherapy and wrote extensively on anxiety, courage and freedom.
Rationale: Viktor Frankl founded logotherapy, emphasizing the will to meaning. Rollo May helped bring European existential thought to American psychotherapy, writing on normal anxiety and the courage to face freedom. Irvin Yalom identified four ultimate concerns: death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness. Martin Buber, a philosopher, described the I-Thou relationship.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Existential Therapy: key figures (Frankl, May, Yalom) and philosophical roots
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

749. nce-s-cou-129 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · existential therapy · hard · In review

A client dreads sweating heavily when giving presentations, and the more he fears it, the more he sweats. His counselor asks him, before his next talk, to try to sweat as much as he possibly can and to show the audience just how much he can sweat. Which Frankl technique is this?
A. Dereflection
Dereflection redirects attention away from oneself and the symptom toward other meanings; it does not ask the client to wish for the symptom.
B. Flooding
Flooding is a behavioral exposure method of prolonged, intense contact with the feared stimulus, not a humorous wish for the symptom.
C. Paradoxical intention ✔ KEY
Frankl's paradoxical intention asks clients to intend the very thing they fear, breaking the cycle of anticipatory anxiety.
D. Ordeal therapy
Ordeal therapy (Haley) attaches a burdensome task to the symptom; it is strategic, not logotherapeutic.
Rationale: In paradoxical intention, Frankl asked clients to wish for or deliberately produce what they fear, often with humor. Doing so interrupts anticipatory anxiety, the fear of the symptom that keeps the symptom going. Frankl paired it with dereflection, which moves attention away from hyper-reflection on oneself.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Existential Therapy: Frankl's logotherapy, paradoxical intention and dereflection
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

750. nce-s-cou-130 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · gestalt therapy · easy · In review

A client speaks of her partner and herself as "we" when describing every feeling and opinion. She says they "never disagree," and she becomes anxious and vague when the counselor asks what she alone wants. In gestalt terms, this blurring of the boundary between self and other is called:
A. Introjection
Introjection is swallowing others' beliefs and standards whole without examining them.
B. Confluence ✔ KEY
Confluence blurs the self-other boundary so that differences are not felt, keeping conflict and separate wants out of awareness.
C. Projection
Projection attributes to others the traits or feelings one disowns in oneself.
D. Deflection
Deflection avoids contact through humor, vagueness or changing the subject.
Rationale: Gestalt therapy names several disturbances at the contact boundary: introjection, projection, retroflection, deflection and confluence. In confluence the person merges with others, seeks constant agreement and loses touch with personal wants. Counselors help such clients notice differences and ask, "What do you feel? What do you want?"
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Gestalt Therapy: contact and resistances to contact (confluence)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

751. nce-s-cou-131 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · gestalt therapy · medium · In review

A client gives a long, detached account of an argument he had with his brother two years ago. As he talks, his voice tightens and he taps his foot quickly. Which response is MOST consistent with gestalt therapy?
A. "What are you aware of right now as you tell me this? Notice your foot." ✔ KEY
This brings him into the here and now and directs attention to present, nonverbal experience, the heart of gestalt awareness work.
B. "Why do you think you and your brother end up fighting like that so often?"
Gestalt counselors avoid "why" questions, which invite intellectualizing rather than present awareness.
C. "What were you telling yourself during the argument that upset you?"
Identifying self-talk is a cognitive-behavioral move focused on the past event rather than present experience.
D. "It sounds as if your brother reminds you of a parent from childhood."
This is a psychodynamic interpretation; gestalt counselors favor client discovery over counselor interpretation.
Rationale: Gestalt therapy holds that awareness in the present moment is itself curative. Counselors shift clients from talking about past events to experiencing what is happening now, often by noticing body language, voice and breath. "What" and "how" questions are preferred to "why" questions, which tend to produce explanations instead of contact.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Gestalt Therapy: the now, awareness, and attention to nonverbal behavior
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

752. nce-s-cou-132 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · gestalt therapy · hard · In review

Arnold Beisser's paradoxical theory of change is a foundation of gestalt practice. Which statement BEST captures it?
A. Change happens when the counselor prescribes the symptom the client most wants to stop
Prescribing the symptom is a strategic family therapy directive, not Beisser's theory.
B. Change happens when clients replace irrational demands with flexible preferences
Replacing demands with preferences is the REBT model of change.
C. Change happens when the counselor interprets resistance until the client gains insight
Interpreting resistance to produce insight is a psychoanalytic method.
D. Change happens when one becomes what one is, not when one tries to be what one is not ✔ KEY
Beisser held that change comes through full awareness and acceptance of who one is now, not through striving to be different.
Rationale: Beisser's paradoxical theory of change states that the more a person tries to be who he or she is not, the more the person stays the same. Change occurs when the person fully experiences and owns current reality. Gestalt counselors therefore do not push for change; they heighten awareness of what is, trusting that integration follows.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Gestalt Therapy: the paradoxical theory of change
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

753. nce-s-cou-133 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · rational emotive behavior therapy · easy · In review

A client who believes it would be unbearable to look foolish is assigned homework: wear a brightly mismatched outfit to the grocery store and loudly ask a clerk where the milk is while standing next to it. She is to notice that she can tolerate others' reactions and still accept herself. This REBT technique is called:
A. Paradoxical intention
Paradoxical intention (Frankl) asks clients to wish for a feared symptom, such as trying to blush or sweat.
B. A shame-attacking exercise ✔ KEY
Shame-attacking exercises have clients do harmless "foolish" acts in public to learn that disapproval is tolerable and not a verdict on their worth.
C. Rational emotive imagery
Rational emotive imagery is done in imagination, not by acting in public.
D. Systematic desensitization
Systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with a graded hierarchy, usually in imagination, to reduce fear.
Rationale: Albert Ellis developed shame-attacking exercises as in vivo homework. Clients deliberately do something they consider shameful but that harms no one, then work on not putting themselves down. REBT relies heavily on such homework to practice new rational beliefs between sessions.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — REBT: behavioral techniques, homework and shame-attacking exercises
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

754. nce-s-cou-134 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · rational emotive behavior therapy · hard · In review

After failing the bar exam, a 27-year-old law graduate says, "I failed, so I'm a failure." Her REBT counselor works toward unconditional self-acceptance (USA). Which goal BEST reflects this concept?
A. Restore her self-esteem by listing past successes that show her real worth
Ellis criticized self-esteem as conditional on achievement; rebuilding it through successes keeps worth tied to performance.
B. Help her see the exam was unimportant so the result need not upset her
REBT does not deny that the outcome is bad; appropriate disappointment is a healthy negative emotion.
C. Rate the failed exam as a poor result while accepting herself as fallible ✔ KEY
USA means rating behaviors and outcomes, not the whole self, and accepting oneself as a fallible human regardless of performance.
D. Trace how her parents' high standards first taught her to fear failure
REBT focuses on present beliefs; tracing childhood origins is not needed for unconditional self-acceptance.
Rationale: Ellis argued that global self-rating is irrational because a person is too complex to sum up with one score. Unconditional self-acceptance asks clients to evaluate their actions and outcomes, sometimes harshly, while accepting themselves without conditions. He contrasted this with self-esteem, which rises and falls with success and approval.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — REBT: unconditional self-acceptance versus self-esteem
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

755. nce-s-cou-135 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · rational emotive behavior therapy · medium · In review

A counselor asks a client to imagine vividly that he is turned down for a date, let himself feel the depressed panic that follows, and then, while keeping the image, change the feeling to disappointment. Afterward they discuss what he told himself to make the change. This REBT technique is:
A. Rational emotive imagery ✔ KEY
Rational emotive imagery has clients hold a vivid image of a feared event and shift an unhealthy emotion to a healthy one by changing the belief.
B. The push-button technique
The Adlerian push-button technique alternates pleasant and unpleasant memories; it does not keep one feared image constant.
C. Covert sensitization
Covert sensitization pairs an unwanted behavior with imagined aversive consequences to reduce that behavior.
D. Systematic desensitization
Systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with graded fear images; it does not ask the client to feel and then transform an emotion.
Rationale: In rational emotive imagery, the client imagines one of the worst things that could happen, allows the unhealthy emotion, and then changes it to a healthy negative emotion such as disappointment or concern. The change happens through a shift in belief, which the client then identifies and practices, often daily as homework.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — REBT: emotive techniques (rational emotive imagery)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

756. nce-s-cou-136 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · solution-focused brief therapy · easy · In review

A client says she has felt sad "every single day" since moving to a new city. Her counselor asks, "Think about this past week. When was the sadness even a little lighter, and what was different then?" This is an example of:
A. A scaling question
Scaling questions ask the client to rate the problem or progress on a numerical scale, such as 0 to 10.
B. The miracle question
The miracle question asks the client to imagine the problem solved overnight and describe what would be different.
C. A coping question
Coping questions ask how the client has kept going despite difficulty, not when the problem was less present.
D. An exception question ✔ KEY
Exception questions search for times the problem was absent or less severe, so the client can repeat what worked.
Rationale: Solution-focused counselors assume that problems are never constant. Exception questions direct attention to times the problem was absent or milder and to what the client was doing then. These exceptions become the raw material for solutions: do more of what works.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Solution-Focused Brief Therapy: exception questions
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

757. nce-s-cou-137 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · solution-focused brief therapy · medium · In review

A father raising three children alone after his wife's death says nothing is going well, and he cannot recall a single time things were better. Which response is MOST consistent with a solution-focused coping question?
A. "Let's find out what in your past is keeping you so stuck right now."
Searching the past for the cause of the problem is problem-focused, which SFBT deliberately avoids.
B. "With so much on you, how have you managed to keep the kids fed and here?" ✔ KEY
A coping question highlights the strength and effort already present when the client sees no exceptions.
C. "On a scale of 0 to 10, how bad would you say things are for you today?"
This is a scaling question, and framing it around how bad things are keeps the focus on the problem.
D. "It sounds like the grief is still very raw. Tell me more about the loss."
This empathic invitation is appropriate in many models but is not an SFBT coping question.
Rationale: When clients cannot identify exceptions, solution-focused counselors use coping questions, such as "How have you managed to keep going?" These questions bring out the client's resources and small successes already present in a hard situation. They respect the difficulty while shifting attention toward competence.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Solution-Focused Brief Therapy: coping questions and client competence
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

758. nce-s-cou-138 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · solution-focused brief therapy · hard · In review

A 16-year-old is sent to counseling by his school after a fight. He says he has no problem and is only there because the principal required it. In de Shazer's terms, what is the counselor-client relationship, and what is the BEST response?
A. Complainant; ask him to watch for times when things go a bit better
A complainant sees a problem but not himself as part of the solution; this teen does not yet see a problem at all.
B. Customer; give him an action task to practice before the next session
A customer sees a problem and is ready to act; assigning tasks to an uncommitted client invites failure.
C. Visitor; compliment him for coming and avoid assigning him any tasks ✔ KEY
A visitor sees no problem to work on; the counselor offers sincere compliments, explores what he might want, and gives no tasks.
D. Customer; confront his denial and set firm goals for his anger at once
Confronting denial is not a solution-focused stance, and the teen is not in a customer relationship.
Rationale: De Shazer described three kinds of relationships: visitor (no complaint or goal yet), complainant (sees a problem but expects others to change) and customer (sees a problem and is willing to act). These describe the relationship at a moment, not fixed client traits. With visitors, counselors build rapport through compliments and curiosity about what the client might want, saving tasks for later.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Solution-Focused Brief Therapy: customer, complainant and visitor relationships; compliments
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

759. nce-s-cou-139 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · narrative therapy · medium · In review

A mother of twins says, "A good mother never needs help, so I'm failing." Her narrative counselor asks, "Where did you learn that idea about good mothers? Who benefits when mothers believe it? Are there times it doesn't fit your life?" The counselor is MAINLY engaged in:
A. Deconstructing a dominant discourse ✔ KEY
Deconstruction questions unpack the taken-for-granted discourses behind a problem story so the client can choose whether to accept them.
B. Disputing an irrational belief
Disputing tests a belief's logic and evidence (REBT); narrative questions trace a belief's cultural origins and effects instead.
C. Interpreting an unconscious conflict
Narrative counselors take a not-knowing stance and do not interpret hidden motives.
D. Naming an Adlerian basic mistake
Basic mistakes in the lifestyle are an Adlerian concept tied to private logic, not cultural discourse.
Rationale: Michael White and David Epston drew on the idea that problem stories are shaped by dominant cultural discourses. Deconstruction exposes where those discourses came from, whose interests they serve and how they have shaped the client's thin, problem-saturated description of herself. This opens space for a thicker, preferred story.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Narrative Therapy: deconstruction and dominant discourses
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

760. nce-s-cou-140 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · narrative therapy · medium · In review

A young adult reclaiming her life from an eating disorder invites three friends to a session. While she talks with the counselor, the friends listen; then they describe what stood out to them, what it brought up in their own lives and how it moved them, and she responds. This narrative practice is known as:
A. Externalizing conversation
Externalizing separates the person from the problem in language; it does not depend on an audience of witnesses.
B. Family sculpting
Family sculpting (Satir) has members arrange one another physically to show relationships.
C. Reflecting team critique
Outsider witnesses do not critique or evaluate the client; reflecting teams also come from Andersen's work with clinicians.
D. Definitional ceremony ✔ KEY
In a definitional ceremony, outsider witnesses hear the preferred story and retell it, which authenticates and thickens it.
Rationale: White adapted the definitional ceremony from anthropologist Barbara Myerhoff. The client tells her preferred story, outsider witnesses retell what resonated with them, and the client then responds to the retellings. The audience helps acknowledge and thicken the new identity claims so they are not held by the client alone.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Narrative therapy: definitional ceremonies and outsider witnesses
⚑ Check: Confirm that Goldenberg (9th ed.) covers definitional ceremonies/outsider witnesses; Corey covers them only briefly. Reflecting-team distractor wording ("critique") chosen so it is clearly not the practice described.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

761. nce-s-cou-141 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · narrative therapy · medium · In review

After a session, a narrative counselor mails a client a letter that quotes the client's own words about how he stood up to "the Anger," notes questions the counselor is still curious about and names the steps he took. What is the MAIN purpose of such therapeutic letters?
A. To give him the counselor's formal diagnosis and expert view of his case
Narrative counselors avoid the expert, diagnostic stance; letters center the client's words, not a diagnosis.
B. To document and thicken his emerging story so it lasts between sessions ✔ KEY
Letters record the alternative story in lasting form, extending and thickening it beyond the session.
C. To assign behavioral homework with rewards for each completed step
Contingent rewards for homework belong to behavior therapy, not narrative letter writing.
D. To keep a legal record of the session in place of case notes
Therapeutic letters are an intervention addressed to the client; they do not replace clinical records.
Rationale: David Epston in particular developed letter writing as a narrative practice. Letters capture unique outcomes and the client's preferred story in a durable, rereadable form, turning a thin problem story into a thicker, richly described one. White and Epston also used certificates and documents to celebrate new identities.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Narrative Therapy: letters and documents that support the alternative story
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

762. nce-s-cou-142 · Social and Cultural Diversity · feminist therapy · easy · In review

Which counselor practice BEST reflects the egalitarian relationship emphasized in feminist therapy?
A. Keeping a neutral blank screen so the client can project onto the counselor
The blank-screen stance is psychoanalytic and widens the power gap feminist counselors try to reduce.
B. Making the counselor's diagnosis the main basis for all treatment decisions
Feminist counselors are cautious about diagnostic labels and do not make the counselor's view the sole authority.
C. Demystifying counseling and treating the client as expert on her life ✔ KEY
Demystifying the process and honoring the client's expertise reduce the power difference and support collaboration.
D. Avoiding any talk of values or social issues so the counselor stays neutral
Feminist counselors see neutrality as impossible and openly address values and social context.
Rationale: Feminist therapy views the counseling relationship as egalitarian. Counselors demystify the process through informed consent, share their orientation and values, use appropriate self-disclosure and treat clients as experts on their own lives. This models healthier uses of power and supports empowerment.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Feminist Therapy: the egalitarian therapeutic relationship
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

763. nce-s-cou-143 · Social and Cultural Diversity · feminist therapy · medium · In review

A home health aide who immigrated five years ago blames herself for "being weak" because she has not confronted an agency that underpays her. Her counselor helps her map the differences in power between her and the agency, including economic, legal and gender factors, and explore ways she might access power. This feminist intervention is:
A. Power analysis ✔ KEY
Power analysis examines how unequal access to power shapes the client's situation and identifies ways to use or gain power.
B. Gender-role analysis
Gender-role analysis explores messages about how women and men should be; this work centers on broader power differences.
C. Cognitive reframing
Reframing offers a new meaning for the same facts but does not map structural power or plan to access it.
D. Assertiveness drills
Assertiveness training may follow, but the intervention described is an analysis of power, not skill rehearsal.
Rationale: In power analysis, feminist counselors help clients see the differences in power between groups in society and in their own relationships, and how these shape their options and self-blame. Clients then identify kinds of power they can use. Shifting the view from personal weakness to social context is a core feminist move.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Feminist Therapy: power analysis and intervention
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

764. nce-s-cou-144 · Social and Cultural Diversity · feminist therapy · medium · In review

Relational-cultural theory (RCT), developed by Jean Baker Miller, Judith Jordan and colleagues at the Stone Center, challenges traditional models of development. According to RCT, psychological growth occurs MAINLY through:
A. Separating from others to achieve independence and a firm, autonomous self
RCT critiques the separation-individuation model that treats autonomy as the goal of maturity.
B. Resolving unconscious drives and conflicts formed in early psychosexual stages
This describes Freudian theory, not RCT's focus on connection.
C. Learning new behaviors through reinforcement in structured, graded tasks
This is a behavioral account of change and omits the relational focus of RCT.
D. Growth-fostering relationships marked by mutual empathy and empowerment ✔ KEY
RCT holds that people grow through and toward connection, in relationships of mutual empathy and mutual empowerment.
Rationale: Relational-cultural theory argues that people grow through connection rather than separation. Growth-fostering relationships involve mutual empathy and mutual empowerment, and chronic disconnection, often linked to marginalization and power, leads to isolation and suffering. RCT is closely tied to feminist therapy and attends to culture and social justice.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Feminist Therapy: relational-cultural theory (Miller, Jordan)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

765. nce-s-cou-145 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · motivational interviewing · medium · In review

Near the end of a session about her drinking, a client says, "I'm going to call the outpatient program on Monday and set up an intake." Using the DARN-CAT framework, which kind of change talk is this?
A. Desire
Desire statements express wanting or wishing ("I want to cut down"), not a pledge to act.
B. Commitment ✔ KEY
"I'm going to" signals an intention to act, which is commitment, a form of mobilizing change talk.
C. Reasons
Reasons statements give specific benefits of change ("I'd sleep better").
D. Taking steps
Taking steps describes an action already done ("I called them yesterday"); this call has not happened yet.
Rationale: Miller and Rollnick group change talk into preparatory talk (Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need) and mobilizing talk (Commitment, Activation, Taking steps). Commitment language such as "I will" or "I'm going to" predicts change more strongly than preparatory talk. Counselors listen for, reflect and strengthen change talk.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Evoking: preparatory (DARN) and mobilizing (CAT) change talk
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

766. nce-s-cou-146 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · motivational interviewing · medium · In review

A father who smokes in the car with his young children says being a present, healthy dad is "the most important thing in my life." Which response BEST develops discrepancy in a way consistent with the spirit of motivational interviewing?
A. "Your kids matter most to you. How does smoking fit with that?" ✔ KEY
This reflects his stated value and invites him to voice the gap between it and his behavior, evoking his own reasons.
B. "You need to know that secondhand smoke in a car harms children's lungs."
Lecturing reflects the righting reflex and tends to provoke sustain talk rather than change talk.
C. "If your kids matter most, then you would have quit smoking long ago."
This is a confrontational argument that challenges his sincerity and is likely to increase discord.
D. "Let's set a quit date now, and I'll give you a list of nicotine aids."
Jumping to planning before he voices his own motivation skips evoking and risks resistance.
Rationale: Developing discrepancy means helping clients notice the gap between their values or goals and their current behavior, so the client, not the counselor, voices the argument for change. The MI spirit of partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation rules out lecturing or confrontation, which tend to trigger sustain talk and discord.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — MI spirit; developing discrepancy between values and behavior
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

767. nce-s-cou-147 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · motivational interviewing · easy · In review

After building rapport with a client who has diabetes, depression and money worries, the counselor and client agree that they will concentrate on his eating and medication habits for now. In the four processes of motivational interviewing, this step is called:
A. Engaging
Engaging is establishing the working relationship, which has already occurred here.
B. Evoking
Evoking draws out the client's own motivation for change once a direction has been chosen.
C. Focusing ✔ KEY
Focusing is developing and keeping a specific direction or change goal for the conversation.
D. Planning
Planning comes last, when the client is ready to commit to a specific plan of action.
Rationale: Miller and Rollnick describe four overlapping processes: engaging (building the relationship), focusing (agreeing on a direction), evoking (drawing out the client's own motivation) and planning (developing commitment and a concrete plan). Each builds on the one before, and counselors may return to earlier processes as needed.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — The four processes: engaging, focusing, evoking, planning
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

768. nce-s-cou-148 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · dialectical behavior therapy · easy · In review

After a client self-harms, her DBT therapist works with her to trace, step by step, her vulnerability factors that day, the prompting event, each thought, feeling and action leading to the behavior, and the consequences that followed. This procedure is called:
A. Radical acceptance
Radical acceptance is a distress tolerance skill of fully accepting reality as it is; it does not map links to a behavior.
B. A thought record
A thought record tracks situations, automatic thoughts and alternative responses (CBT), not a full behavioral sequence.
C. Wise mind practice
Wise mind is a mindfulness skill integrating emotion mind and reasonable mind, not an analysis of a behavior.
D. Behavioral chain analysis ✔ KEY
Chain analysis maps every link from vulnerability and prompting event to the target behavior and its consequences.
Rationale: In DBT, a behavioral chain analysis is done after a target behavior such as self-harm. Therapist and client identify vulnerabilities, the prompting event, the chain of thoughts, emotions, sensations and actions, the behavior and its consequences. Each link becomes a point where a skill could be used instead, and a solution analysis follows.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Dialectical behavior therapy: behavioral chain analysis
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

769. nce-s-cou-149 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · dialectical behavior therapy · medium · In review

A client in a DBT skills group practices asking her roommate to pay his share of the rent. At one point she says, "If you get your half to me by Friday, I'll stop bringing it up and things can get back to normal between us." In the DEAR MAN skill, this statement illustrates:
A. Assert
Assert is clearly asking for what one wants or saying no ("I need your half of the rent").
B. Reinforce ✔ KEY
Reinforce means rewarding the person ahead of time by explaining the positive effects of getting what one asks for.
C. Negotiate
Negotiate is being willing to give to get, such as offering alternatives or a compromise.
D. Express
Express is sharing one's feelings and opinions about the situation using "I" statements.
Rationale: DEAR MAN is a DBT interpersonal effectiveness skill: Describe the situation, Express feelings, Assert the request, Reinforce the other person in advance, stay Mindful, Appear confident and Negotiate. Reinforcing explains what the other person gains by agreeing, which makes a yes more likely.
References: Linehan (DBT Skills Training Manual) — Interpersonal effectiveness: DEAR MAN skills
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

770. nce-s-cou-150 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · dialectical behavior therapy · hard · In review

A client says she freezes and goes silent whenever her manager raises his voice. Her DBT therapist responds, "Growing up, speaking up when your father yelled got you punished, so freezing makes sense given what you learned." In Linehan's levels of validation, this response BEST illustrates:
A. Validating in terms of past learning or biology ✔ KEY
This level explains the response as understandable given the client's history, even if it does not fit the present situation.
B. Normalizing in terms of present circumstances
This level says the response would make sense for anyone in the current situation, without reference to the client's history.
C. Articulating the client's unverbalized feelings
This level puts into words what the client has not said, such as a feeling she has not named.
D. Radical genuineness with the client as an equal
Radical genuineness treats the client as a capable equal rather than fragile; it does not explain a response by history.
Rationale: Linehan described six levels of validation: (1) staying awake and attentive, (2) accurate reflection, (3) articulating the unverbalized, (4) validating in terms of past learning or biology, (5) normalizing in terms of present context, and (6) radical genuineness. Validation balances DBT's change strategies, communicating that the client's responses make sense, which supports the acceptance side of the acceptance-change dialectic.
References: Linehan (DBT Skills Training Manual) — Validation and its levels · Corey (Theory & Practice) — Dialectical behavior therapy: validation strategies and the acceptance-change dialectic
⚑ Check: The six validation levels are set out in Linehan (1997, "Validation and psychotherapy"); confirm the skills manual edition cited presents all six.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

771. nce-s-cou-151 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · termination skills · medium · In review

After four sessions on grief, a 58-year-old client leaves a voicemail cancelling her next appointment and saying she 'just doesn't need counseling anymore.' The counselor believes important work remains. What is the BEST response?
A. Close the file without further contact, since the client has made her choice
Respecting autonomy does not require silence; a brief outreach to offer closure and options is good practice.
B. Reach out, invite a closing session to review progress and offer referral options ✔ KEY
This respects her decision while offering pretermination counseling, a chance to explore her reasons and a path back or elsewhere.
C. Call several times each week until she agrees to resume her regular appointments
Repeated pressure disregards client autonomy and could feel coercive.
D. Mail a letter stating that ending now will most likely cause her grief to worsen
Predicting harm to persuade her to return is a pressure tactic and is not supported by the facts at hand.
Rationale: Clients may end counseling early for many reasons, including satisfaction, cost, discomfort or a rupture in the relationship. The counselor respects the choice but reaches out once to explore the decision, offer a closing session to consolidate gains and provide referrals, leaving the door open to return.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.c Appropriate Termination · Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Termination: premature termination initiated by clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

772. nce-s-cou-152 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · termination skills · easy · In review

After 12 sessions and several changes in approach, a client with social anxiety shows no measurable improvement, and the client and counselor agree that counseling is not helping. According to the ACA Code of Ethics, what should the counselor do?
A. Continue the same sessions, since ending now would amount to abandonment
Ending a relationship that is not helping, with proper preparation and referral, is not abandonment; continuing without benefit is the concern.
B. End services at the next visit without discussion to avoid more expense
An abrupt ending without discussion denies the client pretermination counseling.
C. Keep meeting monthly until the client's insurance benefits are used up
Continuing only to use available benefits does not serve the client and raises ethical concerns.
D. Provide pretermination counseling and recommend other service providers ✔ KEY
The Code directs counselors to end services that are not benefiting the client, with pretermination counseling and referral as needed.
Rationale: ACA Code A.11.c directs counselors to terminate when it is reasonably apparent that the client no longer needs help, is not likely to benefit or is being harmed. Counselors provide pretermination counseling and recommend other service providers when necessary, so the client leaves with a path to help that may fit better.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.c Appropriate Termination
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

773. nce-s-cou-153 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · termination skills · medium · In review

A school counselor's individual sessions with a 7-year-old will end in three weeks because he has met his goals. Which approach to ending is MOST developmentally appropriate?
A. Mark the remaining sessions on a calendar together and plan a goodbye ritual ✔ KEY
Concrete countdowns and a closing ritual give a young child advance notice, predictability and a sense of closure.
B. Tell him at the start of the final session so he has less time to be upset
Last-minute notice gives the child no time to prepare and can feel like abandonment.
C. Avoid mentioning the ending and simply stop scheduling him for sessions
An unexplained stop leaves the child confused and may feel like rejection.
D. Ask his teacher to explain the ending to him after the last session is over
The ending belongs in the relationship; handing it off to someone else after the fact avoids closure.
Rationale: Children understand time concretely, so endings are announced several sessions ahead and made visible, for example by counting down sessions on a calendar. A goodbye ritual, such as a drawing, a memory book or a review of what the child learned, honors the relationship and consolidates gains.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling children: preparing for and ending the relationship
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

774. nce-s-cou-154 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · reflection, paraphrasing and summarizing · hard · In review

A client says, 'I keep picking up extra shifts even though I'm exhausted. My parents gave up everything to bring us to this country.' Which counselor response is the BEST example of a reflection of meaning?
A. You're feeling exhausted and a bit trapped by all the extra shifts you work.
This names emotions, which makes it a reflection of feeling rather than of meaning.
B. You've been working many extra shifts lately, even though you're worn out.
This restates content, which makes it a paraphrase.
C. Working this hard seems to be a way of honoring what your parents sacrificed. ✔ KEY
This captures the value and purpose that give the behavior its significance for the client, the core of reflecting meaning.
D. Perhaps you overwork because part of you fears you'll disappoint your parents.
This offers a new, counselor-generated explanation (a hidden fear), which is an interpretation.
Rationale: Reflection of meaning, in Ivey's microskills, goes beneath content and feeling to the values, purposes and significance a client attaches to experience. It stays close to what the client has implied, whereas interpretation offers a new frame drawn from the counselor's perspective.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling skills: reflection of meaning versus interpretation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

775. nce-s-cou-155 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · reflection, paraphrasing and summarizing · easy · In review

A client says, 'Between my night classes and my daughter's soccer schedule, I haven't had a free evening in a month.' Which counselor response is the BEST paraphrase?
A. Your evenings have been taken up by school and family commitments for weeks. ✔ KEY
This restates the essential content in fresh, concise words, which is what a paraphrase does.
B. Between night classes and soccer, you haven't had a free evening in a month.
Repeating the client's words almost verbatim is parroting, which can sound mechanical.
C. You're feeling worn out and maybe resentful that there's no time for you.
This focuses on emotion, making it a reflection of feeling.
D. It sounds like you may have trouble saying no when others need something.
This adds a counselor hypothesis about the client, which is interpretation.
Rationale: A paraphrase restates the content of a client's message in the counselor's own, usually briefer, words. It shows accurate listening and invites the client to confirm or correct. Verbatim repetition (parroting) adds little and can feel mechanical.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling skills: paraphrasing and the pitfall of parroting
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

776. nce-s-cou-156 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · confrontation and immediacy · medium · In review

A client who was open in earlier sessions has arrived late three weeks in a row, answers in single words and avoids looking at the counselor. The counselor senses growing distance between them. Which response BEST demonstrates immediacy?
A. You've been late three times now, and our policy is that sessions can't run over.
Stating policy addresses logistics, not what is happening in the relationship.
B. Coming late may be your way of resisting the hard work we have started to do here.
This is an interpretation of motive and may increase defensiveness.
C. Let's go back to the goals we set in our first session and review your progress.
Shifting to goals sidesteps the relational shift the counselor is noticing.
D. I'm sensing some distance between us lately, and I wonder what's happening for you. ✔ KEY
The counselor tentatively names what is occurring between them right now and invites the client to explore it.
Rationale: Immediacy is the counselor's direct, tentative comment on what is happening in the counseling relationship in the present moment. Used when tension or distance develops, it brings the relationship itself into the conversation so ruptures can be explored and repaired.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling skills: relationship immediacy
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

777. nce-s-cou-157 · Social and Cultural Diversity · basic attending and listening skills · medium · In review

During intake, a client looks down or past the counselor most of the time and moves her chair back slightly when the counselor leans in. She explains that in her family, looking an elder or professional directly in the eye is considered disrespectful. What should the counselor do?
A. Gently encourage more eye contact to build trust and openness over time
This imposes the counselor's cultural norm on the client.
B. Adjust own eye contact and distance, following the client's comfort cues ✔ KEY
Attending behaviors are adapted to the client's cultural norms for gaze and personal space.
C. Note the gaze avoidance as a possible sign of depression or social anxiety
The client has given a cultural explanation; pathologizing it risks misdiagnosis.
D. Lean in closer to show warmth so that she feels more engaged in session
She has signaled discomfort with closeness; moving in would ignore her cue.
Rationale: Guidelines such as SOLER reflect a particular cultural norm. Comfort with eye contact (kinesics) and conversational distance (proxemics) varies across cultures and individuals, so culturally responsive attending means reading and following the client's cues rather than treating one style as the standard.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Nonverbal communication: proxemics and kinesics
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

778. nce-s-cou-158 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · play therapy · easy · In review

During child-centered play therapy, a 5-year-old holds up a paintbrush and asks the counselor, 'What color should I make the sky?' Which response BEST fits this approach?
A. Blue, just like the real sky outside.
Answering for the child directs the play and takes away a chance for self-direction.
B. Why do you want me to pick for you?
"Why" questions ask young children to explain motives and can feel evaluative.
C. In here, you get to decide that. ✔ KEY
Returning responsibility communicates trust in the child and builds decision-making and self-control.
D. Let's paint it together and find out.
Joining to share the choice still shifts direction away from the child.
Rationale: In child-centered play therapy (Axline, Landreth), the counselor follows the child's lead. Key responses include tracking (describing what the child is doing, such as "You're putting that one on top") and returning responsibility, which hands decisions back to the child to foster autonomy and self-responsibility.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling children: child-centered play therapy responses
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

779. nce-s-cou-159 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · play therapy · medium · In review

A counselor trains parents to hold weekly 30-minute nondirective play sessions with their own child at home, using reflective listening, tracking and limit setting, while the counselor supervises and gives feedback on their skills. Which approach is this?
A. Filial therapy ✔ KEY
Filial therapy, developed by Bernard and Louise Guerney, trains parents as the agents of child-centered play sessions.
B. Theraplay
Theraplay (Jernberg) is an adult-led, attachment-based approach using structured, playful engagement, not nondirective play.
C. Parent-child interaction therapy
PCIT (Eyberg) coaches parents live, usually by earpiece, and includes a parent-directed discipline phase.
D. Sandplay therapy
Sandplay (Kalff, building on Lowenfeld's World Technique) is a Jungian method in which the child builds scenes in a sand tray with the therapist.
Rationale: Filial therapy treats parents as partners: the counselor teaches child-centered play skills, supervises practice sessions and then helps parents generalize the sessions to home. It aims to strengthen the parent-child relationship as the vehicle of change.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling children: filial therapy and sand tray approaches
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

780. nce-s-cou-160 · Human Growth and Development · attachment theory · hard · In review

A 34-year-old client says he badly wants a close relationship, yet he pulls away whenever someone gets close because he expects to be hurt and doubts that he deserves love. In Bartholomew and Horowitz's four-category model of adult attachment, which style BEST fits?
A. Preoccupied
Preoccupied adults see themselves negatively but others positively, so they pursue closeness anxiously rather than withdraw.
B. Dismissing-avoidant
Dismissing adults view themselves positively and downplay any wish for closeness.
C. Secure
Secure adults hold positive views of self and others and are comfortable with intimacy.
D. Fearful-avoidant ✔ KEY
He wants closeness but avoids it, with negative views of both himself and others.
Rationale: Bartholomew and Horowitz crossed a model of self (worthy or unworthy) with a model of others (trustworthy or not). Secure is positive-positive, preoccupied is negative self and positive other, dismissing is positive self and negative other, and fearful is negative on both, producing a desire for closeness alongside avoidance.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Early adulthood: adult attachment styles and intimate relationships
⚑ Check: Confirm Berk 7th ed covers Bartholomew and Horowitz's four-category adult model; the model itself is standard.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

781. nce-s-cou-161 · Human Growth and Development · attachment theory · easy · In review

Bowlby proposed that through repeated experiences with caregivers, a child builds mental representations of whether others are dependable and whether the self is worthy of care, which then guide expectations in later relationships. What did Bowlby call these representations?
A. Secure base
A secure base (emphasized by Ainsworth) is the caregiver from whom a child explores, not the mental representation itself.
B. Internal working models ✔ KEY
Bowlby's internal working models are expectations about self and others built from early caregiving.
C. Object constancy
Object constancy is Mahler's term for holding a stable inner image of the caregiver.
D. Cognitive schemas
Schemas are Piaget's and Beck's terms for organized knowledge or core beliefs, not Bowlby's attachment concept.
Rationale: Bowlby argued that attachment experiences are internalized as working models of self and others. These models operate largely outside awareness and shape how a person seeks support, interprets others' behavior and forms close relationships later in life.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Bowlby's ethological theory of attachment: internal working model
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

782. nce-s-cou-162 · Social and Cultural Diversity · racial and cultural identity models · hard · In review

For two years a Korean American graduate student rejected anything she saw as White culture and worked only within Asian American groups. Lately she feels uneasy with that rigid stance, wonders whether it limits her personal autonomy and is sorting out which values are truly her own. In the Racial/Cultural Identity Development (R/CID) model, she is MOST likely in which stage?
A. Dissonance
Dissonance is the earlier stage in which experiences first challenge a conforming, majority-oriented view.
B. Resistance and immersion
This describes her previous two years of rejecting the dominant culture and endorsing her own group.
C. Introspection ✔ KEY
Discomfort with rigid group views and a search for personal autonomy mark the introspection stage.
D. Integrative awareness
Integrative awareness reflects a secure, flexible identity that she is still working toward.
Rationale: The R/CID model (Atkinson, Morten and Sue, expanded by Sue and Sue) describes five stages: conformity, dissonance, resistance and immersion, introspection and integrative awareness. Introspection follows immersion, as the person questions rigid loyalty to the group and works out an individual identity.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Racial/Cultural Identity Development (R/CID) model
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

783. nce-s-cou-163 · Social and Cultural Diversity · racial and cultural identity models · medium · In review

After a classmate's remark about her family's background, a 15-year-old Mexican American student begins asking her grandparents about their lives in Mexico, joins a Latinx student club and reads Chicano history, though she has not settled what her heritage means to her. In Phinney's model of ethnic identity, she is in which stage?
A. Ethnic identity search (moratorium) ✔ KEY
Active exploration of heritage, often prompted by an encounter, without firm commitment marks the search stage.
B. Unexamined ethnic identity
This first stage involves little interest in or exploration of ethnicity; she is now actively exploring.
C. Achieved ethnic identity
Achievement requires a secure, committed sense of what ethnicity means, which she has not yet reached.
D. Integrative awareness
Integrative awareness is the final stage of the R/CID model, not part of Phinney's model.
Rationale: Phinney applied Marcia's identity statuses to ethnicity: an unexamined identity (diffuse or foreclosed), an ethnic identity search or moratorium often sparked by a significant experience, and an achieved identity marked by clarity and commitment. Exploration supported by family and community fosters well-being.
References: Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Adolescence: ethnic identity (Phinney)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

784. nce-s-cou-164 · Social and Cultural Diversity · multicultural counseling competencies · medium · In review

A counselor who holds several privileged identities is working with a client from a marginalized racial and religious group. She sets aside time to explore with the client how their differences in power and privilege affect trust, communication and the work they are doing together. In the MSJCC, this falls MOST directly within which developmental domain?
A. Counselor self-awareness
Self-awareness concerns the counselor's own identities and biases; here the focus is how the two identities interact.
B. Counseling relationship ✔ KEY
This domain addresses how privileged and marginalized statuses of counselor and client shape the relationship.
C. Client worldview
Client worldview concerns understanding the client's identities, values and experiences of oppression.
D. Counseling and advocacy interventions
This domain covers intervening at individual through international levels, not exploring the dyad itself.
Rationale: The MSJCC places the counselor-client pair in one of four quadrants defined by privileged and marginalized statuses. It then describes four developmental domains: counselor self-awareness, client worldview, the counseling relationship, and counseling and advocacy interventions, with attitudes and beliefs, knowledge, skills and action (AKSA) within each.
References: MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Quadrants and developmental domains: the counseling relationship
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

785. nce-s-cou-165 · Social and Cultural Diversity · multicultural counseling competencies · medium · In review

An older counseling text lists ataque de nervios as a 'culture-bound syndrome.' DSM-5-TR uses a broader term that includes cultural syndromes, cultural idioms of distress and cultural explanations or perceived causes. What is that term?
A. Culture-specific disorders
DSM-5-TR moved away from framing these patterns as disorders tied to one culture.
B. Atypical presentations
This implies a deviation from a supposedly typical norm, the view the newer framework rejects.
C. Ethnic variant syndromes
This is not a DSM-5-TR term.
D. Cultural concepts of distress ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR groups cultural syndromes, idioms of distress and explanations under cultural concepts of distress.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR replaced "culture-bound syndromes" with cultural concepts of distress, recognizing that all distress is culturally shaped and that these concepts may not map onto a single DSM disorder. The Cultural Formulation Interview helps counselors explore the client's own understanding of the problem.
References: DSM-5-TR — Section III: Culture and Psychiatric Diagnosis, cultural concepts of distress
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

786. nce-s-cou-166 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · crisis intervention models · easy · In review

Using James and Gilliland's six-step model of crisis intervention, a counselor has defined the problem from the client's point of view, ensured the client's safety and provided support. What is the counselor's NEXT step?
A. Obtain commitment to a plan
Obtaining commitment is the sixth and final step.
B. Make a concrete plan
Making plans is the fifth step, after alternatives are explored.
C. Examine alternatives ✔ KEY
The fourth step is exploring options, supports and coping mechanisms with the client.
D. Complete a full diagnosis
Formal diagnosis is not a step in the model; assessment runs throughout.
Rationale: James and Gilliland's model has three listening steps (define the problem, ensure client safety, provide support) followed by three acting steps (examine alternatives, make plans, obtain commitment). Assessment of the client's state and safety continues throughout all six steps.
References: James & Gilliland (Crisis Intervention Strategies) — Six-step model: define the problem, ensure safety, provide support, examine alternatives, make plans, obtain commitment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

787. nce-s-cou-167 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · crisis intervention models · hard · In review

In Kanel's ABC model of crisis intervention, a counselor first builds rapport through attending and reflection. The counselor then identifies the precipitating event, the client's perception of it and the resulting distress and impaired functioning. What is this second phase called?
A. Boiling down the problem ✔ KEY
The B phase narrows the focus to the trigger, the client's perception and the subjective distress.
B. Coping
Coping is the C phase, which follows and focuses on current and new coping strategies.
C. Achieving contact
Achieving contact is the A phase, the rapport building described first in the stem.
D. Brief safety planning
Safety is assessed throughout but is not the name of a phase in the ABC model.
Rationale: Kanel's ABC model has three phases: A, achieving (developing and maintaining) contact; B, boiling down the problem by identifying the precipitating event, perceptions and distress; and C, coping, in which the counselor explores past and new coping and builds a plan. Its focus on perception reflects the view that crises arise from how events are interpreted.
References: Kanel (A Guide to Crisis Intervention) — ABC model: A, achieving contact; B, boiling down the problem; C, coping
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

788. nce-s-cou-168 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · medium · In review

Before launching a support group at a refugee resettlement agency, a counselor studies the community's needs, the agency's resources and support, and cultural attitudes toward discussing personal problems in a group. In the ASGW Best Practice Guidelines, this planning task is called:
A. Pre-group screening
Screening assesses individual prospective members, not the community and organizational context.
B. Ecological assessment ✔ KEY
ASGW asks group workers to assess the community, agency and cultural context before forming a group.
C. Professional disclosure
Professional disclosure informs members about the leader and the group; it is not a needs assessment.
D. Group processing
Processing is the later, ongoing reflection on what happens in sessions.
Rationale: The ASGW Best Practice Guidelines organize group work into planning, performing and group processing. In planning, an ecological assessment of community needs, organizational support and cultural factors guides whether and how a group is offered. Processing, by contrast, means regular reflection on sessions with co-leaders, members or supervisors.
References: ASGW Best Practice Guidelines — Best Practice in Planning: ecological assessment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

789. nce-s-cou-169 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · easy · In review
