The T-group (training group), first developed at the National Training Laboratories in Bethel, Maine, used here-and-now feedback to teach human relations skills. Whose field theory and group dynamics research led to this movement?
A. Carl Rogers
Rogers developed the basic encounter group, which grew alongside but separately from T-groups.
B. Jacob Moreno
Moreno developed psychodrama and is credited with coining the term group therapy.
C. Joseph Pratt
Pratt led early educational "classes" for patients with tuberculosis in the early 1900s.
D. Kurt Lewin ✔ KEY
Lewin's field theory and group dynamics work led his colleagues to found NTL and the T-group.
Rationale: Kurt Lewin studied how group forces shape individual behavior. His work led to the National Training Laboratories in 1947, where T-groups used here-and-now feedback to build interpersonal awareness. Rogers later extended the experiential group into the encounter group movement.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — History of group work: Lewin, T-groups and encounter groups
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

790. nce-s-cou-170 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · easy · In review

A counselor suggests that a recently widowed client try a community bereavement group run by and for people who have lost a spouse, with no professional leader. Compared with a counseling or therapy group, what BEST characterizes this kind of group?
A. It uses a professional leader trained to treat diagnosable mental disorders
This describes a psychotherapy group, not a peer-run group.
B. It follows a strict time-limited format with formal screening of all members
Mutual-aid groups are usually open and ongoing, without formal clinical screening.
C. It is peer-led, with members who share a concern offering one another support ✔ KEY
Self-help and mutual-aid groups are led by members who share the problem and help one another.
D. It focuses mainly on reshaping personality through deep insight and analysis
Reconstructive personality change is a goal of some long-term therapy groups, not of mutual-aid groups.
Rationale: Self-help and mutual-aid groups, such as Alcoholics Anonymous or widow-to-widow programs, are organized around a shared concern and led by members rather than professionals. They emphasize support, hope, universality and practical help, and they can complement rather than replace professional counseling.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Group work: self-help and mutual-aid groups
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

791. nce-s-cou-171 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · medium · In review

A 15-year-old in a court-mandated anger management group sits with his hood up and says, 'I'm only here because the judge made me.' What is the leader's BEST initial response?
A. Acknowledge he did not choose to come and invite him to say how that feels ✔ KEY
Openly naming involuntary status respects his autonomy and turns resistance into material for the group.
B. Explain that members who do not take part may be reported back to the court
Leading with threats reinforces the power struggle and deepens resistance.
C. Ask the other members to persuade him that the group will really help him
Recruiting peers to convince him puts him on the spot and can feel like ganging up.
D. Ignore the remark and move on so he gets no attention for his resistance
Ignoring a direct statement misses a chance to engage him and may model avoidance.
Rationale: Adolescents, and especially involuntary members, often test leaders and guard their autonomy. Acknowledging their reluctance openly, respecting choices about what to disclose and inviting them to talk about being sent helps build trust and often reduces resistance more than pressure or avoidance.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Group work with adolescents and involuntary members
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

792. nce-s-cou-172 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · medium · In review

In the ninth session of a cohesive interpersonal group, Malik tells Rosa that her advice-giving feels 'preachy,' and Rosa responds sharply. The room goes quiet. What should the leader do?
A. Move on to a new topic to protect the cohesion the group has built so far
Avoiding conflict teaches members that strong feelings are unsafe and wastes useful material.
B. Help both speak directly to each other and explore what the exchange stirs up ✔ KEY
Keeping the conflict in the here-and-now with direct communication makes it a source of learning.
C. Ask Malik and Rosa to work out their disagreement privately after the session
Moving conflict outside the group fosters subgrouping and removes it from shared work.
D. Point out that Malik's feedback was too harsh and ask him to rephrase it now
Taking sides shuts down exploration and positions the leader as judge.
Rationale: Yalom notes that conflict is inevitable and, in a cohesive group, can be highly productive. The leader keeps it in the here-and-now, encourages members to speak directly and own their reactions, and helps the group examine what the exchange reveals about each person's interpersonal patterns.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — Conflict in the therapy group (the advanced group)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

793. nce-s-cou-173 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · medium · In review

A member describes feeling ignored at family dinners. The leader asks her, 'Is there anyone in this room who you feel might be ignoring you right now?' In Yalom's two-tiered approach to the here-and-now, this question is an example of:
A. Process illumination
Illumination is the second tier, in which the group reflects on and makes sense of what has happened.
B. Universality
Universality is a therapeutic factor, the relief of learning others share one's problems.
C. Catharsis
Catharsis is the expression of strong emotion, not a leader technique for shifting focus.
D. Here-and-now activation ✔ KEY
Steering an outside concern into members' relationships in the room is the first, activating tier.
Rationale: Yalom describes two tiers of here-and-now work. The leader first activates the here-and-now by moving the focus from outside, past events to members' reactions to one another in the room. The leader then illuminates the process, helping members reflect on and understand what just occurred; activation without illumination yields emotion without learning.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — Ch. 6: The here-and-now, activation and illumination of process
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

794. nce-s-cou-174 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · medium · In review

A 9-year-old's frequent stomachaches keep his worried mother home from work. A therapist directs the boy to pretend to have a stomachache at set times and the mother to pretend to comfort him, turning the symptom into play while the mother takes back her caretaking role. This technique is MOST closely associated with:
A. Salvador Minuchin
Minuchin's structural therapy uses enactments, joining and boundary making rather than pretend directives.
B. Murray Bowen
Bowen emphasized differentiation, triangles and genograms, with the therapist as a calm coach.
C. Cloé Madanes ✔ KEY
Madanes developed pretend techniques within strategic family therapy.
D. Virginia Satir
Satir's experiential approach focuses on communication stances, self-esteem and sculpting.
Rationale: Madanes viewed some children's symptoms as attempts to help a parent that also upset the family hierarchy. Pretend techniques ask the child to pretend to have the symptom and the parent to pretend to help, making the symptom voluntary and playful so it loses its function and the parent resumes an appropriate caregiving role.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Strategic family therapy: Madanes and pretend techniques
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

795. nce-s-cou-175 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · medium · In review

In a group setting, a guide uses a client's family chronology to have members role-play scenes from the lives of the client's parents and grandparents, helping the client see them as people and let go of old learnings. This experiential technique, developed by Virginia Satir, is called:
A. Family reconstruction ✔ KEY
Satir's family reconstruction re-enacts multigenerational scenes to free the "star" from outdated patterns.
B. Psychodrama
Psychodrama, created by Jacob Moreno, uses role-play but is not Satir's multigenerational technique.
C. Family sculpting
Sculpting arranges members in a physical tableau of present relationships rather than re-enacting family history.
D. Genogram construction
A genogram maps multigenerational patterns on paper (associated with Bowen) and does not involve role-play.
Rationale: Satir's family reconstruction guides a "star" through key events in three generations, using a family chronology and role players. Family sculpting, also used by Satir and by Duhl and Kantor, positions members physically to show closeness, distance and power. Both are experiential techniques that make family patterns visible and felt.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Experiential family therapy: Satir, family reconstruction and sculpting
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

796. nce-s-cou-176 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · hard · In review

Parents of a 14-year-old have grounded him for longer and longer periods for breaking curfew, with no effect. In MRI brief therapy terms, which outcome would represent second-order change?
A. The parents extend the grounding from one week to a full month
More of the same solution is first-order change in degree, not in kind.
B. The family changes the rules governing how curfew is set and handled ✔ KEY
Altering the rules of the system itself is second-order change.
C. The parents add the loss of his phone to the grounding as a penalty
Adding another penalty stays within the same punitive pattern, so it is first-order.
D. The parents keep the same rules but enforce them more strictly
Stricter enforcement of unchanged rules is a first-order adjustment.
Rationale: Watzlawick, Weakland and Fisch distinguished first-order change, a change within a system whose rules stay the same, from second-order change, a change in the system's rules or structure. MRI therapists look for interventions such as reframing that interrupt "more of the same" attempted solutions.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — MRI interactional view: first-order and second-order change
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

797. nce-s-cou-177 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · behavior therapy · medium · In review

Parents decide to stop going into their 3-year-old's room when she cries at bedtime. On the second and third nights, her crying becomes louder and lasts longer than before. How should the counselor explain this?
A. Spontaneous recovery; the plan has failed and should be stopped now
Spontaneous recovery is the return of a behavior after extinction appeared complete; the plan has not failed.
B. Negative reinforcement; her crying is being made stronger by them
Nothing aversive is being removed after crying, so this is not negative reinforcement.
C. Punishment; ignoring the crying is causing her new emotional harm
Withholding attention is extinction, not punishment, and the increase is predictable.
D. Extinction burst; it is expected and fades if parents stay consistent ✔ KEY
A temporary surge in a behavior when reinforcement stops is an extinction burst.
Rationale: When a previously reinforced behavior no longer produces its reinforcer, it often increases in frequency or intensity before declining, a pattern called an extinction burst. If caregivers give in during the burst, they reinforce a more intense version of the behavior on an intermittent schedule, so consistency is essential.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Behavior therapy: operant extinction and the extinction burst
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

798. nce-s-cou-178 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · behavior therapy · hard · In review

To reduce a child's hand-biting, a behavior analyst delivers a token at the end of every 10-minute interval in which no hand-biting occurs, regardless of what else the child is doing. Which procedure is this?
A. DRA (alternative behavior)
DRA reinforces a specific replacement behavior, such as asking for help, rather than mere absence of the target.
B. DRL (low rates of behavior)
DRL reinforces the target behavior when it occurs at or below a set rate, for behaviors to reduce but not eliminate.
C. DRO (other behavior) ✔ KEY
DRO reinforces the absence of the target behavior over an interval.
D. Premack principle
The Premack principle uses a high-probability activity to reinforce a low-probability one.
Rationale: Differential reinforcement of other behavior (DRO) delivers reinforcement when the target behavior has not occurred for a set interval, sometimes called differential reinforcement of zero rates. DRA reinforces a specified alternative behavior, DRI an incompatible one and DRL a low rate of the target itself.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Behavior therapy: differential reinforcement procedures
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

799. nce-s-cou-179 · Human Growth and Development · psychodynamic and psychoanalytic theory · medium · In review

An 18-month-old who recently toddled off happily to explore now repeatedly returns to his mother, shadows her, wants her to share each discovery and becomes upset when she leaves, yet sometimes pushes her away. In Mahler's separation-individuation theory, he is in which subphase?
A. Rapprochement ✔ KEY
Around 16 to 24 months, awareness of separateness brings renewed clinging alongside a push for autonomy.
B. Practicing
Practicing (about 10 to 16 months) is the earlier, exhilarated period of exploring with little concern for the mother.
C. Differentiation
Differentiation (about 5 to 10 months) is when the infant first begins to distinguish self from mother.
D. Object constancy
Object constancy (about 24 to 36 months) brings a stable inner image of the mother that eases separations.
Rationale: Mahler described separation-individuation subphases following the early autistic and symbiotic phases: differentiation, practicing, rapprochement and the move toward object constancy. The rapprochement crisis, with its mix of clinging and pushing away, is often linked to later difficulties with closeness and separateness.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic therapy: object relations theory and Mahler's separation-individuation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

800. nce-s-cou-180 · Human Growth and Development · psychodynamic and psychoanalytic theory · easy · In review

A 2-year-old insists on bringing a worn stuffed rabbit to child care and clutches it when her father leaves. In Winnicott's object relations theory, what function does this transitional object serve?
A. It signals an insecure attachment that will need professional treatment
Transitional objects are a normal part of development, not a sign of pathology.
B. It soothes her and bridges her move from union with a parent to separateness ✔ KEY
Winnicott saw the transitional object as an intermediate space that helps the child tolerate separation.
C. It reflects fixation at the oral stage caused by weaning that came too early
This applies Freud's psychosexual fixation, not Winnicott's concept.
D. It is a part-object she splits into all-good and all-bad parts to manage fear
Splitting and part-objects come from Melanie Klein, not the transitional object concept.
Rationale: Winnicott described the transitional object as the child's first "not-me" possession, standing between inner and outer reality and helping the child manage the gradual move to independence. It develops within a holding environment provided by a good-enough mother, who meets needs well at first and then fails in small, tolerable ways.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic therapy: object relations (Winnicott, Klein)
⚑ Check: Confirm Corey's object-relations section names Winnicott's transitional object and good-enough mother.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

801. nce-s-cou-181 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · reality therapy and choice theory · easy · In review

Glasser pictured total behavior as a car, with basic needs as the engine and wants as the steering wheel. Which two components are the front wheels, the parts of behavior a person controls most directly?
A. Feeling and physiology
Feeling and physiology are the back wheels; they follow along and change indirectly when acting and thinking change.
B. Wants and needs
In the metaphor, needs are the engine and wants steer the car; they are not components of total behavior.
C. Acting and thinking ✔ KEY
Acting and thinking are the front wheels: the components over which people have the most direct control.
D. Perceiving and remembering
Perception plays a role in choice theory (the perceived world), but it is not one of the four wheels of total behavior.
Rationale: In choice theory, total behavior has four inseparable components: acting, thinking, feeling and physiology. Glasser argued that we have almost total control over acting and thinking and only indirect control over feeling and physiology. Reality therapists therefore focus on what the client is doing and thinking, expecting feelings and body states to follow.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Reality Therapy: choice theory and total behavior
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

802. nce-s-cou-182 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · reality therapy and choice theory · medium · In review

A 17-year-old on probation says nothing matters to him, yet he lights up when he talks about his grandmother and about someday becoming a firefighter. A reality therapist notes that these belong to his quality world. In choice theory, the quality world is BEST described as:
A. A personal album of the people, things and ideas that best satisfy his needs ✔ KEY
Glasser described the quality world as a set of specific pictures of the people, activities, possessions and beliefs that we believe will best satisfy our needs.
B. The stored record of past failures that has built up into a failure identity
Failure identity was an early Glasser concept about how people see themselves, not the store of need-satisfying pictures.
C. An unconscious storehouse of repressed wishes that drives his current choices
Repressed unconscious wishes are a psychoanalytic idea; choice theory emphasizes present, conscious choices.
D. The shared set of perceptions about reality that he holds with his peer group
The quality world is highly individual; it is not a set of perceptions shared with a group.
Rationale: The quality world is the core of choice theory's motivation: everyone carries a personal "album" of pictures of what would satisfy the needs for survival, love and belonging, power, freedom and fun. A reality therapist tries to learn what is in the client's quality world and to become part of it, then helps the client evaluate whether current behavior is getting him what he wants.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Reality Therapy: the quality world
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

803. nce-s-cou-183 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · reality therapy and choice theory · medium · In review

A client agreed to walk for 20 minutes three mornings this week. She returns saying she "just couldn't find the time." Which response BEST reflects the reality therapy principles of accepting no excuses and using no punishment?
A. "That is disappointing. We agreed on this, so I expect you to make up the missed walks."
Expressing disappointment and imposing a make-up penalty is criticism and punishment, which reality therapists avoid because it damages the relationship.
B. "Tell me more about what made this week so hard. Your schedule may explain a great deal."
Inviting a long account of why the plan failed accepts the excuse and keeps the focus off what she will do next.
C. "Maybe this plan asked too much of you. Let's set exercise aside and work on something else."
Dropping the goal is giving up on the client, which Glasser explicitly cautioned against.
D. "Do you still want this? If so, let's make a smaller plan you are sure you can carry out." ✔ KEY
The counselor neither accepts the excuse nor punishes; she checks the want and helps make a simpler, more attainable plan.
Rationale: When a plan is not carried out, reality therapists do not accept excuses, do not criticize or punish, and do not give up. Instead they return to the client's wants, have the client evaluate what she is doing, and make a new plan that is simple, attainable and within her control (the SAMIC qualities of a good plan).
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Reality Therapy: planning and commitment; no excuses, no punishment, do not give up
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

804. nce-s-cou-184 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · reflection, paraphrasing and summarizing · easy · In review

A 56-year-old client says, "My son moved across the country for work last month. The house is so quiet now, and I still catch myself setting four places at dinner." Which response is the BEST reflection of feeling?
A. "Your son moved away for work last month, and the house is quieter now."
This restates the content of what she said (a paraphrase) but does not name the emotion beneath it.
B. "You are feeling a real sense of loss and loneliness with him gone." ✔ KEY
It identifies the underlying emotions (loss, loneliness) that her words and the image of the extra place setting convey.
C. "How often do the two of you talk now that he lives so far away?"
A question gathers information and shifts focus to logistics rather than reflecting her feeling.
D. "Many parents feel this way at first, and it gets easier with time."
Reassurance and normalizing can feel dismissive and do not reflect her specific feeling back to her.
Rationale: A reflection of feeling names the emotion the client is expressing, often one implied rather than stated, so the client feels understood and can explore it further. Paraphrasing captures content, questions gather information, and reassurance can cut exploration short.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling skills: reflection of feeling versus paraphrasing
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

805. nce-s-cou-185 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · reflection, paraphrasing and summarizing · medium · In review

A counselor opens the fourth session by saying, "Last week you talked about the tension with your sister, the late nights at work and how little sleep you are getting, and you decided to try leaving the office by six. Where would you like to begin today?" Which skill is the counselor using, and for what purpose?
A. Paraphrasing, to restate a single message in fresher and shorter words
A paraphrase restates one recent client message; this response pulls together material from an entire prior session.
B. Interpretation, to offer a new frame of reference for the client's issues
The counselor adds no new meaning or explanation; she simply organizes what the client already said.
C. Summarizing, to tie earlier material together and give the session focus ✔ KEY
Summaries condense several themes over a longer span and are often used to open a session, provide continuity and set direction.
D. Immediacy, to address what is happening in the relationship right now
Immediacy concerns the here-and-now counselor-client relationship, which this response does not address.
Rationale: Summarizing condenses several client statements, themes or feelings over a longer stretch of time. Counselors use it to begin a session (linking to the last one), to shift topics, to close a session, and to check shared understanding. It differs from paraphrasing in scope, and from interpretation in that it adds no new frame.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling skills: summarization and its uses
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

806. nce-s-cou-186 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · confrontation and immediacy · medium · In review

A client says, "I'm completely over the breakup," as her eyes fill with tears and she twists a ring on her finger. Which counselor response is the BEST example of a skilled confrontation?
A. "You say you're over it, and yet your eyes are filling with tears." ✔ KEY
It describes the discrepancy between her words and her nonverbal behavior, tentatively and without judgment, and leaves her room to explore it.
B. "You clearly are not over it, and denying it will only make things harder."
This tells the client what she feels and labels her as denying; it is judgmental and likely to provoke defensiveness.
C. "Why are you crying right now if you really are over the breakup?"
"Why" questions about a discrepancy tend to feel accusatory and invite justification rather than exploration.
D. "It sounds like you have worked very hard to move on from this breakup."
This supportive reflection ignores the discrepancy entirely, so it is not a confrontation.
Rationale: In counseling, confrontation means pointing out a discrepancy (between words and nonverbal behavior, between statements, or between words and actions) in a caring, descriptive way. The "you say ... and yet ..." format names both sides without judgment and invites the client to examine the mixed message. Accusing, interpreting or asking "why" tends to raise defenses.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling skills: confrontation of discrepancies
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

807. nce-s-cou-187 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · confrontation and immediacy · hard · In review

Over six sessions, a client has said repairing his marriage is his top goal, yet he has cancelled each couples appointment he scheduled. The alliance is strong. The counselor gently notes this discrepancy, and the client is quiet, then says, "I guess I've been avoiding it because I'm afraid she'll tell me she wants out." What should the counselor do NEXT?
A. Restate the discrepancy more firmly so that its importance is not lost on him
He has already acknowledged the discrepancy; pressing it harder adds pressure without adding understanding.
B. Shift to a lighter topic to ease the tension that the confrontation created
Retreating just as he opens up signals that his fear is too much to talk about and loses the opening the confrontation made.
C. Ask him to commit now to attending the next couples appointment he schedules
Moving straight to a commitment skips exploration of the fear that drives the avoidance and risks hollow compliance.
D. Reflect his fear and explore what avoiding the sessions has protected him from ✔ KEY
Following a confrontation, the counselor attends to the client's response; he has accepted the discrepancy, so exploring the underlying fear deepens the work.
Rationale: A confrontation is only as useful as what follows it. The counselor watches how the client responds (denial, partial acceptance or full recognition) and builds on it. Here the client has recognized the discrepancy and named a fear, so empathic reflection and exploration of that fear come before planning new behavior.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Counseling skills: confrontation and evaluating the client's response
⚑ Check: Applied-skills judgment item; confirm the Gladding locator on confrontation and that "explore before planning" is the clearly best sequencing.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

808. nce-s-cou-188 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · termination skills · hard · In review

A client whose panic attacks resolved months ago has a history of losing caregivers in childhood. Three sessions before a jointly planned ending, she reports two new panic attacks and asks whether she can keep coming "for as long as it takes." What is the BEST response?
A. Agree to continue open-ended weekly counseling, since her symptoms have now returned
Reflexively extending treatment can confirm her fear that she cannot cope without the counselor and skips the meaning of the ending.
B. Explore her feelings about ending, normalize a brief return of symptoms and review gains ✔ KEY
A temporary return of symptoms near termination is a familiar reaction, especially with a history of loss; processing the ending and her skills is the core task.
C. Keep to the plan and avoid discussing the attacks, so as not to reinforce her symptoms
Ignoring the attacks and her feelings about ending leaves important material unprocessed and may feel like another abandonment.
D. Refer her to a new counselor now so that she has ongoing support once the sessions end
An abrupt transfer just before ending sidesteps the termination work and offers no reason why a new counselor is needed.
Rationale: Termination can stir up feelings of loss, particularly for clients with histories of abandonment, and a temporary regression is common. The counselor normalizes this, explores what ending means to the client, reviews her progress and coping skills, and may adjust the pace (for example, spacing sessions) rather than dropping or reflexively extending the plan.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Termination: client reactions and resistance to ending
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

809. nce-s-cou-189 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · termination skills · easy · In review

A client has met his counseling goals. Rather than stopping abruptly, the counselor proposes moving from weekly sessions to sessions every three weeks, followed by a booster session two months later. What is the MAIN purpose of this plan?
A. To let him practice new skills on his own while support is still available ✔ KEY
Spacing sessions and adding a booster lets the client rely on himself while the counselor can still help consolidate gains and plan for setbacks.
B. To keep him from forming an unhealthy dependence in the early sessions
The plan addresses the end of counseling, not the formation of dependence early in treatment.
C. To meet an ACA requirement that each ending include follow-up sessions
The ACA Code of Ethics does not require follow-up sessions for every termination.
D. To delay the ending until he no longer reports any symptoms whatsoever
The goals are already met; waiting for a symptom-free state is not the aim of tapering.
Rationale: Gradually spacing sessions (fading) and scheduling a booster or follow-up session are common termination practices. They allow the client to test and consolidate new skills independently, give room to address relapse prevention, and make the ending less abrupt.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Termination: fading sessions and follow-up
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

810. nce-s-cou-190 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · Adlerian therapy · medium · In review

A client reports frequent headaches that keep her home from social events. Her Adlerian counselor asks, "If these headaches went away tomorrow, what would you be doing differently in your life?" What is the PRIMARY purpose of this question?
A. To help her picture a future with no problem, as in a miracle question
The miracle question is a solution-focused technique for building goals; the Adlerian question has a diagnostic aim.
B. To uncover a repressed conflict that is being converted into pain
Conversion of repressed conflict is a psychoanalytic formulation, not the purpose Adlerians give this question.
C. To learn whether the symptom serves a purpose, such as avoiding a task ✔ KEY
"The Question" helps the counselor see whether the symptom has a social purpose, such as excusing the client from a life task she fears.
D. To rate how much the headaches interfere with her daily functioning
Rating functional impairment is an assessment task; the question is meant to reveal the goal of the symptom.
Rationale: Adlerians view symptoms as purposeful. "The Question" (asking what the client would do if the symptom were gone) helps distinguish problems that may be largely physical from those that serve a goal, such as avoiding friendship, work or love tasks. If the answer names something the client is avoiding, the symptom may be safeguarding her from it.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Adlerian Therapy: "The Question" and the purposeful nature of symptoms
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

811. nce-s-cou-191 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · Adlerian therapy · hard · In review

A teacher consults a school counselor about a 9-year-old who tears up classmates' artwork and makes cruel remarks to the teacher. The teacher says she feels deeply hurt and wonders how a child could treat her this way. Using Dreikurs's goals of misbehavior, which goal is the child MOST likely pursuing?
A. Attention
An attention goal typically leaves the adult feeling annoyed or irritated, not hurt.
B. Power
A power goal typically leaves the adult feeling angry, provoked or challenged.
C. Display of inadequacy
Display of inadequacy leaves the adult feeling hopeless or discouraged as the child gives up.
D. Revenge ✔ KEY
When adults feel hurt, the child is often seeking revenge, trying to hurt others as he feels hurt.
Rationale: Rudolf Dreikurs, who extended Adler's ideas to parenting and schools, described four mistaken goals of misbehavior: attention, power, revenge and display of inadequacy. A practical clue is the adult's own reaction: annoyance (attention), anger (power), hurt (revenge) and hopelessness (inadequacy). Identifying the goal helps adults stop reinforcing it and encourage the child.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Adlerian Therapy: Dreikurs and the goals of misbehavior
⚑ Check: Dreikurs's four goals are standard; confirm that the cited Corey edition covers them (Gladding's child/school chapters are an alternative locator).
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

812. nce-s-cou-192 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · person-centered therapy · medium · In review

A client sees himself as "a calm person who doesn't get angry." When his partner says he shouted during an argument, he insists he was "just being emphatic." In Rogers's theory of personality, this BEST illustrates:
A. Reaction formation against an unacceptable id impulse of anger
Reaction formation (expressing the opposite of an impulse) is a Freudian defense rooted in id-superego conflict, not Rogers's framework.
B. Distortion of an experience that threatens the self-concept ✔ KEY
Rogers held that experiences inconsistent with the self-concept are distorted or denied to awareness, maintaining incongruence.
C. Introjection of a parent's rules, swallowed whole without question
Introjection is a gestalt contact boundary disturbance about uncritically accepting others' values.
D. Minimization, a cognitive distortion that should be disputed
Minimization is a CBT term, and person-centered counselors do not dispute thoughts.
Rationale: In Rogers's theory, when an experience (here, anger) does not fit the self-concept, the person may perceive it selectively (distortion) or keep it out of awareness entirely (denial). The gap between self-concept and experience is incongruence, which produces vulnerability and anxiety. The core conditions make it safe enough to let such experiences into awareness.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-Centered Therapy: incongruence, distortion and denial
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

813. nce-s-cou-193 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · person-centered therapy · hard · In review

A client says, "I suppose I'm kind of annoyed with my sister, but it's not a big deal," while clenching her fist. Which option BEST matches how a person-centered counselor and a gestalt counselor would each MOST likely respond?
A. Person-centered: reflect the annoyance she is starting to own; gestalt: ask her to give her fist a voice ✔ KEY
Person-centered counselors follow and empathically reflect the client's emerging feeling; gestalt counselors direct attention to present bodily awareness and often invite the client to speak as the body part.
B. Person-centered: ask her to exaggerate the clenched fist; gestalt: reflect the annoyance she now owns
The pairing is reversed: exaggeration is a gestalt experiment, and nondirective reflection is person-centered.
C. Person-centered: interpret her anger as displaced; gestalt: dispute her belief that anger is no big deal
Interpreting displacement is psychoanalytic and disputing beliefs is REBT; neither fits these two approaches.
D. Person-centered: advise her on how to talk with her sister; gestalt: explore early memories of the sister
Person-centered counselors avoid advice, and gestalt work stays with present experience rather than early memories.
Rationale: Both approaches are humanistic and value awareness, but they differ in counselor activity. A person-centered counselor stays nondirective, offering empathy so the client can more fully own her feeling. A gestalt counselor is more active, noticing nonverbal behavior and creating experiments, such as giving the fist a voice, to heighten here-and-now awareness.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-Centered Therapy: empathic reflection and the nondirective stance · Corey (Theory & Practice) — Gestalt Therapy: attending to nonverbal behavior and experiments
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

814. nce-s-cou-194 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · existential therapy · easy · In review

A 44-year-old client says, "I have no choice but to stay in a job I hate. My family expects it." Which counselor response is MOST consistent with existential therapy?
A. Dispute the irrational belief that he must meet his family's expectations
Disputing "must" beliefs is the core REBT technique, not the existential focus.
B. Explore how his early bond with his father shaped this need to comply
Tracing present behavior to early relationships is a psychodynamic focus.
C. Help him see that staying is a choice and explore what it means to him ✔ KEY
Existential counselors highlight freedom and responsibility, helping clients recognize that they are choosing even when they claim they have no choice.
D. Rehearse assertive statements he can use when his family raises it
Assertiveness rehearsal is a behavioral skills intervention.
Rationale: Existential therapy holds that people are free and therefore responsible for their choices. Statements such as "I have no choice" are seen as ways of avoiding that responsibility. The counselor helps the client own his choices, face the anxiety that comes with freedom, and decide how he wants to live.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Existential Therapy: freedom and responsibility
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

815. nce-s-cou-195 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · existential therapy · hard · In review

A 67-year-old client recently told his cancer is terminal says, "What's the point of anything now?" He is not suicidal. Which counselor response is MOST characteristic of an existential approach rather than a cognitive behavioral one?
A. "What evidence tells you that nothing has a point? Let's examine it together."
Testing the evidence for a thought is cognitive restructuring, a CBT method.
B. "Facing death has you asking what matters. What gives your days meaning now?" ✔ KEY
The existential counselor treats the question as a genuine confrontation with death and meaning and invites him to explore it.
C. "Let's schedule a few small, pleasant activities each day to lift your mood."
Scheduling pleasant activities is behavioral activation, a CBT strategy for low mood.
D. "Tell me about earlier losses in your life that this news is stirring up."
Linking present reactions to past losses reflects a psychodynamic focus.
Rationale: A CBT counselor might treat "What's the point?" as a hopeless automatic thought to test or as low mood to activate. An existential counselor sees it as an authentic encounter with the givens of death and meaninglessness and helps the client search for meaning, values and connection in the time that remains. Yalom argued that facing death honestly can deepen how one lives, and Frankl that meaning can be found even in unavoidable suffering.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Existential Therapy: death, meaning and the search for meaning
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

816. nce-s-cou-196 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · behavior therapy · medium · In review

Two counselors treat clients who fear elevators. One teaches relaxation and works up a ranked list of feared scenes. The other has the client ride an elevator repeatedly for a long session, without leaving, until the anxiety subsides. Which statement accurately contrasts these approaches?
A. Flooding pairs relaxation with each step; desensitization keeps the client at peak fear
This reverses the methods: relaxation pairing belongs to systematic desensitization.
B. Both rely on reciprocal inhibition, but flooding is limited to scenes that are imagined
Flooding does not rely on a competing relaxation response, and it can be done in vivo or in imagination.
C. Desensitization blocks escape; flooding lets the client stop at any step of a hierarchy
This reverses them: flooding prevents escape, while desensitization moves gradually and lets the client pause.
D. Flooding is intense and blocks escape; desensitization is graded and paired with relaxation ✔ KEY
Flooding uses prolonged, high-intensity exposure with response prevention; systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with a graded hierarchy.
Rationale: Wolpe's systematic desensitization uses relaxation training, an anxiety hierarchy and gradual exposure so that relaxation inhibits anxiety. Flooding exposes the client to a highly feared stimulus for a prolonged period, in vivo or imaginal, while preventing escape, so anxiety extinguishes. Flooding often works faster but is more distressing and needs careful informed consent.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Behavior Therapy: systematic desensitization, in vivo exposure and flooding
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

817. nce-s-cou-197 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · behavior therapy · easy · In review

A counselor, a 13-year-old and his parents write and sign an agreement: on each school night he finishes his homework by 8 p.m., he earns 30 minutes of video games, and his father will check the work and deliver the reward. Which behavioral technique is this?
A. Contingency contract ✔ KEY
A contingency contract is a written agreement that specifies the target behavior, the consequence and who delivers it.
B. Token economy
A token economy uses tokens or points later exchanged for backup reinforcers; no tokens are involved here.
C. Response cost
Response cost removes a reinforcer after an unwanted behavior; this plan adds a reward for a wanted one.
D. Covert sensitization
Covert sensitization pairs an unwanted behavior with an imagined aversive event.
Rationale: Contingency contracts make the "if-then" relationship between behavior and consequence explicit. Effective contracts define the behavior in observable terms, specify the reinforcer, name who monitors and delivers it, and are agreed to by everyone involved, which increases the client's sense of ownership.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Behavior Therapy: operant techniques and contingency contracts
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

818. nce-s-cou-198 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · cognitive behavioral therapy · medium · In review

A client says, "My boss walked right past me this morning without saying hello. I'm going to get fired." Which counselor response BEST illustrates Socratic questioning?
A. "Your boss was probably just busy, so I really doubt you will be fired."
Reassurance supplies the counselor's conclusion instead of helping the client examine the thought himself.
B. "That is catastrophizing, so try replacing it with a positive thought."
Labeling the distortion and prescribing a replacement is didactic, not guided discovery.
C. "What are some other reasons your boss might have walked past you?" ✔ KEY
The open question guides the client to generate alternative explanations and weigh the evidence for himself.
D. "How did you feel in that moment when your boss walked past you?"
Exploring the feeling is useful but does not question the accuracy of the automatic thought.
Rationale: Socratic questioning, central to Beck's guided discovery, uses open questions to help clients examine evidence, consider alternative explanations and reach their own conclusions about a thought. Counselor-supplied reassurance or labeling may be accurate but tends to be less persuasive than conclusions the client reaches.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Cognitive Behavior Therapy: Beck's Socratic dialogue and guided discovery
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

819. nce-s-cou-199 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · cognitive behavioral therapy · medium · In review

A client with depression says she used to love her pottery class and will start going again "once I feel more motivated." Which response BEST reflects behavioral activation?
A. Agree to wait until her mood lifts, since pushing activity now could set her up to fail
Behavioral activation holds that waiting for motivation keeps clients stuck; action is expected to come first.
B. Schedule a pottery session this week and rate her mood and mastery after it ✔ KEY
BA works "outside-in": the client schedules valued activity according to a plan, not a mood, and tracks its effects.
C. First identify and dispute the core belief that is behind her lack of motivation
Disputing core beliefs is cognitive restructuring; BA targets behavior and avoidance directly.
D. Explore the earlier losses that may account for her loss of interest in pottery
Exploring past losses reflects a psychodynamic focus rather than activation.
Rationale: Behavioral activation treats depression by reducing avoidance and increasing contact with rewarding, valued activities. Clients monitor activities and mood, then schedule specific activities according to a plan rather than waiting to feel like it, often rating pleasure and mastery. Motivation tends to follow action rather than precede it.
References: APA CPG — Depression guideline (2019): behavioral therapy, including behavioral activation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

820. nce-s-cou-200 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · cognitive behavioral therapy · easy · In review

On a thought record, a client has written the situation, her automatic thought ("Everyone at the party thought I was boring") and her emotion (embarrassment, 85%). What does a cognitive therapy thought record typically ask her to do NEXT?
A. Trace the thought back to the childhood memory that first produced it
Finding the childhood origin of a thought is not the next step of a thought record.
B. Repeat a positive affirmation until the thought no longer feels true
Affirmations replace the thought without examining it, which is not cognitive restructuring.
C. Describe the thought in more detail without judging if it is accurate
Noticing thoughts without evaluating them is closer to mindfulness or defusion than to a thought record.
D. Weigh the evidence and write a more balanced, alternative response ✔ KEY
Thought records move from identifying the thought to evaluating it and writing an adaptive response, then re-rating the emotion.
Rationale: A thought record structures cognitive restructuring: situation, automatic thought, emotion and its intensity, then evaluation of the thought (evidence for and against, alternative explanations) leading to a balanced or adaptive response, and finally a re-rating of the emotion. It teaches clients to treat thoughts as hypotheses rather than facts.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Cognitive Behavior Therapy: Beck's cognitive therapy and recording automatic thoughts
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

821. nce-s-cou-201 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · psychodynamic and psychoanalytic theory · easy · In review

Freud called it the "fundamental rule" of psychoanalysis: the client reports whatever comes to mind, however trivial, illogical or embarrassing it seems, without censoring it. This technique is called:
A. Free association ✔ KEY
Free association asks the client to say everything that comes to mind, opening a path to unconscious material.
B. Dream analysis
Dream analysis interprets the manifest and latent content of dreams; it is a separate technique.
C. Interpretation
Interpretation is the analyst's explanation of the meaning of material, not the client's uncensored reporting.
D. Catharsis
Catharsis is the release of pent-up emotion, which may occur but is not the reporting rule itself.
Rationale: Free association is the basic method of psychoanalysis. By suspending conscious censorship, the client lets associations lead toward repressed wishes and conflicts. The analyst attends especially to blocks, pauses and changes of topic, which may signal resistance.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic Therapy: free association
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

822. nce-s-cou-202 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · psychodynamic and psychoanalytic theory · hard · In review

After gaining the insight that he ends relationships once they become close, a client begins arriving late and "forgets" a session. Weeks later he describes pulling away from a new partner in the same way. From a psychoanalytic perspective, which statement BEST describes what is happening and how to proceed?
A. The lateness reflects low motivation, so firm attendance rules with consequences should be set
Treating the lateness as a compliance problem misses its unconscious meaning, which is the analyst's main interest.
B. The repetition shows the insight was wrong, so the original interpretation should be dropped
Repetition after insight is expected; it does not by itself show the interpretation was wrong.
C. The lateness is resistance to be explored, and the repeated pattern calls for working through ✔ KEY
Lateness and forgetting after a painful insight are classic resistance, and insight is consolidated by working through the conflict repeatedly.
D. The relapse shows a need for catharsis, so his feelings should be discharged more fully
Emotional discharge alone was abandoned by Freud as a mechanism of lasting change.
Rationale: In psychoanalytic therapy, resistance is anything that keeps unconscious material from awareness, such as lateness, missed sessions or changing the subject, and it is interpreted rather than punished. A single insight rarely changes a pattern; working through is the repeated exploration of the same conflict as it appears in many situations and in the transference until change takes hold.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic Therapy: interpreting resistance and working through
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

823. nce-s-cou-203 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · hard · In review

A 40-year-old moved across the country at 20 and has not spoken to his parents in ten years. He says, "I've put all that behind me." His father also stopped speaking to his own family as a young man, and the client's marriage now swings between intense closeness and angry distance. How would a Bowenian therapist MOST likely understand and approach this?
A. His distance shows a high level of differentiation, so therapy should focus only on the marriage
For Bowen, physical or emotional distance is not differentiation; cutoff reflects unresolved fusion with the family.
B. The family's rigid boundaries should be restructured by having it enact the conflict in session
Boundaries and enactments are structural (Minuchin) concepts, not Bowen's.
C. The marriage problems call for a paradoxical directive to have the couple fight on purpose
Paradoxical directives are a strategic technique; Bowen coaching emphasizes calm, reflective self-work.
D. Cutoff manages unresolved fusion passed down the generations; he would be coached to reconnect ✔ KEY
Emotional cutoff handles fusion by distance, and its repetition across generations reflects multigenerational transmission; Bowen coaching helps clients re-engage their families while staying differentiated.
Rationale: Bowen saw emotional cutoff as a way of managing unresolved attachment by distance, not as a sign of maturity; the fusion tends to reappear in other close relationships, such as a marriage. Multigenerational transmission explains how such patterns and levels of differentiation pass down family lines. Therapy often involves a genogram and coaching the client to make calm, person-to-person contact with family of origin.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Bowen family systems theory: emotional cutoff and multigenerational transmission process
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

824. nce-s-cou-204 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · medium · In review

In a first session with a family, a counselor lets the father speak first as the family expects, picks up the family's own phrases and pace, and follows their story. Afterward she sketches a diagram showing a diffuse boundary between the mother and son and a rigid one around the father. In structural family therapy, these two activities are BEST described as:
A. Triangulating and then detriangulating the parental subsystem
Triangulation and detriangulation are Bowen concepts about drawing in a third person, not this sequence.
B. Joining the family, then mapping its boundaries and subsystems ✔ KEY
Accommodating to the family's style and hierarchy is joining; the boundary diagram is a structural map.
C. Prescribing the symptom, then reframing the family's problem
Symptom prescription and reframing are strategic techniques, and neither occurs here.
D. Building a genogram to trace patterns across three generations
A genogram traces multigenerational patterns (Bowen); a structural map shows current boundaries and alignments.
Rationale: Minuchin's structural therapist first joins the family, accommodating to its style through maintenance, tracking and mimesis, to become accepted as a leader of the therapeutic system. Family mapping then charts current structure: subsystems, hierarchy and boundaries that are clear, diffuse (enmeshed) or rigid (disengaged), guiding later restructuring interventions.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Structural family therapy: joining, accommodating and family mapping
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

825. nce-s-cou-205 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · trauma-informed interventions · medium · In review

At intake, a counselor explains to a client with a history of sexual assault what each part of the interview involves and why questions are asked. She lets the client choose where to sit and whether the door stays open, and says she may skip any question. These practices BEST reflect:
A. Trauma-informed principles of safety, transparency and choice that limit retraumatization ✔ KEY
Explaining procedures, offering choices and control, and attending to physical safety are core trauma-informed practices.
B. Early exposure to trauma cues so that habituation can begin right from the first session
Nothing here exposes the client to trauma cues; the aim is to reduce, not evoke, distress at intake.
C. Analytic neutrality and abstinence so that transference can develop without interference
Neutrality and abstinence are psychoanalytic stances and do not describe sharing control with the client.
D. Standardized intake procedures that apply the very same steps to every client at the agency
Offering individual choices is the opposite of a rigid, uniform procedure.
Rationale: Trauma-informed care assumes that many clients have trauma histories and organizes services to avoid retraumatization. Practices include physical and emotional safety, transparency about what will happen, and collaboration, choice and empowerment, so that clients regain a sense of control that trauma took away.
References: SAMHSA TIP 57 — Trauma-informed care principles: safety, trustworthiness, choice and avoiding retraumatization
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

826. nce-s-cou-206 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · trauma-informed interventions · hard · In review

A veteran with PTSD writes an impact statement about why he thinks a friend died in an ambush and how it changed his beliefs about safety, trust, power, esteem and intimacy. His therapist then helps him identify "stuck points," such as "It was my fault," and examine them with structured worksheets. Which treatment is this?
A. Prolonged exposure therapy
Prolonged exposure (Foa) centers on repeated imaginal and in vivo exposure, not written impact statements and stuck-point worksheets.
B. EMDR
EMDR (Shapiro) uses bilateral stimulation while the client holds the memory in mind, within an eight-phase protocol.
C. Cognitive processing therapy ✔ KEY
CPT (Resick) uses the impact statement, stuck points and worksheets across five themes: safety, trust, power/control, esteem and intimacy.
D. Stress inoculation training
Stress inoculation training (Meichenbaum) builds coping skills in three phases; it does not target stuck points.
Rationale: Cognitive processing therapy, developed by Patricia Resick, is a trauma-focused cognitive therapy recommended in major PTSD practice guidelines. Clients write an impact statement, identify stuck points (often self-blame or overgeneralized beliefs), and use worksheets to challenge them, with later sessions on safety, trust, power and control, esteem and intimacy.
References: APA CPG — PTSD guideline (2017): cognitive processing therapy · VA/DoD CPG — PTSD guideline: trauma-focused psychotherapies (CPT, PE, EMDR)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

827. nce-s-cou-207 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · crisis intervention models · easy · In review

According to classic crisis theory, which statement BEST describes an acute crisis?
A. A sign of underlying mental illness that calls for long-term treatment
Crisis is viewed as a normal response to an overwhelming event, not evidence of psychopathology.
B. A property of the event, so anyone facing it will be in crisis
Crisis depends on the person's perception of the event and coping resources; the same event may not cause a crisis for everyone.
C. A chronic state that lasts until the person receives counseling
Crisis states are time-limited; a person reaches some new equilibrium with or without help.
D. A time-limited state that resolves within weeks, for better or worse ✔ KEY
Caplan described crisis as a temporary disequilibrium that usually resolves within about four to six weeks, in an adaptive or maladaptive direction.
Rationale: Crisis theory, building on Lindemann and Caplan, holds that a crisis arises when a person perceives an event as overwhelming their usual coping. The state is time-limited, commonly cited as about four to six weeks, and resolves at a higher, equal or lower level of functioning. Because it contains both danger and opportunity, brief, prompt intervention can tip the outcome toward growth.
References: James & Gilliland (Crisis Intervention Strategies) — Approaching crisis intervention: definitions of crisis and basic crisis theory
⚑ Check: The "four to six weeks" duration is the commonly taught figure from Caplan; confirm wording against the cited James & Gilliland edition.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

828. nce-s-cou-208 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · crisis intervention models · hard · In review

Hours after a house fire, a client sits staring at the floor, cannot say where she will sleep tonight, and does not respond to questions about whom she might call. Her triage assessment shows severe impairment. Using James and Gilliland's continuum of crisis worker involvement, which stance is MOST appropriate?
A. Nondirective, letting her generate her own plan so that her sense of control is not taken away
A nondirective stance fits clients who are mobile and able to act; she cannot currently generate options.
B. Directive, taking charge to assess safety, give clear guidance and arrange immediate shelter ✔ KEY
When a client is immobile and severely impaired, the worker becomes directive, taking temporary control to meet urgent needs.
C. Collaborative, working as an equal partner to weigh options that she suggests for the night
Collaboration suits clients with partial mobility; she is not yet able to contribute options.
D. Deferred, holding off on any action until a full psychosocial history has been completed
Crisis work addresses immediate safety and needs first; a full history is not a prerequisite for action.
Rationale: James and Gilliland describe a continuum of worker involvement matched to the client's level of mobility, as gauged by triage assessment of affective, behavioral and cognitive functioning. Immobile clients need a directive worker; partially mobile clients, a collaborative one; and mobile clients, a nondirective one. The stance shifts toward less direction as the client regains functioning.
References: James & Gilliland (Crisis Intervention Strategies) — Six-step model: directive, collaborative and nondirective involvement; Triage Assessment Form
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

829. nce-s-cou-209 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · motivational interviewing · medium · In review

Partway through a session, a court-referred client crosses his arms and says, "You're just like my probation officer, always telling me what to do." Which counselor response BEST reflects how motivational interviewing handles discord?
A. "I'm not telling you what to do. I'm only giving you the facts here."
Defending oneself argues with the client and tends to increase discord.
B. "If you don't engage here, I will have to report that to your officer."
A warning or threat is confrontational and escalates the conflict in the relationship.
C. "You're tired of being told what to do. Here, the choices are yours." ✔ KEY
Reflecting his frustration and emphasizing autonomy de-escalates discord without arguing.
D. "Let's get back to your plan. What will you change before next week?"
Pushing ahead ignores the strain in the relationship and is likely to deepen it.
Rationale: In current MI, discord refers to tension in the working relationship, distinct from sustain talk about the behavior. Counselors respond without arguing: reflecting, apologizing, affirming or shifting focus, and emphasizing the client's autonomy. This replaces the older idea of "rolling with resistance" and keeps the counselor from triggering further defensiveness.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Responding to sustain talk and discord; emphasizing autonomy
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

830. nce-s-cou-210 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · motivational interviewing · medium · In review

Asked to rate on a 0 to 10 scale how important it is to her to stop vaping, a 19-year-old says, "Maybe a 3." Which follow-up question is MOST likely to elicit change talk?
A. "Why a 3 and not a 1 or a 2?" ✔ KEY
Asking why the number is not lower invites her to state her own reasons for change, which is change talk.
B. "Why only a 3 and not higher?"
Asking why the number is not higher invites her to defend the status quo, eliciting sustain talk.
C. "What would get you to a 10?"
Jumping to the top of the scale is a large leap that tends to bring out reasons it is not possible.
D. "Isn't a 3 a bit low for you?"
This implies judgment and reflects the righting reflex, which tends to provoke defensiveness.
Rationale: Importance and confidence rulers are a common MI strategy for evoking change talk. The key follow-up is to ask why the client chose that number rather than a lower one, which prompts her to voice her own reasons for change. Asking why the number is not higher tends to elicit sustain talk instead.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Evoking change talk: importance and confidence rulers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

831. nce-s-cou-211 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · medium · In review

A counselor holds individual pre-group interviews for a 12-week interpersonal process group. She spends each interview asking about symptoms, history and current stressors, then tells applicants whether they have been accepted. Her supervisor says an essential element of screening is missing. Which element is it?
A. Requiring a formal DSM-5-TR diagnosis before any applicant joins
A diagnosis is not required for most counseling groups, and it says little about fit with a particular group.
B. Letting applicants ask questions and judge whether the group fits ✔ KEY
Screening is a two-way process: applicants learn about the group and leader and decide whether it meets their needs.
C. Ranking applicants by a personality inventory to pick the strongest group
Selection rests on fit with group goals and readiness, not on ranking applicants by a test score.
D. Asking applicants to agree to meet socially with members between sessions
Outside socializing is not encouraged in therapy groups and is not a screening goal.
Rationale: Pre-group screening selects members whose needs and goals fit the group, who will not impede the process and whose well-being will not be jeopardized by it. It is also a chance for prospective members to interview the leader, learn about the group's purpose and procedures and decide for themselves whether to join. A one-sided interview that only gathers clinical data misses that mutual decision.
References: ASGW Best Practice Guidelines — Planning: group and member preparation (screening and orientation) · ACA Code of Ethics — A.9.a Screening
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

832. nce-s-cou-212 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · easy · In review

A counselor is preparing the informed consent discussion for a new adult therapy group. Which statement BEST belongs in that discussion?
A. The leader guarantees that every member will keep what is said confidential.
Leaders cannot guarantee that other members will keep confidentiality, and consent must state this limit.
B. Once you join, you are expected to attend until the final group session ends.
Members keep the right to leave; consent explains how to leave, not that leaving is barred.
C. You may feel pressure to share, but you decide what and how much to disclose. ✔ KEY
Naming the risk of group pressure and affirming the member's control over disclosure is core group consent content.
D. The leader will decide how much personal material each member shares weekly.
Members, not the leader, decide what they disclose; leaders protect members from coercion.
Rationale: Informed consent for a group covers its purpose, procedures and leader qualifications, the limits of confidentiality among members, and the psychological risks of participation, such as pressure to disclose, confrontation and changes that affect outside relationships. Members are told that they control their own disclosures and how to leave the group if they choose.
References: ASGW Best Practice Guidelines — Planning: group and member preparation (informed consent) · ACA Code of Ethics — A.2.b Types of Information Needed; B.4.a Group Work
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

833. nce-s-cou-213 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · medium · In review

A counselor in a community clinic is planning an open-ended outpatient interpersonal therapy group for adults. Which plan for size and session length is MOST consistent with Yalom's recommendations?
A. About 3 members, meeting weekly for 30 minutes
Three members is too few for rich interaction, and 30 minutes leaves no time to warm up and work.
B. About 15 members, meeting weekly for 45 minutes
Fifteen members is too many for interaction-focused work, and 45 minutes is too short.
C. About 12 members, meeting weekly for 3 hours
Twelve is above the usual range, and sessions beyond about 2 hours tend to tire members.
D. About 7 members, weekly for 80-90 minutes ✔ KEY
Yalom places the ideal interactional group near 7 or 8 members, with sessions of about 80 to 90 minutes.
Rationale: Yalom suggests that an interactional therapy group works best with about 7 or 8 members, within an acceptable range of roughly 5 to 10. Sessions need time for a warm-up period and for working through themes, so most groups meet for 80 to 90 minutes; beyond about 2 hours members tend to become weary. Groups for children or for highly impaired inpatients are usually smaller and shorter.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — Creation of the group: group size and duration of meetings
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

834. nce-s-cou-214 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · medium · In review

In the sixth session of a process group, members keep switching topics whenever anyone mentions loneliness. The leader is considering a self-disclosure. Which disclosure is MOST consistent with Yalom's guidance on leader transparency?
A. "I went through a lonely divorce years ago, so let me tell you how I got through it."
A detailed personal history shifts the focus to the leader and rarely helps members with their own here-and-now work.
B. "I feel a bit shut out as we keep changing topics. I wonder what others feel now." ✔ KEY
A brief here-and-now disclosure of the leader's reaction models openness and invites members to examine the process.
C. "I have struggles of my own lately, so I am one more member of the group tonight."
Presenting oneself as a member blurs the leader role and burdens the group with the leader's problems.
D. "I keep my reactions private so that you can project onto me more freely here."
A blank-screen stance is not what Yalom advises; judicious transparency aids the interactional group.
Rationale: Yalom favors leader self-disclosure that is focused on the here-and-now and offered in the service of members' work, such as sharing a reaction to what is happening in the room. Lengthy disclosure of the leader's past or current personal problems tends to redirect attention, burden members and blur the leader role, while total opacity deprives the group of useful modeling.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — The therapist: transparency and the use of the self
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

835. nce-s-cou-215 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · hard · In review

Near the end of a co-led depression group, a member quietly says she has stockpiled pills and "probably won't be around next week." Other members look stunned. What should the leaders do?
A. Note her comment and plan to raise it with her at the start of next week's session
Waiting a week ignores an imminent risk statement; risk must be assessed immediately.
B. Ask members to share reasons to live so the group can talk her out of the plan now
Peer persuasion is not a risk assessment and puts members in a role they cannot safely fill.
C. Remove her from the group and give her a referral for individual counseling instead
Removal without assessing and managing her immediate safety abandons her at a moment of risk.
D. Acknowledge it, have one leader assess her risk privately now, and help the group process ✔ KEY
Her safety comes first through an immediate individual assessment, while the other leader helps members with their reactions.
Rationale: A disclosure of suicidal intent during group calls for immediate action. The leaders acknowledge what was said, one leader (or the leader right after the group) conducts a private risk assessment and safety planning, and the group is helped to process its reactions now and in later sessions. Co-leadership makes it possible to attend to the individual without abandoning the group.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Group work: handling a member in crisis; co-leadership · C-SSRS — Suicidal ideation with intent and plan: immediate risk assessment
⚑ Check: Best-practice consensus rather than a single named standard; SME to confirm the Gladding locator.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

836. nce-s-cou-216 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · medium · In review

Three members of an interpersonal group have begun meeting for coffee before each session. In group they sit together, trade knowing glances and fall silent when one of them is challenged. Following Yalom, how should the leader BEST respond?
A. Ban all contact between members outside of group sessions for the rest of the group
Outside contact is not itself the problem, and a ban tends to drive it underground.
B. Invite the members to talk openly in group about their outside meetings and their effect ✔ KEY
Bringing the subgroup into the open turns a threat to cohesion into here-and-now material.
C. Meet privately with the three members and ask them to sit apart from each other in group
A private meeting adds secrecy and leaves the rest of the group out of the work.
D. Let the subgroup run its course, since cohesive pairs tend to strengthen the whole group
Secret subgroups whose loyalty outweighs the group's goals tend to undermine cohesion.
Rationale: Subgrouping becomes destructive when members' loyalty to the subgroup outweighs their commitment to the group's goals and when what happens outside stays secret. Yalom advises that extragroup contact be brought back into the group and discussed openly, so that it can be understood rather than forbidden.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — Problem group members and subgrouping; extragroup socializing
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

837. nce-s-cou-217 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · hard · In review

In a long-term group, Theo bristles at every comment from Ines, an assertive older member, and accuses her of "always looking down on me," though others see her remarks as mild. He later realizes she reminds him of his critical older sister. Drawing on Sullivan, Yalom calls Theo's distorted perception of Ines:
A. Parataxic distortion ✔ KEY
Parataxic distortion is perceiving another person through the lens of past relationships rather than as they are.
B. Consensual validation
Consensual validation is the corrective process of checking one's view against others' views, not the distortion.
C. Projective identification
This object relations term involves inducing one's projected feelings in another; Yalom uses Sullivan's term here.
D. Family recapitulation
Corrective recapitulation of the family group is a therapeutic factor, not the term for one member's distortion of another.
Rationale: Yalom borrows Sullivan's term parataxic distortion for the tendency to perceive others in the group through the template of earlier relationships, a form of transference that can occur between members as well as toward the leader. Feedback from other members, a process Sullivan called consensual validation, helps the member see the distortion and test it against reality.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — Interpersonal learning: parataxic distortion and consensual validation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

838. nce-s-cou-218 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · easy · In review

A counselor wants to know whether her 10-week anxiety management group actually reduced members' symptoms. Which evaluation approach BEST answers that question?
A. Hand out a satisfaction survey at the last session of the group
Satisfaction tells whether members liked the group, not whether symptoms changed.
B. Record her own impressions of each member's progress each week
Leader impressions are subjective and open to bias; they do not measure symptom change.
C. Count how many members attended at least eight of ten sessions
Attendance shows engagement, not whether the group reduced symptoms.
D. Give a standardized anxiety measure before and after the group ✔ KEY
A valid symptom measure given at pre- and post-test directly assesses change in the target outcome.
Rationale: Outcome evaluation asks whether the group achieved its goals. Administering a reliable, valid measure of the target problem before and after the group (and, ideally, at points during it) provides evidence of change; satisfaction, attendance and leader impressions are process indicators, not outcome data.
References: ASGW Best Practice Guidelines — Performing and processing: evaluation of group outcomes · Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Program evaluation: outcome evaluation with pretest-posttest measures
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

839. nce-s-cou-219 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · medium · In review

A counselor is launching a video-based support group for caregivers who live across her state. Which step is MOST specific to the safe running of this telehealth group?
A. Ask members to keep their cameras turned off to protect each other's identities
Cameras off removes nonverbal cues and makes it harder to verify who is present and to monitor distress.
B. Skip pre-group screening, since online members can simply log off if it is a poor fit
Screening is as necessary for online groups as for in-person groups.
C. Get each member's location and emergency contact and set privacy rules for joining ✔ KEY
Knowing where members are, having emergency contacts and agreeing on privacy and no-recording rules address telehealth risks.
D. Use any free video app members already know, since familiarity improves attendance
Platforms must meet security and privacy requirements; convenience alone is not sufficient.
Rationale: Distance group work adds risks: members may join from places where others can overhear, could record sessions, and may be far from the counselor in a crisis. Counselors address these in informed consent and planning by verifying identity and location, collecting emergency contacts, using secure platforms and setting norms such as joining from a private space and not recording.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — H.2.a Informed Consent and Disclosure; H.3 Client Verification · ASGW Best Practice Guidelines — Planning: trends and technological changes
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

840. nce-s-cou-220 · Career Development · career development theories (Holland, Super, Krumboltz) · hard · In review

For her first months as a hospital social worker, Amina followed every unit norm and sought her colleagues' approval. Now, secure in the role, she is pushing the team to adopt her ideas for discharge planning and asserting her own views. In Tiedeman and O'Hara's decision-making model, Amina is in which stage?
A. Crystallization
Crystallization is part of anticipation, when options are clarified before any choice is made.
B. Induction
Induction describes her earlier months, when she sought acceptance and conformed to the group.
C. Reformation ✔ KEY
In reformation the person, now accepted, acts assertively to change the group toward her own views.
D. Integration
Integration follows reformation, when individual and group goals are balanced into a stable sense of self.
