The ACA Code bars referral based solely on the counselor's personal values; the counselor must first work to bracket them.
B. Share the counselor's own beliefs openly so the client can weigh them in deciding
Offering personal religious views on the client's decision imposes the counselor's values.
C. Gently point out what the client may lose by leaving her supportive community
Emphasizing losses of only one option steers the client toward the counselor's preference.
D. Seek consultation, set aside personal views, and follow the client's own process ✔ KEY
Recognizing the pull, getting consultation, and keeping the focus on the client's goals reflect self-awareness and A.4.b.
Rationale: Self-awareness includes noticing when personal religious or political values press on clinical work. The ACA Code directs counselors to be aware of their own values and avoid imposing them, seeking training where they are at risk of doing so, and it prohibits referral based solely on the counselor's personal values.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.b Values Within Termination and Referral
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

948. nce-s-cor-028 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · countertransference · easy · In review

A counselor whose parents had a bitter divorce works with a 16-year-old caught in a custody dispute. She finds herself angry at the client's father and urging the teen to "stand up to him." This pattern is BEST described as
A. overidentification ✔ KEY
The counselor is merging her own history with the client's, losing objectivity and taking sides, a form of countertransference.
B. parallel process
Parallel process refers to dynamics in counseling being replicated in supervision, or the reverse.
C. advocacy
Advocacy addresses systemic barriers on behalf of a client; it is not driven by the counselor's unresolved personal history.
D. client transference
Transference is the client's projection onto the counselor; here the reaction originates in the counselor.
Rationale: Overidentification occurs when a counselor sees the client's situation through the lens of his or her own experience, losing the "as if" boundary of empathy. It is a common form of countertransference that can lead the counselor to take sides or push the client toward choices the counselor wished for, so it calls for self-reflection and supervision.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — The counselor as a person: countertransference and overidentification
⚑ Check: Confirm Corey (Theory & Practice) discusses overidentification by name; Corey's Issues & Ethics may be the better home for it.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

949. nce-s-cor-029 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · easy · In review

A client says, "I still smoke weed most nights to fall asleep. Go ahead and give me the lecture." Which counselor response BEST reflects a nonjudgmental stance?
A. No lecture. I'd like to understand what it does for you and how it's working. ✔ KEY
This sets aside evaluation and invites the client's own view of benefits and costs, a nonjudgmental and collaborative stance.
B. I won't lecture, but you know nightly use can make your sleep worse over time.
The "but" delivers the lecture anyway, conveying judgment and likely increasing defensiveness.
C. It sounds like you already know it's a problem, or you wouldn't expect a lecture.
This interprets the comment as an admission of a problem, imposing the counselor's conclusion.
D. Lots of people use cannabis for sleep now, so it isn't a big concern for me.
Dismissing the topic is approval, another kind of judgment, and closes off exploration.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental stance suspends both disapproval and approval in favor of curiosity about the client's experience. With substance use, exploring what the substance does for the client and how it is working invites honest self-evaluation and is consistent with motivational interviewing's spirit of acceptance.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Spirit of MI: acceptance (absolute worth, autonomy support)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

950. nce-s-cor-030 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · medium · In review

A 33-year-old single mother mentions in passing that she does sex work to pay her bills, then says she came to counseling because of anxiety about her son's problems at school. What should the counselor do?
A. Shift the focus to her work, since it is likely the underlying source of her anxiety
Assuming the work is the real problem overrides the client's stated goal and reflects the counselor's judgment.
B. Follow her stated concern while leaving room to discuss work or safety if she wishes ✔ KEY
Respecting the client's agenda without ignoring possible safety needs reflects a nonjudgmental, client-centered stance.
C. Give her referrals for job training so she has other options to support her family
Unrequested job referrals imply her work must change, imposing values she did not ask the counselor to apply.
D. Avoid any mention of her work so that she does not feel judged in this session
Treating the topic as unspeakable can also signal judgment and may miss safety concerns she wants to raise.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental stance means the counselor does not treat a stigmatized behavior as the presumed problem. The client sets the agenda, and the counselor stays open to discussing work, health, or safety when the client chooses, without pathologizing or avoiding the topic.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

951. nce-s-cor-031 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

A client arrives sobbing and breathing rapidly after learning she is being evicted at the end of the week. Which counselor response BEST conveys warmth in this moment?
A. Hand her a list of housing resources so she can start making calls right away
Resources may help later, but moving to tasks while she is flooded ignores her emotional state.
B. Ask her to describe the eviction notice in detail to see what her options are
Detailed fact-gathering before she is calmer is task-focused and can add to her distress.
C. Tell her firmly that panicking will not help and that she needs to calm down
A directive to stop panicking is cold and dismissive, and it rarely reduces distress.
D. Sit with her, speak in a calm, steady voice, and acknowledge how scared she is ✔ KEY
A calm, caring presence and acknowledgment of her fear communicate warmth and help her regulate before problem-solving.
Rationale: Warmth is communicated largely through nonverbal behavior, including tone of voice, pacing, and attentive presence, together with acknowledgment of the client's feelings. In acute distress, a warm and steady presence helps the client regulate enough to engage in the practical problem-solving that follows.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Warmth and nonverbal communication in the helping relationship
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

952. nce-s-cor-032 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · medium · In review

A counselor is meeting with a Spanish-speaking client through a trained professional interpreter. Which practice BEST preserves the client's voice and respects the counseling relationship?
A. Ask the interpreter to summarize what the client says to keep sessions brief
Summaries filter the client's words through the interpreter and lose emotional content.
B. Ask the client's bilingual teenage son to interpret, since the family trusts him
Family members, especially children, compromise accuracy and confidentiality and shift family power roles.
C. Speak directly to the client in the first person rather than to the interpreter ✔ KEY
Addressing the client directly keeps her at the center of the relationship and the interpreter in a conduit role.
D. Speak with the interpreter after sessions to learn the cultural meaning of her words
Relying on the interpreter as cultural expert behind the client's back can sideline her own account of her experience.
Rationale: Interpreted sessions add a third person and can shift power away from the client. Best practice is to use a trained interpreter rather than family, brief the interpreter beforehand, and speak directly to the client in the first person so that the relationship remains between counselor and client.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.2.c Developmental and Cultural Sensitivity · Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Language barriers and use of interpreters
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

953. nce-s-cor-033 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · medium · In review

A counselor who sincerely holds egalitarian values reviews her recorded sessions for supervision. She notices that with her Latino clients she offers fewer reflections, interrupts more often, and moves to advice sooner than with her White clients. She had not been aware of the difference. This pattern BEST illustrates
A. implicit bias operating outside her conscious awareness ✔ KEY
Automatic, unintended differences in behavior toward a group, despite consciously held egalitarian beliefs, are the hallmark of implicit (unconscious) bias.
B. explicit prejudice that she consciously holds but conceals
Explicit prejudice is consciously endorsed. The counselor sincerely holds egalitarian values and was unaware of the pattern.
C. cultural encapsulation produced by a narrow training program
Wrenn's cultural encapsulation describes defining reality through one's own cultural lens. It does not specifically explain unaware, group-specific differences in her microskills.
D. countertransference rooted in conflicts from her own family
Countertransference stems from the counselor's personal history with significant others. Nothing suggests a family conflict; the pattern tracks client ethnicity.
Rationale: Implicit bias refers to attitudes and associations that operate automatically and outside awareness, so well-intentioned counselors can treat groups differently without meaning to. Sue and Sue stress that good intentions do not protect against unintentional bias; recorded sessions, supervision and ongoing self-examination are how counselors detect it.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Implicit bias and unintentional racism in well-intentioned helping professionals
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

954. nce-s-cor-034 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · medium · In review

A 47-year-old client in a larger body seeks counseling for grief after his mother's death. He has not raised any concern about his weight. Over three sessions, the counselor finds herself suggesting exercise plans and asking about his eating. Which action BEST reflects counselor self-awareness?
A. Add a weight-loss goal to the plan, since weight affects mood and grief
This imposes the counselor's agenda on a client who came for grief and acts on the bias rather than examining it.
B. Notice her assumptions about his weight and refocus on the grief he brought ✔ KEY
Recognizing the counselor-driven assumption and returning to the client's own goal is self-aware, client-centered practice consistent with ACA A.4.b.
C. Refer him to a dietitian so his eating habits can be addressed by an expert
A referral the client did not request still acts on the counselor's assumption about his body rather than on his presenting concern.
D. Ask him directly whether his weight played a part in his mother's death
This question extends the counselor's weight focus into his grief and may shame him; it reflects the bias rather than awareness of it.
Rationale: Self-awareness means noticing when personal values or assumptions, including those about body size, are steering the work. ACA Standard A.4.b directs counselors to avoid imposing their own values and to respect the client's goals. The counselor should examine where the weight focus came from and return to the grief the client brought.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · Corey (Theory & Practice) — The counselor as a person: self-awareness and personal values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

955. nce-s-cor-035 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · hard · In review

The week after a national election, a client spends several minutes praising a candidate the counselor strongly opposes. The counselor notices her jaw tightening. The client then asks, "You agree with me, right?" Which counselor response BEST reflects self-aware, ethical practice?
A. Honestly, I see it differently, but I respect your right to your own view.
Sharing political disagreement shifts focus to the counselor and risks imposing values; congruence does not require disclosing every opinion.
B. I do. A lot of people feel that way, so I can see why you are hopeful now.
Feigning agreement is incongruent and also brings the counselor's supposed politics into the session.
C. I keep my politics out of here, but I want to hear what this means for you. ✔ KEY
This gently declines to disclose, keeps the focus on the client, and invites exploration, which manages the counselor's reaction without acting on it.
D. Since we differ on this, another counselor might be a better fit for you.
ACA A.11.b cautions against referral based solely on the counselor's personal values; a political difference is not grounds for referral.
Rationale: Counselors are expected to notice their own value reactions, including political ones, and keep them from steering the session (ACA A.4.b). Self-disclosure of opinions should serve the client, and a politically charged question is usually best met by declining warmly and exploring its meaning for the client. Referral solely because of a values difference is discouraged under A.11.b.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.b Values Within Termination and Referral
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

956. nce-s-cor-036 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

At a community mental health center, a 36-year-old client referred by his caseworker glares at the counselor and says, "You're just another paid stranger. You don't actually care what happens to me." Which counselor response BEST conveys warmth and respect?
A. I have years of training, so you can trust that I know how to help you.
Defending credentials centers the counselor and argues with the client's experience rather than respecting it.
B. I can't work with you if you speak to me in that tone during sessions.
The client is distrustful, not abusive. An early limit on tone reads as punitive and confirms his expectation that no one cares.
C. Let's set that aside and get through the intake questions for today.
Ignoring the statement dismisses the client's concern and treats him as paperwork, the opposite of respect.
D. Sounds like people haven't earned your trust. I'd like to, at your pace. ✔ KEY
This reflects the meaning behind the hostility without defensiveness and communicates a respectful wish to earn trust over time.
Rationale: Warmth and respect are tested most when a client is hostile. A nondefensive response that reflects the client's distrust, treats it as understandable, and leaves the client in control of the pace communicates care. Defending oneself, setting premature limits, or ignoring the comment tend to confirm the client's expectations.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Warmth, respect and working with reluctant or resistant clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

957. nce-s-cor-037 · Social and Cultural Diversity · warmth and respect · medium · In review

A 60-year-old Vietnamese immigrant father comes to counseling about conflict with his teenage son. In the first session he says, "You are the expert. Please tell me what I should do." Which counselor approach BEST combines respect with responsiveness to his request?
A. Offer some concrete suggestions and structure, checking how each idea fits his family ✔ KEY
Honoring his expectation of an active, expert helper while asking how ideas fit his family respects both his cultural frame and his autonomy.
B. Explain that counselors do not give advice and that he must find his own answers
A strictly nondirective stance may be experienced as unhelpful or as a lack of competence, and it dismisses his stated preference.
C. Tell him exactly what rules to set for his son, since he asked for clear direction
Directing without his input ignores his knowledge of his own family and values; structure should still be collaborative.
D. Ask him to first explore his deeper feelings about his son before any guidance
Insisting on emotional exploration before addressing his practical request disregards what he came for and may lead to early dropout.
Rationale: Sue and Sue note that many clients, especially those from cultures that value hierarchy and practical help, expect the counselor to take an active, directive role, and that a purely nondirective style can lead to early termination. Respect means meeting the client's expectations with structure and concrete input while still checking that suggestions fit the client's values.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Culturally appropriate helping styles: directive versus nondirective approaches
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

958. nce-s-cor-038 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

A 38-year-old Army veteran referred for military sexual trauma tells the counselor in her second session, "I'm not ready to talk about what happened. I don't know if I ever will be." Which counselor response BEST respects the client's pace?
A. Avoiding it keeps symptoms going, so let's try to cover the details today.
Pressing for details before the client consents overrides her choice and can feel retraumatizing.
B. That's okay. You decide what we talk about and when, and we can go slowly. ✔ KEY
This affirms her control over disclosure, a core trauma-informed principle, and conveys respect for her readiness.
C. Could you give me just a short outline so I know what we're working with?
Asking for an outline right after she declines still pressures disclosure and disregards her stated limit.
D. Unless you talk about it, I'm not sure that counseling can help you much.
Making help conditional on disclosure is coercive and undermines safety and trust.
Rationale: Respecting a client's pace is especially important with trauma survivors. SAMHSA's trauma-informed principles emphasize safety, trustworthiness, and client voice and choice; counselors let clients control when and how much they disclose, building stabilization and trust first.
References: SAMHSA TIP 57 — Trauma-informed principles: safety, choice and client control over disclosure
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

959. nce-s-cor-039 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · medium · In review

A 26-year-old client in outpatient treatment for opioid use returns after relapsing following 90 days of abstinence. He looks down and says, "You must be so disappointed in me." Which counselor response BEST demonstrates unconditional positive regard?
A. I'm a bit disappointed, but I know you can do better than this next time.
This makes the counselor's regard contingent on his behavior, which is the opposite of unconditional positive regard.
B. Relapse is just part of recovery, so it's really not a big deal at all.
This minimizes a serious event and offers reassurance rather than acceptance of the person and his feelings.
C. My regard for you hasn't changed. I'm glad you came back to talk about it. ✔ KEY
This separates his worth from the relapse and welcomes him back, communicating acceptance that does not depend on his behavior.
D. Let's go over what you did wrong so this does not happen to you again.
Opening with what he did wrong frames the session around judgment; relapse review can come later from a stance of acceptance.
Rationale: Unconditional positive regard is acceptance of the client as a person, not approval of every behavior, and it does not rise and fall with the client's performance. After a relapse, communicating steady regard reduces shame and makes honest exploration of what happened more likely.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: unconditional positive regard and acceptance
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

960. nce-s-cor-040 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · easy · In review

According to Carl Rogers, incongruence between a person's self-concept and actual experience develops primarily when the person
A. fails to resolve unconscious conflicts between the id and superego
This is a psychoanalytic explanation of conflict, not Rogers's account of incongruence.
B. learns maladaptive behavior patterns through repeated reinforcement
This is a behavioral explanation; Rogers focused on the self-concept and conditions of worth.
C. holds irrational beliefs that they must win approval from others
Irrational beliefs about needing approval belong to Ellis's REBT, not person-centered theory.
D. internalizes conditions of worth set by significant others ✔ KEY
Rogers held that conditional regard from significant others leads people to internalize conditions of worth, which produces incongruence.
Rationale: Rogers proposed that when love and approval are conditional, people internalize conditions of worth and deny or distort experiences that do not fit them, creating incongruence. Unconditional positive regard in counseling counters this by allowing clients to accept all of their experience without losing the counselor's regard.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: conditions of worth and incongruence
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

961. nce-s-cor-041 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · easy · In review

In person-centered theory, a counselor who is congruent is one who
A. shares every thought and feeling with the client as soon as it arises
Congruence does not mean impulsively disclosing all reactions; expression should be appropriate and in the client's service.
B. is aware of inner experience and expresses it authentically when fitting ✔ KEY
Congruence is the match between the counselor's inner experience, awareness of it, and outward expression, without a professional facade.
C. hides personal reactions to maintain a neutral and professional stance
Hiding behind a professional facade is the opposite of congruence in Rogers's view.
D. mirrors the client's emotional tone and posture to build rapport fast
Mirroring is a rapport technique; it can be done without any genuineness at all.
Rationale: Rogers described congruence, or genuineness, as the counselor being real: inner experience, awareness and communication are consistent, with no facade. Corey notes that this does not mean impulsively sharing every feeling; genuine expression is appropriate and serves the relationship.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: congruence or genuineness
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

962. nce-s-cor-042 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · hard · In review

A 31-year-old client who says coworkers avoid her asks, "Be honest. Do you find me annoying? Everyone else does." In their sessions, the counselor has felt irritated when the client cuts her off mid-sentence. Which response BEST demonstrates congruence in the client's service?
A. Not at all. I truly enjoy every single minute of our time together in here.
This reassurance contradicts the counselor's actual experience, so it is incongruent and withholds useful feedback.
B. Honestly, yes. You can be pretty exhausting for most people to be around.
This is a global, hurtful judgment rather than a specific, caring observation; genuineness is not the same as bluntness.
C. At times I feel cut off when you jump in. I wonder if others feel that too. ✔ KEY
This honestly shares a specific, behavior-based reaction in the here and now and links it to the client's concern, which is genuine and therapeutic.
D. What makes you want to ask me that question at this point in our work?
Exploring the question can be useful, but used here it sidesteps a direct, sincere request for honest feedback.
Rationale: Congruence means the counselor's responses match inner experience, but it is expressed with care and for the client's benefit. Sharing a specific, behavioral reaction in the moment (immediacy) gives the client accurate interpersonal feedback she may not get elsewhere. False reassurance is incongruent, and blunt global judgments are not genuineness but a failure of respect.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: congruence; appropriate expression of counselor reactions
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

963. nce-s-cor-043 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · therapeutic alliance · medium · In review

A clinic director wants an early indicator of which clients are likely to benefit from counseling, regardless of the counselor's theoretical approach. Based on psychotherapy outcome research, which measure is the MOST useful early predictor?
A. The specific theoretical orientation the counselor practices
Comparative outcome research finds that bona fide approaches produce broadly similar outcomes, so orientation is a weak predictor.
B. A demographic match between the counselor and the client
Demographic matching has shown inconsistent, generally small effects on outcome compared with the alliance.
C. The total length of the initial intake assessment session
Intake length is not an established predictor of counseling outcome.
D. The client's rating of the working alliance in early sessions ✔ KEY
Meta-analyses find that the alliance, especially as rated by the client early in treatment, predicts outcome across approaches.
Rationale: The working alliance is one of the most consistently replicated predictors of counseling outcome. Meta-analyses (e.g., Horvath and colleagues; Flückiger and colleagues) show a moderate, reliable relationship between alliance and outcome across theoretical approaches, and alliance ratings taken early in treatment, often by the third to fifth session, already predict results.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — The working alliance and common factors in counseling outcome
⚑ Check: Alliance-outcome meta-analytic findings (Horvath et al., 2011; Flückiger et al., 2018) are not themselves in the source library; SME should confirm the Gladding locator covers early alliance as an outcome predictor.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

964. nce-s-cor-044 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · therapeutic alliance · hard · In review

In the third session of couples counseling, Dana interrupts her wife and says to the counselor, "Every time she talks, you nod along. You're clearly on her side." What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Acknowledge Dana's experience, invite her to say more, and check in with both partners ✔ KEY
Taking the perceived split seriously and exploring it openly with both partners repairs the alliance with Dana without abandoning her wife.
B. Reassure Dana that counselors stay neutral, then return to where the session left off
Reassurance without exploration dismisses Dana's experience and leaves the split alliance unrepaired.
C. Explain to Dana that her wife's points have simply been clearer and more specific
This confirms Dana's perception that the counselor is siding with her wife and deepens the split.
D. Schedule separate sessions with Dana alone to rebuild her trust before joint work
Moving to private sessions before addressing the issue together can create new imbalances and secrets and delays repair in the room.
Rationale: In couple and family counseling the counselor holds an alliance with each member, and a split alliance, where one member feels less allied with the counselor, is linked to poorer engagement and dropout. The counselor should address the rupture openly and nondefensively in session, maintaining balanced (multipartial) alliances with all members.
References: Friedlander et al. (Alliances in Couple & Family Therapy) — Split alliances and SOFTA safety/emotional connection; repairing in-session ruptures · Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Therapeutic alliance in couple and family therapy; balanced alliances with each member
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

965. nce-s-cor-045 · Social and Cultural Diversity · cultural humility · medium · In review

A 50-year-old Diné (Navajo) client being seen for anxiety mentions that her family is arranging a ceremony with a traditional healer next month. Which counselor response BEST reflects cultural humility?
A. Suggest she wait on the ceremony until counseling has had a chance to work
This ranks the counselor's approach above the client's healing tradition and imposes the counselor's worldview.
B. Describe what she has read about Navajo ceremonies to show her knowledge
Taking an expert stance on the client's culture is the opposite of humility and may be inaccurate for this client and family.
C. Ask what the ceremony means to her and how she wants it to fit with counseling ✔ KEY
This positions the client as the expert on her culture and invites collaboration between traditional and counseling approaches.
D. Note it as possible magical thinking to explore further in the assessment
Pathologizing a culturally normative healing practice reflects cultural bias, not humility.
Rationale: Cultural humility is an other-oriented, lifelong stance of self-reflection in which the counselor treats the client as the expert on her own culture and attends to power differences. Sue and Sue encourage counselors to respect and, where the client wishes, collaborate with Indigenous healing practices rather than dismiss or pathologize them.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling Indigenous clients; respecting traditional and Indigenous healing · MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling relationship: client worldview and cultural healing practices
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

966. nce-s-cor-046 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · easy · In review

A 19-year-old says, "I dropped out of college to stream video games full time. My parents keep calling me lazy." Which counselor response BEST reflects a nonjudgmental stance?
A. Dropping out this young could really limit your options later in life.
This evaluates the decision as a mistake and aligns the counselor with a negative judgment.
B. Your parents may have a point, since streaming is a hard way to earn money.
Siding with the parents judges the client's choice and is likely to harm trust.
C. Good for you. Following your passion is the right call at your age, I think.
Approval is also a judgment; a nonjudgmental stance neither condemns nor endorses the choice.
D. That's a big change. What drew you to streaming, and how is it going so far? ✔ KEY
This acknowledges the change and invites the client's own perspective with curiosity, neither praising nor criticizing.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental stance means suspending evaluation of the client's choices, positive or negative, so the client can explore them openly. Curious, open-ended responses keep the focus on the client's experience; both criticism and praise place the counselor's values at the center.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

967. nce-s-cor-047 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · medium · In review

A client who works two hourly jobs has missed two sessions after short-notice shift changes. She apologizes repeatedly and seems afraid of being dropped. The agency discharges clients after three missed sessions. Which counselor response BEST reflects awareness of power and privilege?
A. Name the shift-work barrier and explore flexible times or telehealth together ✔ KEY
This recognizes a structural barrier rather than blaming the client and uses the counselor's power to adapt services with her.
B. Remind her of the attendance policy and that one more absence ends services
Leading with the policy uses institutional power punitively and ignores the economic constraints driving the absences.
C. Interpret the missed sessions as ambivalence about change to explore in session
Framing a work-schedule barrier as resistance pathologizes the client and overlooks her circumstances.
D. Suggest she ask her manager for a fixed schedule so she can attend reliably
This assumes a level of workplace control that hourly workers often lack, reflecting the counselor's own privileged frame.
Rationale: The MSJCC ask counselors to recognize how privileged and marginalized statuses, including socioeconomic status, shape the counseling relationship and access to services. Counselors hold institutional power and can use it to reduce barriers rather than interpret structural constraints as client resistance.
References: MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling relationship; privileged and marginalized statuses and institutional barriers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

968. nce-s-cor-048 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · countertransference · medium · In review

A counselor working with a 68-year-old recently widowed man, with his permission, has begun calling his bank, drafting his letters, and booking his appointments. She thinks warmly, "He would be lost without me." Which risk does this pattern MOST directly create?
A. Turning the client's gratitude into hostile negative transference
Nothing in the scenario points to hostility; the more direct risk lies in what the client stops doing for himself.
B. Fostering dependence that undermines the client's own competence ✔ KEY
Rescuing driven by the counselor's need to be needed takes over tasks the client could learn to do, encouraging dependence and eroding self-efficacy.
C. Making termination easier because the alliance is so strong
Dependence typically makes termination harder, not easier.
D. Causing the counselor to grow emotionally detached from him
The pattern reflects overinvolvement, not detachment.
Rationale: Countertransference can be positive as well as negative. Corey describes the counselor's need to be needed and rescuing as countertransference that leads counselors to do for clients what clients can do for themselves. The result is dependence and reduced client self-efficacy, which supervision can help the counselor recognize.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Countertransference: the need to be needed and rescuing clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

969. nce-s-cor-049 · Social and Cultural Diversity · cultural humility · medium · In review

A counselor tells a 45-year-old Mexican American client, "It must help to have your big family around you right now." The client replies, "Actually, my family is part of the stress. My friends from work are who I lean on." Which counselor response BEST reflects cultural humility?
A. Families can be complicated, but they usually come through in a real crisis.
This holds on to the counselor's assumption about family support and quietly dismisses the client's correction.
B. I'm sorry to hear that. Maybe we can work on repairing things with them.
This sets a family-repair goal the client did not ask for and still treats family closeness as the expected norm.
C. Thank you for correcting me; I assumed. Tell me about who supports you. ✔ KEY
The counselor owns the assumption without defensiveness, thanks the client, and lets the client define her own support system.
D. That surprises me, since family is so central in Mexican American culture.
This applies a group generalization over the individual's own account, which is stereotyping rather than humility.
Rationale: Cultural humility treats the client as the expert on how culture shows up in her life. When a client corrects an assumption, the humble response is to accept the correction openly, acknowledge the error, and get curious about the client's actual experience. Group-level knowledge can inform hypotheses but cannot override what an individual client says about herself.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Within-group differences; avoiding stereotyping in culturally responsive practice
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

970. nce-s-cor-050 · Social and Cultural Diversity · cultural humility · hard · In review

A Filipina American counselor begins working with a 58-year-old White, heterosexual, Christian man who owns a hardware store in a small farming town and is struggling after his business partner died. The counselor thinks, "His culture is the mainstream one, so there isn't much cultural material to explore." Which stance BEST reflects cultural humility?
A. Explore how his faith, rural roots, class and ideas of manhood shape his grief ✔ KEY
Everyone has a culture. Inviting him to describe how faith, place, class and gender norms shape his loss applies humility to a client from dominant groups.
B. Focus on grief alone, because culture matters mainly for marginalized clients
This treats dominant-group identity as culture-free, the very assumption the counselor should be questioning.
C. Rely on her knowledge of small-town life to anticipate his values and beliefs
Presuming to know his values from group knowledge is the opposite of the other-oriented, open stance humility requires.
D. Begin by discussing her own ethnic identity so he sees what culture involves
Centering the counselor's identity at the outset shifts focus away from the client and does not explore his worldview.
Rationale: Cultural humility is not reserved for clients from marginalized groups. Members of dominant groups also hold cultural identities, such as religion, regional and rural culture, social class and gender-role norms, that shape how they experience distress and help-seeking. Treating the majority culture as a neutral default is a form of cultural encapsulation; a humble counselor stays curious about every client's worldview.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Everyone has a culture; Whiteness as an invisible default and cultural encapsulation · MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Client worldview: privileged and marginalized client identities
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

971. nce-s-cor-051 · Social and Cultural Diversity · cultural humility · easy · In review

Which description BEST captures cultural humility as distinct from cultural competence?
A. A body of knowledge about specific groups that a counselor masters in training
Mastering group-specific knowledge is closer to the knowledge component of cultural competence, not humility.
B. A credential earned after completing a set number of multicultural CE hours
Humility is an ongoing stance, not an endpoint that can be certified by hours of training.
C. A technique of matching clients with counselors who share their background
Matching may help some clients, but it is a service-delivery choice, not the counselor's own stance of humility.
D. A lifelong process of self-reflection, openness, and attention to power ✔ KEY
Cultural humility is defined as an ongoing commitment to self-reflection and self-critique, openness to the client's view, and redressing power imbalances.
Rationale: Cultural humility, a term introduced by Tervalon and Murray-Garcia, emphasizes lifelong self-evaluation and critique, an other-oriented openness to the client's cultural identity, and attention to power imbalances. It complements competence: rather than an endpoint of mastery, it is a continuing way of being with clients that keeps the counselor learning.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Cultural humility versus cultural competence; lifelong self-reflection
⚑ Check: Tervalon & Murray-Garcia (1998) originated the term; confirm the cited Sue & Sue edition discusses cultural humility in these terms.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

972. nce-s-cor-052 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · medium · In review

A 44-year-old man says, "I've been seeing someone else for six months. My wife has no idea. You probably think I'm a terrible person now." Which counselor response BEST reflects a nonjudgmental stance?
A. I don't think that, but you'll need to tell your wife before we can go on.
Making disclosure a condition of counseling imposes the counselor's values and sets an agenda the client has not chosen.
B. You expected me to judge you. I'd like to understand what's happening for you. ✔ KEY
This reflects his fear of judgment and conveys acceptance and curiosity without endorsing or condemning the affair.
C. Affairs are very common, so you really shouldn't feel bad about this at all.
Normalizing and reassuring takes a stance on the behavior and dismisses whatever guilt or conflict he may feel.
D. How do you think your wife would feel if she found out about all of this?
Though phrased as a question, it implies moral evaluation and shifts focus from his experience to an imagined accusation.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental stance means suspending moral evaluation so the client can explore his experience openly. It neither condemns nor approves the behavior. ACA Standard A.4.b asks counselors to avoid imposing their own values; responding to the client's fear of judgment and inviting exploration keeps the focus on his goals.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

973. nce-s-cor-053 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · medium · In review

A 62-year-old client laid off from a factory job says, "Immigrants took all the jobs around here. People like that are ruining this country." The counselor, herself the daughter of immigrants, feels a flash of anger. Which response BEST reflects a nonjudgmental stance while staying ethical?
A. Losing that job hit hard. Tell me what these months have been like for you. ✔ KEY
This attends to the loss and fear beneath the statement, neither endorsing nor attacking his view, and keeps the focus on his experience.
B. I need to tell you that my own parents were immigrants, and that remark hurt.
Disclosing her hurt at this point centers the counselor's reaction and is likely to rupture the relationship before it forms.
C. The research shows immigrants don't really take jobs away from local workers.
Debating the facts turns the session into an argument and signals judgment rather than understanding.
D. It sounds like you're right that outsiders are causing a lot of your problems.
Agreeing with the generalization abandons neutrality and reinforces a blaming belief rather than exploring it.
Rationale: Nonjudgmental does not mean agreeing. The counselor sets aside her reaction in the moment, monitors it, and responds to the client's underlying experience of loss. Consistent with ACA A.4.b, she avoids imposing her values; she can process her own anger in supervision and later explore how his beliefs affect his goals.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · Corey (Theory & Practice) — The counselor as a person: personal values and dealing with difficult client views
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

974. nce-s-cor-054 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · easy · In review

A 67-year-old woman meeting by telehealth after eight months of sobriety says, "I drank at my granddaughter's wedding. I blew everything. I'm back at zero." Which counselor response BEST reflects a nonjudgmental stance?
A. A wedding was a risky place to be. Why didn't you use your coping plan there?
The "why didn't you" question carries blame and is likely to deepen her shame.
B. Well, eight months is good, but you'll need to start counting from day one.
This confirms her all-or-nothing view of the lapse and minimizes the progress she has made.
C. You're being hard on yourself. Let's look at what led up to it, together. ✔ KEY
This acknowledges her self-criticism without blame and invites shared, curious review of the lapse as something to learn from.
D. I'm a little disappointed, but I know you can get back on track this week.
Voicing disappointment adds the counselor's evaluation to her shame, even with encouragement attached.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental response to a lapse counters the abstinence violation effect, the guilt and "I've blown it" thinking that can turn a single lapse into a full relapse. Treating the lapse as information about high-risk situations, rather than as moral failure, keeps the client engaged and supports recovery.
References: Marlatt & Donovan (Relapse Prevention) — Abstinence violation effect; lapse versus relapse
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

975. nce-s-cor-055 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · medium · In review

A middle school counselor receives a 13-year-old sent by the assistant principal after a hallway fight. The student slumps in the chair and says, "Just write me up already. You all work for the office." Which counselor response BEST reflects awareness of power in this setting?
A. Remind the student that cooperating now will help keep the consequences lighter
Using discipline as leverage confirms that the counselor is an arm of the office and uses institutional power coercively.
B. Wait silently until the student is ready to explain what happened in the fight
Silence without explanation leaves the student's assumption about the counselor's role unaddressed.
C. Tell the student that everything said here will stay strictly between the two of them
Promising absolute confidentiality is inaccurate in a school setting and could later break trust.
D. Explain her role apart from discipline, what she would share, and offer choices ✔ KEY
Clarifying her role and the limits of confidentiality, and giving the student some control, directly addresses the power imbalance the student names.
Rationale: In schools, courts and other mandated settings, clients often see counselors as agents of the institution. Naming the counselor's role honestly, explaining what will and will not be shared, and offering real choices reduces the power differential and builds trust. Overpromising confidentiality or leveraging consequences each misuse the counselor's position.
References: MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling relationship: power, privilege and oppression influencing the relationship · ACA Code of Ethics — B.1.d Explanation of Limitations
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

976. nce-s-cor-056 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · hard · In review

A 55-year-old Haitian Creole-speaking woman comes to an intake for depression with her adult son, who offers to interpret. As the session goes on, he answers some questions without asking her and gives brief summaries of her longer replies. What is the BEST course of action?
A. Continue with the son, since he knows her history and she seems comfortable
Comfort does not offset the filtering already happening; her voice and privacy are being shaped by a family member.
B. Arrange a trained interpreter, explaining it protects her privacy and voice ✔ KEY
A trained interpreter renders her words fully and neutrally, restoring her voice and confidentiality that family interpreting compromises.
C. Ask the son to translate word for word and to stop adding his own answers
Instructions do not remove the family role, power dynamics, or limits on what she can disclose in front of her son.
D. Rely on her limited English so that no third party needs to be in the room
Forcing her to use a language she does not command well silences emotional content and deepens the power imbalance.
Rationale: Language carries power: a client who cannot speak for herself in her own language loses control over her story. Family interpreters, however willing, may filter, edit or answer for the client, and their presence limits disclosure of sensitive material. Using a trained professional interpreter is the standard of practice that protects accuracy, confidentiality and the client's voice.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Language barriers; problems with using family members as interpreters · ACA Code of Ethics — A.2.c Developmental and Cultural Sensitivity
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

977. nce-s-cor-057 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · medium · In review

A 50-year-old Black man who was once hospitalized involuntarily says at intake, "You've got all those letters after your name. The last one decided what was wrong with me and never asked me a thing." Which counselor response BEST addresses the power differential?
A. My training is extensive, so you can trust that I'll get the diagnosis right.
Leaning on credentials reasserts the expert power the client distrusts and dismisses his past experience.
B. That provider was probably following protocol, so try not to take it personally.
Defending the system invalidates his experience and aligns the counselor with the institution he distrusts.
C. Let's not focus on the past; what matters is the work we're going to do now.
Redirecting away from his experience avoids the trust issue he has raised and quietly silences it.
D. That sounds like it left you unheard. You know your life best; let's work together. ✔ KEY
This validates his experience, names him as the expert on his life, and invites a collaborative relationship that shares power.
Rationale: Credentials give counselors real institutional power, including the power to diagnose and document. Clients with histories of coercive or dismissive care, often compounded by systemic racism, may reasonably distrust that power. Acknowledging the experience and positioning the client as a collaborator and the expert on his own life helps balance the relationship.
References: MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counseling relationship: counselor and client privileged and marginalized statuses · Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Cultural mistrust and the credibility of the helping professional
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

978. nce-s-cor-058 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · medium · In review

A 78-year-old man tells his 27-year-old counselor, "You're young enough to be my granddaughter. What could you know about burying a wife of 55 years?" Which counselor response BEST conveys empathy?
A. Age doesn't matter much here; I've been trained to work with grief at any age.
Citing training defends the counselor and sidesteps the doubt and loss the client is expressing.
B. You're right, I haven't lived that. I want to understand what losing her is like. ✔ KEY
This honestly acknowledges the generational gap and communicates a sincere wish to enter his world of loss.
C. I lost my grandmother last year, so I do know a little of what you're feeling.
This self-disclosure equates different losses and shifts the focus to the counselor's experience.
D. Would you feel more comfortable seeing a counselor who's closer to your age?
Offering a transfer at the first sign of doubt avoids the relationship rather than responding to his feelings.
Rationale: Empathy does not require shared experience; it requires trying to understand the client's world from his frame of reference. With a client of a different generation, the counselor can honestly acknowledge the difference and convey genuine interest in learning his experience, which often strengthens credibility more than defending one's qualifications.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: accurate empathic understanding of the client's frame of reference
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

979. nce-s-cor-059 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · hard · In review

A counselor at a refugee resettlement agency tells her supervisor that she cries alongside clients as they describe their losses, then feels drained and has trouble thinking clearly in session. The supervisor suggests she shift the balance of her empathy. Which shift is the supervisor MOST likely recommending?
A. More affective empathy, so that clients can see how deeply she shares their pain
She is already highly affectively attuned; adding more emotional sharing would deepen the overwhelm she reports.
B. Expressing sympathy and pity instead, since they are less taxing to the counselor
Sympathy feels for the client from outside their frame of reference and is not a substitute for empathy.
C. More cognitive empathy, grasping the client's view while keeping her own footing ✔ KEY
Cognitive empathy, accurate perspective-taking with emotional separateness, keeps the "as if" quality and protects clear thinking.
D. Emotional detachment, keeping reflections of feeling to an absolute minimum in session
Detachment would abandon empathy altogether and damage the relationship rather than rebalance it.
Rationale: Affective empathy is feeling with the client; cognitive empathy is accurately understanding the client's perspective. Rogers described empathy as sensing the client's world "as if" it were one's own without losing the "as if" quality. When affective resonance turns into personal distress, strengthening the cognitive side helps counselors stay present and effective while reducing burnout and vicarious trauma risk.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: accurate empathic understanding and the "as if" quality · Davis (Multidimensional Empathy) — Perspective taking (cognitive) vs empathic concern and personal distress (affective)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

980. nce-s-cor-060 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · easy · In review

In person-centered counseling, offering unconditional positive regard means the counselor
A. values the client as a person without requiring approval of every behavior ✔ KEY
UPR is acceptance of the person's worth that does not depend on the client's behavior; it is not approval of all actions.
B. agrees with the client's decisions so the client feels supported and safe
UPR does not require agreeing with choices; acceptance of the person is distinct from endorsement of decisions.
C. offers frequent praise to raise the client's self-esteem in each session
Praise is conditional by nature, tied to things the counselor approves of, which is the opposite of unconditional regard.
D. keeps a neutral blank screen so that clients project feelings onto it
The blank screen is a psychoanalytic stance used to foster transference, not person-centered acceptance.
Rationale: Rogers described unconditional positive regard as a nonpossessive caring and acceptance of the client as a person of worth, without conditions. It allows clients to explore feelings and behaviors without fearing the loss of the counselor's regard. Acceptance of the person does not mean approval of every behavior.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: unconditional positive regard and acceptance
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

981. nce-s-cor-061 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · medium · In review

A 23-year-old client starting treatment for panic attacks asks, "Just tell me straight. Is this going to fix me?" The counselor believes the approach is likely to help but cannot be certain it will work for him. Which response BEST demonstrates congruence?
A. Yes, this approach works for nearly everyone, so you'll be panic-free soon.
Overpromising misrepresents what the counselor actually believes and could undermine trust if progress is slow.
B. What do you think it would mean for you if this didn't end up working out?
Deflecting a direct question with a question avoids being genuine with a client who asked for honesty.
C. It's too early in our work for me to give you any kind of answer about that.
This withholds the counselor's honest, informed view, which she does in fact have.
D. I can't promise that, but many people improve, and we'll track how it goes. ✔ KEY
This matches what the counselor genuinely believes, offering honest hope without false certainty.
Rationale: Congruence means the counselor's outward communication matches inner experience. When a client asks a direct question, a genuine counselor answers honestly, which here means conveying realistic hope while admitting uncertainty. False reassurance and evasion are both incongruent and can erode the trust that genuineness is meant to build.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: congruence or genuineness
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

982. nce-s-cor-062 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · therapeutic alliance · hard · In review

A 48-year-old client with marked paranoid features stiffens when the counselor mentions his former employer. "How do you know where I worked? Have you been talking to people about me?" The detail came from the intake form he completed. Which response is MOST likely to protect the working alliance?
A. Reassure him warmly that she is on his side and that he is completely safe here
Effusive warmth and reassurance tend to raise suspicion in clients with paranoid features rather than ease it.
B. Gently note that his reaction may reflect a pattern of mistrust worth exploring
Interpreting his suspicion in this moment feels accusatory and is likely to deepen the rupture.
C. Calmly say it came from his intake form and offer to show him the form itself ✔ KEY
A plain, factual and transparent answer respects his concern and demonstrates that nothing is being hidden.
D. Apologize for bringing it up and move the conversation on to another subject
Dropping the topic without explanation leaves his suspicion intact and can look like evasion.
Rationale: Clients with paranoid features are highly sensitive to hidden motives. A straightforward, consistent and transparent style, explaining exactly where information came from and how it is used, builds trust better than warmth, interpretation or avoidance. Repairing a moment of suspicion this way strengthens the bond component of the alliance.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Working alliance: building trust and repairing ruptures · DSM-5-TR — Paranoid personality disorder: pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others
⚑ Check: The recommendation of a matter-of-fact, transparent (not effusively warm) style with paranoid clients is standard clinical guidance but is not stated in DSM-5-TR itself; DSM is cited for the feature only.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

983. nce-s-cor-063 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · countertransference · medium · In review

A counselor in a community reentry program, herself a mother of young children, is assigned a 35-year-old man who served a sentence for physically abusing a child. She notices she is curt with him, ends sessions early, and dreads his appointments. What is the MOST appropriate action?
A. Refer him to a colleague right away, since her values conflict with his past
ACA A.11.b cautions against referral based solely on the counselor's personal values; she should first examine and manage the reaction.
B. Explore her reaction in supervision and watch how it is affecting his care ✔ KEY
Supervision helps her understand and manage negative countertransference so it stops shaping her behavior toward him.
C. Tell him her feelings openly so he understands the impact of his offense
Disclosing her reaction this way would be punitive and serve her needs rather than his treatment.
D. Keep the shorter sessions, since his offense limits what counseling can do
Continuing reduced care acts out the countertransference and denies him equitable treatment.
Rationale: Negative countertransference toward clients who have caused harm can show up as coldness, shortened sessions and avoidance. The counselor's task is to recognize the reaction, explore it in supervision, and keep it from compromising care. ACA A.11.b asks counselors to refrain from referring prospective and current clients based solely on personally held values; referral is for genuine lack of competence after efforts to manage the reaction.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Countertransference: recognizing and managing negative reactions to clients · ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.b Values Within Termination and Referral
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

984. nce-s-cor-064 · Social and Cultural Diversity · warmth and respect · easy · In review

At his first session, a 26-year-old graduate student from Ghana whose name is Kwabena says, "Most people here just call me Kevin. It's easier." Which counselor response BEST conveys respect?
A. I'm happy to use whichever you prefer. If Kwabena, will you help me say it? ✔ KEY
This leaves the choice with him and shows willingness to learn his name, conveying respect without pressure.
B. Kevin is fine with me, then. It will keep things simple for both of us here.
Accepting the anglicized name for convenience skips asking what he prefers and centers ease over his identity.
C. I'll call you Kwabena, because it's important to honor your true heritage.
Insisting on his birth name overrides his choice; respect means honoring his preference, whatever it is.
D. Do you feel people here haven't respected your culture since you arrived?
Jumping to a probing question about discrimination presumes a problem before learning what he wants to be called.
Rationale: Respect includes honoring how clients wish to be addressed. Rather than defaulting to convenience or imposing a choice, the counselor asks for his preference and offers to learn correct pronunciation. Small acts like this signal that the client's identity matters and that he directs how it is represented.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Building a counseling relationship: warmth and respect
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

985. nce-s-cor-065 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · counselor self-awareness and bias · hard · In review

A counselor in long-term recovery through a 12-step program works at an outpatient clinic. Reviewing her notes, she sees that she steers nearly every client toward meetings and describes clients who prefer SMART Recovery or medication for opioid use disorder as "not ready." Which step BEST reflects counselor self-awareness?
A. Keep recommending 12-step meetings, since her own recovery shows how well that path works
This generalizes from one personal experience to all clients and leaves the bias in place.
B. Tell each client about her own recovery so they understand why she favors 12-step meetings
Self-disclosure here serves to justify the counselor's preference and adds pressure; it does not examine the bias.
C. Recognize that her own path is shaping her advice, and explore each client's preferred route ✔ KEY
Naming how her history colors her judgment, then centering each client's choice, is the core of self-awareness and avoids imposing values.
D. Stop mentioning any mutual-help groups so that she cannot influence clients' choices at all
Withholding useful options overcorrects; the aim is to offer choices without bias, not to remove information.
Rationale: Counselors' personal histories, including their own recovery, can quietly shape what they recommend and how they label clients. Self-awareness means noticing that pattern, examining it (often in supervision), and returning the choice to the client. ACA Standard A.4.b asks counselors to be aware of and avoid imposing their own values, attitudes and beliefs.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · Corey (Theory & Practice) — The counselor as a person: personal needs, values and their influence on counseling
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

986. nce-s-cor-066 · Group Counseling and Group Work · counselor self-awareness and bias · medium · In review

A counselor leading a hospital support group for family caregivers reviews a session recording. She notices that she invites the two members who are nurses to speak more often and responds to them at length, while briefly thanking a member with little formal education. What should the leader do?
A. Reflect on the pattern in supervision and deliberately balance her attention among members ✔ KEY
Examining the bias and then consciously equalizing attention addresses both the leader's self-knowledge and the group climate.
B. Ask the two nurses to share less often so that the other members have more time to speak
This places the burden on members for a pattern the leader created and leaves her own bias unexamined.
C. Tell the whole group she has been favoring some members, and apologize to all of them at once
A group-wide confession without first understanding the pattern may embarrass members and centers the leader.
D. Continue as before, because members with clinical training contribute more useful information
This rationalizes the bias; every member's experience is valuable, and unequal attention signals unequal worth.
Rationale: Group leaders communicate members' worth through whom they call on and how fully they respond. Unequal attention based on education or status is a form of bias that can silence members and weaken cohesion. Best practice asks group workers to know their own values and blind spots and to attend to diversity within the group.
References: ASGW Best Practice Guidelines — Best practice in performing: self-knowledge and attention to diversity among members
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

987. nce-s-cor-067 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · counselor self-awareness and bias · easy · In review

A counselor in training asks her supervisor how to become more aware of her own cultural biases. Which activity MOST directly builds this kind of self-awareness?
A. Reading research summaries that describe the values of many different cultural groups
This builds knowledge about others, a different competency from awareness of one's own biases.
B. Treating every client in exactly the same way so that cultural differences stop mattering
A "colorblind" stance ignores culture and leaves the counselor's own assumptions unexamined.
C. Limiting her caseload to clients whose backgrounds closely match her own life experience
Avoiding difference prevents growth and does nothing to surface her assumptions.
D. Examining how her upbringing shaped her values, through reflection and supervision ✔ KEY
Looking inward at how her own cultural history formed her values and reactions is the essence of counselor self-awareness.
Rationale: Self-awareness is the counselor's understanding of how their own cultural background, values and assumptions shape their perceptions of clients. It grows through deliberate self-reflection, such as journaling or a cultural genogram, and through supervision and feedback. Learning about other groups is valuable but builds knowledge rather than self-awareness.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counselor awareness of own assumptions, values and biases · MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2016) — Counselor self-awareness domain
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

988. nce-s-cor-068 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · hard · In review

A perfectionistic 20-year-old engineering student has felt worthless since childhood. The counselor notices that she becomes animated and praises him when he reports top grades, but grows quiet when he describes setbacks. From a person-centered view, what is the MAIN concern?
A. Praising his achievements may slowly weaken his motivation to keep his grades high
Motivation is not the person-centered concern here; the issue is what her shifting warmth teaches him about his worth.
B. Her responses may repeat the conditions of worth that feed his sense of worthlessness ✔ KEY
Warmth that rises and falls with performance is conditional regard, echoing the conditions of worth that Rogers saw as the root of incongruence.
C. He may come to depend on the counselor's approval more than on support from his peers
Dependence could follow, but the central problem is that her regard has become conditional on achievement.
D. Talking about setbacks at length may reinforce a negative core belief about himself
This is a cognitive framing; person-centered theory sees exploring setbacks in an accepting climate as helpful.
Rationale: Rogers proposed that people internalize conditions of worth when they are valued only for meeting others' standards, producing incongruence and fragile self-regard. Unconditional positive regard offers acceptance that does not depend on performance. A counselor whose warmth tracks the client's achievements can unintentionally recreate the very conditions that brought him to counseling.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: conditions of worth and unconditional positive regard
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

989. nce-s-cor-069 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · easy · In review

Which counselor statement BEST illustrates unconditional positive regard?
A. I'll keep supporting you as long as you keep working on the goals we set together.
Support that depends on meeting goals is conditional regard.
B. I care about you as a person, whether or not we see this choice the same way. ✔ KEY
This separates acceptance of the person from agreement with a choice, which is the heart of unconditional positive regard.
C. You're a model client. You do everything I suggest for you between our sessions.
Praise tied to compliance signals that the client is valued for doing what the counselor wants.
D. I'm proud of you for making the right decision this week instead of the old one.
This evaluates the client's choice as right or wrong, implying regard depends on the "right" behavior.
Rationale: Unconditional positive regard is Rogers' term for accepting and caring for the client as a person without conditions. It does not require approving of every behavior, but the counselor's valuing of the client does not rise or fall with the client's choices. Praise tied to compliance or "right" decisions conveys conditional acceptance.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: unconditional positive regard and acceptance
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

990. nce-s-cor-070 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · medium · In review

In the fifth session, a counselor refers to a grieving client's late son as "Marcus." The client stiffens and says quietly, "His name was Martin." Which counselor response BEST demonstrates congruence?
A. Of course, Martin. Let's go back to what you were saying about the funeral service.
Glossing over the error hides the counselor's real experience and leaves the client's hurt unacknowledged.
B. I see many clients, and names sometimes get mixed up. I'm sorry that it happened.
The excuse is defensive and minimizes the mistake, shifting attention to the counselor's workload.
C. I'm fairly sure the name was written that way in my notes, so I'll check them later.
This deflects responsibility to the paperwork rather than owning the error.
D. I got his name wrong, and I'm sorry. Martin matters, and I want to get it right. ✔ KEY
The counselor openly owns the mistake and conveys real care, so words and inner experience match.
Rationale: Congruence means the counselor is genuine: what they express matches what they actually experience, without a professional facade. When a counselor makes a mistake, a congruent response owns it simply and honestly rather than hiding, excusing or deflecting it. Such moments, handled openly, often strengthen trust.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: congruence, or genuineness
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

991. nce-s-cor-071 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · hard · In review

A trainee tells her supervisor, "To be congruent, I should tell clients every reaction I have toward them as soon as I notice it." Which reply from the supervisor MOST accurately describes congruence in person-centered theory?
A. Congruence means your inner experience and outward expression match, not voicing every feeling ✔ KEY
Rogers described congruence as awareness and genuineness, with no facade; it does not require impulsively sharing every reaction.
B. Congruence is mainly about matching your body language to the client's posture and vocal tone
This describes mirroring, an attending technique, not genuineness.
C. Congruence requires sharing your personal history so the client sees you as an equal partner
Self-disclosure of history is a separate skill and is not what congruence requires.
D. Congruence is reached by keeping a calm, neutral manner no matter what you feel in a session
Hiding behind a neutral front is the professional facade that congruence rejects.
Rationale: In person-centered theory, congruence means the counselor's inner experience, awareness and outward expression are consistent, so there is no false front. It does not mean impulsively sharing every feeling. Counselors use judgment about expressing persistent reactions that are relevant to the relationship, and they do so in a way that serves the client.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: congruence does not mean impulsive sharing of all reactions
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

992. nce-s-cor-072 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · therapeutic alliance · medium · In review

A 45-year-old client seeking help with heavy weekend drinking says his goal is to cut back to two drinks a night, not to quit. He has no history of withdrawal. The counselor believes abstinence would be safer. Which approach BEST strengthens the working alliance?
A. Explain that moderation goals rarely succeed, and make abstinence the first treatment goal
Imposing the counselor's goal undermines agreement on goals, a core component of the alliance.
B. Accept his goal without discussing it at all, so that he does not feel pressured or judged
Silently withholding a relevant concern is not genuine collaboration and skips mutual goal-setting.
C. Share her concern with permission, then agree with him on a goal and tasks he will try ✔ KEY
Offering her view respectfully while negotiating shared goals and tasks builds the agreement and bond the alliance depends on.
D. Put off any goal setting until he has kept a drinking diary for several weeks on his own
Monitoring can help, but delaying all goal discussion leaves the alliance without shared direction.
Rationale: Bordin described the working alliance as agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and an emotional bond. When client and counselor see the goal differently, the counselor can share information with permission while respecting the client's autonomy and negotiating a goal both can work toward. Imposing a goal, or hiding a concern, weakens that collaboration.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — The working alliance: goals, tasks and bond · Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Exchanging information with permission; supporting autonomy in goal choice
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

993. nce-s-cor-073 · Group Counseling and Group Work · therapeutic alliance · medium · In review

At the first meeting of a 10-week court-mandated anger management group, several members say they are only there to get their paperwork signed. Which leader action is MOST likely to begin building a working alliance with the members?
A. Review the attendance rules and the consequences of missing sessions for each member
Rules need to be clear, but leading with consequences emphasizes control rather than shared purpose.
B. Remind them that their anger brought them here, so they should take the group seriously
Lecturing increases defensiveness and does nothing to create agreement on goals.
C. Show a video outlining the curriculum so that members know what the group expects of them
This presents tasks without the members' input, missing agreement on goals and the bond.
D. Acknowledge the mandate and invite each member to name a goal worth working on for them ✔ KEY
Validating the reality of the mandate while eliciting personal goals starts agreement on goals and builds the bond.
Rationale: With mandated members, the alliance begins by acknowledging their situation honestly and finding goals that matter to them within the group's requirements. Bordin's components of goals, tasks and bond apply in groups as in individual work. Leading with rules or lectures tends to deepen resistance rather than engagement.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Working alliance with reluctant and involuntary clients; goals, tasks and bond
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

994. nce-s-cor-074 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

A 34-year-old client who uses a power wheelchair arrives for an intake with a personal care attendant. Which counselor behavior BEST conveys respect?
A. Speaking directly to the client and asking how they would like the room arranged ✔ KEY
Addressing the client directly and inviting their preferences treats them as the expert on their own needs.
B. Directing the intake questions to the attendant, who likely knows the client's needs
Talking past the client to a companion is disrespectful and undermines the client's autonomy.
C. Moving the wheelchair closer to the desk so the client does not have to adjust it
A wheelchair is part of the client's personal space; moving it without asking is intrusive.
D. Telling the client how inspiring it is that they still get out and come to counseling
Calling routine activity "inspiring" is patronizing and frames disability as the client's defining trait.
Rationale: Respect means treating clients as capable adults and the experts on their own lives. With clients who have disabilities, that includes speaking to them directly rather than through companions, asking before offering help, and avoiding patronizing praise. These behaviors communicate that the client, not the disability, is the focus.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counseling individuals with disabilities: addressing the person directly and avoiding paternalism
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

995. nce-s-cor-075 · Group Counseling and Group Work · warmth and respect · medium · In review

In a school counseling group for 14-year-olds coping with family changes, a usually quiet member describes crying the night her father moved out. Another member snickers. Which leader response BEST conveys warmth and respect while protecting the group?
A. Ignore the snicker so that the attention stays on the member who just took a risk
Ignoring the behavior leaves the sharer exposed and implies that mocking is acceptable in the group.
B. Calmly block the snicker, then thank the member for trusting the group with this ✔ KEY
Blocking protects the vulnerable member, and the warm acknowledgment honors her risk and reinforces safety norms.
C. Ask the member who snickered to leave the room until he is able to act respectfully
Removal is a heavy first response that shames the other teen and shifts focus away from the sharer.
D. Ask the group to vote on whether laughing at another member should be against the rules
Putting safety to a vote in the moment leaves the sharer unprotected and makes respect negotiable.
Rationale: Group leaders shape norms of safety and support, especially early and with adolescents.
